Part 1: Key decisions and facts

Go/no-go gates. NO at an early gate costs the least.

# Question Threshold Evidence If NO
1 Is the written Council/Commission delegation of binding technical authority to the arbitration panel signed? Signed by Month 2 (text agreed by Month 1.5 as target); panel 8-12 FTE, rulings within 60 days, 14 days to comply or escalate. Failure trigger in the premortem: Council Legal Service estimates more than 4 months. Signed delegation instrument; Council Legal Service opinion (Month 1); bilateral carrier sessions (Months 0-1). Escalate to the Commission for fast-tracking and pause carrier commitments. If still unsigned after the premortem's 4-month tolerance, re-baseline the governance model (e.g. a heavier legal vehicle, accepting delay) or stop. Note that the delegation precedes Regulation adoption (Month 9), so its legal basis must be confirmed.
2 Have carriers above EUR 50M cross-border revenue signed Commitment Letters (including escrow penalties of 0.5-1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue)? At least 95% of carriers above EUR 50M signed by Month 3 (proposed threshold); no top-5 carrier unsigned at Month 4. Signed Commitment Letters collected at Month 3; written preconditions from DB, SNCF, OBB gathered in Months 0-1. Steering Committee re-baseline at Month 4. Hold co-funding and onboarding commitments. If a top-5 carrier refuses binding rulings, reduce scope to willing carriers/corridors or stop.
3 Does the willingness-to-pay evidence show enough demand for the sum-of-segment through-ticket (EUR 70-90 vs flights at EUR 40-70)? At least 8% of respondents prefer the through-ticket at Month 4 (proposed threshold, to be justified against the 40% target); pilot conversion at least 3% at Month 12 (proposed threshold). Conjoint survey (300-500 respondents per corridor) by Month 4; one-corridor pilot from Month 9 with conversion read at Month 12. Stop scaling marketing beyond the pilot corridor, focus on corridors with weak air competition, and re-scope the 40% target or take a new, unfunded decision on fare support.
4 Does the bottom-up cost model with binding quotes keep demand inside the budget lines? Co-funding grant demand within the EUR 234M grant line (failure level about 20% over); distributor run-rate at or below EUR 50M/year; any projected overrun fits the EUR 215M free contingency. Cost model (Month 2); binding quotes from 8-12 carriers and distributor-operator candidates (Months 4-6); distributor scope decision (Month 2); funding decision on supplementary authority. Downsize: cut the co-funding rate (Tier 2, 20% to 10%) or reduce the distributor to reference scope. If exposure still exceeds the free contingency, either obtain an explicit cap increase before committing awards, or reduce scope. Do not rely on an unsecured supplementary authority.
5 Has the Regulation been adopted by the gate, leaving a workable standards window? Adopted by Month 9; if not adopted by Month 10, pause carrier onboarding commitments and re-baseline. Adoption probability at or below 70% at Month 6 triggers the external standards consortium (proposed thresholds). Parliament/Council adoption record; weekly tracking with TRAN/IMCO rapporteurs; divergence check against shadow standards (liability, data scope, API scope, access definition). Delay: pause onboarding and re-baseline Month 18 and Month 30 (each month of slip removes one standards month). If still unadopted at Month 12, restructure the programme or stop.
6 Are hubs and settlement ready to carry real traffic? At least 2 accredited payment providers operational by Month 12 (fewer than 2 applicants by Month 6 triggers the fallback); 4 hubs operational by Month 9 with booking-failure rate below 2% (target below 0.5%); settlement under 48 h in dry-run before any corridor opens (by Month 18). Accreditation decision (Month 8) and provider go-live (Month 12); hub contracts (Month 3), operational start (Month 9), dual-runs and pilots (Months 15-18); settlement dry-run results. Use the bilateral-settlement or emergency-procurement fallback (EUR 10M clearing reserve). Do not open corridors to through-ticket sales without a settlement route under 48 h. Drop failing hubs from the Month 30 plan and downsize the 90% bookability expectation (below 90% triggers Commission review).

What you need to decide, and by when.

7 open decisions: 4 high and 3 medium severity. Most urgent are the demand-threshold definitions (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) and the reference distributor scope (Month 2 = 2026-12-08). The funding source for overruns beyond free contingency follows at Month 3 (2027-01-08), ahead of co-funding awards. Until then, the plan can safely run shadow standards work, the baseline survey, the DPIA, market sounding and the governance set-up, but should not commit co-funding awards or distributor scope.

1. Who pays beyond the fixed cap (🔴 High)

Decision: If overruns exceed the EUR 215M free contingency, who finances the excess: a formal cap increase, Tier 3 cuts, or hard limits on committed exposure?

Why it is open: Executive summary, plan and pitch call the EUR 1,500M cap fixed. Risk sections rely on a EUR 100-200M supplementary authority (estimate) that is outside the cap, unsecured, and below the EUR 85-235M exposure in a 20-30% overrun.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Pre-agreed Commission/Council top-up that formally lifts the cap. Covers up to EUR 85-235M exposure only if sized for the upper case. Needs a political process before awards are committed. public_budget_cap_eur; fallback_budget_overrun_exceeds_cap; executive summary and pitch wording.
B. Pre-size Tier 3 scope cuts to absorb the full EUR 85-235M. Cap stays fixed. Likely cuts to conformance testing, capacity building or TEN-T extension (Month 36 = 2029-10-08 start). budget_tiers_and_reviews; allocation lines; tent_extension_start.
C. Cap committed co-funding and distributor exposure at the EUR 215M free contingency. Overrun risk is limited by design. Reduces award headroom and may slow smaller-carrier onboarding. alloc_carrier_cofunding_eur; alloc_reference_distributor_eur; premortem FM1.
  • If nobody decides: The cap is treated as fixed with no funded fallback. Tier 3 triggers an ad hoc Commission escalation after contingency is spent.
  • Owner: Programme Steering Committee, escalating to the Commission (DG MOVE).
  • Decide by: Month 3 (2027-01-08), before co-funding awards and distributor commitments are made.
  • Blocks: Co-funding award commitments, Month 12 mid-course review, and the cost-model gate.

2. Reference distributor scope (🔴 High)

Decision: Should the public reference distributor be reference-implementation only, hybrid, or full retail?

Why it is open: The EUR 215M line (~EUR 43M/year) sits between sizings. The self-audit calls it reference-only. The review sizes reference-only at EUR 20-30M/year and full retail at EUR 60-100M/year (estimates). Overrun figures use different bases.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Reference-implementation only. Fits the EUR 215M line with headroom. Weaker public competitor to incumbents. alloc_reference_distributor_eur; post_month60_unfunded_run_cost.
B. Hybrid scope. Uses most of the EUR 215M. Needs a new tripwire base (currently EUR 50M/year). Reference distributor allocation; tripwire; fallback_extended_distributor_operation.
C. Full retail. Above EUR 215M. Needs a cap decision or cuts elsewhere. Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) run cost rises. Budget lines; post_month60_unfunded_run_cost; contingency use.
  • If nobody decides: The EUR 215M line is spent with undefined scope. Overruns are drawn from free contingency by default.
  • Owner: Programme Steering Committee with DG MOVE as sponsor.
  • Decide by: Month 2 (2026-12-08), because the cost model and binding quotes (Months 4-6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) depend on it.
  • Blocks: Cost-model gate, distributor procurement, and the budget-fit gate.

3. Meaning and timing of the Month 24 (2028-10-08) share gate (🔴 High)

Decision: What does the Month 24 (2028-10-08) 15% through-ticket share gate measure, and is it kept before corridors go live?

Why it is open: The gate (15%, proposed threshold) sits at Month 24 (2028-10-08). Consumer go-live is Month 27 (2029-01-08), the API mandate Month 30 (2029-04-08), and providers operate from Month 12 (2027-10-08). The Month 9 (2027-07-08) pilot settlement route is unstated.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Measure share on live pilot corridors only. Gate stays at Month 24 (2028-10-08) and is reachable. The sample is small and unrepresentative of the 40% target. measurement_baseline; payment_fee_subsidy.
B. Move the gate after first go-live (e.g. Month 30+). Measures real capability. Fee subsidy ends at Month 24 (2028-10-08) before the gate reads, so the subsidy end date must be revisited. measurement_baseline; payment_fee_subsidy; co-funding review timing.
C. Keep the all-journeys gate at Month 24 (2028-10-08). Likely missed by design. Triggers co-funding hold and subsidy end. No change; premortem FM3 stays.
  • If nobody decides: The gate stays as written, is likely missed, and triggers the co-funding hold and subsidy end.
  • Owner: Programme Steering Committee, advised by the Measurement and Evaluation Lead.
  • Decide by: Month 9 (2027-07-08), when the validated baseline is available. The pilot settlement route is needed earlier.
  • Blocks: Month 24 (2028-10-08) interim gate, fee-subsidy continuation, and Month 12 (2027-10-08) pilot conversion test.

4. Demand thresholds (🔴 High)

Decision: Which separately named demand thresholds (metric, month, owner) replace the reused 8%?

Why it is open: 8% is used for stated preference (Month 4 = 2027-02-08), share (Month 24 = 2028-10-08) and modal shift (Month 48 = 2030-10-08). Stated preference at 8% proves little against the 40% target. Pilot conversion (3%) and the 15% gate are proposed thresholds.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Three distinct thresholds: preference at Month 4 (2027-02-08), pilot conversion 3% at Month 12 (2027-10-08), share 15% gate / 8% stop at Month 24 (2028-10-08). Clear stop rules. The Month 4 (2027-02-08) level must be justified against the 40% target. measurement_baseline; review and premortem A3/FM3/FM6.
B. Raise the stated-preference threshold. Stricter early stop. Higher chance of stopping marketing beyond the pilot. Review Critical Assumptions; premortem A3.
C. Defer the Month 4 (2027-02-08) threshold and rely on the Month 12 (2027-10-08) pilot. Less early information. Marketing spend risk before Month 12 (2027-10-08). Survey window; consumer rollout phasing.
  • If nobody decides: The ambiguous 8% remains. The Month 4 (2027-02-08) survey result cannot reliably drive a stop or go.
  • Owner: Programme Steering Committee, with the Measurement and Evaluation Lead.
  • Decide by: Month 1 (2026-11-08), so the survey design (Months 1-4 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-02-08) uses the right threshold.
  • Blocks: Willingness-to-pay gate at Month 4 (2027-02-08) and the pilot conversion read at Month 12 (2027-10-08).

5. Carrier co-funding triggers and increase (🟡 Medium)

Decision: What single demand metric and early-warning and failure levels apply to co-funding, and is any increase in grants funded?

Why it is open: Triggers of EUR 290M, EUR 310M and ~EUR 348M are all in use. Only EUR 234M is grants. A rise from EUR 234M to EUR 280M at Month 18 (2028-04-08) has no source and conflicts with the Tier 2 rate cut.

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Grant demand vs EUR 234M with one warning and one failure level; no increase. Simple control. Under-subscription is handled by milestone rules, not extra money. alloc_carrier_cofunding_eur; premortem FM1; self-audit.
B. Allow the increase to EUR 280M, funded from free contingency. Uses EUR 46M of the EUR 215M free contingency. Reduces overrun headroom. contingency_free_eur; co-funding line; Tier 2 text.
C. Fund the increase by reallocating from other lines. Cap neutral. Cuts another line by EUR 46M. Allocation lines; review.
  • If nobody decides: Overlapping triggers stay and the increase is unfunded. Tier 2 timing is disputed at Month 12 (2027-10-08).
  • Owner: Programme Steering Committee.
  • Decide by: Month 6 (2027-04-08), before the Month 12 (2027-10-08) Tier 2 trigger and award commitments.
  • Blocks: Tier 2 trigger at Month 12 (2027-10-08) and the Month 18 (2028-04-08) grant review.

6. Corridor go-live definitions (🟡 Medium)

Decision: How are consumer go-live, API mandate and full through-ticketing defined, and which corridor goes first?

Why it is open: The executive summary has first-corridor go-live at Month 30 (2029-04-08). Canonical facts have four-corridor consumer go-live at Month 27 (2029-01-08), the API mandate at Month 30 (2029-04-08) and full through-ticketing at Month 60 (2031-10-08).

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Three terms: consumer go-live Month 27 (2029-01-08), API mandate Month 30 (2029-04-08) (90% bookable), full through-ticketing Month 60 (2031-10-08) (40%). Aligns with canonical facts. The 5% first-corridor traffic target needs re-anchoring. Executive summary deliverables; pitch; review.
B. Staggered corridor go-live with a named first corridor. Lower risk per corridor. Changes the Month 27 (2029-01-08) four-corridor consumer date. consumer_app_timeline; milestones.
  • If nobody decides: The two timelines stay inconsistent. Gate measurement and onboarding plans diverge.
  • Owner: Project Sponsor (DG MOVE) with the Programme Steering Committee.
  • Decide by: Month 6 (2027-04-08), before the app and hub schedules are baselined.
  • Blocks: Consumer rollout plan and the corridor-opening settlement gate.

7. Hub end state (🟡 Medium)

Decision: At Month 48 (2030-10-08), should hubs be moved to full cost recovery, kept with a subsidy, or sunset with carrier migration?

Why it is open: The hub timeline has sunset/cost-recovery at Month 48 (2030-10-08). Fee revenue covers ~61% of opex (gap ~EUR 1.9M/year for 4 hubs, estimate), and TEN-T carriers join via hubs from Month 36 (2029-10-08).

Option Consequences What changes in the plan
A. Raise fees to full cost recovery. Removes the subsidy gap. Raises costs for smaller carriers and may deter onboarding. hub_economics_gap; hub_timeline.
B. Continue a subsidy in the post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding decision. Adds ~EUR 1.9M/year to the ~EUR 45M/year unfunded run cost. post_month60_unfunded_run_cost; hub_timeline.
C. True sunset with migration to native interfaces. Conflicts with TEN-T hubs and hubs after Month 60 (2031-10-08). Needs migration support funding. hub_scope_and_funding; tent_extension_start.
  • If nobody decides: Hubs keep running past Month 48 (2030-10-08) with an unfunded gap.
  • Owner: Programme Steering Committee, with the Commission for the post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding.
  • Decide by: Month 30 (2029-04-08), alongside the TEN-T hub decision. The funding model decision is due Month 48 (2030-10-08).
  • Blocks: TEN-T hub decision at Month 30 (2029-04-08) and the Month 48 (2030-10-08) funding model decision.

Choices made on your behalf

Set when the scenario was selected, not by you. Confirm or change them.

Lever Chosen Strongest alternative Why it matters Revisit by
OSDM access terms and enforcement Certification-based tiered access with carrier audit rights over distributors. A regulated reference price and service-level schedule enforced by national regulators. It avoids fixing a price before the Regulation and real cost data exist, but enforcement is softer. Month 9 (2027-07-08), at the Regulation adoption gate.
Clearing and settlement Competing accredited payment institutions under common settlement rules. A single publicly governed clearing entity with a guarantee fund. It avoids new-entity licensing delay, but depends on at least 2 providers being operational by Month 12 (2027-10-08). Month 6 (2027-04-08), the applicant-count fallback tripwire.
Funding allocation and incentives Milestone-based co-funding that prioritises smaller and state-weak carriers. A competitive pool paid on verified through-ticket volume. It determines who receives the EUR 290M co-funding line and how overrun risk is shaped. Month 12 mid-course review.
Legacy carrier IT migration Regional shared booking hubs (4 at launch). A publicly hosted gateway translating legacy systems. It lets smaller carriers meet the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate, but creates a hub operating gap. Month 30 (2029-04-08), TEN-T hub decision.
Governance vehicle A time-boxed arbitration panel layered on existing institutions. A joint undertaking with its own budget authority and tie-breaking power. It avoids a new legal entity, but the panel has no enforcement authority of its own. Month 2 (2026-12-08), the delegation signature gate.

payment_accreditation_timeline Market sounding Months 0-1 (2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08); call for applicants Month 2 (2026-12-08); decision Month 8 (2027-06-08); at least 2 accredited providers operational Month 12 (2027-10-08) decision Risk 8 and Issue 7; Q2 requires accreditation done by Months 12-18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08) to leave 12 months of production before Month 30 (2029-04-08).

Switching up to EUR 1M per incident (EUR 5-10M if sole provider fails), covered by the EUR 10M reserve in the clearing line, excess from free contingency estimate Issue 7 gives EUR 1-2M reserve and EUR 5-10M single-provider cost; the reserve is set at EUR 10M, which covers the upper single-provider case. Fits the cap but bilateral settlement is slower and risks the Month 30 (2029-04-08) date.
through_fare_rule Through-fare = sum of segment prices with total and breakdown shown before purchase; no regulated ceilings; reduction-card recognition worth ~10-15% effective discount decision Pragmatic Foundation avoids price-fixing and antitrust risk; the 10-15% discount is an estimate from Q5. Planning comparison EUR 70-90 through-fare vs EUR 50-80 air fare, with a EUR 5-15 convenience premium (estimate).

Any resulting slip of Months 18/30/60 (2028-04-08, 2029-04-08, 2031-10-08) breaches the user's dates and needs a new decision from the Commission.

technical_sla API: p95 latency under 2 s, uptime 99.95%, at least 500 req/s per corridor; hubs: 99.9% uptime, under 2 h recovery; inventory freshness under 5 min; disruption latency under 2 min; settlement under 48 h proposed threshold Risks 12 and 18 and Q8; hub uptime of 99.9% is lower than the API figure by design.

Strategic Decision 10 was not set in the scenario, so this is a plan choice. DG Comp comfort letter targeted for Months 2-6 (2026-12-08 to 2027-04-08) (outcome not assured).

Risk 4's EUR 200-400M minus EUR 215M free contingency = up to 185M (the lower end of 200M is just within it); would need a new funding decision or scope cut, and cannot be combined with other contingency draws.

Focus and Context

Why this programme exists: The EU's proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail aims to unlock cross-border rail mobility by mandating non-discriminatory access to carrier inventory, fares and post-sale operations for any compliant distributor. The programme delivers the shared infrastructure (APIs, clearing, data layer, standards, payments, governance) to make that regulation operational and achieve 40% through-ticket market share, halved distributor complaints, and modal shift from short-haul air by 2031. It is a five-year, EUR 1.5 billion public coordination initiative spanning 27 member states, 25+ carriers and 4 priority corridors, with binding milestones at Months 18, 30 and 60 (2028-04-08, 2029-04-08, 2031-10-08).

Purpose and Goals

Establish the technical, commercial and governance infrastructure for any EU-regulated distributor to sell single-payment through-tickets across multiple carriers with continuity-of-journey rights and non-discriminatory access. Specific goals: (1) 40% through-ticket share of cross-border rail journeys by Month 60 (2031-10-08); (2) Distributor complaints ≤50% of baseline by Month 60 (2031-10-08); (3) Binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-08); (4) Mandatory API exposure by Month 30 to 90 (2029-04-08 to 2034-04-08)%+ of corridor traffic; (5) Modal shift 5–15% from short-haul air (planning range, not commitment).

Key Deliverables and Outcomes

• Binding technical standards (OSDM-compatible access, settlement, refund rules) by Month 18 (2028-04-08).
• Mandatory API exposure covering 90%+ of priority-corridor traffic by Month 30 (2029-04-08).
• Clearing and settlement mechanism via 2+ accredited payment institutions operational by Month 12 (2027-10-08).
• Regional hubs enabling 12–18 legacy-IT carriers to meet Month 30 (2029-04-08) deadline.
• Public reference distributor app live and multilingual support operational by Month 15 (2028-01-08).
• First corridor (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln) through-ticketing go-live by Month 30 (2029-04-08).
• Four-corridor full deployment by Month 60 (2031-10-08) with 40% through-ticket share.

Timeline and Budget

Duration: 60 months (Month 0: 2026-10-08 to Month 60: 2031-10-08). Public Budget: EUR 1,500 million fixed cap (user constraint), allocated: standards EUR 280M, clearing EUR 120M, distributor EUR 215M, capacity EUR 100M, consumer rollout EUR 150M, carrier co-funding EUR 290M, data layer EUR 60M, governance EUR 60M, contingency EUR 225M (EUR 215M free, EUR 10M earmarked). Critical Gates: Regulation adoption Month 9 (2027-07-08), council delegation Month 2 (2026-12-08), Commitment Letters Month 3 (2027-01-08), hub go-live Month 9 (2027-07-08), payment accreditation Month 12 (2027-10-08), standards Month 18 (2028-04-08), API mandate Month 30 (2029-04-08), full deployment Month 60 (2031-10-08). Private IT Spend: EUR 0.5–2 billion (estimate, planning value EUR 1.25 billion), outside the cap.

Risks and Mitigations

Risk 1 – Regulation Adoption Delay: If adopted past Month 9 (2027-07-08), the standards window shrinks from 9 months (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 to Month 18 = 2028-04-08) by one month per month of slip (adoption at Month 12 = 2027-10-08 leaves 6 months; Months 14-15 = 2027-12-08 to 2028-01-08 leaves 3-4), threatening Month 18 (2028-04-08) completion; a pause gate applies at Month 10 (2027-08-08) because of lost margin and rework risk. Mitigation: Weekly adoption tracking from Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); shadow standards pre-work; external standards consortium by Month 8.5 (2027-06-23) if needed.
Risk 2 – Payment Accreditation Shortfall: If <2 providers apply, fallback to bilateral settlement or custom procurement adds 6–12 month delay, jeopardizing Month 30 (2029-04-08). Mitigation: Market sounding Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); formal call Month 2 (2026-12-08); contingency procurement by Month 6 (2027-04-08) if <2 applicants.
Risk 3 – Budget Overrun (20–30%): EUR 300–450 million overrun exceeds EUR 215M free contingency by EUR 85–235M. Mitigation: Monthly burn-rate dashboards Month 3 (2027-01-08); Tier contingency actions (Tier 1–3) pre-approved; supplementary authority request Month 12 (2027-10-08) if Tier 2 triggered.

Audience Tailoring

Tailored for DG MOVE leadership, national transport ministers, and the Steering Committee. Tone: formal, institutional, risk-aware. Focus: critical prerequisites, budget discipline, contingency triggers, decision deadlines. Avoids technical detail; emphasizes governance, ROI and political commitment required.

Action Orientation

Immediately (This Month): Initiate weekly Regulation adoption tracking with Parliament TRAN rapporteurs and member-state transport ministers; draft Council Delegation legal document; hire PMO leadership and arbitration-panel chair. Months 1–2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08): Establish Steering Committee; commission cost model, killer-application research, GDPR DPIA; issue hub RFPs and open the payment-provider accreditation call at Month 2 (2026-12-08). Month 1.5 (2026-11-23): Target for legal review complete and delegation text agreed. Month 2 (2026-12-08): Delegation signed; announce delegation, Commitment Letter deadline, governance framework. Month 3 (2027-01-08): Collect signed Commitment Letters; award hub contracts (payment-provider accreditation is decided at Month 8 (2027-06-08)); finalize contingency budgets and triggers. Owner: DG MOVE Programme Director. Gate: If delegation not signed by Month 2 (2026-12-08), escalate to Commission for Council fast-tracking.

Overall Takeaway

The Pragmatic Foundation is a realistic, risk-managed path to EU cross-border rail through-ticketing that delivers binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-08), mandatory APIs by Month 30 (2029-04-08), and 40% through-ticket share by Month 60 (2031-10-08). It balances progress against delivery risk by avoiding heavy legal set-up (e.g. new joint undertakings), using existing payment-services markets, including smaller carriers via regional hubs, and protecting critical-path milestones through early governance clarity and monthly budget discipline. Success requires securing three hard prerequisites (Council delegation, Commitment Letters, Regulation adoption) by Months 2–9 (2026-12-08 to 2027-07-08) and locking the killer-application validation by Month 12 (2027-10-08). Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability requires decision by Month 48 (2030-10-08).

Part 2: Supporting analysis

Persuasive elevator pitch.

European Cross-Border Rail Through-Ticketing Programme

Project Overview

Break the fragmentation barrier: unlock 40% of European cross-border rail journeys with one ticket, one payment, one promise. Today, passengers buying a multi-carrier journey across Europe face multiple bookings, multiple payments, and zero continuity rights if a connection fails. This programme delivers the technical, commercial and governance infrastructure to fix that by Month 60 (2031-10-08): a shared real-time inventory layer, certified distributor access, accredited payment providers, passenger-rights protection, and regional hubs enabling smaller carriers to participate immediately.

The Pragmatic Foundation approach avoids years of legal set-up by using existing institutions, tiered access certification instead of price-fixing, and milestone-based carrier co-funding rather than heavy new entities. With a EUR 1.5 billion public coordination budget and a realistic path to the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandatory API deadline, this programme makes rail competitive with short-haul flying across four priority corridors and builds the foundation for EU-wide through-ticketing. It is not the most aggressive option on any lever—it is the realistic one that protects the critical path, includes smaller operators, and actually gets built.

Target Audience

Primary audience: DG MOVE, the Commission and Parliament's TRAN committee, member-state governments and transport ministers evaluating the Regulation and programme commitment.

Secondary audience: Major carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, ÖBB, Renfe, Trenitalia, NS, SJ) and distributors (Trainline, Omio) assessing participation risk and benefit.

Tertiary audience: National transport regulators and consumer bodies assessing consumer and competition safeguards.

The pitch appeals to each stakeholder group distinctly: to the Commission and member states, the fiscal discipline and milestone-based approach prove manageability; to carriers, the tiered access and co-funding reduce integration burden; to regulators and consumers, the accessibility and passenger-rights backstop show inclusion and protection. The emphasis on realistic execution speaks to all audiences sceptical of over-ambitious EU programmes.

Risks and Mitigation Strategies

  • Regulation adoption slips past Month 9 (2027-07-08): Standards work runs in shadow from Month 0 (2026-10-08); if adoption is delayed past Month 10 (2027-08-08), carrier onboarding pauses and the critical path resets, extending the Month 30 (2029-04-08) milestone. Mitigation: Hire external standards consortium by Month 8 (2027-06-08) if needed; negotiate phase-in periods with Parliament.

  • Arbitration panel cannot enforce against large incumbents: A panel with technical binding power but no commercial control may lack teeth when SNCF or Deutsche Bahn resist access terms. Mitigation: Secure written Commission delegation with escalation to DG COMP for repeated non-compliance; tie carrier co-funding to compliance with access decisions.

  • Budget overrun of 20–30% (EUR 300–450 million) exceeds the EUR 215 million free contingency: A supplementary authority of EUR 100–200 million (estimate) may still not close the gap. Mitigation: Freeze co-funding at 10% after Month 24 (2028-10-08) if quarterly spend exceeds 115% pro-rata; seek early mid-course reviews at Months 12 and 24 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08).

  • Smaller carriers cannot meet Month 30 (2029-04-08) API deadline without hub infrastructure: Regional hub delays leave 12–18 carriers behind. Mitigation: Contract hubs by Month 3 (2027-01-08); run 2–4 week dual-runs before go-live and suspend onboarding if booking-failure exceeds 2% for one week.

  • GDPR or competition-law challenge to the shared data layer: A court ruling that the neutral data operator or fare-sharing rules violate competition law could unwind the clearing model. Mitigation: Complete DPIA by Month 2 (2026-12-08); reach EDPB/DPA consensus by Month 4 (2027-02-08); consult DG COMP on data scope by Month 6 (2027-04-08); seek formal clarity or block exemption if time allows.

Metrics for Success

  • Through-ticket share: 40% of cross-border rail journeys sold as through-tickets by Month 60 (2031-10-08), validated by quarterly carrier and distributor reporting with independent auditor spot-checks. Interim gate: at least 15% by Month 24 (2028-10-08). Below 15% triggers co-funding review.

  • Distributor complaints: Reduced to at or below 50% of the Month 9 (2027-07-08) validated baseline by Month 60 (2031-10-08), measured by standardised complaint taxonomy across the public reference distributor, Trainline, Omio and national platforms.

  • Corridor bookability: At least 90% of traffic on each priority corridor bookable end-to-end by Month 30 (2029-04-08); below 90% triggers Commission review.

  • Carrier conformance: 100% of carriers above EUR 50 million cross-border revenue meeting the conformance testing standard by Month 30 (2029-04-08); smaller carriers via hubs or native implementation by Month 30 (2029-04-08), measured through the 90% corridor-bookability threshold, with any smaller-carrier exemption documented and time-limited.

  • API and clearing performance: p95 search latency under 2 seconds, 99.95% uptime, hub recovery under 2 hours, settlement completion under 48 hours.

  • Accessibility: Assistance confirmation within 24 hours at 90%+ rate; delivery at 95%+; complaint rate under 2%.

  • Budget adherence: Spend within the EUR 1.5 billion cap with free contingency of EUR 215 million; quarterly reviews at Months 12, 24, 36 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08, 2029-10-08); overrun triggers Tier 1–3 spending cuts.

  • Stakeholder trust: Dispute resolution time under 60 days; absence of antitrust complaints; carrier and distributor participation above 85% of eligible operators.

Stakeholder Benefits

For carriers: Reduced compliance cost via tiered access certification (no early price-fixing) and milestone-based co-funding (EUR 234 million grants for API and system integration). Smaller carriers access regional hubs (EUR 44 million) rather than building native APIs alone. Larger carriers gain guaranteed non-discriminatory access to all distributors and visibility into through-ticket demand. Revenue upside from 40% through-ticket share and the modal-shift opportunity.

For distributors: Non-discriminatory OSDM API access for any distributor that passes conformance testing, enabling Trainline, Omio and smaller platforms to sell the same through-products. Early API access (Month 15 = 2028-01-08) with integration incentive payments tied to verified through-ticket sales.

For passengers: Single booking reference, single payment and continuity-of-journey rights (reroute under 4 hours, refund under 10 days) across carriers—eliminating the multiple-booking pain point. Accessibility assistance confirmed within 24 hours.

For member states and regulators: Strengthened capacity through twinning and a lead-authority network for cross-border dispute resolution, reducing fragmentation of enforcement. Clear standards by Month 18 (2028-04-08) remove regulatory uncertainty.

For smaller and newer entrants (startups, regional operators): The public reference distributor and open conformance testing level the playing field; hub access and capacity-building funding (EUR 100 million) support operators excluded from traditional distribution channels.

For transport policy: A realistic, achievable path to the EU Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing; 40% through-ticket penetration and a 5–15% modal shift from short-haul air (planning range, estimate) support decarbonisation and mobility objectives without requiring aggressive price controls or new central institutions.

Ethical Considerations

Non-discrimination and access: The certification-based tiered access scheme is designed to prevent the discriminatory practices (slow inventory feeds, higher latency, limited itineraries) that incumbents can impose. Auditable conformance testing and carrier audits of distributors create mutual accountability. A neutral data-layer operator with segregated carrier data access logs prevents any carrier from seeing competitors' commercial inputs. This protects competition and smaller market entrants.

Passenger protection: The single-contact passenger-rights backstop gives travellers one clear promise: if a connection is missed, the selling distributor handles rerouting and refunds, with cost recovered from the liable carrier. This removes the risk that passengers are passed between carriers. GDPR safeguards (90-day PII deletion, with extension only for active refund or complaints) prevent long-term personal data pooling.

Accessibility and inclusion: Assistance booking is embedded in the standard interface, not an add-on; confirmation within 24 hours is mandatory. The public reference distributor and accessibility data in the shared layer ensure that persons with reduced mobility are not left behind by commercial platforms.

Fiscal discipline and public accountability: The EUR 1.5 billion budget is fixed; quarterly spending reviews and Tier 1–3 cuts if spend exceeds 115% pro-rata prevent unchecked cost growth. The arbitration panel's technical decisions are published and subject to Commission review; no decisions are made in private.

Realistic pragmatism: The Pragmatic Foundation scenario avoids fixing prices before the legislation and cost data exist, which would risk both economic inefficiency and legal challenge. It uses existing institutions (accredited payment providers, national regulators, the EU Agency for Railways) rather than building new central entities, reducing the legal set-up burden and leaving sovereignty with member states. This builds trust by showing restraint.

Collaboration Opportunities

With carriers: Seek Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08) naming native API, hub or gateway pathway; participate in the quarterly Steering Committee and carrier roundtables (dedicated slots for smaller operators). Co-invest in integration through milestone-based grants and hub access.

With distributors (Trainline, Omio, national platforms): Sign integration roadmaps by Month 3 with early API access (Month 15 = 2028-01-08) in exchange for through-ticket sales commitments. Distributor advisory council meets monthly with veto over consumer-facing design. Co-market the through-ticket with shared campaign budgets (EUR 10–20 million, estimate).

With payment institutions: Apply for accreditation by Month 2 (2026-12-08) to operate split-payment and refund orchestration as a competitive service; at least two accredited providers are required. Fee subsidy covers 60% of transaction fees (Months 0–24 = 2026-10-08 to 2028-10-08) to lower adoption barriers.

With member states and regulators: Participate in the Standing Regulators Committee; apply for twinning and capacity-building grants (EUR 100 million) to align enforcement procedures. Designate a lead regulator for cross-border access disputes.

With data and accessibility bodies: Support EDPB/DPA consensus-building (Months 0–4 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-02-08) on Standard Contractual Clauses and data-sharing scope. Accessibility working group meets monthly; organisations can propose standards and test cases.

With research and academia: Independent evaluator hired Month 3 (2027-01-08) to build counterfactual model of modal shift and validate the 40% through-ticket target. Open access to anonymised programme data for peer-reviewed research on modal shift, competition effects and accessibility outcomes.

Long-term Vision

Months 0–30 (2026-10-08 to 2029-04-08) (Foundation Phase): Establishes the binding technical standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08), mandatory OSDM APIs (Month 30 = 2029-04-08), accredited payment providers, certified distributor access and regional hubs. By Month 30 (2029-04-08), any conformant distributor can sell through-tickets across any participating carrier on the four priority corridors (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon, Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin), with passenger-rights protection and accessibility confirmation.

Months 30–60 (2029-04-08 to 2031-10-08) (Scale and Impact Phase): Expands through-ticketing from early-adopter corridors to mainstream market share. The 40% through-ticket target is reached by Month 60 (2031-10-08). Accessibility delivery matures above 95%; distributor complaints fall to half the baseline. A 5–15% modal shift from short-haul air is achieved through superior pricing and convenience.

Month 36 (2029-10-08) onwards (TEN-T Extension): Begins expansion beyond the four priority corridors to the full Trans-European Transport Network, supported by EUR 12 million TEN-T hubs reserved at launch and community co-funding. Regional and smaller operators join via the certified hub pathway.

Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) and Beyond (Sustainability Transition): The programme transitions from public coordination funding to a cost-recovery model: payment providers recover fees from carriers and distributors; hub operators aim to move to fee-based models; the shared data layer and public reference distributor seek sustainable funding (EUR 45 million/year, estimate; funding model to be decided by Month 48 = 2030-10-08). Multimodal hooks to buses, ferries and short-haul air create seamless mobility, with rail as the spine. The through-ticket becomes the default for European cross-border travel, driving further modal shift and supporting EU decarbonisation targets. Lessons learned feed into global standards (UIC/OSJD) and regional initiatives (e.g. Rail Baltica, Nordic corridors) beyond the EU.

Call to Action

  • Carriers: Commit Binding Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08) naming your native API or hub pathway and IT investment.

  • Distributors (Trainline, Omio, national platforms): Sign the integration roadmap with early API access and incentive payment tied to through-ticket volumes from Month 18 (2028-04-08).

  • Member states: Prepare national regulator capacity: fund DPA twinning and appoint a lead regulator for cross-border access disputes.

  • Payment institutions: Apply for accreditation by Month 2 (2026-12-08)—at least two competitive providers are essential to the clearing model.

  • Programme launch: The programme launches formally at Month 1 (2026-11-08); the arbitration panel delegation must be signed by Month 2 (2026-12-08) for standards work to start on schedule.

  • Coordination hub: Visit the programme's coordination hub (launch Month 2 = 2026-12-08) for the full standards roadmap, hub eligibility criteria, and co-funding application templates.

Goal Statement: Deliver the Pragmatic Foundation programme for EU cross-border rail through-ticketing, starting Month 0 (2026-10-08): binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-08), mandatory OSDM API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-08), and full through-ticketing on four priority corridors by Month 60 (2031-10-08), within the EUR 1,500 million public cap, reaching 40% through-ticket share.

SMART Criteria

  • Specific: Establish technical, commercial and governance arrangements so any compliant distributor can sell multi-carrier through-tickets (single booking reference, single payment, continuity-of-journey rights) on the four priority corridors, with TEN-T extension starting Month 36 (2029-10-08).
  • Measurable: 40% of cross-border rail journeys sold as through-tickets by Month 60 (2031-10-08); distributor complaints at or below 50% of the Month 9 (2027-07-08) validated baseline; at least 90% of corridor traffic bookable end-to-end at Month 30 (2029-04-08) (proposed threshold); spend within the EUR 1,500 million cap.
  • Achievable: Uses a realistic scenario: certification-based access, accredited payment institutions, regional hubs and an arbitration panel avoid new legal entities. Limits: pending Regulation, legacy carrier IT, and a fixed budget with EUR 225 million contingency. Modal shift of 5-15% is a planning range only (estimate).
  • Relevant: Removes the fragmentation that blocks single through-tickets across national operators, supports the proposed EU Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing for Rail, and makes rail more attractive than short-haul flying.
  • Time-bound: Five-year programme from Month 0 (2026-10-08) (project start ASAP). Standards by Month 18 (2028-04-08), API mandate by Month 30 (2029-04-08), TEN-T extension start Month 36 (2029-10-08), full corridor through-ticketing by Month 60 (2031-10-08).

Dependencies

  • Adoption of the Regulation by Parliament and Council by Month 9 (2027-07-08) (proposed gate; pause carrier onboarding commitments if not adopted by Month 10 = 2027-08-08)
  • Written Council/Commission delegation of binding technical authority to the arbitration panel by Month 2 (2026-12-08)
  • Carrier Commitment Letters signed by carriers above EUR 50M cross-border revenue by Month 3 (2027-01-08) (proposed threshold)
  • Accredited payment institutions operational (at least 2 by Month 12 = 2027-10-08)
  • Hub operators contracted and operational for carriers with legacy booking systems
  • Agreed through-ticket definition and validated measurement baseline

Resources Required

  • EUR 1,500 million public budget incl. EUR 225 million contingency held at DG MOVE
  • OSDM standards and conformance testing labs
  • Shared data layer: API hosting, availability cache, 24/7 operations centre, neutral operator
  • Regional booking hubs (4 at launch, 2 TEN-T hubs reserved)
  • Programme management office, arbitration panel and consumer app/support teams

Related Goals

  • Extension of through-ticketing to the full TEN-T network from Month 36 (2029-10-08)
  • Multimodal hooks for buses, ferries and short-haul air
  • Modal shift from short-haul air to rail (planning range 5-15%)
  • Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainable funding of distributor, hubs and data layer (about EUR 45M/year unfunded, estimate)
  • Accessible travel for persons with reduced mobility

Tags

  • rail
  • through-ticketing
  • OSDM
  • EU regulation
  • passenger rights

Risk Assessment and Mitigation Strategies

Key Risks

  • Regulation adoption slips past Month 9 (2027-07-08), compressing the standards window
  • Arbitration panel lacks enforcement power over large incumbents
  • Budget overrun of 20-30% exceeds the EUR 215 million free contingency
  • Hub or legacy-IT delays leave smaller carriers behind at Month 30 (2029-04-08)
  • GDPR or competition-law challenge to the shared data layer

Diverse Risks

  • Payment provider accreditation draws fewer than 2 applicants
  • Distributors (Trainline, Omio) delay integration or demand preferential access
  • Through-fares fail to compete with airlines, so modal shift falls short
  • Accessibility assistance confirmed but not delivered on platforms
  • Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding cliff for distributor, hubs and data layer

Mitigation Plans

  • Run shadow standards pre-work from Month 0 (2026-10-08); track legislation; hire an external standards consortium if adoption passes Month 8 (2027-06-08)
  • Secure written delegation by Month 2 (2026-12-08) and Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08) with escrow penalties (proposed threshold)
  • Build a cost model by Month 2 (2026-12-08); hold mid-course reviews at Months 12 and 24 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08); apply Tier 1-3 cuts at 115% of pro-rata spend; seek supplementary authority if needed
  • Contract hubs by Month 3 (2027-01-08), run 2-4 week dual-runs, and suspend onboarding if the booking-failure rate exceeds 2% for a week
  • Complete the DPIA, reach EDPB/DPA consensus on SCCs by Month 4 (2027-02-08), and consult competition authorities on data-sharing scope
  • Use bilateral settlement or emergency procurement as a fallback; fund distributor co-marketing; set accessibility SLAs; decide the post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding model by Month 48 (2030-10-08)

Stakeholder Analysis

Primary Stakeholders

  • DG MOVE (programme owner and budget holder)
  • EU Agency for Railways (technical secretariat)
  • Programme management office and arbitration panel
  • National rail carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, Trenitalia, Renfe, ÖBB, NS, SJ and others)
  • Distributors (Trainline, Omio, public reference distributor)

Secondary Stakeholders

  • CER and smaller carriers
  • National regulators
  • BEUC and disability-rights bodies
  • Payment institutions and hub operators
  • EDPB, national data protection authorities and competition authorities

Engagement Strategies

  • Weekly reporting to DG MOVE and the Agency; quarterly Steering Committee
  • Quarterly roundtables with major carriers and dedicated slots for smaller carriers
  • Distributor advisory council with early API access in return for integration commitments
  • Monthly Standing Regulators Committee and twinning for weaker regulators
  • Accessibility and consumer working groups; milestone updates to Parliament TRAN committee

Regulatory and Compliance Requirements

Permits and Licenses

  • Payment institution licences (PSD2) for accredited providers
  • Written Council/Commission delegation for the arbitration panel
  • Competition authority comfort letter or clearance for data sharing
  • Distributor certification under the tiered access scheme
  • Non-EU participation agreements (e.g. Swiss SBB) for Wien-Munchen-Zurich

Compliance Standards

  • Proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail
  • GDPR (DPIA, SCCs, 90-day PII deletion)
  • EU rail passenger rights rules
  • Articles 101/102 TFEU competition law
  • Accessibility requirements (WCAG 2.1 AA, 24 h assistance confirmation)

Regulatory Bodies

  • European Commission (DG MOVE, DG COMP)
  • EU Agency for Railways
  • National rail regulators
  • European Data Protection Board and national DPAs
  • National competition authorities

Compliance Actions

  • Complete DPIA Months 0-2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) and reach DPA consensus by Month 4 (2027-02-08)
  • Seek competition-authority consultation on data scope by Month 6 (2027-04-08)
  • Run payment accreditation: call Month 2 (2026-12-08), decision Month 8 (2027-06-08)
  • Embed GDPR, accessibility and liability insurance checks in the conformance checklist
  • Anchor binding standards at Month 18 (2028-04-08) and quarterly compliance reviews

Primary Decisions

The vital few decisions that have the most impact.

The Critical levers (access terms, clearing and settlement, funding allocation, legacy IT migration, governance) address the programme's core tensions: enforceable openness versus incumbent buy-in, central versus federated risk, a fixed budget versus carrier readiness, and decision authority versus the Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline. High levers refine delivery, rights, data and fares. No major dimension is missing, though consumer-facing rollout and communication are only lightly covered.

Decision 1: OSDM Access Terms and Enforcement Model

Lever ID: 3356b1d1-4008-4b3c-8245-318c0e4cc69d

The Core Decision: Defines what "non-discriminatory" access to inventory, fares and post-sale functions means in practice, who audits it, and what sanctions apply. Success is measured by time-to-onboard for a new distributor, inventory parity and API latency against carriers' own channels, and the share of distributor complaints resolved. The choice sets the credibility of the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandatory API exposure milestone.

Why It Matters: This lever sets how non-discriminatory distributor access to real-time inventory, fares and post-sale operations is defined and enforced. Tight, regulator-audited terms speed distributor onboarding and support the goal of halving complaints, but they raise compliance cost and legal friction for incumbents. Looser, negotiated terms win early carrier buy-in but leave room for the discriminatory practices the proposed regulation is meant to end.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Mandate a single regulated reference price and service-level schedule for API access, enforced by national regulators with EU Agency for Railways audit rights over inventory parity and latency.
  2. Let carriers publish their own FRAND-style access terms within a common template, with a complaints-driven review by regulators and penalties only after repeated findings of discrimination.
  3. Tie API access terms to a certification scheme under which distributors earn tiered inventory access by meeting conformance and consumer-protection tests, with carriers able to audit distributors in return.

Trade-Off / Risk: A regulated price schedule gives distributors certainty, but fixing terms before the legislation is final and before real cost data exists risks mispricing access, and national regulators differ widely in resources and appetite to enforce.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Strengthens Competition-Law Firewalls for Shared Fare and Inventory Data by giving data-sharing clear rules, and works with Member-State Regulator Capacity and Cross-Border Enforcement Cooperation, since auditable terms only deter discrimination if regulators can enforce them.

Conflict: Strict, regulator-audited terms strain Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives, because incumbents bear compliance costs and may demand compensation. They also pull against Legacy Carrier IT Migration Pathway, where slower carriers cannot yet meet parity and latency obligations.

Justification: Critical, Critical because it defines non-discriminatory access, the core of the regulation, and sets the credibility of the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API milestone. It links to competition firewalls, regulator capacity, funding and legacy migration, and controls the compliance-cost versus carrier buy-in trade-off.

Decision 2: Clearing and Settlement Architecture

Lever ID: 562282e0-88fd-478f-b1b7-4f2d657224bb

The Core Decision: Chooses the money-flow backbone for single-payment through-tickets: who holds passenger funds, how revenue is apportioned across carriers, and how refunds are reversed. Key metrics are settlement cycle time, refund turnaround, dispute rate and default exposure. The choice drives trust among carriers and distributors, and it sets licensing, capital and governance needs that can lengthen the critical path.

Why It Matters: This lever determines how revenue from a single payment is split across carriers and how refunds are reversed. A central public clearing house gives uniform rules and visibility but concentrates operational and credit risk in one entity. A federated model reuses existing bilateral settlement between carriers and is quicker to start, but it leaves reconciliation disputes and refund delays that undermine through-ticket confidence.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Establish a single publicly governed clearing entity that receives passenger payments, applies agreed apportionment rules and pays carriers on a fixed cycle, with a guarantee fund for defaults.
  2. Extend existing bilateral and multilateral carrier settlement arrangements with a common message standard and an independent dispute-resolution body, avoiding any new central payment entity.
  3. Contract regulated payment institutions to run split-payment and refund orchestration as a competitive service, with carriers choosing among accredited providers that meet common settlement rules.

Trade-Off / Risk: Central clearing simplifies refunds and apportionment, but it demands licensing, capital and carrier trust that take years to build and could delay the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate if made a precondition.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Passenger-Rights Backstop and Liability Allocation, since fault-based reimbursements and pooled guarantees run through the clearing mechanism, and supports Through-Fare Composition and Reduction Card Rules by providing the apportionment logic for split revenue.

Conflict: A central clearing entity competes with Programme Governance Vehicle and Decision Rights for institutional design and risk ownership. Making it a precondition could delay Corridor Sequencing and Onboarding Gates and the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate.

Justification: Critical, Critical because it is the money-flow backbone for single-payment through-tickets. It enables the passenger-rights backstop and fare apportionment, and it sets licensing and capital needs that can lengthen the critical path to Month 30 (2029-04-08). It controls the central-versus-federated risk trade-off.

Decision 3: Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives

Lever ID: 26395e1c-310a-4258-92c2-0f80537b7c92

The Core Decision: Determines how the €1.5 billion public budget (user constraint) is divided among standards, conformance testing, the clearing mechanism, the public reference distributor, capacity building and carrier co-funding. Key metrics are the share of funds reaching smaller carriers, disbursement tied to API and data-quality milestones (Months 18 and 30 = 2028-04-08, 2029-04-08), additionality of subsidies against private IT spend, and avoidance of paying for work already planned.

Why It Matters: This lever sets how the €1.5 billion public budget (user constraint) is split between standards, shared infrastructure, public distribution, capacity building and direct co-funding of carrier integration. Subsidising carrier IT work reduces resistance and speeds up integration but could duplicate private investment that carriers must fund anyway. Concentrating on shared infrastructure keeps public money visible but leaves smaller carriers unable to comply.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Reserve most of the budget for shared infrastructure, conformance testing and the clearing mechanism, leaving carrier-side integration to be funded privately under the mandate.
  2. Make a significant portion of the budget available as milestone-based co-funding for carriers, prioritising smaller and state-weak operators, conditional on meeting API and data-quality deadlines.
  3. Hold back a competitive pool of funds that carriers and distributors bid for to deliver jointly proposed integration projects, with payment tied to verified through-ticket volumes.

Trade-Off / Risk: Co-funding carrier integration lowers adoption barriers, but it risks subsidising work that incumbents would have to do anyway, while volume-linked payments reward corridors that were already succeeding.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Legacy Carrier IT Migration Pathway, since milestone co-funding can finance gateway or hub onboarding for weaker operators. Also strengthens Corridor Sequencing and Onboarding Gates, because payments can be released only when readiness gates are passed.

Conflict: Competes with Role of the Public Reference Distributor and Clearing and Settlement Architecture for a fixed budget; generous carrier co-funding leaves less for shared infrastructure, while volume-linked payments may favour corridors that were already succeeding.

Justification: Critical, Critical because it allocates the fixed €1.5 billion budget (user constraint) across clearing, distributor, standards and carrier co-funding. It is a hub that competes with other levers for money and releases payments against gates and milestones, controlling the cost versus scope trade-off.

Decision 4: Legacy Carrier IT Migration Pathway

Lever ID: 1a590841-cc26-4b57-b4a4-02fa39c06ba1

The Core Decision: Chooses how carriers with ageing booking back-ends reach the standard OSDM-compatible interface: native builds, a public gateway or regional hubs. It sets the size of the private IT bill, the pace at which the long tail of operators joins before the mandatory API date (Month 30 = 2029-04-08), and operational dependency on gateway or hub operators. Metrics are carriers conformant by deadline and migration cost per carrier.

Why It Matters: Carriers differ greatly in the age and openness of their booking back-ends, so the migration route sets both the private IT bill and how quickly the long tail of smaller operators can join. Forcing native implementations preserves carrier control but leaves weaker operators behind. Shared adapters reduce effort but create a dependency on whoever operates them.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Require every carrier to build and operate its own native interface, using public funds only for standards work and testing, and accept uneven readiness among smaller operators.
  2. Fund a publicly hosted gateway that translates legacy carrier systems into the standard interface, which smaller carriers can use until they modernise their back-ends.
  3. Offer regional shared booking-service hubs, run by consortia of neighbouring carriers or by procured third-party operators, that host inventory and fare logic for several carriers behind one interface.

Trade-Off / Risk: A shared gateway lowers the entry barrier for smaller carriers, but it risks becoming a permanent crutch and a single point of failure, undermining the incentive to modernise that the mandatory API date is meant to create.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Works with Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives, which can subsidise gateway or hub use, and with OSDM Access Terms and Enforcement Model, because a translation layer lets smaller carriers meet non-discriminatory access duties on time.

Conflict: Shared gateways or hubs can weaken the modernisation incentive behind OSDM Access Terms and Enforcement Model. They also create a single point of failure that undermines Real-Time Inventory and Disruption Data Model quality commitments.

Justification: Critical, Critical because the slowest carrier back-ends constrain corridor gates, data freshness, access obligations and ticket validation. The choice between native builds, a gateway and hubs sets the private IT bill and whether the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate is achievable.

Decision 5: Programme Governance Vehicle and Decision Rights

Lever ID: 1771a340-d031-467b-8348-a1a87115d3f2

The Core Decision: Sets who holds binding decision rights over standards, conformance and funding disputes, and how fast contested technical choices are settled. The choice shapes legal set-up time before the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards milestone, accountability for the €1.5 billion public budget (user constraint), and incumbents' ability to stall. Metrics: dispute resolution time, milestone adherence and stakeholder trust.

Why It Matters: Choosing who holds binding decision rights (the Commission directly, a dedicated joint body, or an agency-hosted board) determines how quickly standards disputes between carriers and distributors are resolved. A heavier vehicle adds legal set-up time before the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards milestone, while a lighter one risks lacking authority when large incumbents resist.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Run the programme from DG MOVE with the EU Agency for Railways as technical secretariat, using advisory working groups and keeping all binding decisions inside existing EU institutional procedures.
  2. Establish a dedicated joint undertaking with carrier, distributor and consumer seats, giving it its own budget authority, staff and a tie-breaking mechanism for contested technical decisions.
  3. Create a small independent standards arbitration panel with time-boxed rulings, layered on top of existing institutions, so disputes resolve quickly without building a full new legal entity.

Trade-Off / Risk: A dedicated body gives clearer accountability and budget control, but its legal creation can consume the first year, whereas reusing existing institutions starts faster yet leaves incumbents able to stall contested decisions.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Provides the authority that makes OSDM Access Terms and Enforcement Model and Corridor Sequencing and Onboarding Gates enforceable, and gives Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives a clear budget holder to release payments against milestones.

Conflict: A heavier vehicle's set-up time conflicts with the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards deadline and delays Corridor Sequencing and Onboarding Gates; a lighter one leaves it dependent on Member-State Regulator Capacity and Cross-Border Enforcement Cooperation for real enforcement.

Justification: Critical, Critical because it sets who can bind incumbents, resolve standards disputes and hold the €1.5 billion budget (user constraint). It makes access terms and gating enforceable, and its set-up time directly threatens the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards milestone.

Secondary Decisions

These decisions are less significant, but still worth considering.

Decision 6: Role of the Public Reference Distributor

Lever ID: 64d93888-c3bb-4a65-810d-da8fb4b8aa70

The Core Decision: Sets the mandate, scale and lifespan of the publicly funded distributor: neutral benchmark, full retail channel or last-resort service. It determines the budget share absorbed by consumer-facing operations, long-term operating liability, and the signal sent to commercial platforms. Metrics include conformance reuse by small operators, accessibility-assisted bookings served, and through-ticket share attributable to the public channel.

Why It Matters: This lever decides whether the publicly funded distributor is a neutral benchmark, a full consumer-facing retail service, or a fallback. A full retail service gives travellers a direct, rights-compliant channel and can show what good looks like. It also risks crowding out Trainline, Omio and similar platforms, whose cooperation is needed to reach the 40% through-ticket share, and it creates a long-term operating liability.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Build the reference distributor as a fully branded consumer booking service funded from the programme budget and operated by a dedicated public entity, with a sunset review once market share is reached.
  2. Limit it to an open-source reference implementation and a conformance sandbox that commercial distributors and small operators can reuse, with no direct consumer sales.
  3. Run it as a consumer service of last resort that sells only the corridor itineraries and accessibility-assisted journeys that commercial distributors decline to carry, funded by a per-ticket levy.

Trade-Off / Risk: A public retail service shows regulatory seriousness, but if it competes directly with commercial distributors the program risks losing their cooperation, while a code-only reference does little for passengers who need a trustworthy channel.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Assistance Booking and Accessibility Integration, since a public channel can serve assisted journeys that commercial sellers decline, and supports OSDM Access Terms and Enforcement Model by showing what compliant access and conformance testing look like.

Conflict: A full retail service competes with commercial distributors and strains Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives by drawing budget into running costs. It also risks Competition-Law Firewalls for Shared Fare and Inventory Data if its privileged data access looks discriminatory.

Justification: Medium, Matters for budget share and the signal sent to Trainline and Omio, but it is an optimisation of one channel. It is less central than the access, settlement and funding levers, and its main effects run through them.

Decision 7: Corridor Sequencing and Onboarding Gates

Lever ID: a612a767-6705-46c6-9709-af45f933b2f9

The Core Decision: Controls the order, pace and entry criteria for going live on Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon and Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin. It balances credible journey continuity against momentum. Metrics include carriers passing conformance on schedule, share of corridor itineraries bookable end to end, and clarity of what travellers can buy. It also decides how early learning feeds the later TEN-T extension.

Why It Matters: This lever sets the order and pace of corridor rollout and what carriers must pass before going live. Holding the four starting corridors to strict gates builds a credible base, but waiting for the weakest carrier can stall momentum. Letting the fastest carriers go first yields early results but can create a two-speed network in which the through-ticket works only on parts of a journey.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Launch the four named corridors together under common gates, so that no corridor goes live until every carrier on it passes conformance and settlement integration tests.
  2. Go live corridor by corridor as each reaches readiness, starting with the one with the most advanced OSDM implementations, and use its results to set gates for the others.
  3. Start with a small number of high-demand city pairs across several corridors, selected on competition with short-haul air, and expand along routes once through-ticket volumes show demand.

Trade-Off / Risk: Gating by weakest carrier protects journey continuity, but a single slow operator can hold up every corridor, while staggered launches make it harder to explain to travellers what is actually bookable.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Works with Outcome Measurement, Baselines and Attribution, since staged launches create comparable early data, and with Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives, since funding can be tied to passing gates and rewarding readiness.

Conflict: Strict common gates collide with Legacy Carrier IT Migration Pathway, as the slowest carrier holds up every corridor. Staggered or city-pair launches conflict with Through-Fare Composition and Reduction Card Rules, because partial coverage complicates consistent fares and traveller messaging.

Justification: High, Governs the momentum versus journey-continuity trade-off and links to legacy migration, funding release, measurement and fare consistency. It is largely a downstream delivery lever that depends on governance and funding choices, so it ranks High rather than Critical.

Decision 8: Passenger-Rights Backstop and Liability Allocation

Lever ID: 24c81358-0ae3-43a8-9ff9-f2b64e410eba

The Core Decision: Allocates responsibility and funding for rerouting, care and refunds when a missed connection occurs on a multi-carrier through-ticket. It must align with the revised EU rail passenger rights rules and give travellers one clear promise. Metrics include time to reroute or refund, claim dispute rate, distributor willingness to sell risky itineraries, and backstop cost per ticket sold.

Why It Matters: This lever determines who is responsible when a missed connection occurs on a through-ticket sold by a third party covering several carriers. A single point of liability and a guaranteed rerouting or refund gives travellers real protection but must be funded and must be reconciled with the revised rail passenger rights rules. Distributing liability among carriers keeps costs with the cause of the delay but weakens the passenger-facing promise.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Make the selling distributor the single point of contact for rerouting and refunds, with carriers reimbursing it through the clearing mechanism according to a fixed fault-allocation schedule.
  2. Fund a pooled EU-level guarantee mechanism that pays out to passengers first and then recovers costs from the responsible carriers, administered alongside the clearing entity.
  3. Assign the first carrier on the through-ticket as accountable for the whole journey, with national enforcement bodies handling complaints in that carrier's home state.

Trade-Off / Risk: A single point of contact is easy for passengers to understand, but without a funded way of recovering costs from the carriers at fault, distributors may decline to sell risky itineraries or carriers may contest every claim.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Builds on Clearing and Settlement Architecture, which provides the reimbursement and recovery channel, and reinforces Real-Time Inventory and Disruption Data Model, since reliable disruption data lets fault be allocated and rerouting triggered quickly.

Conflict: A strong single-contact or pooled guarantee increases financial exposure, tensioning with Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives, and may clash with Member-State Regulator Capacity and Cross-Border Enforcement Cooperation, as national bodies interpret rights and fault differently.

Justification: High, Delivers the continuity-of-journey promise that makes through-tickets trustworthy and sets financial exposure. It depends on clearing and disruption data and tensions with funding and regulator consistency, so it has many strong interactions, but it builds on upstream choices.

Decision 9: Through-Fare Composition and Reduction Card Rules

Lever ID: f3c80ae9-6a26-4bb0-af61-d6d24fc3ab81

The Core Decision: Sets how prices from several carriers become one through-fare, and how national reduction cards are recognised across borders. It decides whether passengers see a single, competitive price against airlines and how much pricing freedom carriers keep. Metrics include through-fare price versus competing air fares on priority corridors, reduction-card recognition coverage, and the revenue shifts passed to clearing.

Why It Matters: Rules for assembling a through-fare from several carriers' prices decide whether passengers see one price that competes with a flight. They also set how much pricing freedom carriers keep. Recognising reduction cards across borders adds appeal but shifts revenue between carriers, which the clearing mechanism then has to absorb.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Allow through-fares to be the sum of each carrier's segment price, with only a transparency duty requiring the total and its breakdown to be shown before purchase.
  2. Designate a lead carrier per journey that sets one through-fare under agreed apportionment rules, with the lead carrier bearing the pricing risk across the other segments.
  3. Introduce a regulated cross-border fare product with a ceiling tied to distance bands on priority corridors, and require mutual recognition of national reduction cards at a defined discount.

Trade-Off / Risk: A summed-segment model is easiest to adopt but rarely beats airline pricing on competitive short-haul routes, while regulated fare ceilings could achieve the modal-shift goal yet invite competition-law challenge and carrier resistance.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Supports the 40% through-ticket target when combined with Clearing and Settlement Architecture, which can apportion revenue automatically, and with Outcome Measurement, Baselines and Attribution, which can show whether fare rules drive modal shift.

Conflict: Regulated fare ceilings or lead-carrier pricing collide with Competition-Law Firewalls for Shared Fare and Inventory Data, since coordinated pricing invites antitrust scrutiny. Reduction-card recognition also adds revenue-allocation load on Clearing and Settlement Architecture.

Justification: High, Determines whether passengers see a single competitive price against air fares, so it bears directly on the 40% and modal-shift targets. It trades carrier pricing freedom against antitrust risk and loads clearing, but it is narrower in scope than the foundation levers.

Decision 10: Real-Time Inventory and Disruption Data Model

Lever ID: 6c3c7ad8-741d-48bb-9754-1963cc5f7790

The Core Decision: Defines the architecture of the shared data layer: federated queries, a central availability cache or event-streamed disruption data. It governs search latency, accuracy of seat availability for distributors, speed of detecting missed connections for rights claims, and who bears data-quality liability. Metrics are search response time, oversell and booking-failure rates, and disruption-event latency.

Why It Matters: The shared data layer can hold inventory centrally, leave it with carriers behind federated queries, or stream events as they occur. This choice sets search speed, the accuracy of availability shown to distributors, and how quickly a missed connection is detected for rights purposes. Each model also changes who bears data-quality liability.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Use federated queries in which each carrier keeps authoritative inventory and national access points route requests, accepting variable response times between operators.
  2. Maintain a European availability cache that carriers feed continuously, so distributors search one fast source and only confirm final bookings with the carrier.
  3. Build an event-streaming disruption mesh in which delays, cancellations and platform changes are published as they occur, with data quality commitments written into carrier access terms.

Trade-Off / Risk: A central cache gives distributors fast, uniform search, but stale availability turns into oversold seats and disputes, while federated queries avoid duplication yet let the slowest carrier define the passenger experience on every through-journey.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Feeds Passenger-Rights Backstop and Liability Allocation with timely missed-connection evidence, and supports Assistance Booking and Accessibility Integration by enabling live platform, lift and assistance updates for travellers with reduced mobility.

Conflict: A central cache or shared mesh raises concerns under Competition-Law Firewalls for Shared Fare and Inventory Data, because pooled commercial data can enable collusion. It also depends on Legacy Carrier IT Migration Pathway, since slow back-ends limit data freshness.

Justification: High, Defines the shared data layer architecture, which drives search quality, oversell rates and disruption evidence for rights claims. It feeds the backstop and accessibility, and it depends on legacy migration and the competition firewalls, making it a major technical hub.

Decision 11: Ticket Format, Validation and Passenger Data Model

Lever ID: 5b18310c-0cc6-4816-b164-8513132f11a3

The Core Decision: Specifies what a through-ticket is, how any carrier's staff or validators verify it on board, and what passenger data flows between carriers. It drives interoperability on trains, GDPR exposure and the cost of upgrading inspection devices. Metrics include ticket acceptance rate across carriers, validator coverage by deadline, validation performance in low-connectivity areas, and the volume of personal data shared.

Why It Matters: What a through-ticket physically is, and how it is checked on board, determines whether a passenger holding one ticket is accepted by every carrier's staff and validators. The same choice defines how much personal data moves between carriers, which brings GDPR obligations. A common format simplifies inspection but requires new validator software on many networks.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Mandate a common offline-verifiable barcode ticket format that any carrier's handheld device can validate, with carriers given a transition period to update inspection equipment.
  2. Link tickets to a digital identity wallet credential, so inspection checks the passenger's entitlement online and avoids passing full booking records between carriers.
  3. Keep each carrier's native ticket format but require a standard machine-readable wrapper and a shared validation service that carriers query in real time on boarding.

Trade-Off / Risk: An offline barcode works in tunnels and border areas with weak coverage but needs broad device upgrades, while wallet-based or service-based validation reduces data sharing at the cost of dependence on connectivity on the very corridors being prioritised.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Enables Passenger-Rights Backstop and Liability Allocation by giving a verifiable single-ticket entitlement that proves continuity of journey, and supports Clearing and Settlement Architecture through reliable usage records for apportioning revenue.

Conflict: A mandated common barcode requires validator upgrades that compete for money with Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives and burden Legacy Carrier IT Migration Pathway. Online wallet or service validation instead depends on connectivity along prioritised corridors, affecting Corridor Sequencing and Onboarding Gates.

Justification: Medium, Important for on-board acceptance and GDPR exposure, and it supports the backstop and clearing records. It is a largely technical standard choice with a contained set of conflicts (validator upgrade cost), so it is useful but not a core strategic driver.

Decision 12: Assistance Booking and Accessibility Integration

Lever ID: 1747a9ca-836b-49cd-bd26-b7907b8f9425

The Core Decision: Defines how passengers with reduced mobility request, receive confirmation of and rely on assistance within a through-ticket purchase. Scope covers request formats, response windows, cross-border handovers between carriers and stations, and accessibility data. Success metrics: share of requests confirmed before payment, share of confirmed assistance actually delivered on the platform, and accessibility-related complaint rates.

Why It Matters: How assistance for persons with reduced mobility is requested and confirmed through the booking flow determines whether through-tickets are usable by those passengers. Treating it as a core booking step increases cost and complexity for carriers. Treating it as an add-on keeps rollout simple but risks leaving the group out of the through-ticket benefit.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Make assistance requests a mandatory field in the standard booking interface, with each carrier required to confirm or reject within a defined response window before payment completes.
  2. Establish a single European assistance coordination desk that receives requests from all distributors and arranges handovers between carriers and stations across borders.
  3. Publish a station and rolling-stock accessibility registry through the data layer, so distributors can offer only itineraries whose transfers and vehicles match the passenger's declared needs.

Trade-Off / Risk: Embedding assistance in the booking step gives certainty before payment, but it depends on station staffing that this program funds only indirectly, so a confirmed request can still fail on the platform.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Amplifies Real-Time Inventory and Disruption Data Model by feeding accessibility and assistance status into the shared data layer, and strengthens Passenger-Rights Backstop and Liability Allocation by giving a clear record of confirmed assistance obligations.
