Conflict: Mandatory confirmation windows add cost and latency for carriers, trading off against Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives, and may slow Legacy Carrier IT Migration Pathway where older systems cannot return timely confirmations.

Justification: Medium, Essential for inclusion and a stated scope item, but it is a feature-level lever. Its connections to the data layer, backstop and funding are real but limited, and it does not govern the programme's main structural trade-offs.

Decision 13: Competition-Law Firewalls for Shared Fare and Inventory Data

Lever ID: 7236cb11-ae18-4988-a1d5-2c201a5f57f1

The Core Decision: Determines what commercially sensitive data (fares, load factors, sales volumes) the shared layer may expose among competing carriers, and the safeguards that keep it pro-competitive rather than a facilitator of coordination. It sets the usable data depth for distributors and the legal risk for participants. Metrics: regulator acceptance, absence of antitrust challenges, and distributor data usability.

Why It Matters: A shared real-time data layer exposes commercially sensitive fares, load factors and sales volumes among carriers that also compete. The safeguards chosen determine whether regulators view the layer as pro-competitive access or as a facilitator of coordination, and how much data distributors can actually use.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Restrict shared data to the minimum needed for booking and clearing, with aggregated or delayed reporting for any competitively sensitive fields, validated by an upfront competition-authority consultation.
  2. Place the data layer under an independent neutral operator that holds carrier data in segregated form and publishes audited access logs, so no carrier sees another's commercial inputs.
  3. Seek a formal block-exemption-style clearance from the Commission for the full data-sharing scheme, accepting a longer legal lead time in exchange for durable certainty for all participants.

Trade-Off / Risk: Tight data minimisation lowers antitrust risk but can starve distributors of the inventory detail needed for good through-fare offers, while broad sharing improves search quality at the cost of enforcement exposure.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Gives legal certainty to OSDM Access Terms and Enforcement Model and Clearing and Settlement Architecture, since clear data boundaries let carriers join without fearing antitrust exposure, and supports the neutral positioning of Role of the Public Reference Distributor.

Conflict: Tight minimisation limits the detail available to Real-Time Inventory and Disruption Data Model and Through-Fare Composition and Reduction Card Rules, weakening search quality, while formal clearance routes lengthen lead time against the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards target.

Justification: High, Sets the legal feasibility of the shared data layer and trades antitrust safety against data usability. It gives certainty to access terms, clearing and the data model, but its effect is mostly as an enabling constraint rather than a primary driver.

Decision 14: Outcome Measurement, Baselines and Attribution

Lever ID: 9022ccc5-3420-4db6-a573-6d0a33ee3351

The Core Decision: Establishes how the programme's three headline targets (40% through-ticket share, halved distributor complaints, modal shift from air) are baselined, defined, tracked and attributed. It fixes what counts as a through-ticket, the data sources and the evaluation design. Metrics: baseline set early, methodology acceptance by stakeholders, and timely triggers for mid-course correction.

Why It Matters: The programme targets a 40% through-ticket share, halved distributor complaints and modal shift from air, yet cross-border sales data are fragmented and no common baseline is assumed to exist. The measurement approach determines whether results can be credibly attributed to the programme, and whether mid-course corrections are triggered early enough.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Define the baseline in the first months through mandatory carrier and distributor reporting templates, then track the three headline targets quarterly using a single published methodology.
  2. Commission an independent evaluator to build a counterfactual using comparison routes outside the rollout corridors, separating programme effects from fuel prices, aviation taxes and capacity changes.
  3. Tie a portion of carrier incentive payments to audited through-ticket volumes and complaint resolution data, so reporting accuracy becomes a financial interest rather than a compliance burden.

Trade-Off / Risk: Counterfactual evaluation produces credible attribution of modal shift, but it takes longer and costs more, while simple self-reported tracking is quick yet vulnerable to definitional disputes over what counts as a through-ticket.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Supplies evidence that lets Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives reward verified results, and informs Corridor Sequencing and Onboarding Gates by showing which corridors are performing and where expansion is justified.

Conflict: Mandatory reporting templates and audited volumes burden carriers during Legacy Carrier IT Migration Pathway, and counterfactual evaluation competes for budget and time with Member-State Regulator Capacity and Cross-Border Enforcement Cooperation.

Justification: Medium, Needed to define the through-ticket and verify the three headline targets, and it informs incentive payments and corridor expansion. It is an enabling and monitoring lever that does not shape the main delivery trade-offs.

Decision 15: Member-State Regulator Capacity and Cross-Border Enforcement Cooperation

Lever ID: 3561617d-7835-4c9b-83f3-cd6cb00513a6

The Core Decision: Aligns national regulators' capacity, procedures and cooperation so access, refund and accessibility duties are enforced consistently across borders. Options range from training and twinning to a lead-authority network or agency-level mediation. Metrics: time to resolve discriminatory-access complaints, consistency of outcomes across states, and the number of cross-border cases escalated.

Why It Matters: National regulators will enforce access, refund and accessibility duties differently unless capacity and procedures are aligned. The cooperation model chosen affects consistency of enforcement across borders and how quickly a distributor's complaint about discriminatory access can be resolved.

Strategic Choices:

  1. Fund bilateral twinning between stronger and weaker national regulators, with shared training and common inspection checklists, leaving enforcement decisions entirely with each national authority.
  2. Create a standing network of regulators with a lead-authority rule for cross-border cases, so one regulator handles a dispute and its decision is recognised in all participating states.
  3. Give the EU Agency for Railways a limited supervisory and mediation role over cross-border access disputes, with escalation to the Commission for repeated non-compliance by any carrier.

Trade-Off / Risk: A lead-authority network speeds cross-border resolution, but it needs mutual recognition that some member states may resist on sovereignty grounds, while twinning alone builds capacity without fixing inconsistent enforcement outcomes.

Strategic Connections:

Synergy: Gives real force to OSDM Access Terms and Enforcement Model and Passenger-Rights Backstop and Liability Allocation, because consistent national enforcement makes access and refund duties credible for distributors and passengers.

Conflict: Lead-authority recognition and agency supervisory roles may collide with sovereignty concerns and with the decision rights set in Programme Governance Vehicle and Decision Rights, risking overlapping or contested authority over disputes.

Justification: High, Determines whether access, refund and accessibility duties are enforced consistently across states, which gives force to access terms and the backstop. It involves sovereignty tensions with governance, so it carries significant systemic weight.

Choosing our strategic path.

The Strategic Context

Understanding the core ambitions and constraints that guide our decision.

Ambition and Scale: Very high. EU-wide, multi-stakeholder public infrastructure and governance programme covering 27 member states and about 25+ carriers. It spans a shared real-time data layer, clearing and settlement, a passenger-rights backstop, a public reference distributor and multimodal hooks. Public coordination budget is €1.5 billion (user constraint). Milestones: binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-08), mandatory API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-08), full corridor through-ticketing by Month 60 (2031-10-08). Outcome targets: 40% of cross-border journeys sold as through-tickets, distributor complaints halved, and modal shift from air.

Risk and Novelty: Moderate to high. The legislative basis is only proposed (Commission proposals published May 2026; adoption by Parliament and Council still pending, so the final text is not confirmed). OSDM is an existing standard, but a pan-European through-ticketing and clearing regime with non-discriminatory access is novel. Key risks are incumbent resistance, uneven carrier IT maturity, regulator capacity differences and legal set-up delays. The brief explicitly asks for a realistic scenario, not the most aggressive one.

Complexity and Constraints: Very high complexity. Legacy booking back-ends vary widely. Multiple legal regimes apply (competition law, payment services licensing, passenger rights). Fixed €1.5 billion public budget, with private carrier IT spend estimated separately. Hard milestones at Months 18, 30 and 60 (2028-04-08, 2029-04-08, 2031-10-08). Phased corridor rollout. Needs conformance testing, member-state capacity building and consumer-side rollout. The critical path is sensitive to governance and clearing set-up time.

Domain and Tone: Public policy and regulatory transport infrastructure with a business and governance framing. Formal, institutional, stakeholder-heavy tone. Digital systems (APIs, payments) are tied to physical rail operations and corridors.

Holistic Profile: A large, politically sensitive, regulation-aligned EU programme that must deliver on fixed milestones with a fixed public budget. It needs credible enforcement of non-discrimination but should avoid fixing prices or building heavy new legal entities before the legislation is final. The brief calls for a balanced, risk-managed path that supports smaller carriers and protects the Month 30 (2029-04-08) deadline while still moving toward the 40% target.

The Path Forward

This scenario aligns best with the project's characteristics and goals.

The Pragmatic Foundation: Certified Access, Competitive Settlement

Strategic Logic: This path avoids fixing prices before the legislation is final and before real cost data exists. It ties inventory access to a distributor certification scheme, uses accredited payment institutions for split payment and refunds so no new central payment entity is needed, and co-funds carriers against milestones with priority for smaller and state-weak operators. Regional hubs let smaller carriers meet the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API date without a permanent central gateway. A time-boxed arbitration panel on top of existing institutions resolves contested technical decisions without a new legal entity. This is the realistic, recommended path: it balances progress against delivery risk, and it does not need the most aggressive option on any lever.

Fit Score: 9/10

Why This Path Was Chosen: Certification-based tiered access, accredited payment providers, milestone co-funding for smaller carriers, regional hubs and a lightweight arbitration panel avoid long legal set-up and early price-fixing. It still gives enforceable access rules and a path to the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate and the through-ticket targets. It matches the 'realistic, not most aggressive' brief.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • OSDM Access Terms and Enforcement Model: Tie API access terms to a certification scheme under which distributors earn tiered inventory access by meeting conformance and consumer-protection tests, with carriers able to audit distributors in return.
  • Clearing and Settlement Architecture: Contract regulated payment institutions to run split-payment and refund orchestration as a competitive service, with carriers choosing among accredited providers that meet common settlement rules.
  • Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives: Make a significant portion of the budget available as milestone-based co-funding for carriers, prioritising smaller and state-weak operators, conditional on meeting API and data-quality deadlines.
  • Legacy Carrier IT Migration Pathway: Offer regional shared booking-service hubs, run by consortia of neighbouring carriers or by procured third-party operators, that host inventory and fare logic for several carriers behind one interface.
  • Programme Governance Vehicle and Decision Rights: Create a small independent standards arbitration panel with time-boxed rulings, layered on top of existing institutions, so disputes resolve quickly without building a full new legal entity.

The Decisive Factors:

  • Balanced ambition and risk: The programme is large and carries fixed milestones (Months 18, 30, 60 = 2028-04-08, 2029-04-08, 2031-10-08) and a €1.5 billion budget (user constraint). The Pragmatic Foundation advances every lever without requiring the most aggressive option on any of them, as the brief asks.
  • Legislation still pending: The Commission proposals (May 2026) have not been adopted. Tiered, certification-based access avoids fixing a regulated price before the final text and real cost data exist.
  • Protects the critical path: Accredited payment institutions and a time-boxed arbitration panel avoid new legal entities and licensing delays that could threaten the Month 18 (2028-04-08) and Month 30 (2029-04-08) milestones.
  • Inclusive adoption: Milestone-based co-funding and regional hubs address the long tail of smaller carriers without creating a permanent single-point-of-failure gateway.
  • Why not The Pioneer's Gambit: Its central clearing entity, joint undertaking and regulated price add legal set-up time and execution risk, and its volume-linked funding favours corridors that already succeed.
  • Why not The Consolidator's Compact: Its self-published terms, complaints-driven enforcement and incumbent-influenced governance make the 40% and halved-complaints targets unlikely.

Alternative Paths

The Pioneer's Gambit: Central Rails, Market-Driven Delivery

Strategic Logic: This path builds central institutions first: a regulated access price, a publicly governed clearing entity and a joint undertaking with its own budget authority and tie-breaking power. It rewards carriers and distributors only for verified through-ticket volume, so public money follows outcomes. It accepts the risks of a long legal set-up (the joint undertaking and clearing licensing could consume much of the first year, which threatens the Month 30 = 2029-04-08 API mandate), uneven readiness among smaller carriers, and funding that favours corridors already succeeding. In return it offers the strongest chance of reaching the 40% target and the strongest enforcement of non-discrimination.

Fit Score: 3/10

Assessment of this Path: It pairs the strongest enforcement with a regulated price, a new central clearing entity and a joint undertaking. The legal and licensing set-up would likely use up much of the first year and threaten the Month 18 (2028-04-08) and Month 30 (2029-04-08) milestones. It also fixes prices before the legislation or cost data exist and leaves smaller carriers behind, which makes it the most aggressive option and not a realistic one.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • OSDM Access Terms and Enforcement Model: Mandate a single regulated reference price and service-level schedule for API access, enforced by national regulators with EU Agency for Railways audit rights over inventory parity and latency.
  • Clearing and Settlement Architecture: Establish a single publicly governed clearing entity that receives passenger payments, applies agreed apportionment rules and pays carriers on a fixed cycle, with a guarantee fund for defaults.
  • Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives: Hold back a competitive pool of funds that carriers and distributors bid for to deliver jointly proposed integration projects, with payment tied to verified through-ticket volumes.
  • Legacy Carrier IT Migration Pathway: Require every carrier to build and operate its own native interface, using public funds only for standards work and testing, and accept uneven readiness among smaller operators.
  • Programme Governance Vehicle and Decision Rights: Establish a dedicated joint undertaking with carrier, distributor and consumer seats, giving it its own budget authority, staff and a tie-breaking mechanism for contested technical decisions.

The Consolidator's Compact: Proven Tools, Protected Deadlines

Strategic Logic: This path puts schedule certainty and cost control first by relying on what already exists. Carriers publish their own access terms within a common template, settle through existing arrangements with a common message standard, and run under current EU institutional procedures. Public money goes to shared infrastructure and testing, and a publicly hosted gateway lets smaller carriers meet the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate. The cost is weaker enforcement against discrimination and slower, incumbent-influenced decisions. The 40% through-ticket target and the halving of distributor complaints are therefore less likely to be met.

Fit Score: 5/10

Assessment of this Path: It protects schedule and cost, but self-published access terms, penalties only after repeated findings, incumbent-influenced governance and no carrier co-funding undercut the non-discrimination goal. The 40% through-ticket and halved-complaints targets would likely be missed. It is safe but under-ambitious for the programme's goals.

Key Strategic Decisions:

  • OSDM Access Terms and Enforcement Model: Let carriers publish their own FRAND-style access terms within a common template, with a complaints-driven review by regulators and penalties only after repeated findings of discrimination.
  • Clearing and Settlement Architecture: Extend existing bilateral and multilateral carrier settlement arrangements with a common message standard and an independent dispute-resolution body, avoiding any new central payment entity.
  • Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives: Reserve most of the budget for shared infrastructure, conformance testing and the clearing mechanism, leaving carrier-side integration to be funded privately under the mandate.
  • Legacy Carrier IT Migration Pathway: Fund a publicly hosted gateway that translates legacy carrier systems into the standard interface, which smaller carriers can use until they modernise their back-ends.
  • Programme Governance Vehicle and Decision Rights: Run the programme from DG MOVE with the EU Agency for Railways as technical secretariat, using advisory working groups and keeping all binding decisions inside existing EU institutional procedures.

Purpose

Purpose: business

Purpose Detailed: Large-scale, multi-stakeholder public infrastructure and governance initiative. It covers an OSDM-compatible shared real-time data layer, an inter-carrier clearing and settlement mechanism, a passenger-rights backstop, a public reference distributor and consumer-side rollout. The aim is to let any compliant distributor sell through-tickets across EU carriers. It runs over a five-year horizon (binding standards by Month 18 = 2028-04-08, mandatory API exposure by Month 30 = 2029-04-08, full corridor through-ticketing by Month 60 = 2031-10-08) with a €1.5 billion public coordination budget (user constraint). Private carrier IT investment is estimated separately. The targets are 40% of cross-border journeys sold as through-tickets, distributor complaints halved, and a modal shift from short-haul air to rail. This is a societal, governmental and economic-scale transport infrastructure and regulatory program, so it is categorized as business.

Topic: Coordinated European program for cross-border rail through-ticketing and digital booking (aligned with the EC proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail)

Domain

Primary domain: Rail Ticketing Interoperability

Secondary domains: Transport Regulation, Clearing and Settlement, Passenger Rights Law

Rationale: Rail Ticketing Interoperability is the only outcome-role candidate and matches the core mechanism of cross-border through-ticketing. Transport Regulation, Data Interoperability Architecture, Clearing and Settlement and Public Program Management are constraints or methods subordinate to that goal.

Disciplines this project involves:

Domain Importance Specificity Role Reason
Rail Ticketing Interoperability 5 5 outcome Core mechanism: OSDM-compatible through-ticketing, distribution, and booking across carriers on cross-border corridors.
Transport Regulation 5 4 constraint Must align with the EC proposed rail booking regulation, passenger rights, and national regulators.
Data Interoperability Architecture 5 4 method Shared real-time data layer with OSDM-compatible APIs demands standards-based API and data architecture.
Clearing and Settlement 4 4 method Inter-carrier revenue clearing and single-payment settlement underpin through-ticket sales.
Passenger Rights Law 4 4 constraint Continuity-of-journey, refund harmonisation and passenger-rights backstop require EU consumer and transport law expertise.
Competition Law 4 4 constraint Non-discriminatory distributor access and inter-carrier data and fare sharing raise antitrust and access obligations.
Payment Systems 4 4 method Single-payment settlement and refunds across carriers require payment orchestration and split-payment design.
Public Program Management 4 3 method Coordinating a €1.5 billion, multi-stakeholder, five-year program across member states requires program governance.
Accessibility Compliance 3 4 constraint Persons with reduced mobility assistance booking must meet accessibility rules and disability-rights requirements.

Plan Type

This plan requires one or more physical locations. It cannot be executed digitally.

Explanation: The plan is classified as physical. Although it centres on digital artefacts (OSDM-compatible APIs, a shared real-time data layer, booking systems and a clearing and settlement mechanism), it is a multi-year, EU-wide rail transport programme with many physical dependencies, and it cannot be executed entirely online. (1) Rail operations and the passenger journey: the goal is to make real cross-border train travel easier and to shift travellers from short-haul flights to trains. The outcome is physical movement of passengers on trains across the Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon and Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin corridors, and later across the TEN-T network. (2) Physical stations and rolling stock: through-ticketing with continuity-of-journey rights, disruption handling, a passenger-rights backstop, bicycle reservations and assistance for persons with reduced mobility all need on-the-ground operations. These include station staff, boarding and assistance services, bicycle spaces on trains, and ticket validation and inspection on board. (3) Integration with other transport modes: the scope includes hooks for buses, ferries and short-haul air, which are physical services at terminals, ports and airports. (4) Conformance and field testing: conformance testing of carrier systems and pilots on live corridors need test environments, devices (validators, handheld inspection devices, kiosks and ticket machines) and real-world trials with operators and passengers. (5) Hardware and facilities: carrier IT investment, data centres, development workspaces, and the physical hardware that standards work and software development depend on. (6) In-person governance and stakeholder coordination: the programme involves DG MOVE, the EU Agency for Railways, CER, national operators, national regulators, BEUC and disability-rights bodies. It also includes member-state capacity building, which implies workshops, meetings in Brussels and national capitals, and regulator engagement. (7) Consumer-side rollout: apps, multilingual support and complaint handling are digital, but rollout also needs physical channels, such as station information, staff training and call centres. (8) Large-scale delivery with a €1.5 billion public budget (user constraint) over five years requires offices, staff, procurement and site work. Software and API development have physical elements of their own: workspaces, hardware and real-device testing. Under the "any doubt means physical" rule, and because the programme's real-world outcomes depend on physical trains, stations, people and locations, it is physical.

Physical Locations

This plan implies one or more physical locations.

Requirements for physical locations

  • Major EU transport hubs and capital cities with strong rail infrastructure
  • Four priority cross-border rail corridors: Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon, Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin
  • Access to national rail operators and regulatory authorities
  • Proximity to conformance testing facilities and carrier IT operations centres
  • Capacity for multi-stakeholder governance coordination (DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways, CER, national regulators, BEUC)
  • Integration with broader TEN-T network infrastructure
  • Accessibility to member-state capacity-building venues and workshops

Location 1

Belgium

Brussels

Brussels, European Quarter or near Central Station

Rationale: Brussels is the primary hub for EU institutional coordination (DG MOVE, Commission, Council). It is central to the Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln corridor and sits at the intersection of major cross-border rail networks. Hosting the programme governance vehicle, arbitration panel and stakeholder coordination here ensures proximity to decision-makers and regulatory authorities while serving the initial priority corridors.

Rationale: Cologne terminates one of the four priority corridors (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln). Frankfurt is Deutsche Bahn's operational hub and a major European rail and logistics centre. Either location enables conformance testing, carrier IT coordination and integration of one of the most complex multicarrier operations (SNCF, SNCB, NS, Deutsche Bahn) within the priority network.

Location Summary

The programme is physically rooted in the four priority cross-border rail corridors and the broader TEN-T network. Governance and standards coordination are centred in Brussels (proximity to EU institutions and DG MOVE). Conformance testing, carrier IT integration and initial corridor rollout are deployed across the corridor hubs: Cologne/Frankfurt for the Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln route, Vienna for Wien–München–Zürich, and Madrid/Barcelona and Copenhagen/Hamburg/Berlin for the southern and northern corridors respectively. Each location serves as a base for carrier onboarding, regulatory liaison, and real-world testing against live rail operations, while the regional shared booking hubs (per the Pragmatic Foundation scenario) are sited in consortia-run facilities near major operators in each corridor region.

Currency Strategy

This plan involves money.

Currencies

  • EUR: Primary currency for EU budget allocation, programme-level disbursement, milestone payments, carrier co-funding and consolidated financial reporting. Covers most priority corridors and eurozone operations.
  • DKK: Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin corridor; DSB and Danish regional operators; local capacity building and hub operations in Denmark.
  • SEK: Swedish railways (SJ) and TEN-T network extensions into Sweden; local procurement and capacity building in Sweden.
  • CHF: Wien–München–Zürich corridor; SBB (Swiss Federal Railways) and Swiss carrier operations; local contracting and hub operations outside the eurozone.
  • PLN: Poland's TEN-T network extension and carrier participation; national regulator capacity building and later-phase corridor rollout.
  • CZK: Czechia's TEN-T participation and regional carrier operations; local procurement and capacity building in central Europe.
  • HUF: Hungary's TEN-T network and carrier integration; central European capacity building and procurement.
  • BGN: Bulgaria's TEN-T participation and later-phase rollout; national capacity building in southeast Europe.
  • RON: Romania's TEN-T network extension and carrier participation; southeast European capacity building and procurement.

Primary currency: EUR

Currency strategy: EUR is used as the consolidated reporting and settlement currency for all public disbursements, milestone payments and programme-level accountability. Non-eurozone transactions (local procurement, regional hub operations, smaller carrier co-funding, national capacity building in Denmark, Sweden, Switzerland, Poland, Czechia, Hungary, Bulgaria and Romania) occur in local currencies and are budgeted and tracked in EUR equivalents using fixed monthly conversion rates to prevent currency fluctuation from consuming the fixed €1.5 billion budget (user constraint). Accredited payment institutions selected under the Pragmatic Foundation scenario handle multi-currency refunds and carrier settlements; apportionment rules specify whether currency conversion costs are borne by the responsible carrier, distributor or a defined pool. No hedging or alternative currency arrangements are required; all transactions follow standard EU budget execution procedures and member-state reimbursement protocols.

Identify Risks

Risk 1 - Regulatory & Permitting

The Commission's proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail (May 2026) has not been adopted by Parliament and Council. Parliamentary amendments, member-state negotiations and legal review could extend adoption into Month 6–12 (2027-04-08 to 2027-10-08). If adoption slips beyond Month 9 (2027-07-08), there is insufficient time to complete binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) and produce tested implementations before the mandatory API exposure deadline (Month 30 = 2029-04-08). Final text divergence could also require rework of standards and access-term rules.

Impact: Delay of final regulation beyond Month 9 (2027-07-08) reduces the window for standards-setting from 9 months to 3–4 months, leaving no margin for stakeholder consultation or dispute resolution. This forces either rushed, untested standards (risking carrier non-compliance) or missed Month 18 (2028-04-08) target. A slipped deadline signals weakness to incumbents and distributors, undermining buy-in for later gates. Estimated impact: Month 18 (2028-04-08) standard missed or delivered without consensus, and Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate questioned by carriers and member-state regulators.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Establish direct liaison between DG MOVE and the rapporteurs of TRAN and IMCO in Parliament, and key member-state transport ministers, to track adoption progress from Month 0 (2026-10-08) onward. Conduct a shadow legislative tracking process in parallel with Commission procedures, and begin technical standards pre-work (gap analysis against OSDM, access-term sketches) in Month 0–3 (2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08) under a 'without prejudice' frame, so standards can be finalised immediately upon adoption. If adoption slips beyond Month 8 (2027-06-08), invoke contingency: contract a rapid standards review by an external consortium and trigger early carrier engagement workshops to assess readiness and unblock technical surprises.

Risk 2 - Governance & Institutional

The Pragmatic Foundation scenario proposes a lightweight arbitration panel layered on existing institutions (DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways) to avoid new legal entities and the set-up delays they incur. However, establishing binding authority for technical disputes without explicit legal power or a formal board can lead to non-compliance when large incumbents contest rulings. Additionally, member-state sovereignty concerns and differing national regulatory powers may limit enforcement of arbitration outcomes, especially in cross-border access and refund disputes. The lack of a dedicated budget holder and staff resource could slow decision cycles.

Impact: Contested technical decisions drag on 2–6 months without binding resolution, holding up corridor gates and carrier onboarding. Incumbents can challenge arbitration findings, forcing escalation to Commission or court, which delays implementation further. An estimated 2–4 month slippage per major dispute (e.g., inventory parity thresholds, refund timing rules) compounds across Month 18–30 (2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08). Non-compliance by a major carrier (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, Trenitalia) on access terms could force renegotiation of the entire access model.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Secure explicit written mandate from the Commission and Council, before Month 1 (2026-11-08), delegating binding technical decision authority to the arbitration panel, with time limits (e.g., 60 days to ruling, 14 days to comply or escalate). Draft a Memorandum of Understanding among DG MOVE, the EU Agency for Railways and the panel, specifying governance, staffing, budget and escalation to the Commission for non-compliance. Allocate 8–12 FTE to the panel in Month 1–2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08), with authority to call emergency meetings. Pre-emptively schedule carrier engagement workshops (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) on access terms, inventory rules and settlement so contested areas surface early and can be negotiated before the panel is forced to arbitrate.

Risk 3 - Technical & Integration

Carriers' booking back-ends range from modern (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn newer systems) to legacy mainframe (some regional operators, ÖBB, older systems). The Pragmatic Foundation proposes regional shared hubs to bridge weaker operators until they modernise, but the effectiveness of a hub translation layer depends on how faithfully it maps legacy inventory and business rules to OSDM. Mapping errors (oversold seats, missing restrictions, incorrect pricing) break through-tickets and trigger rights claims. Additionally, hub operators may lack incentive to innovate, becoming bottleneck dependencies.

Impact: A regional hub mapping error (e.g., missing seat allocation logic or double-booking of restricted inventory) causes 5–15% of booked through-tickets to fail at final confirmation or on boarding, triggering passenger complaints, refund disputes and distributor liability claims. Each corridor's hub failure holds up 1–3 months of onboarding while the mapping is debugged. If a hub operates as a single point of failure (e.g., covering 4–6 operators) its outage grounds through-ticketing for that region for 6–48 hours at a time, causing estimated cascading refund obligations of €100,000–500,000 per incident. Estimated recovery cost per hub: €0.5–2 million over Years 1–3.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Define hub API specifications and test harnesses in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) in close collaboration with legacy operators and hub operators; use an external test lab to validate mapping correctness against real inventory samples from each carrier before go-live. Mandate dual-run (hub and native) for 2–4 weeks per carrier to detect mapping errors before traffic is cut over. Establish a hub incident response team with on-call escalation to the carrier's inventory team, and set target resolution time of 2 hours for critical failures. Require hub operators to carry E&O liability insurance covering overstated availability and inventory errors.

Risk 4 - Financial & Budget

The €1.5 billion public coordination budget (user constraint) is fixed over five years and must cover standards work, conformance testing, the clearing mechanism, a public reference distributor, member-state capacity building and consumer-side rollout. The Pragmatic Foundation allocates milestone-based co-funding to smaller carriers. However, actual carrier IT integration costs and the scale of public reference distributor operations are not yet estimated. If private carrier spend is significantly higher than expected, or if the reference distributor must operate longer than planned (because commercial distributors cannot scale fast enough), budget pressure could force cuts to capacity building or conformance testing, slowing smaller carriers' adoption.

Impact: If co-funding commitments to carriers exceed budget by 20–30% (€300–450 million shortfall), conformance testing budget is cut by 40–50%, slowing certification of smaller operators by 6–12 months and pushing some past the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate. The public reference distributor, intended as a temporary benchmark, may need to operate until Month 48 (2030-10-08) or beyond to capture the 40% through-ticket target, consuming €200–400 million in operating costs not provisioned. Estimated shortfall risk: €150–500 million before Month 36 (2029-10-08).

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Commission a detailed cost model in Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) estimating private carrier IT spend by carrier size, public reference distributor annual operating cost, and per-carrier co-funding need for gateway/hub use, with sensitivity to currency fluctuations across non-eurozone carriers (DKK, SEK, CHF). Define a baseline budget burn and trigger points for mid-course reviews (Month 12 = 2027-10-08, Month 24 = 2028-10-08). Establish a contingency reserve of 10–15% (€150–225 million) held at DG MOVE for urgent gaps. Tie co-funding disbursement to verified milestone completion (API exposure, data-quality attestation) to avoid moral hazard and ensure funds are spent on integration, not diverted.

Risk 5 - Competitive & Market

The programme aims for 40% of cross-border journeys sold as through-tickets within five years, and modal shift from short-haul flights. These targets assume that through-tickets become cheaper, faster or more convenient than stitching together separate operator tickets or buying a competing flight. However, through-fares are constrained by sum-of-segment pricing (the Pragmatic Foundation scenario allows transparency but not regulated fare ceilings), and commercial distributors (Trainline, Omio) may not have sufficient incentive to promote the programme if their margins are compressed. Airlines also have strong incentive to compete aggressively on price and frequency on the priority corridors.

Impact: If through-fares remain 10–25% more expensive than sum-of-separate-operator-tickets or competing flights, the 40% target is unachievable; instead, uptake plateaus at 15–25%, missing the headline goal. Airlines respond with aggressive pricing and increased frequency on Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich and Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon by Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), capturing price-sensitive passengers. Commercial distributors capture only the convenience premium, while the public reference distributor is forced to maintain higher volumes to show success, consuming extra budget. Estimated shortfall: 5–15 percentage points below target by Month 60 (2031-10-08).

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Conduct a detailed competitive pricing and margin analysis in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) comparing through-fares to competing flights and separate tickets, with sensitivities to fuel prices, aviation taxes and seat load factors. Model the effect of reduction-card harmonisation and cross-border accessibility assistance on price perception. Work with Trainline and Omio in Month 3–6 (2027-01-08 to 2027-04-08) to understand margin requirements and agree on promotional commitments in exchange for early API access or preferred inventory terms. Reserve a portion of the public reference distributor budget for targeted campaigns on the priority corridors where air competition is strongest, positioned as 'train travel made simple' rather than price-focused.

Risk 6 - Operational & Implementation

The programme requires simultaneous capacity building in member-state regulators (up to 27 different legal systems, enforcement traditions and data-protection practices), technical standards alignment across 25+ carriers, conformance testing infrastructure, clearing and settlement integration, and consumer-side rollout (apps, multilingual support, complaint handling). Coordination across Brussels, Vienna, Cologne, Madrid, Copenhagen and other hubs involves constant travel, workshops and real-time decision-making. A complex governance structure with multiple working groups, advisory bodies and decision forums can lead to meetings overhead, slow circulation of minutes and decisions, and stakeholder fatigue.

Impact: Governance overhead and working-group proliferation consume 20–30% of programme staff time without proportional output, slowing standards finalisation by 3–6 months. Regulator capacity building courses are planned but poorly attended or not funded by member states, leaving weaker regulators (e.g., in southeastern Europe) unable to enforce access duties, creating a two-tier compliance landscape. Conformance testing backlogs build up, delaying carrier certification and forcing gate relaxation. Consumer-side rollout (app, support, complaint handling) is under-resourced and launches late, leaving passengers confused about which itineraries are actually bookable. Estimated delay impact: Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate at risk if more than 3–4 carriers slip, and consumer satisfaction targets missed.

Likelihood: High

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish a lean core programme management office (PMO) of 10–15 FTE in Month 1 (2026-11-08) based in Brussels, with decision authority over meeting schedules, agendas and minutes circulation. Implement a project tracking tool (e.g., Asana, Monday.com) visible to all stakeholders, with weekly status dashboards, red-flag escalation, and a single clearinghouse for decisions to avoid re-litigation in parallel forums. Fund regulator capacity building as a dedicated workstream with identified trainers and attendees in Month 2–3 (2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08), with follow-up coaching for slower regulators in Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08). Establish a conformance testing steering committee that tracks carrier readiness weekly and flags slippage to funding levers (co-funding holds) by Month 12 (2027-10-08). Ring-fence consumer-side rollout as a separate project with dedicated budget and a clear go-live date (Month 27 = 2029-01-08) for pilot corridors.

Risk 7 - Legal & Regulatory

Cross-border rail journeys involve passenger data flows across 27 member states with varying GDPR interpretations, data residency rules and consent regimes. A through-ticket clearinghouse or hub necessarily sees passenger PII (name, contact, payment details, accessibility needs), and distributing that data among carriers for fulfillment (assistance, refunds, disruption messaging) creates both compliance risk and consumer trust vulnerability. National data protection authorities may impose conflicting requirements on data location, retention and consent, especially for accessibility information and refund-related communications.

Impact: A data protection authority in one member state (e.g., Austria, Poland) challenges the data-sharing architecture and issues a ban on cross-border data flow without explicit consent, forcing a redesign 6–12 months into implementation. This delays Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards approval or creates a workaround that weakens the through-ticket continuity (e.g., no automatic assistance rerouting, no real-time disruption messaging to passengers). Compliance costs to carriers (consent management, data minimization, audit trails) increase by 10–20%, adding €50–150 million to private IT budgets and deterring smaller carriers. Estimated delay: 3–6 months if a standards revision is needed; consumer trust impact if passengers feel data is misused.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Commission a GDPR and data-protection impact assessment (DPIA) in Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08), mapping which PII flows are necessary for booking, fulfillment, refund and accessibility, and identifying minimum-data designs for each. Conduct an early engagement with the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) and national authorities in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) to achieve informal consensus on data residency, cross-border transfer mechanisms (Standard Contractual Clauses, Binding Corporate Rules) and consent regimes before standards are finalised. Embed a data-protection specialist in the standards working group, and include GDPR compliance in the conformance checklist so carriers are audited on consent, retention and breach notification.

Risk 8 - Supply Chain & Integration

The through-ticketing programme depends on payment institutions (for split-payment orchestration), clearing systems (message standards, revenue apportionment), IT service providers (hub operations, testing infrastructure), and telecom/data-centre operators (APIs, data-layer hosting). The Pragmatic Foundation proposes accredited payment institutions, but there is no pre-established market of providers meeting the requirements (multi-currency, multi-carrier settlement, EU licensing, SLA guarantees). If accreditation is lengthy or few providers apply, the programme is forced to fall back on bilateral carrier-to-carrier settlement (weaker, slower) or delay clearing until custom providers are built.

Impact: Accreditation process takes 6–12 months (Month 2–14 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-12-08), and only 1–2 providers come forward initially, leaving little choice. If an accredited provider fails or withdraws (e.g., due to compliance costs or low transaction volumes early on), switching to a replacement during Month 18–30 (2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08) is disruptive and could delay the API mandate. A shortage of qualified testing infrastructure labs delays conformance testing by 2–4 months per carrier. Estimated impact: Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandatory API exposure at risk if settling mechanism is not fully operational, and carrier onboarding gates slip by 4–8 weeks per carrier.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Launch a market sounding in Month 0–1 (2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) to identify potential payment and clearing-service providers, communicate accreditation criteria and timeline, and gauge provider interest. Draft accreditation rules in Month 1–3 (2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) in consultation with licensed payment institutions and the ECB, and issue a call for applicants by Month 2 (2026-12-08) with a target decision by Month 8 (2027-06-08). Require at least 2–3 accredited providers by Month 12 (2027-10-08), with contractual provisions for continuity and redundancy if any withdraw. For testing infrastructure, procure a European network of conformance testing labs in Month 1–3 (2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) with SLAs guaranteeing carrier test slots within 6 weeks of booking.

Risk 9 - Operational & Implementation

The programme aims to harmonise refund policies, disruption handling and passenger-rights claims across carriers and distributors, but existing EU rail passenger rights rules (Regulation 1371/2007) differ from the revised text (adopted 2023, effective 2025), and member states have not yet harmonised enforcement. Some carriers interpret care obligations narrowly (meal vouchers only), others broadly (hotel, transport). A through-ticket sold by a distributor that promises continuity-of-journey rights must resolve claims faster and more consistently than multi-operator journeys today, but carriers have no shared process and national enforcement is fragmented.

Impact: A passenger's through-ticket is disrupted, and the distributor and two carriers trade blame for 4–8 weeks while the passenger waits for refund or compensation. Public complaints about slow, inconsistent refunds and unmet care obligations force intervention by national regulators, creating reputational damage and media coverage. If refund disputes consume more than 10–15% of through-tickets sold, the programme's credibility collapses and distributors withdraw. Estimated impact: 5–10% of through-tickets disputed, average claim resolution 8–12 weeks (vs. target of <10 days), and estimated liability pool of €20–50 million in years 2–3.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Develop a common refund and rights-claim protocol in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) specifying: (1) single point of contact (distributor or carrier, clearly assigned per journey); (2) required response time (48 hours acknowledgement, 10 days decision); (3) evidence collection (real-time disruption data, booking record); (4) apportionment rules (who bears cost of rerouting, care, refund). Draft a Memorandum of Understanding binding all carriers and accredited distributors, with penalties (e.g., 0.5–1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue) for consistent non-compliance. Establish a dispute-resolution panel (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) with rotating carrier and distributor representatives, empowered to rule on contested claims within 5 days. Fund a pilot pilot on one corridor (e.g., Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam) in Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08) to test the process and refine timelines before full rollout.

Risk 10 - Market & Competition

The programme creates a shared real-time inventory and fare data layer with strict non-discrimination rules to prevent incumbents from blocking distributor access. However, competition law (Articles 101 and 102 TFEU) and merger control could be triggered if competitors (carriers) coordinate on fares, load factors or ancillary services through the shared layer. Even with safeguards (data minimisation, neutral operator, access logs), regulators (DG Comp, national authorities) may open investigations into anticompetitive data sharing, especially if modal-shift goals incentivise carriers to act in concert on pricing.

Impact: DG Comp or a national competition authority initiates an investigation into alleged data-sharing collusion in Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08), creating legal uncertainty and requiring carriers to curtail data contributions until cleared. An investigation lasting 12–24 months delays full data-layer rollout and carrier integration, pushing the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate at risk. In a worst-case scenario, a decision orders the data layer to be redesigned or dismantled, requiring a 6–12 month overhaul. Legal and compliance costs to the programme rise by €10–30 million, and carrier trust erodes. Estimated delay impact: Month 30–42 (2029-04-08 to 2030-04-08) if investigation and remedy take 12 months.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Secure a formal block-exemption letter or comfort letter from DG Comp in Month 2–6 (2026-12-08 to 2027-04-08) specifying the data-sharing scope and safeguards that will prevent antitrust scrutiny. Draft a detailed competition-law analysis (submitted to DG Comp as a pre-filing memo) explaining why the data layer is pro-competitive (enables distributor entry, combats incumbent lock-in) and what access and confidentiality rules preclude collusion. If a full block exemption is not feasible within timeline, seek a negative-clearance decision or a comfort letter. Establish a designated neutral operator for the data layer with clear governance rules (no preferential access, transparent logging of all queries) to demonstrate independence. Include antitrust compliance audits in the conformance testing process.

Risk 11 - Stakeholder & Political

The programme must balance incumbent carriers' IT investment burden (estimated €500 million to €2 billion private spend, not in the €1.5 billion public budget), smaller carriers' adoption risk (especially weaker operators in southern and eastern Europe), and distributors' margin pressure. Political pressure from member states (especially those with large incumbent carriers) and from transport unions (fearing job losses in disrupted operations) could slow decision-making or force compromises that weaken non-discrimination rules. If a major carrier (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, ÖBB) signals non-compliance or demands exemptions, other incumbents follow, fracturing the coalition.

Impact: Deutsche Bahn or SNCF announces in Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08) that API integration will not meet the Month 30 (2029-04-08) deadline due to legacy system incompatibility, forcing a renegotiation of the mandate timeline. Other carriers use this as justification for slower rollout, and the Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln corridor gates slip by 6–12 months. Political pressure from Germany or France results in weaker enforcement provisions in the final Regulation or in exemptions for 'strategic' operators. Distributor confidence erodes, and commercial platforms hold back full investment, forcing the public reference distributor to expand beyond its intended scope. Estimated impact: Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate becomes advisory rather than binding, and 40% through-ticket target drops to 25–30%.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: High

Action: Establish a formal carrier engagement and negotiation stream in Month 1 (2026-11-08) with quarterly roundtables between DG MOVE, CER and the largest carriers (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, Trenitalia, Renfe, ÖBB, NS, SJ, SNCB). Use these forums to identify IT cost-sharing opportunities (e.g., shared hubs, co-funding for legacy migration) and to air concerns early before they harden into political demands. Engage transport unions from Month 2 (2026-12-08) onward with transparency about job impacts and a commitment to funding transition support (retraining, consultation). Build political cover by securing visible member-state support (e.g., Belgium, Netherlands, Austria) early and regularly reporting programme progress to the European Parliament's TRAN committee. If a major carrier signals non-compliance, escalate immediately to the Commission and invoke contingency funding levers (co-funding holds) to signal consequences.

Risk 12 - Technical & Integration

The shared real-time data layer exposes inventory, fares and disruption data via OSDM-compatible APIs to distributors and other carriers. API reliability, latency and uptime directly affect passenger experience and distributor confidence. If APIs are slow (>5 seconds per search), unreliable (>99.9% uptime target unmet), or return stale data (seats unavailable when booking), through-tickets fail, passengers complain and distributors lose confidence. Legacy carriers' systems may not support the required API throughput (estimated 100–500 requests/second per corridor during peak hours), requiring expensive infrastructure upgrades.

Impact: API latency exceeds 5 seconds during peak hours (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), causing 10–20% of search sessions to timeout. Distributors report poor user experience and pull back from promoting through-tickets. An unplanned API outage of 4–8 hours affects 10,000–50,000 daily searches, generating escalations to DG MOVE and negative media coverage. A cache or hub serving a corridor fails and takes 12–48 hours to recover, stranding all through-ticket bookings on that route. Estimated impact: distributor frustration and withdrawal, passenger complaints, and potential Month 30 (2029-04-08) credibility hit.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Define API performance SLAs in Month 2–3 (2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08): latency <2 seconds (p95), uptime 99.95%, throughput ≥500 req/s per corridor. Conduct a carrier infrastructure assessment (Month 3–4 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08) to identify systems that cannot meet these targets and prioritise co-funding for upgrades. Procure a European-wide API hosting and caching infrastructure in Month 2–6 (2026-12-08 to 2027-04-08) with guaranteed SLAs, redundancy across data centres and failover protocols. Establish a 24/7 API operations centre in Month 6 (2027-04-08) with escalation to carriers within 15 minutes of any incident. Conduct load testing and chaos engineering exercises quarterly starting Month 9 (2027-07-08) to identify weak points before they affect production.

Risk 13 - Financial & Budget

The programme uses accredited payment institutions to handle split-payment orchestration and refund processing, avoiding the licensing delays of a central clearing entity. However, payment institutions charge transaction fees (estimated 0.5–2% per transaction, or €5–20 million annually for anticipated through-ticket volumes). These costs must come from the €1.5 billion public budget or be borne by carriers and distributors, who will pass them to passengers in higher fares. Additionally, multi-currency settlement across 9+ currencies (EUR, DKK, SEK, CHF, PLN, CZK, HUF, BGN, RON) incurs foreign-exchange costs and conversion-rate volatility that could consume €2–5 million annually.

Impact: Transaction fees to payment institutions total €80–120 million over five years, consuming 5–8% of the fixed public budget and requiring cuts elsewhere (e.g., conformance testing, capacity building). If passengers see higher through-fares as a result of bundled fees, the 40% target becomes harder to reach. Currency volatility in Years 2–5 causes €10–25 million in unexpected FX losses if not hedged, further straining the budget. A less efficient payment infrastructure (e.g., settling only nightly instead of real-time) delays carrier payouts by 1–3 days, undermining cash-flow confidence and raising financing costs for smaller carriers.

Likelihood: High

Severity: Low

Action: Model transaction fee scenarios in Month 1–2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08) and negotiate fee caps (e.g., 0.3–0.5% per transaction) into the accreditation criteria. Establish a fee-sharing formula in which the programme subsidises 50–70% of payment-institution fees for the first 2 years (Month 0–24 = 2026-10-08 to 2028-10-08), with carriers and distributors bearing the remainder, conditional on through-ticket volumes reaching 15% (Month 24 = 2028-10-08 baseline). For FX management, implement a quarterly hedging policy that caps exposure to non-EUR currencies at 5–10% of quarterly disbursements, using EUR-denominated forward contracts. Require accredited payment institutions to offer real-time settlement (intraday clearing) at no extra cost as part of the accreditation SLA.

Risk 14 - Operational & Implementation

The programme's consumer-side rollout includes a multilingual booking app, customer support in 24+ languages, and complaint handling across member-state jurisdictions. Launching a consumer product at EU scale within Months 15–27 (2028-01-08 to 2029-01-08) requires design iteration, user testing, platform scaling and localization. If the app is poorly designed, slow or untrustworthy, it will damage the programme's credibility and reduce through-ticket adoption. Supporting passengers in multiple languages and navigating cross-border disputes requires a large, trained support team.

Impact: The app is released 3–6 months late (Month 21–24 = 2028-07-08 to 2028-10-08 instead of Month 15 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-10-08 instead of 2028-01-08), missing the momentum of early corridor launches. Initial user satisfaction is low (3.5/5 stars) due to poor search, confusing refund flows or missing accessibility features, discouraging adoption. Support queue times exceed 2 hours, and a backlog of unresolved complaints (1,000+) accumulates within 3 months of launch. Estimated impact: 20–30% reduction in through-ticket volumes driven through the public reference distributor, and reputational damage requiring a costly app redesign and support surge.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish a dedicated consumer product team in Month 1 (2026-11-08) with 20–30 FTE (product managers, engineers, UX designers, localization specialists). Conduct user research and wireframing in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08), then build a minimum viable product (MVP) for pilot testing on one corridor by Month 9 (2027-07-08). Iterate based on user feedback during Month 10–12 (2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08), and begin full-scale localization and platform scaling in Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08). Launch the public app by Month 15 (2028-01-08) with a phased rollout (four priority corridors first, then TEN-T) and a commitment to sub-1-hour support response time for critical issues. Budget €20–30 million for app development, infrastructure and support over Months 15–27 (2028-01-08 to 2029-01-08).

Risk 15 - Measurement & Evaluation

The programme targets 40% of cross-border journeys sold as through-tickets, halved distributor complaints, and modal shift from air. However, baseline data on current cross-border rail sales, complaint volumes and modal split do not exist in a consolidated form. Carriers report different metrics, distributors guard proprietary data and aviation data come from EUROSTAT (not real-time). Defining and tracking the targets consistently requires establishing common data collection, but carriers may resist mandatory reporting if they fear exposure of commercial sensitivities.

Impact: Baseline is not established until Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08), delaying mid-course correction insights until Year 2. Without a clear baseline, disputes arise over whether targets are being met, undermining credibility of progress reports. If carriers refuse to report through-ticket volumes, the programme relies on distributor data only, missing operator-to-operator sales and understating true market share. An estimated 15–25% undercount of true through-ticket share is possible, requiring either disclaimer caveats or expensive corrective measurement programmes. By Month 36–48 (2029-10-08 to 2030-10-08), claims about achieving targets become contested and politically vulnerable.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Low

Action: Commission a baseline survey in Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) asking carriers, distributors and airports for current cross-border sales volumes, complaint handling metrics and modal split estimates (with confidentiality protections for sensitive data). Define 'through-ticket' operationally in Month 1–2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08): e.g., 'single booking reference, single payment, continuity-of-journey rights for a multi-carrier journey.' Mandate that all participating carriers and distributors report through-ticket volumes monthly starting Month 18 (2028-04-08), with data aggregated and published quarterly with a 1-month lag (to protect commercial sensitivity). Hire an independent evaluation firm in Month 3 (2027-01-08) to build a counterfactual model comparing through-ticket adoption on priority corridors to control routes outside the rollout, capturing the modal-shift impact separately from fuel prices and capacity changes. Reserve €5–10 million of the public budget for measurement and evaluation.

Risk 16 - Regulatory & Permitting

The four priority corridors (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon, Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin) cross multiple national rail regulators with different inspection powers, license frameworks and operational safety requirements. A through-ticket system must be compatible with each regulator's safety and operational standards, and any accident or incident (e.g., through-ticket passenger injured due to missed connection, or accessibility failure) could trigger a formal investigation that holds others liable. Regulatory fragmentation also means that a carrier can argue that through-ticket obligations (e.g., guaranteed rerouting in under 2 hours) are incompatible with its national safety rules.

Impact: A regulator (e.g., Austria's regulator for ÖBB) issues a preliminary ruling that passenger-rights obligations for through-tickets exceed its domestic safety and operational standards, creating ambiguity that slows carrier buy-in. A passenger incident (e.g., an assisted-travel passenger misses their connection due to a system error and incurs costs) triggers a formal investigation by a national authority, creating reputational damage and forcing a public response from the programme. If regulators diverge on how to interpret through-ticket liability, the backwards-compatibility of the system with national frameworks is questioned, and carriers demand exemptions. Estimated impact: 2–4 month delay in one corridor's rollout if a regulator requires a safety impact assessment or compliance review.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: High

Action: Engage the four priority corridors' national regulators in Month 1–3 (2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) with a technical briefing on through-ticket design, passenger-rights obligations and safety implications. Commission a cross-border safety and liability impact assessment (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) reviewing how through-ticket obligations interact with each regulator's standards, and propose harmonised rules (e.g., maximum rerouting time, accessibility obligations) that all regulators agree to in advance. Establish a Standing Regulators Committee (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) chaired by the EU Agency for Railways, meeting monthly to resolve operational and safety questions before they become disputes. Include through-ticket safety and liability rules in the binding standards document (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) so they are legally anchored and not subject to later re-interpretation by individual regulators.

Risk 17 - Operational & Implementation

Smaller carriers in southern, central and eastern Europe (e.g., regional operators in Romania, Bulgaria, Poland) have ageing IT systems, limited staff expertise and lower revenue resilience than incumbent operators. The Pragmatic Foundation proposes regional shared booking hubs to lower their IT barrier, but if hub operators do not effectively support smaller carriers, or if hub outages disproportionately affect them, adoption remains incomplete. Additionally, these carriers may lack the internal resources to comply with new operational requirements (real-time inventory updates, structured refund processing, accessibility assistance protocols), requiring the programme to provide hands-on capacity building and potentially longer timelines.

Impact: By Month 24 (2028-10-08), only 50–60% of smaller carriers have completed through-ticket integration, compared to 90%+ for major operators, creating a two-tier network in which through-tickets are reliable only on the major corridors. Regional hubs become bottlenecks, with queues of smaller carriers waiting for hub integration and testing slots. A hub failure affecting 4–6 regional operators leaves a significant portion of the TEN-T network unable to support through-tickets, and rollout extension beyond the four priority corridors slips by 6–12 months (pushing to Month 42–48 = 2030-04-08 to 2030-10-08 instead of Month 36 = 2029-10-08). Smaller carriers, unable to compete on through-tickets, resist ongoing API obligations and push back against access-enforcement audits, creating enforcement challenges.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Establish a dedicated Smaller Carriers Support Programme in Month 1 (2026-11-08) with 5–10 FTE regional coordinators (based in Budapest, Warsaw, Sofia, Bucharest) providing hands-on mentoring. Fund a 'migration grant' of €100,000–500,000 per smaller carrier for IT integration, legacy system upgrades and staff training (Month 6–24 = 2027-04-08 to 2028-10-08). Develop a simplified OSDM-lite interface for carriers with very old systems, reducing integration complexity (but maintaining data parity and access obligations). Schedule regional hubs' technical support team to rotate and spend 1–2 weeks per quarter on-site with smaller carriers to debug integration issues and plan upgrades. Establish a peer-mentoring network pairing larger, more advanced carriers with smaller ones to share integration lessons learned (Month 9–18 = 2027-07-08 to 2028-04-08).

Risk 18 - Technical & Integration

Real-time inventory and disruption data is critical for booking, refund decisions and accessibility assistance. The Pragmatic Foundation proposes a federated-query or event-streaming architecture. However, implementing a reliable, sub-second-latency data layer across 25+ carriers with heterogeneous IT systems and network infrastructure (especially in less-developed regions like central and southeastern Europe) is technically challenging. If inventory data is stale (>5 minutes old), overbooking and availability errors increase. If disruption events (delays, cancellations, platform changes) are not published in real time, missed-connection detection is late and passenger communication is delayed.

Impact: A regional carrier's integration with the event-streaming disruption layer has a 2–4 month implementation delay due to network limitations and legacy system incompatibility (Month 12–16 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-02-08 instead of Month 12 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-02-08 instead of 2027-10-08). Stale inventory data (20–30 minutes old) causes 5–10% of bookings to fail at final confirmation, generating passenger refunds and complaints. A cascade of missed-connection claims arises when disruption data is delayed by 10–15 minutes, too late for rerouting systems to react. Estimated impact: 2–4 month slippage in data-layer rollout, 5–10% booking-failure rate during the first 6 months of operation (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), and €5–15 million in unplanned refunds and customer compensation.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Conduct a detailed data-layer architecture workshop in Month 2–3 (2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08) with carrier CIOs and IT teams to assess feasibility of event-streaming vs. federated-query models, identify network and system bottlenecks, and estimate implementation timelines per carrier. Choose a phased approach: launch with a central availability cache for the four priority corridors (higher readiness), deferring event-streaming for disruption data to Month 21–24 (2028-07-08 to 2028-10-08) once infrastructure is proven. Fund a European data-centre network and CDN edge caches to reduce latency (Month 3–6 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-04-08) with redundancy so no single-point failure affects any corridor. Establish data-quality SLAs: inventory freshness <5 minutes, disruption event latency <2 minutes, and require carriers to publish status updates within 5 minutes of any operational change. Test the data layer monthly with synthetic load starting Month 12 (2027-10-08).

Risk 19 - Operational & Implementation

The programme's success depends on distributors (Trainline, Omio, commercial platforms) actively promoting and selling through-tickets. These platforms earn revenue from booking margins, and if through-fares are commoditized or margins are squeezed by low prices or high processing fees, their incentive to invest in integration and marketing diminishes. They may also resist integration timelines if their own IT backlogs are heavy, or demand preferential access to inventory or pricing in exchange for early buy-in.

Impact: Trainline or Omio signal in Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08) that full API integration will not be complete until Month 24–27 (2028-10-08 to 2029-01-08), after the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards deadline and risking the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate. They demand preferential inventory access (e.g., advanced notice of discount fares) in exchange for early implementation, which regulators view as discriminatory. If major distributors do not promote through-tickets actively, uptake remains low (15–25% instead of 40%), forcing the public reference distributor to expand and consume more budget. Estimated impact: distributor commitment delays by 4–8 weeks, and the 40% target becomes unachievable without heavy public spending and forced distributor participation.

Likelihood: Medium

Severity: Medium

Action: Engage Trainline, Omio and other commercial distributors in formal working groups (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) to understand their IT priorities, margin sensitivities and promotional incentives. Offer early API access (Month 9–12 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08) to platforms that commit to integration and promotion by Month 18 (2028-04-08). Establish a distributor advisory council (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) that provides input on data formats, settlement timing and consumer features, ensuring their concerns are heard early. Agree on margin-support measures in Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08), such as co-marketing funds (€5–10 million) for the first 24 months (through Month 24 = 2028-10-08), conditional on through-ticket volumes and customer satisfaction targets. Reserve slots in the conformance testing schedule for distributors' internal systems and provide free technical support to accelerate their integration.

Risk 20 - Social & Stakeholder

The programme commits to accessibility for persons with reduced mobility, including booking systems that allow request and confirmation of assistance, real-time accessibility data on stations and rolling stock, and cross-border assistance coordination. However, accessibility is often treated as a compliance checklist rather than a core service, and carriers' existing assistance infrastructure varies widely. If the programme launches with poor accessibility, it signals exclusion and invites complaints from disability-rights organizations (BEUC, national advocacy groups) that can slow deployment and create reputational damage.

Impact: Accessibility data is incomplete or inaccurate at launch (Month 18 = 2028-04-08), forcing distributors to exclude accessible itineraries from search results, leaving persons with reduced mobility with fewer options than before the programme. Assistance confirmation windows are too long (e.g., 48 hours instead of 24 hours), making it impossible for passengers to book confidently for last-minute journeys. Cross-border assistance handovers fail (e.g., a passenger arrives at a station after assistance is withdrawn), generating complaints and safety incidents. Disability-rights organizations issue a formal complaint to the Commission, triggering an investigation and negative media coverage. Estimated reputational impact: 10–20% reduction in public support and political pressure for the programme's continuation or expansion.

Likelihood: Low

Severity: High

Action: Establish an Accessibility Working Group in Month 0 (2026-10-08) with representatives from BEUC, national disability-rights organizations, accessibility experts and carriers. Define accessibility requirements in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) covering booking interfaces, assistance request/confirmation timelines, station and vehicle accessibility data, and cross-border coordination. Include accessibility in the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) as a non-negotiable requirement, not optional. Fund a €10–15 million accessibility infrastructure programme (Month 6–24 = 2027-04-08 to 2028-10-08) to support carriers' deployment of assistance request systems and accessibility data publishing. Pilot accessibility features on one corridor (e.g., Wien–München) in Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08) with feedback from disability-rights organizations before full rollout. Include accessibility metrics (assisted-journey booking rate, assistance confirmation rate, assistance delivery rate) in the quarterly measurement dashboard.

Risk summary

This €1.5 billion, five-year EU rail infrastructure programme faces compounded risks spanning regulatory, technical, financial, governance and operational domains. The most critical risks are: (1) Regulatory adoption delay—the Commission's proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services is not yet adopted, and delays beyond Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) threaten the Month 18 (2028-04-08) binding standards milestone and the entire timeline; (2) Incumbent carrier resistance and legacy IT migration—the slowest carriers' ageing booking back-ends constrain the critical path, and strategic delay by dominant operators could force gate relaxation or sideline smaller carriers; (3) Governance and decision authority deadlock—establishing binding decision rights without either light-touch institutional lag or heavy legal set-up delays is the fulcrum for all downstream delivery, and sovereignty tensions over cross-border enforcement could paralyze dispute resolution. The Pragmatic Foundation scenario mitigates these by using accredited payment institutions (avoiding new licensing delays), tiered certification-based access (deferring price regulation until legislation is final), milestone co-funding (incentivizing smaller carriers), and a lightweight arbitration panel (avoiding new legal entities). Secondary risks include uneven regulator capacity, passenger data GDPR exposure, clearing settlement disputes, and unproven modal-shift assumptions. Together, these risks demand early governance clarity, decisive regulation adoption, carrier buy-in strategy and realistic measurement baselines.

Make Assumptions

Question 1 - The €1.5 billion public coordination budget is fixed over five years (Month 0–60 = 2026-10-08 to 2031-10-08). Does this budget include funding for all programme elements (standards, conformance testing, clearing mechanism, public reference distributor, capacity building, consumer rollout, and carrier co-funding), or is it limited to specific components? Are carrier-specific IT adaptation costs (estimated at €500 million to €2 billion) explicitly excluded and borne entirely by private spend?

Assumptions: Assumption: The €1.5 billion covers all public-side coordination, governance, testing infrastructure and consumer-facing operations. Carrier IT integration costs are borne separately by carriers, with the public budget providing only co-funding grants (estimated 15–25% of carrier integration cost per Funding Allocation lever). This interpretation treats the budget as comprehensive for public obligations but allows private spend to lie outside it. If carrier co-funding consumes more than 30–40% of the budget, conformance testing and standards work face cuts.

Assessments: Title: Budget Adequacy and Allocation Trade-Off Assessment Description: Evaluation of whether €1.5 billion is sufficient to cover all public programme obligations while funding strategic carrier co-funding without creating unsustainable cuts to standards, testing or consumer-side rollout. Details: At a baseline budget burn of €250–300 million per year, the €1.5 billion fund sustains five years only if spending is tightly distributed. Early estimates suggest: standards and conformance testing (€200–300 million), clearing and settlement infrastructure (€100–200 million), public reference distributor operations (€300–500 million over five years), member-state capacity building (€100–150 million), consumer rollout and apps (€150–200 million). This totals €850–1,350 million, leaving €150–650 million for carrier co-funding and contingency. If carrier co-funding demand exceeds €400 million (plausible for 15–20 smaller operators), the budget faces a 20–30% shortfall. Mid-course review triggers should be set at Month 12 (2027-10-08) and Month 24 (2028-10-08) to assess actual spending against forecast and adjust co-funding rates downward if burn-rate exceeds plan. Risk mitigation: reserve 10–15% contingency and tie disbursements to verified milestone completion.
