Question 2 - The programme has three hard milestones: binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-08), mandatory API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-08), and full corridor through-ticketing by Month 60 (2031-10-08). Are these deadlines fixed and non-negotiable (e.g., regulatory requirements embedded in the final Regulation), or are they planning targets that can slip if technical or governance barriers emerge? What is the definition of 'mandatory API exposure' – does every participating carrier's system must be live and operational, or does 80–90% compliance suffice?

Assumptions: Assumption: The three milestones are treated as regulatory targets tied to the adopted Regulation, and thus legally binding once Parliament and Council finalize the text (expected Month 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08 per Risk 1). The 'mandatory API exposure' milestone requires that every carrier that is required to participate under the Regulation has either live OSDM-compatible API access or validated exemption (e.g., hub access for legacy systems). Exemptions must be documented and time-limited. In practice, 90%+ of corridor traffic must be bookable end-to-end by Month 30 (2029-04-08); <90% compliance triggers a Commission review and possible enforcement action. Slippage beyond these dates carries legal and reputational consequences (enforcement directives, fines for non-compliant carriers, political damage).

Assessments: Title: Timeline Criticality and Milestone Dependency Assessment Description: Evaluation of how fixed milestones constrain delivery decisions and identify which upstream activities (governance setup, standards finalization, payment-institution accreditation) are on the critical path. Details: The Month 18 (2028-04-08) binding standards deadline requires that substantive standards-setting work begin no later than Month 4–5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08), leaving Month 0–3 (2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08) for governance setup, legislative tracking and pre-work. A 3-month delay in regulation adoption (to Month 9 = 2027-07-08) compresses standards-setting from 9 months to 6 months, creating quality and consensus risk. The Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate is gated by: (1) standards finalization (Month 18 = 2028-04-08, hard prerequisite); (2) carrier readiness (estimated 80–95% achievable by Month 28–30 = 2029-02-08 to 2029-04-08 for major operators, 60–80% for smaller operators via hubs); (3) payment-institution accreditation (must be complete by Month 12–18 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08 to allow 12-month production deployment). The critical path is: regulation adoption → governance setup (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) → standards finalization (Month 4–18 = 2027-02-08 to 2028-04-08) → carrier integration (Month 18–30 = 2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08). Any slip in regulation adoption, governance authority or standards consensus cascades directly to Month 30 (2029-04-08) risk. Mitigation: establish monthly milestone tracking, trigger early escalation for >2-week slippage, and resource dispute resolution to prevent re-litigation of settled technical issues.

Question 3 - The Pragmatic Foundation scenario proposes regional shared booking hubs operated by consortia or third parties, allowing smaller carriers to meet the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API deadline without native builds. What is the target coverage of these hubs – should they serve all carriers below a certain size threshold (e.g., <5% cross-border market share), and how many hubs are needed across the four priority corridors and the broader TEN-T network? Are hub operators expected to be for-profit entities charging usage fees to carriers, or non-profit consortia funded from the programme budget?

Assumptions: Assumption: Regional hubs are intended to serve carriers with legacy IT systems that cannot achieve native OSDM compliance by Month 30 (2029-04-08). A 'hub-eligible' carrier is defined as one with: (1) annual cross-border revenue <€50 million, or (2) booking-system architecture >10 years old (mainframe, non-standard protocols), or (3) IT staff capacity <10 FTE. Estimated 12–18 carriers across 27 member states meet this criterion. Hub footprint: 4–6 regional hubs covering the four priority corridors (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon, Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin) plus 2–3 additional hubs for TEN-T extensions (central Europe, southeast Europe, Nordic). Hub operators are initially non-profit, funded by the programme (€20–40 million over five years), with transition to cost-recovery pricing by Year 4 (Month 48 = 2030-10-08). Carriers using hubs pay usage fees (€0.10–0.30 per booking, or a fixed annual fee of €50,000–200,000 depending on volume).

Assessments: Title: Legacy IT Migration and Hub Dependency Assessment Description: Evaluation of how regional hubs reduce the private IT burden for smaller carriers but create dependency risks, single-point-of-failure exposure and long-term operational liabilities. Details: Regional hubs reduce the barrier to through-ticket compliance for 12–18 smaller carriers, enabling ~85–95% of cross-border traffic (by volume, not headcount) to be covered by Month 30 (2029-04-08). Without hubs, only 60–70% of carriers would be ready, creating a fragmented, unreliable through-ticket network. Hub benefits: carriers avoid €500,000–2 million native integration costs, accelerate deployment by 6–12 months, and reduce integration risk. Hub risks: (1) a hub failure affects 4–6 dependent carriers simultaneously, with estimated 12–48 hour recovery time; (2) hub operators may become permanent dependencies (disincentivizing native modernization), increasing long-term costs; (3) mapping errors in legacy system translation cause 2–5% booking failures per region; (4) hub capacity constraints (if hub receives 10,000+ bookings/day per operator) create latency and search timeout; (5) governance ambiguity if a hub operator withdraws mid-deployment. Mitigation: hub SLAs must specify 99.9% uptime, <2-second latency, and incident recovery <2 hours; require hub operators to maintain redundancy (dual data centres); set sunset clause (hub operation expires Month 48 = 2030-10-08, carriers must migrate to native or new hub by then); allocate €5–10 million for hub resilience and training. Cost: €5–8 million per hub over five years.

Question 4 - The programme involves 27 member states and an estimated 25+ rail carriers with varying regulatory frameworks, enforcement traditions and data-protection practices. What governance model ensures that standards, access terms and passenger-rights rules are enforced consistently across borders without paralyzing decision-making? Should there be a single dispute-resolution forum (e.g., the arbitration panel), or should each member state's regulator handle disputes arising in their jurisdiction?

Assumptions: Assumption: The Pragmatic Foundation scenario establishes a lightweight arbitration panel (8–12 FTE, based in Brussels) with time-boxed decision authority (60 days to ruling) over contested technical and standards disputes. Operational and commercial disputes (e.g., carrier A accuses carrier B of discriminatory API access pricing, or passenger refund claim disputed between distributor and carrier) are handled by national regulators in the first instance, with EU Agency for Railways mediation and escalation to the Commission for cross-border cases. The panel operates under explicit written delegation from the Commission and Council, with power to issue binding rulings on technical disputes (inventory parity thresholds, API latency SLs, settlement message formats) but not commercial terms (which remain subject to negotiation and FRAND compliance). Member-state regulators commit to enforcing panel rulings consistently; non-compliance is escalated to Commission enforcement action.

Assessments: Title: Governance Authority and Cross-Border Enforcement Assessment Description: Evaluation of how a lightweight arbitration panel can maintain decision speed and authority while respecting member-state sovereignty and regulatory diversity, and whether it avoids both lengthy legal setup and disputes-driven gridlock. Details: A lightweight panel (8–12 FTE) can meet its 60-day decision target if: (1) disputes are pre-structured (technical vs. commercial), (2) carrier and distributor working groups pre-negotiate solutions before formal arbitration, (3) the panel has clear authority (written delegation from Commission), and (4) escalation to Commission is rarely needed. Advantages: avoids 12–18 month joint-undertaking legal setup, preserves existing national regulatory roles, keeps decision speed high. Risks: (1) if a major incumbent (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF) contests a technical ruling, national regulators may not enforce consistently, and the panel lacks direct enforcement power; (2) sovereignty concerns in some member states could limit acceptance of binding rulings; (3) the panel's credibility depends entirely on Commission backing, and if DG MOVE's leadership changes, enforcement commitment may waver. Mitigation: secure explicit written delegation from Council (Month 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08), establish a Standing Regulators Committee with the panel, and pre-negotiate a carrier Memorandum of Understanding (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) in which carriers agree to binding arbitration and accept penalties for non-compliance (e.g., 0.5–1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue held in escrow for compliance infractions). Cost: €2–3 million over five years for panel operations.

Question 5 - The programme aims to shift passengers from short-haul air travel to rail, reducing environmental impact and achieving modal shift on priority corridors. However, through-ticket pricing is constrained by sum-of-segment fares without regulated ceilings (per the Pragmatic Foundation scenario). What evidence or modelling exists that through-fares will be cheaper, faster or more convenient than competing flights or existing multi-operator tickets? If modelling suggests through-fares will be 10–25% more expensive than flights, should the programme introduce regulated fare ceilings or subsidies to achieve the modal-shift target?

Assumptions: Assumption: Through-tickets will be more convenient (single booking, single payment, continuity-of-journey protection) and faster than buying separate operator tickets, but unlikely to undercut airline prices on all corridors without external intervention. On Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln: through-fare estimated at €60–90 (12 hours train), vs. €40–70 airline (4 hours) depending on load factors and aviation fuel price. Without via modal-shift incentive (e.g., reduction-card harmonization, accessibility assistance, environmental messaging), price-sensitive passengers choose flights. Pragmatic Foundation accepts that the 40% through-ticket target is achievable only on selected high-demand city pairs (e.g., Paris–Brussels, Amsterdam–Köln) and corridors with weak airline competition (e.g., some segments of Wien–München–Zürich where rail has historic dominance). Modal shift is estimated at 5–15% reduction in short-haul air trips on priority corridors by Month 60 (2031-10-08), vs. the headline ambition of >25% shift. The programme does not introduce regulated fare ceilings (to avoid antitrust risk and incumbent resistance) but relies on: (1) reduction-card harmonization (estimated 10–15% effective discount across borders), (2) environmental branding and sustainability messaging, (3) convenience and reliability of through-ticketing attracting premium passengers willing to pay for single-booking convenience, and (4) early public distributor campaigns on price-sensitive routes.

Assessments: Title: Modal Shift and Through-Fare Competitiveness Assessment Description: Evaluation of whether sum-of-segment through-fares, without regulated ceilings, are sufficient to achieve modal shift from short-haul air, or whether the target is aspirational and dependent on external factors (fuel prices, aviation taxes, consumer preferences). Details: Modelling of Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln and Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon corridors (estimated 3–5 million passengers per year) suggests: baseline short-haul air market = 40–50% of the 6–10 million cross-modal annual journeys. A through-fare of €70–90 (sum of segment pricing) competes with airline fares of €50–80 on price-competitive days but loses to budget airlines at €30–50. Convenience premium (single booking, luggage handling integration, real-time disruption communication) is valued at ~€5–15 per journey (estimate based on comparable mobility studies). Estimated modal shift with no additional levers: 5–10% (0.3–1 million annual journeys) by Month 60 (2031-10-08). With reduction-card harmonization and environmental messaging: 10–20% shift. With regulated fare ceilings (not adopted here): 15–30% shift. The Pragmatic Foundation scenario accepts the 5–20% outcome and repositions the 40% target as '40% of cross-border rail journeys sold as through-tickets (not necessarily 40% modal shift from air).' This allows the programme to succeed on volume metrics even if modal shift falls short. Risk: political disappointment if modal shift lags expectations (e.g., 10% actual vs. 25% promised), inviting calls for price regulation or subsidies. Mitigation: clarify headline targets early (through-ticket share vs. modal shift are separate metrics), conduct quarterly competitive pricing analysis, and reserve campaign budget (€10–20 million over five years) for targeted air-route competition on high-sensitivity corridors.

Question 6 - Passenger data flows across the through-ticketing system include names, contact details, payment information, accessibility needs and disruption-related communications. How are GDPR compliance and cross-border data governance handled, especially for data subjects in smaller member states with stricter national data-protection interpretations? Are there any proposed data-residency rules (e.g., PII must not leave certain member states) that could conflict with the shared data layer and clearing mechanism?

Assumptions: Assumption: Through-ticketing requires that passenger PII (name, contact, payment card, accessibility attributes) flow among: (1) the booking distributor, (2) the selling carrier, (3) the connecting carrier(s), (4) the payment institution (for split payments), and (5) the clearing entity (for revenue apportionment and refund reversal). Each actor is a data controller or joint controller under GDPR Article 26. A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) is commissioned in Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) to identify: (1) minimum necessary PII per transaction (baseline: name, contact, booking reference, seat/assistance notes; extended: payment details to clearing entity only), (2) data residency constraints per member state (none formally mandated by EU law, but Poland and Hungary have expressed preferences to keep citizen data in EU data centres), and (3) consent regimes (passive consent at booking time is insufficient; explicit consent for cross-border data sharing may be required). Safeguards: Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) govern cross-border transfers among carriers and payment institutions; Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) for large multi-country operators; deletion protocols (PII deleted 90 days post-journey unless refund or complaint is pending, then 12 months).

Assessments: Title: GDPR Compliance and Cross-Border Data Governance Assessment Description: Evaluation of data-protection risks and mitigation costs for passenger PII flows across multiple carriers, payment institutions and member-state regulators, and the potential for conflicting national data-protection rules to fragment the shared data layer. Details: A full through-ticketing transaction involves 5–8 data controllers (distributor, carriers, payment institution, clearing entity, national regulators for complaint handling). GDPR compliance costs estimated at €2–5 million upfront (DPIA, legal review, consent-management infrastructure) and €500,000–1 million annually for audits and breach response. Risk vectors: (1) a national DPA (e.g., Austria's, Bulgaria's) challenges cross-border data flow and imposes local-consent or data-residency requirements, forcing a redesign; (2) payment institutions refuse to sign on if data-governance is ambiguous, delaying settlement infrastructure; (3) accessibility data (mobility needs, assistance requests) is treated as special category under GDPR Article 9 and requires heightened consent, creating friction at booking time and reducing assisted-journey uptake. Mitigation: secure early EDPB and national DPA consensus (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) on common data-flow model and SCCs; implement privacy-by-design (data minimization, pseudonymization where feasible); establish a data-governance officer role within the programme and a quarterly data-protection audit; include GDPR compliance in the conformance checklist so carriers are tested on data-handling practices. Cost: €5–10 million over five years.

Question 7 - The programme involves multiple stakeholder groups (DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways, CER, national operators, distributors, BEUC, disability-rights bodies, national regulators). How are stakeholder interests balanced, especially when conflicts arise (e.g., incumbents resist non-discriminatory access, distributors demand preferential inventory access, smaller carriers lack resources for integration)? What is the mechanism for escalating and resolving stakeholder disputes before they paralyze programme delivery?

Assumptions: Assumption: Stakeholder engagement follows a tiered structure: (1) Working Groups (Month 0 = 2026-10-08 onward): technical and standards groups (OSDM, clearing, data-layer design) with carrier, distributor and standards-body participation; Governance and Stakeholder Group with all major actors; Consumer and Accessibility Group with BEUC and disability-rights representation; (2) Steering Committee (quarterly, Month 1 = 2026-11-08 onward): senior representatives from DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways, CER and 2–3 carrier representatives, distributors, regulators, addressing strategic conflicts and funding decisions; (3) Escalation Path: contested disputes are escalated from working groups to the Steering Committee (within 2 weeks), and if unresolved, to the arbitration panel for technical or to the Commission for institutional disputes. Conflict resolution relies on transparent interest articulation (each stakeholder states their requirements clearly), early negotiation (disputes are surfaced in Month 2–6 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-04-08, not left until Month 12+), and fallback to binding arbitration if voluntary consensus fails. Smaller carriers and distributors are given explicit voice (dedicated SME representative slots in working groups) and early funding certainty (co-funding commitments announced in Month 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) to reduce uncertainty and buy-in resistance.

Assessments: Title: Stakeholder Involvement and Conflict Resolution Assessment Description: Evaluation of how a multi-level stakeholder engagement structure prevents gridlock, ensures smaller players and consumers are heard, and resolves conflicts without paralyzing programme delivery. Details: Stakeholder involvement is the programme's highest-complexity axis: 25+ carriers, ~10 major distributors, 27 national regulators, multiple EU institutions, and advocacy groups all have competing interests. A tiered governance structure (working groups → steering committee → arbitration/Commission) allows most decisions to be made at the working-group level through technical consensus, escalating only contested issues. Working groups with carrier participation must include representation from: (1) large incumbents (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, Trenitalia, Renfe, ÖBB, NS, SJ, SNCB), (2) medium operators (3–4 elected from CER membership), and (3) smaller/regional operators (2–3 SME representatives rotated). Distributors (Trainline, Omio, smaller platforms) have dedicated working group seats and quarterly steering-committee briefings. BEUC and 2–3 disability-rights organizations attend consumer working group and quarterly steering reviews. National regulators are linked via the Standing Regulators Committee. Risks: (1) working groups can become talking shops if decisions are re-litigated at Steering Committee level (mitigation: Steering Committee has authority to close technical decisions after working-group consensus, with only major policy reversals escalated); (2) smaller carriers and distributors can feel unheard if sessions are dominated by incumbents (mitigation: 50% time ring-fenced for SME/distributor concerns, rotating facilitation); (3) consensus-seeking can delay decisions (mitigation: time-boxed working-group decisions with majority voting as fallback, not consensus-only). Estimated governance-overhead time: 15–20% of programme staff effort, or ~€5–10 million over five years.

Question 8 - The programme's operational systems include: OSDM-compatible real-time APIs for inventory, fares and disruption; a shared data layer accessible to distributors; accredited payment institutions for split-payment settlement; and integration with a clearing and settlement mechanism. What are the operational governance boundaries – who owns and operates these systems, who is responsible for SLA breaches (latency, uptime, data quality), and how are disputes between operators escalated? Should there be a single operator for each system, or competitive redundancy among providers?

Assumptions: Assumption: Operational systems are governed as follows: (1) OSDM API standards and conformance testing: owned by the programme via the EU Agency for Railways, with testing infrastructure procured from independent labs (European Network of Conformance Labs, MOD 0–3 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08); (2) Real-time data layer (inventory, fares, disruption): federated architecture with carriers holding authoritative data and national access points routing queries, or a central European cache (if architecture choice leans toward cache) operated by a procured neutral-operator entity under programme governance; (3) Payment institutions and settlement: competitive market of 2–3 accredited providers selected via public call (Month 2–8 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-06-08), each meeting common SLAs (settlement cycle, multi-currency support, error handling, dispute resolution); (4) Clearing mechanism: programme-owned reference implementation (rules and apportionment logic) operated by a dedicated entity (could be EU Agency for Railways, a private contractor, or a public-private partnership) under close programme oversight. Each system has defined SLAs (e.g., API latency <2 seconds p95, uptime 99.95%, settlement <48 hours) backed by financial penalties (e.g., 0.5–1% of quarterly fees withheld for breach). Disputes: carrier/distributor disputes with a payment institution go to the accredited provider's internal dispute resolution (first), then to the programme's Independent Dispute Panel if unresolved (48–72 hour resolution target).

Assessments: Title: Operational Systems Architecture and Ownership Assessment Description: Evaluation of how operational systems (APIs, data layer, payments, clearing) are owned, operated and governed to ensure reliability, accountability and rapid escalation without creating single points of failure or blocking incumbent lock-in. Details: Operational architecture is critical to programme success, as every through-ticket depends on these systems functioning reliably. Key design choices: (1) Federated vs. central data layer: Federated (carriers keep data, queries route through access points) is resilient but can be slow; Central cache (European availability cache fed by carriers) is fast but creates single-point-of-failure risk and concentration of commercially sensitive data. Pragmatic Foundation leans toward federated for launch (Month 18–30 = 2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08) with optional cache layer added later if performance demands. (2) Competitive vs. monopoly payment providers: Competitive (2–3 accredited providers, carriers choose) encourages innovation and avoids monopoly risk, but requires harmonized settlement rules across providers and complicates dispute resolution if provider A claims provider B caused a refund delay. Pragmatic Foundation requires competitive providers with common SLA framework and Programme-run dispute panel as tiebreaker. (3) Ownership: Systems are programme-owned (rules, standards, governance) but operationally contracted (testing labs, payment institutions, potentially data-layer operators). This separates policy control from operational delivery and allows competition while maintaining standards. Risks: (1) a payment provider withdraws mid-programme (e.g., due to low transaction volumes or compliance costs), forcing carrier migration to a successor, causing 2–4 week disruption; (2) API latency degrades during holiday peak periods due to traffic surge, causing search timeouts and distributor complaints; (3) data-layer inconsistency (carrier A updates inventory, but access point Y serves stale data to a distributor) causes overbooking and refund disputes. Mitigation: require redundancy (payment providers must have failover partners), load-test APIs quarterly starting Month 9 (2027-07-08), establish 24/7 ops centres for critical systems, and mandate incident communication protocols (carrier notified <15 minutes of issue, distributors and passengers <30 minutes). Cost for operations: €10–15 million over five years.

Distill Assumptions

  • €1.5 billion public budget is fixed over five years; carrier integration costs borne separately by private spend.
  • Binding standards required by Month 18 (2028-04-08); mandatory API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-08); full corridor through-ticketing by Month 60 (2031-10-08).
  • Regional shared booking hubs serve 12–18 smaller legacy-IT carriers unable to achieve native OSDM compliance by Month 30 (2029-04-08).
  • Lightweight arbitration panel (8–12 FTE) resolves technical disputes in 60 days; national regulators enforce outcomes.
  • Through-tickets priced as sum of segment fares; no regulated ceilings; modal shift estimated 5–20%, not guaranteed 25%+.
  • Passenger PII flows across 5–8 data controllers; GDPR compliance via Standard Contractual Clauses and Data Protection Impact Assessment.
  • Tiered stakeholder governance: working groups → steering committee → arbitration panel; conflicts escalated within 2 weeks.
  • Accredited payment institutions (2–3 providers) run settlement; carriers choose among common SLA-compliant options.
  • Federated real-time data layer with carriers holding authoritative inventory; access points route distributor queries.
  • Certification-based distributor access: tiered inventory access earned through conformance and consumer-protection testing.
  • Milestone-based carrier co-funding prioritizes smaller operators; 15–25% of carrier integration cost covered by public budget.
  • Critical path: regulation adoption → governance setup (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) → standards (Month 4–18 = 2027-02-08 to 2028-04-08) → carrier integration (Month 18–30 = 2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08).
  • 40% through-ticket target is cross-border rail volume share, distinct from modal-shift metric; easier to achieve.
  • Conformance testing and standards work funded from public budget; carrier-specific IT costs borne by private investment.
  • Governance delays >2 weeks trigger escalation; Month 18 (2028-04-08) and Month 30 (2029-04-08) milestones are legally binding per final Regulation.

Review Assumptions

Domain of the expert reviewer

Large-scale public infrastructure programme management and EU policy delivery. Expertise spans multi-stakeholder coordination, regulatory adoption risk, fixed-budget constraint management, cross-border institutional alignment, and technical delivery on binding political milestones. The review prioritizes the tension between infrastructure ambition (€1.5 billion over five years, 27 member states, 25+ carriers, three hard regulatory deadlines) and realistic delivery risk.

Domain-specific considerations

  • Regulatory adoption and legislative uncertainty: the programme's legal foundation (Commission proposed Regulation on Digital Booking) remains unadopted; delays beyond Month 9 (2027-07-08) compress the standards-setting window from 9 months to 3–4, directly threatening the Month 18 (2028-04-08) binding-standards milestone.
  • Fixed-budget constraint under escalating scope: €1.5 billion must cover standards, conformance, clearing, public distributor, capacity building and consumer rollout; carrier co-funding demand and unplanned costs (e.g., extended distributor operation, hub resilience upgrades) could consume 20–30% contingency by Month 24 (2028-10-08).
  • Legacy-IT heterogeneity and critical-path bottleneck: the slowest carrier's booking-system modernisation constrains regional hub performance and data-layer reliability; uneven readiness among smaller operators (especially in southeast Europe) creates two-tier compliance by Month 30 (2029-04-08).
  • Lightweight governance without enforcement power: the proposed arbitration panel avoids legal setup delays but lacks direct enforcement authority over incumbents; non-compliance by a major carrier (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF) could force renegotiation and delay gates without clear escalation path.
  • Modal-shift assumption mismatch: the headline '40% through-ticket share' is volume-based, not modal-shift; actual air-to-rail shift estimated 5–20%, not the implied 25%+ needed to justify infrastructure investment on competition-with-air grounds.

Issue 1 - Regulation Adoption Delay Threatens Critical-Path Milestones

The Commission's proposed Regulation on Digital Booking (May 2026) has not been adopted by Parliament and Council. Parliamentary amendments, member-state negotiations and legal review could extend adoption to Month 6–12 (2027-04-08 to 2027-10-08). If adoption slips beyond Month 9 (2027-07-08), the window for binding standards-setting (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 deadline) shrinks from 9 months to 3–4 months, eliminating margin for stakeholder consultation or dispute resolution. This is the single highest-impact upstream risk, as it compresses every downstream activity.

Recommendation: Establish direct liaison with TRAN and IMCO rapporteurs and key member-state transport ministers from Month 0 (2026-10-08) to track adoption progress weekly. Conduct parallel 'shadow standards' pre-work (Month 0–3 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08) on OSDM alignment, access-term sketches and settlement architecture under a 'without-prejudice' frame, so standards can be finalised within 2–3 weeks of regulation adoption. If adoption slips beyond Month 8 (2027-06-08), trigger contingency: contract an external standards-review consortium and accelerate carrier engagement workshops to Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08). Set a hard gate: if regulation is not adopted by Month 10 (2027-08-08), pause carrier onboarding commitments and conduct a revised critical-path review.

Sensitivity: Baseline: regulation adopted Month 6–7 (2027-04-08 to 2027-05-08), allowing 11–12 months for standards-setting. If adoption slips to Month 9 (2027-07-08), standards-setting window is compressed by 2–3 months, increasing quality risk and stakeholder consensus failure. If adoption slips to Month 12 (2027-10-08) or beyond, the Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline becomes unachievable, forcing either rushed standards (high non-compliance risk) or formal delay (triggering Commission intervention and carrier resistance). Estimated impact on project timeline: delay of Month 18–30 (2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08) milestones by 2–6 months, or risk of missed deadline with low-compliance implementation.

Issue 2 - €1.5 Billion Budget Fragility and Carrier Co-Funding Demand Mismatch

The €1.5 billion (user constraint) must cover 7 major programmes: standards (€200–300M), conformance testing (€100–150M), clearing/settlement (€100–200M), public reference distributor operations (€300–500M over 5 years), member-state capacity building (€100–150M), consumer rollout and apps (€150–200M), and carrier co-funding. Early baseline suggests €850–1,350M for core infrastructure, leaving only €150–650M for co-funding. However, 12–18 smaller carriers requiring co-funding to meet Month 30 (2029-04-08) via hubs or gateway integration could demand €150–300M (€5–15M per carrier for IT modernisation or hub fees). A 20–30% budget shortfall (€300–450M) is plausible by Month 24 (2028-10-08), forcing cuts to conformance testing (delaying certification), capacity building (weaker regulator enforcement), or distributor operations (shrinking public channel reach).

Recommendation: Commission a detailed activity-based cost model in Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) covering: (1) carrier co-funding need per carrier size and legacy-IT status (baseline estimate: €2–8M per SME, €10–15M per medium operator); (2) hub operating cost and capacity per regional hub (baseline: €5–8M per hub over 5 years); (3) public distributor annual operating cost (baseline: €60–100M/year for full retail channel, €20–30M/year for reference-implementation only). Establish quarterly budget-tracking dashboards (Month 3 = 2027-01-08 onward) with burn-rate forecasts and trigger points: if quarterly spend >115% of pro-rata budget, initiate cost-reduction review within 1 week. Define contingency tiers: (1) Tier 1 (10–15% overrun): defer consumer-app polish, reduce distributor marketing; (2) Tier 2 (15–25% overrun): reduce carrier co-funding rate from 20–25% to 10–15%, prioritise top 5 corridors only; (3) Tier 3 (>25% overrun): suspend new hub openings, scale back capacity building to priority member states. Secure commitment from DG MOVE to seek supplementary budget authority by Month 12 (2027-10-08) if Tier 2 triggers.

Sensitivity: Baseline budget burn: €250–300M/year over 5 years. If carrier co-funding demand exceeds €300M (plausible if hub fees are underestimated or more operators qualify), shortfall is €300–450M by Month 36 (2029-10-08). Impact on ROI and timeline: conformance-testing cuts delay 40% of carrier certifications by 4–8 weeks per carrier, extending Month 30 (2029-04-08) readiness gate by 8–16 weeks for slower operators. Public distributor reductions (e.g., scaling from €80M/year to €50M/year) reduce market-presence investment, lowering through-ticket volumes by estimated 5–10 percentage points. Currency volatility (DKK, SEK, CHF, PLN against EUR) could consume €10–20M annually if not hedged, further reducing effective spending power by 2–3%.

Issue 3 - Lightweight Arbitration Panel Lacks Enforcement Authority Over Incumbents; Governance Deadlock Risk

The Pragmatic Foundation proposes a small arbitration panel (8–12 FTE) with time-boxed (60-day) binding authority over technical disputes, avoiding the 12–18 month legal setup of a dedicated joint undertaking. However, the panel has no direct enforcement power: if Deutsche Bahn or SNCF contests a ruling on inventory-parity thresholds or refund-timing rules, the panel's only escalation is to the Commission, which takes 2–4 months to respond. Meanwhile, the carrier can continue non-compliant practices, and other incumbents follow, fracturing the coalition. Without explicit written delegation from the Council (not yet secured), the panel's authority is questioned, and member-state regulators may not enforce consistently. A major dispute (e.g., SNCF refuses to meet the 2-second API-latency SLA) unresolved by Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08) cascades to standards finalisation disputes and delays the entire Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline.

Recommendation: Secure explicit written delegation of binding technical-decision authority from both the Commission and Council in Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08), specifying: (1) scope (technical standards, conformance rules, settlement message formats), (2) authority limits (not commercial terms like pricing), (3) time limits (60-day decision cycle, 14-day compliance deadline, escalation path to Commission if carrier does not comply), (4) standing (panel rulings are binding on all participants unless formally overturned by Commission within 30 days). Draft a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) among DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways and the panel, with staffing and budget locked in Month 1–2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08). Require all participating carriers to sign a binding Commitment Letter (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08) accepting arbitration and penalties for non-compliance (0.5–1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue held in escrow). Establish a Standing Regulators Committee (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) with power to enforce panel rulings consistently; escalate any member state's non-enforcement to the Commission within 2 weeks. If a major carrier signals non-compliance in Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08), invoke immediate co-funding hold and regulatory escalation.

Sensitivity: Baseline scenario: panel has clear delegation, carriers sign MOU, disputes resolved within 60 days, no major non-compliance. If delegation is delayed to Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08), panel credibility is questioned early, and carriers negotiate weaker access terms. Estimated impact: Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards missed or delivered without incumbents' buy-in, increasing non-compliance risk. If a major incumbent (40–50% of cross-border traffic) contests a panel ruling and escalation to Commission takes 8–12 weeks instead of the assumed 4 weeks, the month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate is at risk (estimated 2–4 month slip). If enforcement is not consistent across all member states (e.g., Austria enforces a ruling but Germany does not), the through-ticket system is perceived as two-tier, reducing distributor investment and passenger trust.

Issue 4 - Modal-Shift Target Mismatch: 40% Through-Ticket Share Does Not Guarantee Air-to-Rail Competition Gain

The programme's headline targets are: '40% of cross-border journeys sold as through-tickets' and 'modal shift from short-haul air.' These are conflated in political messaging but operationally distinct. The 40% is achievable through volume (capturing passengers already choosing rail), but modal shift requires through-fares to be competitive or more convenient than flights. Modelling of priority corridors (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon) suggests through-fares will be €70–90, competing with airline fares of €50–80 on price-competitive days but losing to budget airlines at €30–50. Without regulated fare ceilings (rejected in Pragmatic Foundation to avoid antitrust risk), modal shift is estimated at 5–20%, not the implied 25%+. The programme can hit 40% through-ticket volume by capturing convenience-premium passengers and capturing share from multi-operator rail bookings, but the environmental and capacity-benefit case (implicit in the infrastructure investment) relies on modal shift that may not materialise.

Recommendation: Decouple the two targets operationally in Month 1–2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08): define '40% through-ticket share of cross-border rail journeys sold' (volume metric, achievable via sum-of-segment pricing and convenience) separately from 'modal shift: reduce short-haul air trips by 15–25% on priority corridors' (mode-choice metric, dependent on price and fuel prices). Conduct a detailed competitive pricing analysis in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) for each priority corridor, modelling through-fare competitiveness against airlines under scenarios of fuel-price change (±30%), aviation-tax policy (current vs. proposed CO2-tax levels), and airline capacity (current vs. 20% capacity increase). Use scenarios to set realistic modal-shift targets: if fuel prices rise 30% (baseline: €60/barrel), modal shift to 15–20% is plausible; if fuel is flat, expect 5–10%. Communicate this clearly to stakeholders by Month 6 (2027-04-08). Reserve €10–20M from the programme budget for targeted air-route competition campaigns (e.g., on Paris–Brussels, Amsterdam–Köln) where air is strongest; position as 'train travel convenience' rather than price-focused. If actual modal shift by Month 48 (2030-10-08) is <10%, trigger a mid-course review: consider revenue-recovery mechanisms (e.g., reduction-card pooling) or price-support measures (subsidised through-fares on pilot routes) to meet the implicit environmental target.

Sensitivity: Baseline modelling: through-fare €70–90 vs. airline €50–80, resulting in 5–15% modal shift (conservative). If fuel prices rise to €100/barrel by Month 36 (2029-10-08), airlines raise fares to €70–100, and modal shift rises to 15–25% (aligned with target). If fuel prices fall to €40/barrel, airline fares drop to €35–50, and modal shift remains 2–5%, missing the environmental goal. Estimated ROI impact: if modal shift is 5% instead of 20%, the infrastructure investment per diverted passenger rises 4-fold, reducing cost-benefit ratio and inviting criticism. Through-ticket volume of 40% is still achievable and valuable (capturing rail-to-rail switching), but the mode-shift case—implicit in the €1.5B public investment—may not hold unless fuel prices or aviation taxes rise unexpectedly.

Issue 5 - GDPR and Cross-Border Data-Governance Uncertainty; Risk of Regulatory Intervention Halting Core Systems

Passenger PII (name, contact, payment, accessibility needs) flows across 5–8 entities: distributors, carriers, payment institutions, clearing mechanism, and national regulators for dispute handling. Each is a data controller or joint controller under GDPR Article 26. Data Protection Authorities in some member states (Austria, Poland, Bulgaria) have expressed preferences for data residency (citizen PII not to leave EU data centres) and have scrutinised cross-border data flows in other EU programmes. A DPIA (Data Protection Impact Assessment) has not yet been commissioned, and no consensus exists on data-flow minimisation or consent regimes. If a national DPA challenges the data-sharing architecture and issues a directive to restrict cross-border flows (e.g., requiring explicit opt-in consent for each journey), the clearing mechanism and distributor APIs could be held up 6–12 months for redesign. Accessibility data (mobility needs, assistance requests) is classified as special category under GDPR Article 9, requiring heightened consent and potentially creating friction at booking time.

Recommendation: Commission a comprehensive DPIA and cross-border data-governance consultation in Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08), engaging the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) and national authorities (Austria, Poland, Bulgaria, France, Germany). Define minimum-necessary PII per transaction in Month 1 (2026-11-08): baseline (name, contact, booking reference, seat/assistance notes); extended (payment details to accredited payment institutions only, carrier PII for refund/disruption communication only). Seek early consensus on Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) for cross-border carrier-to-carrier and carrier-to-clearing transfers by Month 4 (2027-02-08). Separate accessibility data governance: treat accessibility attributes (mobility, assistance needs) as special category requiring explicit consent, but allow consent at booking time (passive opt-in for future assistance offers, explicit opt-out for data retention >90 days). Draft data-governance rules as part of the binding standards document (Month 18 = 2028-04-08), so DPAs review them alongside legal framework, not separately post-facto. Allocate €2–3M from the public budget for privacy infrastructure (consent management, data-minimisation tools, breach-response protocols). Include GDPR compliance and data-handling practices in the conformance checklist starting Month 18 (2028-04-08).

Sensitivity: Baseline scenario: EDPB provides early consensus, SCCs are pre-agreed, and GDPR compliance is absorbed into the standards-development process with no additional delays. If a member state (e.g., Poland) issues a unilateral data-residency requirement in Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08), data-layer architecture must be redesigned to keep citizen data in local data centres, requiring 3–6 month engineering rework and potentially fragmenting the shared layer (EU-wide availability cache becomes multi-regional). If a DPA investigation into alleged non-compliance is opened in Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08), it can delay standards approval and carrier certification until cleared, adding 6–12 months to the critical path. Estimated impact: if data governance is not resolved by Month 6 (2027-04-08), payment-institution accreditation is held up, and Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate is at risk by 2–4 months.

Issue 6 - Smaller-Carrier Adoption Cliff and Regional-Hub Dependency: Month 30 (2029-04-08) Readiness Uneven

The Pragmatic Foundation proposes regional shared booking hubs for 12–18 smaller legacy-IT carriers that cannot achieve native OSDM compliance by Month 30 (2029-04-08). However, hub implementation depends on: (1) hub operators being procured and operational by Month 9 (2027-07-08), (2) legacy-system mapping being accurate (avoiding oversold seats, missed restrictions), (3) smaller carriers having internal resources to integrate with hubs (many lack dedicated IT staff). If hub procurement slips to Month 12 (2027-10-08) or later, integration timelines compress to 6–9 months for 12–18 carriers, creating congestion in testing and deployment. If hub mapping errors are detected only during live operation (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), recovery takes 4–8 weeks per carrier, and some operators slip past the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate. Result: a two-tier network in which through-tickets are reliable on major corridors (90%+ carrier readiness) but fragile on smaller routes (60–70% readiness), undermining passenger confidence and creating liability disputes over who is responsible for booking failures.

Recommendation: Accelerate hub-operator procurement to Month 1–3 (2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08), and secure legal commitments (Statements of Work) with hub operators by Month 4 (2027-02-08), specifying: (1) operational start date (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), (2) SLAs (99.9% uptime, <2-second latency, <2-hour incident recovery), (3) capacity (minimum 10,000 bookings/day per operator without degradation), (4) redundancy (dual data centres, failover protocols). Define hub-eligible carriers early (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) using clear criteria: annual cross-border revenue <€50M, booking-system age >10 years, or IT staff <10 FTE. Conduct joint technical workshops (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) pairing hub operators and eligible carriers to identify integration blockers (network latency, API compatibility, data format mismatch) early. Allocate €5–10M for hub resilience and capacity upgrades (Month 6–18 = 2027-04-08 to 2028-04-08). Establish a Smaller-Carriers Support Team (3–5 FTE regional coordinators) based in hub regions (Budapest, Warsaw, Sofia, Bucharest) providing on-site mentoring and troubleshooting during integration (Month 6–30 = 2027-04-08 to 2029-04-08). Schedule mandatory pilot tests (Month 15–18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08) of each hub's integration with 2–3 eligible carriers before the conformance-testing phase. If a hub is not ready by Month 9 (2027-07-08), escalate to the Steering Committee and consider alternative integration paths (gateway use, bilateral pairings with larger operators) for affected carriers.

Sensitivity: Baseline: hub operators procured by Month 3 (2027-01-08), integration begins Month 6, 85–90% of smaller carriers ready by Month 30 (2029-04-08). If hub procurement slips to Month 6 (2027-04-08), integration window is reduced to 9 months for 12–18 carriers, and readiness at Month 30 (2029-04-08) drops to 70–80% (20–30% slip past deadline). If hub mapping errors cause 2–5% booking-failure rate post-launch (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), recovery takes 4–8 weeks per carrier and adds 8–16 week delay for affected corridors. Estimated impact: each month of hub-procurement delay reduces smaller-carrier readiness by 3–5 percentage points; if <75% of smaller carriers are ready by Month 30 (2029-04-08), the TEN-T extension beyond priority corridors slips by 6–12 months (to Month 36–42 = 2029-10-08 to 2030-04-08).

Issue 7 - Accredited Payment-Institution Accreditation Timeline Risk; Settlement Mechanism Delayed

The Pragmatic Foundation proposes competitive accredited payment institutions (2–3 providers) running split-payment and refund orchestration, avoiding the licensing and setup delays of a central clearing entity. However, accreditation is a phased process: (1) market sounding (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08), (2) criteria definition (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08), (3) application call (Month 2–6 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-04-08), (4) decision (Month 8 = 2027-06-08). If only 1–2 providers apply (plausible if transaction volumes are low or compliance costs are high), there is little competitive choice. If a provider withdraws or fails after accreditation (e.g., due to low volumes, operational incident, or acquisition), switching to a replacement during Month 18–30 (2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08) creates 2–4 week disruption and requires carrier re-integration. Additionally, settlement transaction fees (estimated 0.5–2% per transaction, or €80–120M over five years) consume 5–8% of the fixed €1.5B budget, forcing cuts elsewhere.

Recommendation: Launch market sounding in Month 0–1 (2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) with published accreditation criteria specifying: multi-currency support (EUR, DKK, SEK, CHF, PLN, CZK, HUF, BGN, RON), settlement cycle (<48 hours), refund processing (<10 days), error handling (dispute resolution <5 days), SLAs (99.95% uptime), and financial stability (must be licensed payment institution under PSD2). Issue the call for applications by Month 2 (2026-12-08) with a target decision by Month 8 (2027-06-08). Require at least 2 accredited providers to be operational by Month 12 (2027-10-08), with contractual provisions for redundancy: if one provider fails, carriers automatically failover to a backup, with the programme funding the transition cost (up to €1M per incident). Negotiate transaction-fee caps during accreditation (target: 0.3–0.5% per transaction, not >0.7%). Establish a fee-subsidy model: programme covers 50–70% of payment-institution fees in Years 1–2 (Month 0–24 = 2026-10-08 to 2028-10-08), with carriers and distributors bearing the remainder, conditional on through-ticket volumes reaching 15% by Month 24 (2028-10-08). Reserve €1–2M for contingency provider-switching costs. If fewer than 2 qualified providers apply by Month 6 (2027-04-08), escalate to DG MOVE and consider fallback options: temporary settlement via existing carrier-to-carrier bilateral arrangements (slower, but known), or emergency procurement of a custom settlement service.

Sensitivity: Baseline: 2–3 providers accredited, fees capped at 0.5% of transaction value, settlement operational by Month 12 (2027-10-08). If only 1 provider qualifies, the programme has no backup if that provider fails or withdraws; estimated switching cost €5–10M if replacement is needed in Month 18–30 (2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08). If accreditation takes until Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08) instead of Month 8 (2027-06-08), settlement infrastructure deployment is compressed from 12 months to 6–9 months, reducing testing and integration quality. If transaction fees average 1.0% (not the 0.5% target), the five-year cost is €160–240M, consuming 10–16% of the public budget and forcing cuts to conformance testing or distributor operations (estimated 10–20% reduction in testing capacity or distributor market reach).

Issue 8 - Unresolved Definition of 'Through-Ticket' and '40% Target': Measurement Baseline Delay Threatens Mid-Course Correction

The programme targets '40% of cross-border journeys sold as through-tickets' by Month 60 (2031-10-08), but no consensus definition of 'through-ticket' exists. Is it: (1) a single booking reference and payment? (2) guaranteed continuity-of-journey rights? (3) sale through a distributor platform (vs. direct operator sale)? Carriers and distributors propose different definitions to optimise their interests. Additionally, baseline data on current cross-border rail sales, complaint volumes and modal split do not exist in consolidated form; carriers report proprietary metrics, distributors guard booking data, aviation data come from EUROSTAT (1-month lag). If the baseline is not established until Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08), mid-course correction insights are delayed until Year 2 (Month 12–18 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08), and stakeholder disputes over whether targets are being met undermine programme credibility. An estimated 15–25% undercount of true through-ticket share is plausible if carriers refuse to report volumes or if definitions vary by country.

Recommendation: Define 'through-ticket' operationally in Month 1–2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08) with stakeholder consensus: 'single booking reference, single point of payment, continuity-of-journey protection (rerouting/refund if connection missed), sold through any distributor or operator platform.' Publish this definition in the binding standards document (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) so it is legally anchored. Commission a baseline survey in Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) asking carriers, distributors and airports for current cross-border sales volumes, complaint-handling metrics and modal-split estimates, with strict confidentiality protections (aggregated reporting, no carrier-level disclosure). Mandate that all participating carriers and accredited distributors report through-ticket volumes monthly starting Month 18 (2028-04-08), with data aggregated and published quarterly with a 1-month lag (to protect commercial sensitivity). Hire an independent evaluation firm in Month 3 (2027-01-08) to build a counterfactual model comparing through-ticket adoption on priority corridors to control routes outside the rollout, separating programme effects from fuel prices and aviation-capacity changes. Establish a Measurement Steering Group (quarterly, Month 3 = 2027-01-08 onward) to oversee baseline validation, definition refinement and quarterly progress dashboards. Reserve €5–10M of the public budget for measurement and evaluation.

Sensitivity: Baseline scenario: 'through-ticket' defined by Month 2 (2026-12-08), baseline established by Month 9 (2027-07-08), monthly reporting begins Month 18 (2028-04-08). If definition is delayed to Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08), stakeholder disputes consume resources and push baseline survey to Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), delaying insights to Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08). If carriers refuse to report volumes (claiming commercial sensitivity), the programme relies on distributor data only, undercounting true market share by 15–25% and making it impossible to verify whether 40% target is being met. Estimated impact: if mid-course correction is delayed 6 months due to measurement uncertainty, and the target is actually 30% (not 40%), the programme does not detect this until Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), leaving only 6–12 months to adjust strategy (add co-funding, accelerate distributor campaigns, introduce fare-support measures) before it is too late to course-correct.

Issue 9 - Distributor Incentive and Involvement Uncertainty: Trainline and Omio Buy-In Not Secured

The programme's success depends on distributors (Trainline, Omio, commercial platforms) actively promoting and selling through-tickets. However, their involvement is assumed but not contractually secured. If distributor margins are compressed by low through-fares or high processing fees, their incentive to invest in integration and marketing diminishes. Trainline and Omio may also resist integration timelines if their own IT backlogs are heavy, or demand preferential inventory access (which regulators view as discriminatory). If either major distributor signals non-compliance (e.g., 'full API integration will not be ready until Month 24–27 = 2028-10-08 to 2029-01-08 instead of Month 18 = 2028-04-08') in Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08), other distributors may follow, and the programme is forced to expand the public reference distributor to fill the gap, consuming extra budget and crowding out commercial platforms.

Recommendation: Establish formal Distributor Advisory Working Groups in Month 1 (2026-11-08) with Trainline, Omio, smaller platforms and commercial aggregators. Conduct detailed margin and IT-capacity analysis in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) to understand their integration costs, margin requirements and timeline constraints. Offer early API access (Month 9–12 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08) and data-access priority to platforms that commit to full integration and promotion by Month 18 (2028-04-08). Agree on margin-support measures in Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08): co-marketing funds (€5–10M over 24 months), performance bonuses for through-ticket volumes, and transaction-fee waivers (programme covers payment-institution fees for first 12–18 months). Establish a Distributor Commitment Letter (Month 3–4 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08) specifying integration timeline, promotion commitment and penalties for non-compliance (e.g., loss of early API access, withholding of co-marketing funds). Reserve time-slots in the conformance-testing schedule for distributors' internal systems (Month 12–18 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08), with free technical support to accelerate integration. Monitor distributor progress quarterly (Month 3 = 2027-01-08 onward) and escalate any major slippage to the Steering Committee within 2 weeks.

Sensitivity: Baseline: Trainline and Omio commit to integration by Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08), both platforms live by Month 18 (2028-04-08). If distributor commitment is delayed to Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), and either Trainline or Omio signals non-compliance, the programme must increase public-distributor operations by 20–30%, adding €60–90M to operating costs and consuming 4–6% of the public budget. If through-ticket volumes on distributor platforms are <50% of the total (due to poor integration or insufficient promotion), the 40% target becomes achievable only through the public channel and operator direct sales, which are less scalable and create sustainability risk (public distributor must operate for 5+ years, not 3 as planned).

Issue 10 - Member-State Regulator Capacity Gaps and Enforcement Inconsistency; Cross-Border Dispute Resolution Unproven

National regulators across 27 member states vary widely in resources, enforcement powers and interpretation of passenger rights. Some (France, Germany, Netherlands, Austria) have strong rail regulators; others (especially in southeast Europe and smaller member states) have limited staff and expertise. If enforcement of non-discrimination duties and passenger-rights claims is inconsistent across borders, the through-ticket system is perceived as unreliable and passengers lose confidence. Additionally, cross-border disputes (e.g., a distributor complains that a carrier in another member state is denying API access) have no clear resolution path under the Pragmatic Foundation; escalation to the EU Agency for Railways is slow (4–8 weeks), and national regulators may not recognise arbitration panel rulings without explicit legal backing.

Recommendation: Establish a Member-State Regulator Capacity Building Programme in Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08), funded with €10–15M over five years. Conduct a capacity audit (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08) identifying regulator gaps (staff, budget, IT systems, enforcement experience). Fund twinning partnerships (Month 3–6 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-04-08) pairing stronger and weaker regulators, with shared training (access-enforcement, data-quality auditing, complaint handling), common inspection checklists and experience exchange. Establish a Standing Regulators Committee (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) meeting monthly, chaired by the EU Agency for Railways, to harmonise enforcement procedures and resolve cross-border disputes. Define a lead-authority rule for cross-border cases (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08): if a distributor complains that a carrier in Austria is denying API access, the Austrian regulator takes the lead, with support from the EU Agency for Railways and other affected-member-state regulators. Agree that lead-authority decisions are recognised across all member states (no re-litigation). Include enforcement capacity and cross-border-dispute procedures in the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08). Schedule regulator capacity reviews quarterly (starting Month 6 = 2027-04-08) to assess progress and identify ongoing gaps; if a regulator is not meeting standards (e.g., >60-day case resolution time), escalate to the Commission for targeted support or enforcement authority adjustment.

Sensitivity: Baseline: regulators are trained by Month 12 (2027-10-08), enforcement procedures harmonised by Month 18 (2028-04-08), cross-border disputes resolved within 30 days. If regulator capacity building is delayed to Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) or underfunded, enforcement remains patchy; disputes in weak-capacity member states (Poland, Bulgaria, Romania) take 60–120 days to resolve (vs. 30-day target), delaying carrier compliance and distributor onboarding. If one regulator refuses to recognise arbitration panel rulings (e.g., asserting national sovereignty), the cross-border dispute-resolution system breaks down, and carriers in that member state can maintain discriminatory practices without consequence. Estimated impact: 10–20% of disputes unresolved within SLA, driving distributor complaints and reputation damage; smaller carriers in weak-capacity regions slip past Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate, fragmenting the network.

Issue 11 - Passenger-Rights Backstop Funding and Liability Exposure Under-Estimated; Refund Disputes Could Consume Contingency

The programme promises continuity-of-journey rights: if a passenger misses a connection on a multi-carrier through-ticket, they are rerouted or refunded. However, the cost of rerouting (care, alternative transport, hotel) and the liability for false promises (e.g., a distributor sells a risky itinerary with tight connections, and the connection fails) are not fully budgeted. The Pragmatic Foundation proposes that distributors bear first-line liability and recover costs from carriers via the clearing mechanism, but if disputes are frequent (e.g., 10–15% of through-tickets result in claims), refund processing becomes a bottleneck, and the programme's credibility is undermined. Additionally, if accessibility assistance is promised but not delivered (e.g., a station lifts are out of order on boarding day), the programme faces both liability and reputational damage.

Recommendation: Establish a Passenger-Rights Backstop and Liability Framework in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08), specifying: (1) who is the single point of contact for rerouting/refunds (distributor or first carrier), (2) required response time (rerouting decision <4 hours, refund <10 days), (3) financial responsibility (distributor advances cost, then recovers from responsible carrier via clearing), (4) pooled guarantee mechanism (if a carrier is insolvent, a pooled fund covers passenger refunds). Conduct an actuarial study (Month 3–6 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-04-08) estimating refund volumes and costs: baseline assumption is 3–5% of through-tickets result in claims (conservative estimate based on existing multi-carrier journeys); average claim cost is €50–200 (rerouting, care, refund). This suggests €10–40M in refund costs over five years, or €2–8M annually. Reserve €5–10M in contingency for higher-than-expected refund volumes. Establish a Dispute Resolution Panel (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) with rotating carrier and distributor representatives, empowered to rule on contested claims within 5 days. Pilot the refund process on one corridor (e.g., Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam) in Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08) to test procedures and refine timelines. Include refund-processing metrics (claim response time, resolution time, dispute rate) in the quarterly measurement dashboard starting Month 18 (2028-04-08). If actual claim rates exceed 8% by Month 24 (2028-10-08), or average resolution time >15 days, escalate to Steering Committee and consider capacity-building for dispute handlers or procedural simplification.

Sensitivity: Baseline: 3–5% claim rate, €50–150 average cost, €5–15M total five-year cost. If claim rate is 8–10% (e.g., due to tight connections or aggressive through-fare marketing), five-year costs rise to €20–40M, consuming 1–3% of the public budget and crowding out other spending (e.g., capacity building). If average claim resolution time is 20–30 days (not the 10-day target), passengers complain and distributor confidence erodes, reducing through-ticket sales by 5–10 percentage points. If a major carrier (accounting for 30–40% of through-tickets) contests a high volume of claims (e.g., 15–20% vs. expected 3–5%), the clearing entity is forced to arbitrate hundreds of monthly disputes, creating a processing backlog and refund delays. Estimated impact: uncontrolled refund exposure could consume 5–8% of the public budget and delay through-ticket expansion; poor claim resolution damages programme credibility and lowers adoption by 10–20%.

Issue 12 - Technology Infrastructure Scalability and Performance Risk: API Latency and Data-Layer Reliability Under Peak Load

The shared real-time data layer and OSDM APIs must handle peak-hour search traffic estimated at 100–500 requests per second per corridor during holiday periods. Legacy carriers' infrastructure is not designed for this scale; a carrier with 20-year-old booking systems may struggle to support >10 req/s without degradation. If API latency exceeds 5 seconds during peak hours (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), searches timeout, distributors report poor user experience and pull back investment. A hub or cache serving a corridor fails and takes 12–48 hours to recover, stranding all through-ticket bookings on that route and generating cascading refund obligations. Data-quality issues (stale inventory, 20–30 minutes old) cause 5–10% of bookings to fail at confirmation, creating disputes and refund costs.

Recommendation: Conduct carrier infrastructure assessment in Month 3–4 (2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08) to identify systems that cannot meet the required API performance SLAs (latency <2 seconds p95, throughput ≥500 req/s, uptime 99.95%). For carriers that fail, co-fund infrastructure upgrades (€500K–2M per carrier) in Month 6–18 (2027-04-08 to 2028-04-08). Procure a European-wide API hosting and caching infrastructure in Month 2–6 (2026-12-08 to 2027-04-08) with guaranteed SLAs, redundancy across ≥3 data centres per region (EU-West, EU-Central, EU-East), and automatic failover (target <30 seconds). Establish 24/7 API operations centre in Month 6 (2027-04-08) with escalation to carriers within 15 minutes of any incident. Define data-quality SLAs: inventory freshness <5 minutes, disruption-event latency <2 minutes. Conduct monthly load testing and quarterly chaos-engineering exercises (starting Month 9 = 2027-07-08) to identify weak points before they affect production. Budget €10–15M for infrastructure procuracy, operations and testing over five years. If a carrier cannot meet performance SLAs by Month 24 (2028-10-08), delay its integration to Month 30 (2029-04-08) and route its traffic through a hub or federated access point (accepting slightly higher latency).

Sensitivity: Baseline: API infrastructure procured by Month 6 (2027-04-08), load testing validates performance by Month 12 (2027-10-08), production launch Month 18 (2028-04-08) with target <2-second latency. If infrastructure procurement slips to Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08), production deployment is delayed from Month 18 (2028-04-08) to Month 21–24 (2028-07-08 to 2028-10-08), compressing the Month 30 (2029-04-08) integration window for slower carriers. If 20% of carriers' back-ends require co-funded upgrades and the budget is insufficient (e.g., only 10 carriers can be funded due to cost limits), the slower carriers slip past the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate, reducing through-ticket coverage from 90% to 70–75% of cross-border traffic. If API latency is 3–5 seconds instead of 2 seconds (due to network constraints or hub congestion), distributor-side search timeouts increase from <1% to 5–10%, reducing user satisfaction and lowering through-ticket volumes by 10–20%.

Issue 13 - Accessibility Integration Complexity and Assistance-Delivery Risk; Exclusion of Vulnerable Populations

The programme commits to accessibility for persons with reduced mobility, including booking-system requests for assistance, cross-border assistance coordination, and real-time accessibility data on stations and rolling stock. However, accessibility is often under-resourced: carriers' existing assistance infrastructure varies widely (good in western Europe, limited in southeast Europe). If the programme launches with incomplete accessibility data or slow assistance-confirmation windows (e.g., 48 hours instead of 24 hours), persons with reduced mobility face barriers that non-disabled passengers do not, creating exclusion and inviting complaints from BEUC and national disability-rights organizations. Cross-border assistance handovers are particularly risky: if a passenger's confirmed assistance (e.g., platform lift) is not available on boarding day due to equipment failure, the passenger is stranded and the programme is liable.

Recommendation: Establish an Accessibility Working Group in Month 0 (2026-10-08) with BEUC, national disability-rights organizations, carriers and accessibility experts. Define accessibility requirements in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08): booking-interface accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA standard), assistance-request/confirmation timelines (<24 hours for confirmation, <48 hours for rerouting), station and vehicle accessibility data (lift, accessible toilet, accessible seating availability, staff assistance capability). Include accessibility as a binding non-negotiable requirement in the standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08), not optional. Fund a €10–15M Accessibility Infrastructure Programme (Month 6–24 = 2027-04-08 to 2028-10-08) supporting carriers' deployment of assistance-request systems and accessibility-data APIs. Pilot accessibility features on one corridor (e.g., Wien–München) in Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08) with real passengers and feedback from disability-rights organizations. Establish accessibility-specific SLAs: assistance-confirmation rate >90%, assistance-delivery rate >95%, assistance-related complaint rate <2%. Include accessibility metrics in the quarterly measurement dashboard. If a carrier cannot meet accessibility SLAs by Month 24 (2028-10-08), conditional funding is withheld until compliance is demonstrated.

Sensitivity: Baseline: accessibility requirements defined by Month 4 (2027-02-08), pilot corridor operational by Month 18, 90 (2028-04-08, 2034-04-08)%+ of carriers meet accessibility SLAs by Month 30 (2029-04-08). If accessibility requirements are delayed to Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) or weakened (e.g., assistance confirmation window extended to 48 hours), uptake among persons with reduced mobility lags other passenger groups by 15–25 percentage points. If cross-border assistance handovers fail at a rate >5% (e.g., a passenger arrives at a connecting station and assistance is not available), incidents escalate to disability-rights organizations and media, damaging the programme's reputation. Estimated impact: if accessibility is poorly integrated, the programme excludes 5–10% of potential passengers (persons with mobility limitations) and invites regulatory intervention by national disability-rights authorities.

Issue 14 - Incumbent Carrier Non-Compliance Risk: Month 18 (2028-04-08) Standards Deadline Under Threat if Major Carriers Demand Exemptions or Extensions

The programme's credibility depends on binding standards and mandatory API exposure deadlines (Month 18 = 2028-04-08, Month 30 = 2029-04-08). However, large incumbents (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, Trenitalia, ÖBB, Renfe) have significant political leverage: if one signals non-compliance or demands extensions, others follow, and the Commission is forced to negotiate weaker terms or grant exemptions. Political pressure from member states (especially Germany and France) could soften enforcement. If SNCF announces in Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08) that API integration will not be ready until Month 36 (2029-10-08) due to legacy system incompatibility, the entire timeline becomes discretionary, and carriers see no consequences for slippage.

Recommendation: Establish formal carrier engagement and negotiation stream in Month 1 (2026-11-08) with quarterly roundtables between DG MOVE, CER and the 8 largest carriers (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, Trenitalia, Renfe, ÖBB, NS, SJ, SNCB). Use these forums to: (1) understand IT cost-sharing opportunities (e.g., hub use for phased integration, gateway sharing for legacy systems), (2) air concerns early before they harden into political positions, (3) offer co-funding and timeline flexibility (e.g., carrier A gets extra 6 months if it demonstrates genuine technical blocker, but loses co-funding premium). Build political cover by securing visible member-state support (Belgium, Netherlands, Austria, Spain) early and regularly reporting programme progress to European Parliament's TRAN committee. Establish a 'Major Carrier Commitment Protocol' (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08) requiring all carriers >€100M annual cross-border revenue to sign a binding letter specifying compliance timeline, API readiness date (no later than Month 30 = 2029-04-08), and acceptance of arbitration outcomes. If a major carrier signals non-compliance in Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08), escalate immediately to Commission with evidence (missed milestones, insufficient investment) and invoke contingency: hold co-funding, public channel bypasses (public distributor offers competing service), or regulatory escalation (Commission mandates compliance and threatens fines). Communicate non-compliance risk to stakeholders transparently so distributor and passenger expectations are managed.

Sensitivity: Baseline: major carriers commit to Month 30 (2029-04-08) compliance in Month 1–3 (2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08), no major signalling of non-compliance by Month 18 (2028-04-08). If SNCF or Deutsche Bahn signals non-compliance in Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08), and Commission negotiates an extension (e.g., to Month 36 = 2029-10-08), other carriers follow, and the mandatory deadline becomes advisory, reducing compliance rate from 90%+ to 70–80%. If political pressure forces the Commission to grant exemptions (e.g., SNCF exempt from API mandate on domestic routes), the through-ticket system is fragmented and unreliable, and the 40% target becomes unachievable. Estimated impact: if non-compliance by 1–2 major carriers is not addressed firmly, the entire Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate is undermined, and the programme's credibility is damaged for years.

Issue 15 - Consumer-Facing Rollout Delay: App Launch and Support Capacity Underfunded

The programme's consumer-side rollout includes a multilingual booking app, customer support in 24+ languages, and complaint handling across member-state jurisdictions. Launching a consumer product at EU scale within Months 15–27 (2028-01-08 to 2029-01-08) is ambitious: design iteration, user testing, platform scaling and localization typically take 12–18 months for a new product. If the app is released 3–6 months late (Month 21–24 = 2028-07-08 to 2028-10-08 instead of Month 15 = 2028-01-08), momentum from early corridor launches is lost. If the app is poorly designed, slow or untrustworthy (e.g., confusing refund flow, missing accessibility features), user ratings are low (3.5/5 stars), and distributor confidence is shaken. Support capacity is often under-estimated: if support queue times exceed 2 hours and a backlog of 1,000+ unresolved complaints accumulates within 3 months of launch, reputational damage is significant.

Recommendation: Establish a dedicated Consumer Product Team in Month 1 (2026-11-08) with 20–30 FTE (product managers, engineers, UX designers, localization specialists, support staff). Conduct user research and personas in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08), then wireframe and prototype in Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08). Build a minimum viable product (MVP) for pilot testing on one corridor by Month 9 (2027-07-08). Iterate based on user feedback during Month 10–12 (2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08), then begin full-scale localization and platform scaling in Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08). Target public app launch by Month 15 (2028-01-08) with phased rollout (four priority corridors first, then TEN-T). Budget €20–30M for app development, infrastructure and support over Months 15–27 (2028-01-08 to 2029-01-08). Establish a support team with sub-1-hour response-time target for critical issues, tiered escalation (level-1 FAQs, level-2 human support, level-3 dispute resolution). Conduct app-store and third-party reviews throughout the pilot and post-launch periods (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 onward) to catch usability issues early. If user satisfaction is <4.0/5 stars at Month 18 (2028-04-08), pause rollout and conduct a 4–6 week redesign cycle before resuming.

Sensitivity: Baseline: app launched Month 15, 1 (2028-01-08, 2026-11-08)-hour support response time, user satisfaction >4.2/5 stars. If app launch slips to Month 18–21 (2028-04-08 to 2028-07-08), early-corridor momentum is lost and through-ticket volumes drop by 10–15 percentage points (passengers use manual, multi-step booking instead). If user satisfaction is <4.0/5 stars and is publicised (app-store reviews, media coverage), distributor confidence is shaken and commercial platforms reduce co-marketing investment by 20–30%. If support queue times exceed 4 hours and complaints backlog reaches 2,000+ by Month 21 (2028-07-08), resolving the backlog takes 4–8 weeks and generates negative media coverage. Estimated impact: consumer-product delays or poor quality reduce through-ticket volumes by 10–20 percentage points and require budget surge for reputation repair (€5–10M in crisis messaging and support surge).

Issue 16 - Unclear Private-Sector Financial Commitment: Carrier IT Investment Estimates (€500M–€2B) Not Binding; Funding Gaps Possible

The programme assumes that carrier IT integration costs (€500M–€2B private spend, estimated separately from the €1.5B public budget) are borne entirely by carriers. However, no binding commitments exist: carriers can delay or under-invest if they perceive weak enforcement of the mandatory API deadline or if co-funding is insufficient to offset their costs. Smaller carriers, especially in southeast Europe and with weak financial positions, may claim they cannot afford integration and lobby for further public funding or exemptions. If actual private spend is 30–50% lower than estimated (e.g., €350M–€1B instead of €500M–€2B), integration is incomplete by Month 30 (2029-04-08), and through-ticket coverage is fragmented.
