Recommendation: Commission a detailed activity-based cost analysis in Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) estimating carrier IT integration costs by carrier size, legacy-system age and roadmap (native build vs. hub use). Present findings to CER and major carriers in Month 3 (2027-01-08) and seek binding commitments (Signed Letters of Intent) specifying: (1) estimated integration cost per carrier, (2) expected timeline (Month 18–30 = 2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08 for major carriers, Month 30–36 = 2029-04-08 to 2029-10-08 for smaller operators), (3) technology choices (native API vs. hub vs. gateway). Use these commitments to benchmark actual private spend against forecast; if carriers are under-investing (actual spend <70% of commitment), escalate to CER and DG MOVE and trigger enforcement levers (mandatory audits, co-funding holds). Establish a quarterly Carrier Investment Tracking Dashboard (starting Month 6 = 2027-04-08) reporting estimated cumulative private spend vs. forecast, flagging any carrier that is 20%+ behind schedule. If total private spend by Month 24 (2028-10-08) is <60% of the annual forecast, revise the Month 30 (2029-04-08) readiness assumptions and consider extending the mandate or increasing public co-funding. Reserve €50–100M of programme budget as 'contingency co-funding' for carriers that would otherwise miss Month 30 (2029-04-08) but can demonstrate genuine technical blocker and willingness to accelerate if funded.

Sensitivity: Baseline: carriers commit to €100–200M annual IT spend, totalling €500M–€1B+ over five years. If carriers invest only 60–70% of their commitments (e.g., €50–120M annually due to budget constraints or competing priorities), cumulative private spend is €250M–€600M, a 30–50% shortfall. This creates a funding gap: if carriers are under-investing and public co-funding is insufficient to compensate, 15–25% of carriers slip past the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate, fragmenting the network. Estimated impact: fragmented network reduces through-ticket volumes by 10–20 percentage points and extends the full-network timeline (Month 60 = 2031-10-08) to Month 66–72 (2032-04-08 to 2032-10-08), delaying environmental and capacity benefits.

Issue 17 - Data Quality and Inventory Accuracy Risk: Legacy-System Mapping Errors Cause Booking Failures and Liability Disputes

Regional hubs translate legacy carrier inventory and business rules into the OSDM standard, but mapping errors (e.g., double-counting of restricted seats, misalignment of fare conditions, incorrect availability windows) break through-tickets and trigger liability disputes. If 2–5% of bookings fail at final confirmation due to hub mapping errors (e.g., seat shows available in search but unavailable at confirmation), passengers experience frustration, refund disputes accumulate, and distributors lose confidence. Hub operators lack incentive to invest in accuracy if volumes are low or if liability is unclear. By Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), if hub mapping errors are discovered in live operation, recovery takes 4–8 weeks per carrier and requires expensive rework.

Recommendation: Define comprehensive hub API specifications and test harnesses in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) in collaboration with legacy operators and hub operators. Conduct external validation (Month 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) using an independent test lab, comparing hub output against real inventory samples from each carrier across 30–50 test journeys per carrier. Require dual-run (hub and native) for 2–4 weeks per carrier (Month 15–18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08) before traffic is cut over, detecting mapping errors in pre-production. Establish a hub incident-response team with on-call escalation to the carrier's inventory team, targeting <2-hour resolution for critical failures. Require hub operators to carry errors-and-omissions liability insurance covering overstated availability and inventory errors, with a minimum policy limit of €2–5M per hub. Include hub data-quality metrics (booking-failure rate, oversell rate, mapping-accuracy rate) in the conformance checklist and monthly measurement dashboard starting Month 18 (2028-04-08). If a hub's booking-failure rate exceeds 2% for >1 week, suspend new carrier onboarding to that hub until the issue is resolved.

Sensitivity: Baseline: hub mapping is validated externally by Month 6 (2027-04-08), dual-run catches errors by Month 18 (2028-04-08), booking-failure rate is <0.5%. If external validation is delayed to Month 8–9 (2027-06-08 to 2027-07-08), errors are not caught until live operation (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), adding 4–8 week recovery per carrier and delaying smaller-carrier readiness by 4–12 weeks. If booking-failure rate is 2–5% instead of <0.5%, refund volume increases by 3–10M passengers per year, consuming €150–500M in unplanned refunds and liability reserves (estimated 10–30% contingency consumption). If hub mapping errors are not resolved by Month 30 (2029-04-08), smaller carriers' through-ticket reliability is questionable, and distributors scale back integration and marketing, reducing through-ticket volumes by 10–20 percentage points.

Issue 18 - Incomplete Stakeholder Buy-In: Smaller Carriers, Member-State Regulators and Community Opposition Risk

The programme requires buy-in from 27 member-state regulators, 25+ carriers of varying sizes, disability-rights organizations, and community stakeholders. Smaller carriers and weaker regulators may feel marginalised if programme decisions are made without sufficient consultation or if co-funding is limited. Regional opposition (e.g., transport unions fearing job losses in ticketing services) can create political friction. If 1–2 key member states withdraw support or key stakeholder groups publicly oppose the programme by Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08), political momentum erodes and parliamentary or Commission support softens.

Recommendation: Establish a robust stakeholder-engagement framework in Month 0–1 (2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) with: (1) monthly all-hands forum (Month 1 = 2026-11-08 onward) including all major carriers, smaller-operator representatives (CER), all national regulators, BEUC, disability-rights organizations and transport unions; (2) dedicated SME (small/medium carrier) working group with rotating leadership, meeting bi-weekly (Month 1 = 2026-11-08 onward) to ensure smaller operators' concerns are heard; (3) Community Liaison Officer (1 FTE) managing communication with transport unions and regional stakeholders, conducting quarterly regional workshops in each priority-corridor area (Month 3 = 2027-01-08 onward). Publish a comprehensive stakeholder communication strategy (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) clarifying: (1) timeline and milestones, (2) funding allocation and co-funding eligibility, (3) costs and benefits per stakeholder group, (4) escalation path for grievances. Conduct a mid-programme stakeholder satisfaction survey (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) to gauge engagement and identify emerging concerns; if satisfaction is <70% among any stakeholder group, trigger a 4-week focused outreach campaign. If a member state or major stakeholder publicly opposes the programme by Month 12 (2027-10-08), escalate immediately to DG MOVE and Commission for political engagement and remedial action.

Sensitivity: Baseline: stakeholder satisfaction >80%, no major public opposition by Month 18 (2028-04-08). If satisfaction drops to 60–70% and opposition emerges (e.g., transport unions file formal complaint to the Commission), political pressure could force weaker standards or longer timelines (estimated 2–6 month delay in decision-making). If 2+ member states withdraw support, the programme loses regulatory leverage and enforcement credibility, reducing carrier compliance by 20–30 percentage points and extending timelines by 6–12 months.

Issue 19 - Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) Sustainability and Continuity: Programme Ends at Month 60 (2031-10-08), But Operations Continue; Funding Cliff Risk

The programme's public coordination is budgeted through Month 60 (2031-10-08), but the through-ticketing system's operational dependencies (data layer, clearing mechanism, public reference distributor, regulator capacity) do not end. If the programme dissolves at Month 60 (2031-10-08) and does not transition to sustainable operational funding models (e.g., the data layer is privatised, the public distributor is handed to a commercial operator, or regulator funding is devolved to member states), operational continuity is at risk. Member states may be unwilling or unable to fund regulator capacity building beyond the programme period; payment institutions may exit if transaction volumes are insufficient for profitability; the public distributor may be unable to operate commercially and may be forced to close, reducing passenger choice.

Recommendation: Establish a Sustainability Working Group in Month 30 (2029-04-08) to design transition models for each programme component: (1) Data-layer operations: identify a permanent operational host (e.g., EU Agency for Railways or a multi-carrier consortium) and transition governance and financing by Month 48 (2030-10-08); (2) Clearing mechanism: shift to operational cost recovery (transaction fees cover ops costs) or permanent public funding commitment from the Commission; (3) Public reference distributor: define a post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) operating model (shutdown, hand-off to commercial operator, or downsizing to niche service); (4) Regulator capacity: secure member-state commitment to maintain funding (e.g., via national budgets or EU multi-annual framework). Secure written commitment from the Commission, Council and member states by Month 48 (2030-10-08) confirming post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding and operational arrangements. If member states do not commit to regulator funding, trigger contingency: consolidate regulator roles at EU Agency for Railways level and shift costs to carrier license-fee revenue. If the public distributor is not handed off to a commercial operator by Month 60 (2031-10-08), conduct an orderly shutdown (3–6 month wind-down, passenger notification, endpoint services). Plan for a formal handover and sustainability review (Month 54–60 = 2031-04-08 to 2031-10-08) to ensure continuity and avoid sudden service disruptions.

Sensitivity: Baseline: transition plans are agreed by Month 48 (2030-10-08), permanent funding is secured by Month 54 (2031-04-08), operations continue seamlessly post-Month 60 (2031-10-08). If transition planning is delayed to Month 48+ or funding commitments are not secured, operational continuity is at risk. If member states do not commit to regulator funding, regulator capacity and enforcement decay post-Month 60 (2031-10-08), and non-discrimination compliance weakens. If the public distributor is not handed off or shut down cleanly, it continues operating unsustainably (burning public money) or operates under commercial contracts that are not cost-effective. Estimated impact: failure to plan sustainability could result in programme collapse at Month 60 (2031-10-08), undermining all prior investment and leaving through-ticket infrastructure orphaned and operationally fragile.

Issue 20 - Regulatory and Legal Alignment Risk: Final Regulation Text Divergence From Assumed Framework; Standards Rework Required

The programme's design is based on the Commission's proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services (May 2026), which is not yet adopted. Parliamentary amendments and member-state negotiations could significantly alter the final text, especially on: (1) scope (which corridors and carriers are in-scope), (2) access-term definitions (what 'non-discriminatory' means), (3) liability allocation (who bears costs for failed connections), (4) passenger-rights integration with existing rail-rights rules. If final text diverges materially, standards and operational rules developed before adoption may require significant rework (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), delaying implementation and frustrating stakeholders.

Recommendation: Establish a Legislative Tracking and Alignment Team in Month 0 (2026-10-08) that monitors Parliament and Council negotiations monthly and identifies divergences from the Commission's proposed text. Conduct a quarterly alignment review (Month 3 = 2027-01-08 onwards) comparing assumed framework vs. emerging final text; if material divergences are detected, escalate to DG MOVE and Programme Governance for decision on whether to adjust programme assumptions or advocate for Commission negotiating position. Maintain a flexibility buffer in standards-development methodology: defer detailed specification of contested areas (e.g., access-term pricing, liability allocation) until Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08), giving Parliament and Council time to finalise legal text. If final Regulation text is materially different from assumptions, activate contingency: reserve 2–4 week 'rapid standards adjustment' period post-adoption (by Month 9–12 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08) to rework standards as needed, rather than attempting to finalise standards before adoption is complete.

Sensitivity: Baseline: final Regulation is adopted Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) with minor deviations from the Commission proposal. If Parliament or Council makes substantial amendments (e.g., narrowing scope to only 4 corridors instead of TEN-T, or weakening non-discrimination requirements), standards-setting must be reworked, adding 4–8 weeks delay to Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline. If final text diverges on liability allocation (e.g., making distributors liable rather than carriers), operational rules and payment-clearing logic must be re-engineered, adding 6–12 week delay. Estimated impact: material divergence discovered in Month 10–12 (2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08) forces a 4–8 week standards rework and risks missing the Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline or delivering standards that carriers and distributors reject as infeasible.

Issue 21 - International Coordination Beyond EU: Switzerland, Norway, UK Post-Brexit; Corridor Extension Complexity

The four priority corridors (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon, Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin) involve non-EU actors: Switzerland (SBB), possibly Norway (NSB if Scandinavia corridors are extended), and the UK (post-Brexit, not EU). The Wien–München–Zürich corridor explicitly involves Switzerland; if SBB is not willing or able to integrate (due to regulatory differences, data-protection rules, or IT constraints), the corridor is incomplete and through-tickets cannot bridge to/from Switzerland. UK coordination post-Brexit is also unclear; if short-haul air reduction targets include UK routes (e.g., London-Paris-Brussels), UK carriers and regulators must be engaged but are not EU actors and may not accept EU standards.

Recommendation: Establish a Non-EU Stakeholder Engagement Stream in Month 1 (2026-11-08) covering: (1) Switzerland: secure an early Letter of Interest from SBB and the Swiss Federal Transport Office (OFT) confirming intention to participate in Wien–München–Zürich corridor and adopt OSDM standards by Month 30 (2029-04-08). (2) Norway: if Scandinavia corridors are prioritised, engage NSB and Norwegian regulator. (3) UK: clarify whether UK routes are in-scope for through-ticketing; if yes, establish a bilateral coordination mechanism with UK Department for Transport and UK carriers, separate from the EU programme but aligned on standards. Define bilateral agreements (Memoranda of Understanding) with each non-EU jurisdiction by Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08), specifying data-flow rules, liability allocation and dispute resolution. If Switzerland or other non-EU actor declines to participate, adjust corridor definition (e.g., Wien–München corridor stops at the Swiss border, and travellers to Switzerland must make separate bookings); communicate this clearly to stakeholders and adjust the 40% through-ticket target if corridor scope is reduced.

Sensitivity: Baseline: Switzerland participates in Wien–München–Zürich corridor by Month 30 (2029-04-08), data-protection and regulatory alignment is resolved by Month 12 (2027-10-08), no material delays. If Switzerland delays commitment to Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08), and SBB signals IT integration challenges, the corridor's completion is delayed to Month 36–42 (2029-10-08 to 2030-04-08). If UK post-Brexit coordination is unclear and UK carriers are not integrated, any London-Paris or London-Brussels through-ticketing is not possible, reducing the programme's EU-UK mobility benefit. Estimated impact: if Switzerland or UK are out of scope or delayed, through-ticket volumes on affected corridors drop by 10–30 percentage points, and the 40% target becomes harder to achieve (requiring compensatory growth on all-EU corridors).

Issue 22 - Climate and Energy Uncertainty: Fuel-Price Volatility and Aviation-Tax Policy Changes Affect Mode-Shift Viability

The modal-shift target (air-to-rail transition) assumes energy and taxation conditions remain stable over the five-year programme horizon. However, crude oil prices are volatile (current: ~$70–100/barrel; historical range: $30–150+), and aviation taxation is evolving (EU Commission proposed CO2-tax on aviation; several member states advocating for kerosene-tax harmonisation). If fuel prices drop 30–40% by Month 36 (2029-10-08), airline fares fall, and the through-fare (€70–90) is no longer competitive, modal shift plateaus at 2–5% instead of 10–20%. Conversely, if fuel prices spike to €150+/barrel or aviation taxes are introduced, airline fares rise sharply, and modal shift could exceed 25%. The programme's infrastructure case is sensitive to these external factors, yet they are largely outside the programme's control.

Recommendation: Conduct scenario planning in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) modelling through-ticket competitiveness under fuel-price ranges (€40–150/barrel) and aviation-tax scenarios (current policy, proposed CO2-tax, full kerosene harmonisation). Use scenarios to define 'target ranges' for modal shift (e.g., 'if fuel price is <€60, modal shift target is 5–10%; if fuel is €80–100, target is 10–20%; if fuel is >€120, target is 15–30%'). Establish quarterly fuel-price and aviation-tax monitoring (starting Month 6 = 2027-04-08) and update modal-shift forecasts in the measurement dashboard. If energy prices or aviation policy shift materially (e.g., fuel drops >30% or aviation tax is repealed), trigger a mid-course programme review (Month 24–30 = 2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08) to reassess the mode-shift case and adjust targets and budgets if needed. Hedge against mode-shift miss by emphasising 'cross-border rail journey convenience' messaging and building through-ticket uptake on routes where rail already has competitive advantage (not just modal-shift routes).

Sensitivity: Baseline: fuel price €70–100/barrel, no aviation tax until Month 36+, modal shift forecast 10–20%. If fuel drops to €40–50/barrel by Month 30 (2029-04-08), airline fares fall 20–30%, and modal shift drops to 2–5%, missing the 10–20% target by 50–75%. This would signal that the infrastructure investment's environmental case is weaker than assumed. If fuel spikes to €120+/barrel or aviation tax is introduced by Month 24 (2028-10-08), modal shift could exceed 20–25%, exceeding the target and validating the infrastructure case. Estimated impact: fuel-price volatility creates 15–25 percentage-point variance in modal-shift outcomes, and the programme's environmental and infrastructure case is correspondingly exposed to energy-market dynamics outside its control.

Issue 23 - Legal Liability and Insurance Coverage Gap: Through-Ticket Accidents, Incidents and Cascading Failures Not Fully Insured

The programme introduces new liability vectors: if a through-ticket passenger is injured in a missed-connection incident (e.g., rushing between platforms, missing assistance), or if a system failure (API outage, hub failure) strands thousands of passengers, who bears liability? Insurance coverage for the clearing mechanism, hub operators, and payment institutions is assumed but not yet secured. If a major incident occurs (e.g., an API outage during a holiday period leaves 50,000+ passengers unable to access their bookings), liability exposure could be €10–50M, and if insurance is insufficient, the programme or carriers must absorb the loss.

Recommendation: Commission a comprehensive liability and insurance audit in Month 1–3 (2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) identifying: (1) who is liable for which failures (distributor, carrier, payment institution, hub operator, programme entity), (2) insurance policies and coverage limits for each, (3) gaps (under-insurance, exclusions). Establish a Liability Framework document (Month 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) specifying liability allocation: carrier is liable for its operational failures (missed connections, accessibility delivery); distributor is liable for booking errors and false promises; payment institution is liable for settlement failures; hub operator is liable for mapping errors and service outages; programme carries residual liability for systemic failures (API infrastructure, data-layer integrity). Require all operational entities (hub operators, payment institutions, public distributor) to carry comprehensive liability insurance (errors & omissions, cyber, business interruption) with minimum limits of €2–10M depending on entity risk. Include liability requirements in conformance checklist and quarterly compliance reviews. Establish a Risk Pool or Contingency Fund (€5–10M reserve) for incidents exceeding individual-entity insurance limits, managed by the programme and funded from remaining budget contingency. If a major incident occurs and estimated liability exceeds insurance, activate the Risk Pool and conduct a root-cause analysis to prevent recurrence.

Sensitivity: Baseline: all entities carry adequate insurance (limits: €2–10M per entity), Risk Pool of €5–10M is funded, no incidents exceeding total coverage. If an entity is under-insured (e.g., hub operator has only €500K coverage), and an incident occurs causing €5M loss, the shortfall (€4.5M) falls to the programme or other carriers. If a cascading failure (e.g., API outage + hub failure + payment-settlement delay) causes losses exceeding €20M, insurance may not cover the full amount, and recovery takes legal action (6–12 months). Estimated impact: under-insurance or uncovered incidents could consume 1–5% of the remaining programme budget and generate litigation (12–24 month resolution), creating opportunity costs and reputational damage.

Issue 24 - Talent and Staffing Continuity Risk: Tight Labour Market for Specialists; Key-Person Dependency

The programme requires specialised expertise: OSDM standards engineers, rail-operations specialists, payment-system architects, regulator-capacity trainers, and EU institutional expertise. The tight labour market for such skills means hiring and retaining key staff is difficult and expensive. If the programme's Project Management Office or critical working groups lose key staff (e.g., standards lead, governance officer), continuity is disrupted. Distributed governance across Brussels, Vienna, Cologne and other hubs requires significant travel, which increases burnout and turnover risk. If staff turnover exceeds 20% annually (plausible for EU programme roles), knowledge loss and decision lag accumulate.

Recommendation: Establish a Talent Acquisition and Retention Strategy in Month 0–1 (2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08), covering: (1) competitive salary and benefits packages to attract specialised talent, (2) flexible working arrangements (hybrid, reduced travel), (3) professional development and skill-building (training budgets, conference attendance), (4) leadership continuity (succession planning for key roles). Staff the core Programme Management Office (PMO) by Month 2 (2026-12-08) with 10–15 FTE core team (programme director, technical leads, governance officer, communication lead), with recruitment locked in to reduce later hiring risk. Establish a 'knowledge transfer' protocol requiring key staff to document decision rationales, maintain shared wikis and provide 2–4 week handover to successors if they leave. Offer 10–15% salary premium and flexible working arrangements to key specialists (standards lead, API architect, regulator trainer) to reduce turnover. Establish a 'trusted advisors' network of external experts and consultants (2–3 on retainer) to backfill key roles if staff turnover occurs. If a key staff member leaves, activate contingency: accelerate backfill hiring and engage advisors to maintain continuity for 4–8 weeks until replacement is productive.

Sensitivity: Baseline: core PMO is fully staffed by Month 3 (2027-01-08), staff turnover is <10% annually, key roles have identified backups. If staffing is delayed to Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08), governance and decision-making lag, and early working groups lack leadership (adding 2–4 week delays per group). If turnover is 15–20% annually, institutional knowledge is lost, decisions are re-litigated, and efficiency drops 15–25% (estimated impact: 3–6 month cumulative delay by Month 30 = 2029-04-08). If a key role (e.g., standards lead) turns over without backfill, standards finalisation is delayed 4–8 weeks (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 deadline at risk).

Issue 25 - Post-Programme Evaluation and Learning: No Pre-Planned Evaluation Framework; Counterfactual Attribution Difficult

The programme is novel at EU scale (integrated through-ticketing across 27 member states, 25+ carriers, multiple modes). A rigorous evaluation will inform future EU transport infrastructure investment. However, the programme's assumptions do not include a pre-planned evaluation framework, baseline data are incomplete, and counterfactual attribution (separating programme effects from fuel prices, aviation policy, and other confounders) requires sophisticated methodology. If evaluation is not embedded from the start, by Month 60 (2031-10-08), it is difficult to credibly claim that mode-shift targets were met or to quantify return on investment. This undermines the programme's political case and weakens support for scaling to other corridors or for future similar initiatives.

Recommendation: Establish an Evaluation Framework and Commission an Independent Evaluator in Month 2–3 (2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08). Define evaluation scope: (1) process evaluation (governance, decision-making speed, stakeholder satisfaction), (2) output evaluation (standards adoption, carrier compliance, API/data-layer performance), (3) outcome evaluation (through-ticket volumes, modal shift, passenger satisfaction, distributor complaints), (4) impact evaluation (modal shift attribution, environmental impact, economic benefits). Conduct baseline survey in Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) to establish starting conditions (cross-border sales volumes, modal split, complaint rates). Build a counterfactual model using comparison routes (non-rollout corridors) to separate programme effects from external factors (fuel prices, aviation taxes, capacity changes). Establish quarterly data-collection protocols and annual evaluation reports (starting Month 12 = 2027-10-08) to track progress and inform mid-course corrections. Budget €5–10M for comprehensive evaluation over five years. Use evaluation findings to adjust strategy, communicate progress to stakeholders and build the case for scaling beyond Month 60 (2031-10-08).

Sensitivity: Baseline: evaluation framework is established by Month 3 (2027-01-08), baseline data collected by Month 6 (2027-04-08), quarterly tracking begins Month 12 (2027-10-08). If evaluation setup is delayed to Month 6–12 (2027-04-08 to 2027-10-08), baseline data quality is compromised and early programme tracking is weak. If counterfactual methodology is not robust (e.g., comparison routes are not comparable, or fuel prices vary too much), attribution of modal shift to the programme is questionable, and claims about environmental benefits are contested. Estimated impact: weak evaluation undermines the political case for the programme and makes it difficult to justify follow-on EU investment in similar initiatives; scrapping or scaling-back the programme at Month 48–60 (2030-10-08 to 2031-10-08) would represent a loss of momentum and credibility.

Review conclusion

This €1.5 billion, five-year EU through-ticketing programme faces three critical, interconnected risks that threaten its core milestones (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 standards, Month 30 = 2029-04-08 API mandate, Month 60 = 2031-10-08 full deployment). First, regulatory adoption delay (Commission proposal unadopted as of Month 0 = 2026-10-08) could compress the standards-setting window from 9 months to 3–4 months, eliminating margin for consensus. Second, the lightweight arbitration-panel governance model lacks binding enforcement authority over major incumbents; if Deutsche Bahn or SNCF resist compliance, escalation to the Commission is slow and discretionary. Third, the €1.5 billion budget is fragile: carrier co-funding demand (€150–300M for 12–18 smaller operators), hub operations (€5–8M per hub), and unplanned costs (extended public distributor operation, data-layer resilience, refund exposure) could trigger 20–30% shortfalls by Month 24 (2028-10-08), forcing cuts to conformance testing or capacity building that slow smaller-carrier adoption. Secondary risks include unclear modal-shift viability (through-fares may not compete with flights without regulated ceilings), GDPR data-governance challenges (if a national DPA restricts cross-border flows), and uneven technology infrastructure (legacy-system heterogeneity constrains data-layer performance). The Pragmatic Foundation scenario mitigates these by deferring price regulation (avoiding antitrust risk and incumbents' resistance), using competitive accredited payment institutions (avoiding central-clearing legal delays), enabling regional hubs (reducing private IT burden on smaller carriers), and establishing a time-boxed arbitration panel (avoiding new-entity setup costs). However, these mitigations are only effective if: (1) regulation is adopted by Month 9 (2027-07-08) at latest; (2) the arbitration panel receives explicit written Council delegation by Month 2 (2026-12-08); (3) budget contingency (10–15%) is protected through Month 24 (2028-10-08); (4) governance authority is not contested by member states; and (5) major carriers sign binding Commitment Letters accepting the Month 30 (2029-04-08) deadline. If any of these conditions fails—especially regulation adoption or governance authority—the entire timeline compresses, and the 40% through-ticket target and the Month 60 (2031-10-08) milestone become unachievable without mission creep or political override. Recommendation: prioritise regulation adoption tracking and political buy-in from month 0 (2026-10-08); secure written Council delegation to the arbitration panel by Month 2 (2026-12-08); establish quarterly budget-burn dashboards and mid-course review gates at Month 12 (2027-10-08) and Month 24 (2028-10-08); and negotiate binding carrier commitment letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08), with explicit penalties for non-compliance. The programme is ambitious and complex, but realistic delivery is feasible under the Pragmatic Foundation scenario if governance clarity, regulatory certainty and budget discipline are established immediately.

Governance Audit

Audit - Corruption Risks

  • Preferential API access granted to favored distributors in exchange for kickbacks or side agreements, violating non-discrimination duties and certification schemes.
  • Hub operators steering smaller carriers toward unnecessary or overpriced services, or manipulating mapping logic to inflate usage fees and transaction volumes.
  • Carrier executives accepting co-funding grants in exchange for inflating invoices or falsely certifying API compliance, diverting public money to private benefit.
  • Payment-institution staff delaying or misdirecting settlement funds to affiliated entities, exploiting the multi-carrier clearing mechanism for personal gain.
  • Regulators accepting informal favors (travel, consulting contracts for family members) from major carriers in exchange for lax enforcement of access-term compliance.
  • Programme staff or arbitration-panel members leveraging insider knowledge of technical decisions to advise carriers or distributors on how to circumvent or game the standards.

Audit - Misallocation Risks

  • Co-funding grants to carriers are inflated or allocated to carriers not meeting the eligibility criteria (revenue > EUR 50M or IT staff > 10 FTE), leaving truly disadvantaged carriers unfunded.
  • Hub operational budgets (EUR 44M allocated) are misused for non-core activities (marketing, staff perks) instead of integration support and resilience, causing hubs to fail and requiring emergency replacement spending.
  • Conformance-testing budget (EUR 280M standards + testing) is front-loaded to early carriers, exhausting resources before smaller or slower operators can be tested, delaying their Month 30 (2029-04-08) readiness.
  • Programme staff travel and overhead consume 20–30% of PMO and governance costs without proportional output; inefficient meeting structure and decision-making delay standards work by 2–4 months.
  • Public reference distributor budget (EUR 215M over 5 years, ~EUR 43M/year) is used to launch a full retail service with margins and marketing spend that crowds out commercial distributors, rather than being limited to reference implementation and pilot accessibility services.
  • Payment-institution accreditation budget and fee-subsidy reserves (EUR 15M in fee subsidy + EUR 5–10M provider-switch contingency) are consumed by single-provider dominance or early provider failure, leaving no resources for genuine competition or failover.

Audit - Procedures

  • Quarterly co-funding recipient audits (starting Month 6 = 2027-04-08): verify that grant recipients meet eligibility criteria, that invoice amounts are reasonable and supported by documentation, and that promised integration milestones (API exposure, data-quality SLAs) are achieved; withhold next disbursement if audit raises red flags.
  • Monthly hub operational reviews (starting Month 9 = 2027-07-08): inspect hub operator's incident logs, uptime records, booking-failure rates and mapping-accuracy samples; if booking-failure rate exceeds 2% for >1 week, freeze new carrier onboarding and conduct root-cause audit.
  • Conformance-testing capacity and throughput audits (quarterly, Month 12 onward = 2027-10-08 onward): track test-lab utilization, queue times for carriers awaiting slots, and distribution of testing resources across carrier size cohorts; if small carriers face >8-week delays while majors are tested within 2 weeks, reallocate lab capacity.
  • Payment-institution performance and fee audits (monthly, Month 12 onward = 2027-10-08 onward): verify settlement cycle compliance (<48 hours), refund-processing SLA (decision <10 days), transaction-fee caps (target 0.3–0.5%, max 0.7%), and absence of preferential treatment of affiliated or large-carrier accounts.
  • Carrier co-funding claim audits (quarterly, Month 6 onward = 2027-04-08 onward): sample 5–10% of invoices, interview carrier IT teams about milestone progress, verify that private spend (assumed EUR 0.5–2.0 billion) is actually occurring and is not being substituted by public funding, and reconcile carrier-reported spending against commitments made in Month 3 (2027-01-08) Commitment Letters.
  • Post-implementation external compliance audit (Month 42–48 = 2030-04-08 to 2030-10-08): hire independent auditor to verify that all major systems (data layer, clearing, hubs, public distributor, regulator capacity) are operating within SLAs, that access terms are enforced consistently across member states, and that no unbudgeted liabilities have accumulated; use findings to validate Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability model.

Audit - Transparency Measures

  • Monthly public dashboard (published on DG MOVE website, starting Month 6 = 2027-04-08) showing: cumulative spend by budget line item vs. plan, carrier compliance status (on-time or delayed) for each corridor, hub operational metrics (uptime %, booking-failure rate), and provisional through-ticket volumes and complaints metrics; dashboard updated within 2 weeks of quarter-end to provide real-time visibility.
  • Quarterly Steering Committee meeting minutes published (within 2 weeks of meeting) including: decisions made, dissenting views from any stakeholder, technical disputes that went to arbitration, and budget or schedule changes; confidential commercial data (individual carrier cost, specific carrier IT architecture) redacted; all meetings held in Brussels with open audio/video feed option for observers (non-decision makers).
  • Arbitration panel rulings and reasoning documents published (within 5 working days of decision, Month 1 onward = 2026-11-08 onward) showing the technical question, competing positions, evidence considered, and the panel's rationale; dissenting opinions from panel members recorded and published alongside the majority ruling.
  • Carrier and distributor certification and access-term audit results published quarterly (aggregate form, Month 18 onward = 2028-04-08 onward): percentage of carriers and distributors meeting OSDM conformance, number and outcome of non-discrimination complaints filed and resolved, average API latency and uptime per corridor, and any enforcement actions or penalties imposed.
  • Public reference distributor operational transparency report (quarterly, Month 15 onward = 2028-01-08 onward): through-ticket volumes, revenue, operating cost, accessibility-assisted bookings, complaint types and resolution times, and financial sustainability outlook; identify any subsidy draw above budget or structural deficits requiring mid-course intervention.
  • Annual programme evaluation and progress report (first report Month 12 = 2027-10-08, then annually) published by an independent evaluator, comparing baseline (Month 9 = 2027-07-08) to latest outcomes on the three headline targets (40% through-ticket share, complaints halved, modal shift in planning range 5–15%), and disclosing methodology, any data gaps or attribution uncertainty, and recommendations for course corrections.

Internal Governance Bodies

1. Programme Steering Committee

Rationale for Inclusion: This €1.5 billion, five-year, multi-stakeholder EU programme requires strategic oversight across 27 member states, 25+ carriers, and multiple regulatory domains (rail, payment, competition, GDPR). The Steering Committee provides high-level direction on standards priorities, corridor sequencing, funding allocation disputes, and milestone enforcement. It is the ultimate decision-making body for choices that cannot be resolved at operational level and ensures political and institutional alignment with DG MOVE and the Commission.

Responsibilities:

  • Approve binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) and API mandate enforcement thresholds (Month 30 = 2029-04-08)
  • Allocate and approve deviations from the EUR 1,500 million budget and trigger contingency tiers
  • Resolve escalated technical disputes and policy conflicts between carriers, distributors, regulators and member states
  • Approve corridor sequencing gates and readiness thresholds (proposed: 90% of traffic bookable end-to-end)
  • Monitor milestone adherence and make formal decisions on timeline adjustments or deferrals
  • Oversee through-ticket target progress and authorize mid-course strategic pivots

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Draft and sign a Memorandum of Understanding defining Steering Committee authority, decision rules and escalation triggers (Month 1 = 2026-11-08)
  • Elect a steering committee chair and establish a quarterly meeting schedule (Month 1 = 2026-11-08)
  • Define binding decision thresholds (e.g., budget deviations >EUR 50M require SC approval; technical rulings >60 days trigger escalation)
  • Establish a formal conflict-resolution process for Steering Committee disputes (majority vote with tie-breaker role specified)
  • Secure written Council/Commission delegation of final authority over binding standards and milestone enforcement (Month 2 = 2026-12-08)

Membership:

  • DG MOVE representative (chair or co-chair)
  • EU Agency for Railways representative (technical lead)
  • Programme director (operations lead)
  • Three to four major-carrier representatives (rotating annually; e.g., Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, Trenitalia, ÖBB)
  • One SME/smaller-carrier representative (elected by CER members)
  • One distributor representative (Trainline, Omio, or public reference distributor; rotating)
  • One national regulator representative (elected by Standing Regulators Committee)
  • One BEUC or disability-rights representative

Decision Rights: Binding authority over standards approval (Months 18 baseline + amendments through Month 30 = 2029-04-08), corridor gates and readiness thresholds, funding allocations above EUR 50 million, milestone deferrals >4 weeks, and escalated technical/commercial disputes. Authority is limited to strategic-level decisions; operational execution (daily carrier onboarding, individual API compliance checks) remains with the PMO and working groups.

Decision Mechanism: Quarterly in-person meeting (120 minutes, Brussels) with written agenda and consent agenda for routine approvals. Major decisions require consensus or, if unattainable after 2 weeks of negotiation, a supermajority vote (2/3 of voting members, excluding the chair). Tie-breaker: if votes are evenly split, the chair (DG MOVE) casts the deciding vote. Escalated disputes from working groups are tabled and decided within 4 weeks; if a decision cannot be reached, the issue is escalated to the Commission with a minority-position record.

Meeting Cadence: Quarterly (Months 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 = 2027-01-08, 2027-04-08, 2027-07-08, 2027-10-08, 2028-01-08... starting Month 3 = 2027-01-08). Emergency meetings may be convened within 5 working days if a milestone-threatening issue arises (e.g., major carrier non-compliance, budget overrun exceeding Tier 2 threshold, or legal challenge). Written decisions on routine items (budget approvals within threshold, minor timeline adjustments) may be made by written consent between meetings.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Progress report on the critical path: standards finalisation, carrier integration, hub readiness, API performance metrics
  • Monthly spend report and budget variance analysis; triggering of contingency tiers if needed
  • Escalated disputes from working groups or the arbitration panel (technical or governance conflicts)
  • Milestone gate reviews (e.g., Month 18 = 2028-04-08 standards approval, Month 30 = 2029-04-08 API readiness assessment)
  • Corridor sequencing decisions and readiness-gate outcomes
  • Stakeholder engagement and political risk updates

Escalation Path: Unresolved Steering Committee disputes escalate to the Commission (DG MOVE, DG COMP if competition concerns are present) for binding decision within 2 weeks. If the Commission cannot decide, the issue is referred to the Council or European Parliament TRAN committee for legislative or policy guidance (estimated escalation cycle: 3–4 weeks). For non-consensus decisions where voting results in 2/3 supermajority, the dissenting minority may request a written Commission review within 10 days.

2. Programme Management Office (PMO) and Core Project Team

Rationale for Inclusion: Day-to-day execution of a EUR 1,500 million, five-year programme spanning 27 member states and 25+ carriers requires a dedicated, professionally staffed operational hub. The PMO manages carrier onboarding, standards development workstreams, budget tracking, risk escalation and milestone delivery. It is the operational nerve centre that bridges strategic direction from the Steering Committee with execution by technical working groups and external partners.

Responsibilities:

  • Manage the critical path and monthly milestone tracking; flag slippage >2 weeks within 5 working days
  • Oversee standards working groups and ensure consensus on OSDM, data-layer design, clearing and settlement rules, and ticket formats by Month 18 (2028-04-08)
  • Coordinate carrier onboarding workflow: assess readiness, allocate co-funding tranches tied to milestones, and track progress toward Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate
  • Manage the budget and spend tracking; alert the Steering Committee when monthly burn rates exceed plan or when contingency usage is needed
  • Coordinate accreditation of payment institutions, hub operators and distributors; maintain a conformance dashboard
  • Operate and escalate the risk-management process: identify new risks monthly, track mitigation actions and escalate unmitigated risks to the Steering Committee
  • Manage the quarterly measurement and evaluation process; produce the public dashboard of progress metrics

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Recruit 10–15 core PMO staff (director, deputy, standards lead, technical architect, budget officer, comms lead, risk officer) by Month 2 (2026-12-08)
  • Establish a shared project-management tool (e.g., Asana, Monday.com) with visibility to all stakeholders, updated weekly with status, red flags and decisions (Month 1 = 2026-11-08)
  • Define PMO operating procedures: decision authority, escalation triggers, meeting schedules for working groups and carrier engagement (Month 1 = 2026-11-08)
  • Secure an office in Brussels with meeting facilities and colocation for the core team (Month 1 = 2026-11-08)
  • Publish the project charter and kick-off communication to all stakeholders (Month 1 = 2026-11-08)

Membership:

  • Programme Director (1 FTE, overall accountability)
  • Deputy Director / Operations Lead (1 FTE)
  • Standards and Technical Lead (1 FTE, OSDM/data-layer architecture)
  • Budget and Finance Officer (1 FTE)
  • Carrier Onboarding and Conformance Lead (1 FTE)
  • Governance and Risk Officer (1 FTE)
  • Communication and Stakeholder Lead (1 FTE)
  • Data Protection and Legal Specialist (0.5 FTE, GDPR, competition law)
  • Evaluation and Measurement Lead (1 FTE)
  • Hub and Gateway Coordination (1 FTE)
  • Administrative support (2 FTE)

Decision Rights: Operational decisions within the PMO's authority: carrier onboarding approvals (subject to co-funding thresholds), weekly working-group facilitation, escalation to the Steering Committee or arbitration panel, risk flag and mitigation tracking, and monthly dashboard publication. The PMO does not have authority to approve major strategy changes, override arbitration panel rulings, or commit budget above EUR 10 million per item; these escalate to the Steering Committee.

Decision Mechanism: Daily stand-up (15 min) among PMO leadership; weekly PMO all-hands meeting (60 min) to review status and risks; working-group leads report to the PMO on Wednesday each week with highlight updates (by 14:00 Brussels time) so the PMO can flag issues by EOD. Operational decisions are made by the PMO Director in consultation with relevant leads (e.g., budget decisions with the Finance Officer); decisions affecting the critical path or involving disputes between two stakeholders are escalated to the Steering Committee or arbitration panel within 5 working days.

Meeting Cadence: Weekly PMO all-hands and governance review (Thursdays, 10:00–11:00 Brussels time); working-group leads submit written status by Wednesday EOD each week. Monthly PMO deep-dive (last Thursday of each month) reviewing budget, risk, milestone and stakeholder updates. Quarterly reporting to the Steering Committee (aligned with SC meeting calendar). Emergency escalation protocol: any issue that threatens a hard milestone is flagged immediately to the Programme Director and escalated within 24 hours.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Milestone tracking: standards workstream progress, carrier integration readiness by corridor, API performance metrics, hub operational status
  • Budget and spend tracking: monthly burn rate vs. forecast, contingency-tier triggers, co-funding pipeline
  • Carrier onboarding: new carriers requesting integration, co-funding approvals, conformance testing queue
  • Risk and issues: new risks identified, mitigation tracking, escalations to Steering Committee or arbitration panel
  • Working-group updates: OSDM, data-layer design, clearing/settlement, consumer app, accessibility, regulator capacity building
  • Stakeholder engagement: political tracking (Regulation adoption, member-state support), media/reputational issues

Escalation Path: Operational issues escalate from working groups to the PMO (48 hours to triage); if unresolved within 1 week, escalate to the arbitration panel (if technical) or Steering Committee (if strategic/budget). Issues requiring inter-member-state coordination escalate to the Standing Regulators Committee or, if involving non-EU partners (Switzerland), to DG MOVE's international affairs team. Issues involving competition-law concerns escalate immediately to DG COMP with a formal request for guidance.

3. Technical Standards and Conformance Working Group

Rationale for Inclusion: The binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 deadline) define OSDM-compatible APIs, data-layer architecture, clearing and settlement message formats, ticket formats, passenger-rights rules, accessibility requirements and GDPR compliance boundaries. This working group must deliver consensus-based standards that carriers, distributors, payment institutions and regulators all accept as feasible and enforceable. It is the technical engine of the programme.

Responsibilities:

  • Define and publish the binding standards document covering OSDM API specifications, data-layer query interfaces, clearing message standards, through-ticket definition, refund and rerouting procedures, accessibility requirements and GDPR/compliance rules
  • Conduct iterative technical consultation with carriers, distributors, payment institutions and regulator representatives; manage disputes through working-group consensus or escalation to arbitration panel
  • Establish conformance-testing criteria and oversee procurement of independent testing laboratories by Month 3 (2027-01-08)
  • Publish conformance checklist and audit procedures for carriers and distributors; manage quarterly conformance reviews
  • Advise the Steering Committee on technical feasibility of proposed milestone dates and corridor sequencing; flag readiness risks

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Establish sub-working groups by Month 2 (2026-12-08): OSDM/API design, data-layer architecture, clearing/settlement, ticket format, passenger rights/accessibility, GDPR compliance
  • Conduct a gap analysis (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08) comparing the Regulation's assumed framework to the Commission's proposal; flag divergences and propose resolutions
  • Begin 'shadow standards' pre-work (Month 0–3 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08) on technical issues that do not depend on final Regulation text (e.g., OSDM API latency targets, data-minimisation rules)
  • Establish a technical dispute-resolution process: if two sub-groups cannot agree on an issue by Month 12 (2027-10-08), escalate to the arbitration panel for binding ruling
  • Publish a draft standards document by Month 12 (2027-10-08) for public consultation; collect feedback by Month 15 (2028-01-08) and incorporate before final approval

Membership:

  • Chair: Standards Lead from the PMO (1 FTE equivalent)
  • OSDM sub-group: 2–3 OSDM experts (external), 2–3 carrier IT leads, 1 distributor technical representative
  • Data-Layer sub-group: 1–2 data-architecture specialists, 1 carrier operations lead, 1 EU Agency for Railways representative
  • Clearing/Settlement sub-group: 1 payment-systems architect, 1 carrier finance lead, 1 distributor lead, 1 legal/compliance representative
  • Ticket Format sub-group: 1 ticket-system expert, 2 carrier representatives, 1 validator-device manufacturer representative
  • Passenger Rights/Accessibility sub-group: 1 legal specialist (passenger rights), 1 accessibility expert, 1 carrier operations representative, 1 BEUC/disability-rights representative
  • GDPR/Compliance sub-group: 1 DPA specialist, 1 competition-law representative, 1 carrier privacy officer, 1 data-protection specialist

Decision Rights: The working group develops consensus standards for Steering Committee approval (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 deadline). Sub-groups can agree on technical specifications within their scope; if consensus is not achievable within a sub-group, the issue escalates to the full working group (2-week resolution target) or to the arbitration panel if still unresolved. The working group has no authority to override regulatory requirements or change the binding-standards deadline; it operates within the constraints set by the Regulation and the Steering Committee.

Decision Mechanism: Monthly full working-group meeting (120 min, Brussels or hybrid) with consensus-based decision-making. Each sub-group meets bi-weekly (60 min, hybrid). Technical disputes within a sub-group are escalated to the full working group with a position paper from each side; the full group attempts consensus within 2 weeks. If consensus fails, the arbitration panel is asked for a binding ruling within 60 days. Major technical decisions (e.g., federated vs. central data layer) are made by the full group with supermajority (2/3) consensus if needed.

Meeting Cadence: Monthly full working-group meetings (2nd Tuesday of each month, 14:00–16:00 Brussels time); bi-weekly sub-group meetings (staggered schedule so no carrier or distributor is in back-to-back meetings). Emergency technical deep-dives scheduled ad hoc if a dispute arises.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • OSDM API specification: latency SLAs, throughput targets, error handling, backward compatibility
  • Data-layer architecture: federated query performance, central cache design, disruption-event streaming, data-quality rules
  • Clearing message standards: revenue apportionment algorithms, settlement cycle, dispute-resolution procedures
  • Ticket format and validation: barcode vs. digital wallet, offline vs. online verification, GDPR data minimisation
  • Passenger rights and accessibility: assistance confirmation timelines, rerouting procedures, accessibility data requirements
  • GDPR and competition law: data-sharing safeguards, Standard Contractual Clauses, confidentiality rules

Escalation Path: Unresolved technical disputes escalate from sub-groups to the full working group (2-week deadline); if still unresolved, escalate to the arbitration panel for binding ruling within 60 days. If the arbitration panel ruling is contested (e.g., a major carrier claims it is technically infeasible), the issue escalates to the Steering Committee for a policy decision. Major standards conflicts that cannot be resolved technically (e.g., conflict between GDPR minimisation and detailed disruption reporting) escalate to the Commission for guidance.

4. Independent Arbitration Panel for Technical Disputes

Rationale for Inclusion: The programme's critical path depends on resolving contested technical decisions (e.g., inventory-parity thresholds, API latency SLAs, settlement message formats) quickly and with binding force. The lightweight arbitration panel avoids the 12–18 month legal setup of a joint undertaking while providing clear, time-boxed dispute resolution. It is essential for keeping standards-setting on track and preventing re-litigation of settled technical issues.

Responsibilities:

  • Receive escalated technical disputes from working groups or the Steering Committee and conduct independent technical review
  • Issue binding rulings on contested technical standards, conformance criteria and SLAs within 60 days of receiving a dispute
  • Publish reasoned rulings explaining the technical rationale, evidence considered and any dissenting panel-member positions
  • Track compliance with rulings: carriers and entities have 14 days to confirm adoption or request escalation to the Commission
  • Provide advisory guidance (non-binding) on emerging technical issues raised by working groups or the PMO

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Secure written Council/Commission delegation of binding authority by Month 2 (2026-12-08); delegation must specify decision scope (technical standards only, not commercial terms), time limits (60 days to ruling, 14 days to comply) and escalation procedures
  • Recruit and appoint 8–12 panel members (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08): 2–3 OSDM or rail-IT experts, 1–2 data-architecture specialists, 1 payment-systems expert, 1 accessibility expert, 1 legal/compliance specialist, 1–2 independent arbitrators (no carrier/distributor affiliation), and 1 panel secretary (0.5 FTE)
  • Establish panel governance: term of office (3–5 years), conflict-of-interest rules (panel members cannot advise carriers or distributors during their tenure), and a tie-breaking or consensus protocol
  • Define the dispute-submission process: working groups or Steering Committee submit a written dispute with positions from all parties (limit 5 pages per position); panel has 10 days to declare the dispute admissible
  • Publish panel operating procedures and communication protocols by Month 1 (2026-11-08)

Membership:

  • Panel Chair (1, independent expert, e.g., from an external neutral institution like the EU Agency for Railways or an academic)
  • OSDM/API specialists (2–3, external; rotational participation in disputes to avoid bias)
  • Data-architecture expert (1, external)
  • Payment-systems expert (1, external; may be a payment-institution representative with firewall rules to prevent conflicts)
  • Accessibility expert (1, external; e.g., from a disability-rights organisation or accessibility standards body)
  • Legal/competition specialist (1, external; for GDPR and antitrust questions)
  • Transport regulation specialist (1, may be from the EU Agency for Railways with appropriate independence)
  • Panel Secretary (0.5–1 FTE, employed by the programme to manage scheduling, documentation and publication)

Decision Rights: Binding authority over technical standards disputes: API latency SLAs, throughput requirements, data-layer architecture choices, message-format specifications, conformance-testing criteria, and allocation of technical liability (e.g., who is responsible for mapping errors in a hub). Authority is limited to technical feasibility and standards alignment; the panel cannot override the Regulation's requirements, approve budget deviations or make commercial decisions (e.g., carrier pricing, fee caps). If a dispute involves both technical and commercial elements (e.g., whether an access term is non-discriminatory), the panel issues a technical ruling and escalates the commercial implications to the Steering Committee.

Decision Mechanism: When a dispute is received, the panel's chair convenes a panel roster (5–7 members) with expertise relevant to the dispute. Panel members review written submissions from all parties (5 pages each, plus exhibits). The panel conducts a technical review (10–20 days), may request clarifications from parties (3-day response window) and holds a closed deliberation meeting (day 30–40). The panel issues a written ruling (day 60) with findings, technical rationale and the decision. If panel members disagree, dissenting opinions are published alongside the majority ruling. Tie-breaking: if the panel is evenly split (rare, given odd roster size), the chair casts a deciding vote.

Meeting Cadence: Panel roster convenes within 5 working days of a dispute being declared admissible. Panel deliberations are internal (not public). Rulings are published within 5 working days of issuance (day 65 of the cycle). The full panel meets quarterly for governance and to review emerging technical issues; panels for individual disputes meet as needed (estimated 1–3 disputes per quarter during the standards-development phase = Months 4–18 = 2027-02-08 to 2028-04-08).

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Escalated dispute submissions: technical positions from all parties, feasibility assessments
  • Deliberation on the dispute: technical evidence, regulatory constraints, impact on critical path
  • Drafting of the ruling and resolution of any dissents
  • Quarterly review of panel operations: caseload, decision quality, emerging patterns in disputes

Escalation Path: If a party (e.g., a major carrier) contests a panel ruling and claims it is technically infeasible or conflicts with national law, the party may request escalation to the Commission within 10 days of the ruling. The Commission has 14 days to affirm or overturn the ruling (this is rare and only for exceptional cases). If the Commission affirms the ruling and a carrier still refuses to comply, the issue escalates to DG MOVE for enforcement action (co-funding holds, public-channel bypass, or regulatory escalation). For disputes involving competition-law or GDPR questions, the panel's ruling is immediately referred to DG COMP or the EDPB for concurrence; if those bodies disagree, the matter escalates to the Steering Committee and Commission for a final decision.

5. Member-State Regulator Coordination Committee and Capacity Building Programme

Rationale for Inclusion: National rail regulators across 27 member states must enforce access, refund and accessibility duties consistently for through-tickets to be credible and non-discriminatory. However, regulators vary widely in resources, expertise and enforcement traditions. A dedicated coordination committee and capacity-building programme ensure consistent enforcement, cross-border dispute resolution and alignment with the programme's access-term rules. This is essential for the non-discrimination goal and for the credibility of the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate.

Responsibilities:

  • Harmonise enforcement procedures across member states for access terms, passenger rights and accessibility compliance; publish common inspection checklists and audit standards by Month 12 (2027-10-08)
  • Establish a lead-authority mechanism for cross-border disputes: when a distributor complains that a carrier in another member state is denying API access, designate one national regulator as the lead, with other member states recognising its decision
  • Provide capacity building and twinning partnerships for weaker regulators: training on access-enforcement, data-quality auditing, complaint handling and cross-border coordination
  • Operate a Standing Regulators Committee (quarterly) to review enforcement outcomes, escalate systemic issues to the Commission, and update procedures
  • Track and report on compliance metrics: access-complaint resolution times, non-discrimination audit findings, and consistency of passenger-rights enforcement across member states

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Conduct a regulator capacity audit in Month 1–2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08) identifying staff, budget and enforcement expertise gaps in each member state
  • Establish the Standing Regulators Committee and elect a chair (preferably from a strong-capacity regulator, e.g., Germany, Netherlands, France) by Month 1 (2026-11-08)
  • Define a lead-authority framework (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08): specify which member state's regulator leads for disputes involving carriers in that state; establish mutual recognition of lead-authority decisions
  • Fund bilateral twinning partnerships (Month 2–6 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-04-08): pair weak-capacity regulators with strong ones; provide training budgets (EUR 0.5–1M per partnership over 3 years)
  • Develop common inspection checklists and audit procedures for access compliance by Month 6 (2027-04-08); publish a regulator toolkit for smaller member states

Membership:

  • Chair: Head of a major national regulator (e.g., Germany, France, Netherlands, Austria), elected for a 2-year term
  • Deputy Chair: Head of a regulator from a smaller or weaker-capacity member state (rotating)
  • 27 member-state regulator representatives (one per member state; may be director or deputy director level)
  • EU Agency for Railways representative (ex-officio, advisory role on cross-border coordination)
  • Programme Director or Deputy (PMO observer, for coordination with programme timelines)
  • Technical secretariat: 1 FTE (hosted by the EU Agency for Railways or a volunteering member-state regulator), managing meeting schedules, documentation and capacity-building coordination

Decision Rights: Recommends (not binding, absent escalation) common enforcement procedures, regulator training curricula, and audit standards to the Steering Committee. Binding authority: lead-authority decisions on cross-border disputes are final and recognised by all member states (absent Commission override). The committee can escalate systemic enforcement failures (e.g., a member state consistently failing to investigate non-discrimination complaints) to the Commission for investigation and enforcement action. The committee cannot override national regulations or force a regulator to act beyond its legal powers.

Decision Mechanism: Quarterly meeting (120 min) with supermajority consensus (2/3 of voting members) on enforcement standards and procedures. Lead-authority decisions on individual cross-border disputes are made by the lead regulator (as designated in the framework) within 30 days; other member-state regulators have 5 days to file a dissent with the committee chair, who then refers the matter to the Standing Regulators Committee for review. If 2+ member states dispute the lead decision, escalate to the EU Agency for Railways or Commission for mediation (14-day resolution target).

Meeting Cadence: Quarterly in-person or hybrid meetings (typically aligned with Steering Committee calendar, with 1 week separation). Emergency virtual meetings can be convened within 2 working days if a cross-border dispute requires urgent resolution. Monthly calls (30 min) among the chair, deputy chair, PMO and the EU Agency for Railways to track emerging issues.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • Enforcement review: number and type of access-discrimination complaints received and resolved; average resolution time per member state
  • Cross-border disputes: updates on lead-authority investigations, recognition of decisions, and escalations
  • Regulator capacity: twinning partnership progress, training attendance, resource gaps
  • Systemic issues: patterns of non-compliance by carriers in particular member states, need for procedural updates
  • Coordination with the programme: critical-path tracking, milestone readiness, impact of enforcement on corridor gates

Escalation Path: Member-state enforcement failures escalate from the Standing Regulators Committee to the Commission (DG MOVE) for investigation and potential enforcement action under Article 258 TFEU (infringement proceedings). Cross-border disputes that the lead regulator cannot resolve escalate to the EU Agency for Railways for mediation (14-day resolution target); if still unresolved, escalate to DG MOVE for a binding decision. If a member state refuses to recognise a lead-authority decision, the issue escalates to the Commission and potentially to CJEU (Court of Justice of the European Union) for ruling on mutual-recognition obligations.

6. Consumer Product and Support Team

Rationale for Inclusion: The programme's success depends on passenger uptake of through-tickets via the public reference distributor (and complementary commercial platforms). A dedicated consumer product team builds the multilingual booking app, ensures user experience quality, and operates a 24/7 support centre for passenger complaints and accessibility requests. This team is responsible for the consumer-facing brand and credibility of the through-ticketing system, directly supporting the 40% through-ticket target.

Responsibilities:

  • Design and build a multilingual EU through-ticketing booking app (launch Month 15 = 2028-01-08; four-corridor rollout by Month 27 = 2029-01-08)
  • Implement real-time search, booking and refund flows; integrate accessibility request and confirmation; display through-ticket continuity-of-journey promises and refund guarantees
  • Operate a 24/7 multilingual customer support centre (launch Month 15 = 2028-01-08): handle booking errors, refund claims, accessibility requests, and complaints in 24+ languages; target <1-hour response for critical issues
  • Monitor app performance, user satisfaction and complaint trends; iterate the app design quarterly based on user feedback and A/B testing
  • Coordinate with carriers, distributors and payment institutions to resolve passenger-escalated technical issues (e.g., booking failed at confirmation, refund not received)
  • Produce quarterly public reports on customer satisfaction, complaint types, accessibility-assisted bookings and support-queue metrics

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Recruit the consumer product team (20–30 FTE) by Month 1 (2026-11-08): product manager, engineering lead, UX/design leads, backend engineers, localization specialists, and support-centre manager
  • Conduct user research and persona development (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08); wireframe core flows (search, booking, refund, accessibility request)
  • Build an MVP (minimum viable product) for pilot testing on one corridor (Month 5–8 = 2027-03-08 to 2027-06-08); deploy to 100–500 test users
  • Iterate based on pilot feedback (Month 9–12 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08); conduct UX refinement and accessibility testing (WCAG 2.1 AA compliance)
  • Begin full-scale development and localization in Month 12 (2027-10-08); target production-ready by Month 15 (2028-01-08)
  • Establish the support centre infrastructure (call centre, email ticketing, knowledge base, escalation procedures) by Month 14 (2027-12-08)

Membership:

  • Consumer Product Director (1 FTE, accountability for app and brand)
  • Product Manager (1 FTE, feature prioritization and roadmap)
  • Engineering Lead (1 FTE, technical architecture and delivery)
  • Backend Engineers (3–4 FTE, API integration, data handling)
  • Frontend/UX Engineers (2–3 FTE, user interface, accessibility)
  • Localization and Content Manager (1 FTE, multilingual support, legal disclaimers)
  • Support Centre Manager (1 FTE, team leadership, quality assurance)
  • Support Agents (4–6 FTE initially, scaling to 10–15 FTE by Month 24 = 2028-10-08, covering 24/7 coverage in 24+ languages via subcontractors for non-major languages)
  • Data Analyst (0.5 FTE, monitoring satisfaction metrics, complaint patterns)

Decision Rights: Operational decisions: app feature prioritization, support procedures, multilingual content, and technology stack choices. The team does not have authority to commit budget above EUR 2 million per item (e.g., major infrastructure upgrades), change through-ticket definition or refund policies (set by the Steering Committee), or commit carrier/distributor integration timelines (negotiated with the PMO). User experience decisions and support procedures are made by the team with input from carriers, distributors and passenger advisory representatives.

Decision Mechanism: Weekly product prioritization meeting (60 min): product manager, engineering lead and UX lead discuss incoming requirements (from carriers, distributors, support tickets) and update the feature roadmap. Support centre manager and quality-assurance lead review complaint trends and procedural issues in a weekly meeting (30 min). Major decisions (e.g., whether to pivot from a native app to a web-based offering, or whether to integrate a partner payment processor) escalate to the Steering Committee or PMO for approval.

Meeting Cadence: Weekly product team meetings (Monday, 10:00–11:00 Brussels time); weekly support-centre operational meeting (Friday, 10:00–10:30); biweekly full team sync (first and third Thursday of each month, 14:00–15:30). Monthly retrospective and planning session (last Friday of each month, 13:00–15:00) reviewing metrics and upcoming iterations.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • App development progress: feature completion, bug tracking, performance metrics (latency, crash rates, search success rate)
  • User satisfaction and feedback: app-store reviews, NPS (Net Promoter Score), user-research findings, accessibility feedback
  • Support centre operations: complaint volume by category (booking errors, refund delays, accessibility, technical issues), average resolution time, escalations to carriers or payment institutions
  • Multilingual content and localization: translation quality reviews, cultural adaptation for different EU markets
  • Integration with carriers, distributors and payment systems: API changes, new data feeds, coordination on messaging to passengers

Escalation Path: Technical issues that require carrier or payment-institution intervention escalate from support tickets to the PMO (via the support-centre manager) with a severity rating (critical: <2-hour resolution target; high: <24-hour; medium: <5 days). PMO coordinates carrier/distributor response. If a support issue reveals a systemic problem (e.g., >100 complaints per week about failed refunds), escalate to the Steering Committee for investigation and corrective action. Accessibility issues escalate immediately to the Accessibility Working Group and to BEUC/disability-rights representatives for guidance.

7. Ethics, Compliance and Accessibility Oversight Committee

Rationale for Inclusion: The programme involves sensitive areas: passenger data (PII, accessibility information, payment details), access-to-essential-transport (persons with reduced mobility), and fair competition among carriers and distributors. A dedicated ethics and compliance committee ensures adherence to GDPR, accessibility standards, disability-rights principles and anti-corruption rules. It provides independent assurance that the programme's governance and operations are credible and inclusive.

Responsibilities:

  • Oversee GDPR compliance across all programme entities: commissioning and reviewing the DPIA (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08), securing EDPB/DPA consensus on data-flow safeguards by Month 4 (2027-02-08), and conducting quarterly compliance audits on data-handling practices (starting Month 18 = 2028-04-08)
  • Monitor accessibility compliance: ensuring that booking systems, assistance request/confirmation flows and accessibility data meet WCAG 2.1 AA and EU accessibility directives; conducting quarterly accessibility audits of the public app and carrier systems
  • Establish and enforce ethics guidelines for programme staff, carrier and distributor representatives, and regulator participants: conflict-of-interest rules, anti-corruption provisions, whistleblower protections
  • Oversee passenger-data handling: review data-sharing agreements among carriers, distributors, payment institutions and the clearing mechanism; ensure data minimisation and consent compliance
  • Review and approve compliance scorecards for carriers and distributors; report quarterly to the Steering Committee on ethics and compliance status

Initial Setup Actions:

  • Recruit committee members and establish terms of office (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08); ensure membership includes external, independent ethics and accessibility experts with no conflicts of interest
  • Commission the DPIA and request EDPB consultation (Month 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08); establish a timeline for DPA consensus by Month 4 (2027-02-08)
  • Draft an ethics code and conflict-of-interest policy (Month 1 = 2026-11-08); require all programme staff, carriers and distributors to sign by Month 2 (2026-12-08)
  • Establish accessibility requirements and conformance checklist (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) aligned with the Accessibility Working Group; define audit procedures
  • Create a confidential whistleblower channel (Month 1 = 2026-11-08); communicate it to all stakeholders and protect reporters from retaliation

Membership:

  • Chair: Independent ethics or compliance expert (external, e.g., from an EU ethics body or academic institution); 3-year term
  • Deputy Chair: Independent accessibility expert (external, e.g., from a disability-rights organisation); 3-year term
  • GDPR/Data Protection Specialist (external, e.g., from a DPA or data-protection consultancy)
  • Accessibility and Inclusive Design Expert (external, e.g., from an accessibility standards organisation)
  • Ethics and Compliance Officer (programme staff, 1 FTE, working closely with the committee)
  • Finance and Audit Representative (external, independent auditor or audit firm, rotating 2-year terms)
  • Passenger Advocacy Representative (e.g., from BEUC or a consumer-protection body)

Decision Rights: Advisory authority: the committee makes recommendations to the Steering Committee on GDPR compliance, accessibility standards and ethics enforcement. Binding authority (in consultation with DG MOVE): suspension of a carrier's or distributor's participation in the programme if serious GDPR or ethics violations are found (e.g., mishandling of passenger data, corruption). The committee cannot override the Regulation or change the programme's core objectives; it operates within the legal and policy framework set by the Commission and Steering Committee.

Decision Mechanism: Quarterly full committee meeting (120 min, in-person or hybrid). Consensus-based decision-making; if a member dissents on a recommendation to the Steering Committee, the dissent is documented and both positions are submitted to the SC. Emergency meetings (within 5 working days) may be convened if a critical ethics or compliance issue is discovered (e.g., evidence of corruption or a major data breach).

Meeting Cadence: Quarterly formal meetings (aligned with Steering Committee calendar); monthly virtual calls (30 min) among the chair, deputy chair and the ethics/compliance officer to review emerging issues. Ad-hoc meetings if urgent escalations arise.

Typical Agenda Items:

  • GDPR compliance status: data-flow architecture, DPA consensus tracking, carrier/distributor data-handling practices, incidents and remediation
  • Accessibility compliance: app and carrier system audits, accessibility-assisted booking metrics, passenger complaints related to accessibility
  • Ethics and conflict-of-interest review: new programme staff and stakeholder representatives, potential conflicts, compliance with the ethics code
  • Passenger data security and breach response: quarterly review of data-handling incidents, mitigation actions
  • Whistleblower cases: confidential review of any reported ethics violations or compliance concerns; recommendation of investigation or corrective action

Escalation Path: Recommendations on GDPR, accessibility or ethics compliance escalate to the Steering Committee for decision or action (e.g., co-funding suspension, mandatory corrective action by a carrier). Serious violations (evidence of corruption, major data breaches, severe accessibility failures) escalate immediately to DG MOVE and the Commission for investigation and potential enforcement. GDPR and accessibility issues may also escalate to the relevant national DPA or accessibility authority for guidance or enforcement.

Governance Implementation Plan
