1. Project Sponsor (DG MOVE) formally initiates the programme and establishes initial programme authority. Publish the project charter, confirm programme start date (Month 0 = 2026-10-08), approve the governance structure, and designate the Programme Director role with interim decision authority during set-up.

Responsible Body/Role: Project Sponsor (DG MOVE)

Suggested Timeframe: Within 1 week of project start (Month 0.1 = 2026-10-11)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Signed Project Charter
  • Programme Director Role Specification and Interim Authority Memorandum
  • Initial Communication to All Stakeholders (Regulation text, timeline, governance overview)

Dependencies:

  • Project start decision
  • Identified Project Sponsor and initial programme leadership

2. Programme Director (once designated) establishes the core Programme Management Office (PMO) and convenes a governance-setup task force. Define PMO staffing plan, office location (Brussels), project-management tools and reporting cadence. Initiate recruitment of 10–15 core PMO staff (director, deputy, standards lead, technical architect, budget officer, communications lead, risk officer).

Responsible Body/Role: Programme Director

Suggested Timeframe: Within 2 weeks of project start (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • PMO Organization Chart and Staffing Plan
  • Office/Meeting Facilities Lease Agreement (Brussels)
  • Project Management Tool Setup (Asana, Monday.com, or equivalent)
  • PMO Recruitment Initiation (job descriptions, outreach)

Dependencies:

  • Project Sponsor authorization
  • Budget authorization for PMO operations

3. Programme Director drafts the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) governing the Programme Steering Committee (SteerCo): authority, decision rights, decision-making rules, escalation procedures, meeting cadence. Define quorum, tie-breaking provisions and record-keeping protocols.

Responsible Body/Role: Programme Director (with input from Legal Counsel and DG MOVE)

Suggested Timeframe: Within 3 weeks of project start (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08)

Key Outputs/Deliverables:

  • Draft Steering Committee MOU (authority, scope, decision rules)
  • Proposed Steering Committee Membership List
  • Nominated Steering Committee Chair (to be approved by DG MOVE)

Dependencies:

  • Project Charter approved
  • PMO established
  • Understanding of stakeholder landscape (carriers, regulators, distributors)

4. Senior Management (DG MOVE) formally appoints the Steering Committee Chair and confirms initial membership. Chair must be a senior DG MOVE or Commission representative; deputy chair a representative from a smaller/weaker-capacity member state or regulator. Secure written commitment from all nominated members (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08).

Responsible Body/Role: Project Sponsor (DG MOVE) / Senior Management

Standards Working Group, in collaboration with legal counsel and the EU Agency for Railways, conducts a gap analysis comparing the Commission's proposed Regulation (May 2026) to OSDM standards and legacy-carrier IT capabilities. Identify areas where standards development can proceed immediately ('shadow work') versus areas dependent on final Regulation text. Publish findings by Month 3 (2027-01-08).

Programme Director recruits and appoints the independent Arbitration Panel members (8–12 FTE: chair, OSDM/API experts, data-architect specialist, payment-systems expert, accessibility expert, legal/competition specialist, regulator representative, and secretary). Distribute for signature by Month 3 (2027-01-08).

Programme Director commissions a detailed activity-based cost model estimating: carrier IT integration costs by carrier size and legacy-system status; hub operating costs per region; public reference distributor annual operating costs; payment-institution transaction fees. Issue a Request for Information (RFI) outlining accreditation criteria: multi-currency support (EUR, DKK, SEK, CHF, PLN, CZK, HUF, BGN, RON), settlement cycle <48 hours, refund processing <10 days, SLAs (99.95% uptime), financial stability (PSD2 license required). Budget per hub: EUR 6M over 5 years; total hub budget EUR 24M launch + EUR 20M reserved for two TEN-T hubs (decisions at Month 30 = 2029-04-08).

Decision Escalation Matrix

Budget Overrun Exceeding Contingency Threshold Escalation Level: Programme Steering Committee Approval Process: Written decision within 5 working days. Supermajority vote (2/3 of members) if consensus cannot be reached. Escalation to the Commission (DG MOVE) if Tier 3 contingency (>25% overrun) is triggered or if free contingency is exhausted. Rationale: The fixed EUR 1,500 million budget is a hard user constraint. Overruns exceeding 15% (Tier 2) threaten funding for standards work, conformance testing, and carrier co-funding. Monthly budget tracking triggers escalation when spend exceeds 115% of pro-rata forecast. A Tier 2 or Tier 3 event requires immediate strategic decisions (cut co-funding rates, defer TEN-T extension, seek supplementary authority) that only the Steering Committee can authorise. Negative Consequences: Unmitigated budget overruns force arbitrary cuts to conformance testing (delaying smaller-carrier certification by 6–12 months), capacity building (weakening regulator enforcement), or consumer rollout (reducing through-ticket adoption). A EUR 300–450M overrun (Tier 3) exceeds free contingency and risks programme failure or compressed delivery without quality assurance.

Carrier Non-Compliance or Major Incumbent Signalling Delay Past Month 30 (2029-04-08) Mandatory API Deadline Escalation Level: Programme Steering Committee, with escalation to the Commission (DG MOVE) and potential enforcement action (co-funding hold, public-channel competition, regulatory escalation) Approval Process: Steering Committee convenes an emergency meeting within 5 working days of non-compliance signal. Reviews evidence (missed integration milestones, insufficient IT investment, formal delay announcement). If a major carrier (>30% of corridor traffic) signals non-compliance, Steering Committee authorises contingency levers: hold co-funding tranches, escalate to the Commission for enforcement negotiations, and consider public distributor expansion to bypass the non-compliant carrier. Rationale: Large incumbents (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, Trenitalia, ÖBB) have political leverage and can stall the entire programme if they contest compliance deadlines or demand exemptions. The Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate is legally binding under the adopted Regulation. If a major carrier continues non-compliant practices after an arbitration panel ruling, the programme's credibility collapses and smaller carriers lose incentive to integrate. Negative Consequences: Non-compliance by one major carrier (accounting for 30–40% of cross-border traffic) fractures the coalition. The Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate becomes advisory rather than binding, and competing carriers demand similar extensions, reducing API coverage from 90% to 70–80% of cross-border journeys. The 40% through-ticket target becomes unachievable.

Regulation Adoption Delayed or Materially Divergent from Assumed Framework Escalation Level: Programme Steering Committee and Project Sponsor (DG MOVE), with parliamentary liaison and member-state coordination Approval Process: Steering Committee reviews the regulatory status quarterly (starting Month 3 = 2027-01-08). If adoption slips to Month 9 (2027-07-08) or later, the Committee convenes an emergency session to activate contingency: (1) accelerate shadow standards work (already underway from Month 0 = 2026-10-08) and contract external standards consortium for rapid finalisation; (2) pause new carrier onboarding commitments until final Regulation text is clear. If final text diverges materially on scope, access terms, or liability, the Committee authorises a 2–4 week 'rapid standards adjustment' post-adoption (by Month 12 = 2027-10-08) rather than attempting finalisation before text is confirmed. Rationale: The Commission's proposed Regulation (May 2026) remains unadopted as of Month 0 (2026-10-08). Parliament and Council negotiations could extend adoption to Month 6–12 (2027-04-08 to 2027-10-08), compressing the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards-setting window from 9 months to 3–4 months. A hard gate of Month 9 (2027-07-08) ensures that if adoption slips further, the critical path is re-baselined before momentum is lost. Negative Consequences: If adoption occurs after Month 9 (2027-07-08), standards-setting margin is eliminated. Either rushed, low-quality standards (risking non-compliance by carriers) or a formal Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline miss results. Material divergence in final text (e.g., narrowed scope or weaker non-discrimination rules) invalidates much of the pre-work and requires rework, adding 4–8 weeks and threatening the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate.

Arbitration Panel Ruling Contested or Rejected by a Major Carrier or Member State; Governance Deadlock Escalation Level: Commission (DG MOVE, and DG COMP if competition concerns arise) for binding decision and enforcement authority Approval Process: If a carrier or member-state regulator contests an arbitration panel ruling (issued within 60 days) within 10 days, the issue escalates to the Commission with a written statement from the panel, the dissenting party and any affected stakeholders. The Commission has 14 days to affirm or overturn the ruling. If affirmed and a carrier continues non-compliant practices, the Commission can impose remedial action: mandatory corrective measures, interim API access revocation, or escalation to national enforcement authorities. Rationale: The lightweight arbitration panel lacks direct enforcement authority. If a major incumbent contests a technical ruling (e.g., on inventory-parity thresholds or API latency SLAs) and refuses to comply, the panel's only recourse is escalation to the Commission. Without explicit written Council delegation (target Month 2 = 2026-12-08) and carrier Commitment Letters with penalty provisions, the panel cannot compel compliance. Negative Consequences: Unresolved disputes cascade: a contested ruling on, e.g., API latency (2 seconds vs. 3 seconds) holds up standards approval, carrier integration and the Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline. Escalation to the Commission for mediation takes 2–4 months, and if the carrier is politically protected (e.g., a national champion), the Commission may negotiate weaker terms, undermining the non-discrimination goal. The programme's authority is questioned by other carriers, and compliance rates drop.

GDPR or Competition-Law Challenge to the Shared Data Layer; Regulatory Investigation or Mandated Redesign Escalation Level: European Commission (DG COMP for competition law; EDPB for GDPR), with programme suspension contingency Approval Process: If a competition authority or data protection authority initiates a formal investigation into alleged data-sharing collusion or GDPR non-compliance (estimated Month 12–18 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08 risk window), the Steering Committee is notified immediately. The Committee authorises the programme's legal team and DG MOVE to engage in the investigation. If the authority issues a preliminary ruling requiring redesign or forbearance, the Committee convenes an emergency session within 5 working days to assess impact on the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate and authorise contingency measures: data-layer architecture redesign, temporary suspension of shared data (revert to pure federated queries), or timeline extension to Month 36 (2029-10-08). Rationale: The shared real-time data layer exposes carrier fares, load factors and sales volumes—commercially sensitive information. Even with safeguards (data minimisation, neutral operator, access logs), a competition investigation can create legal uncertainty and force carriers to curtail data contributions. Similarly, a GDPR challenge over cross-border PII flows or consent regimes can disrupt payment-institution accreditation and clearing operations. Negative Consequences: A competition authority investigation lasting 12–24 months delays full data-layer rollout. Carriers become unwilling to participate, reducing inventory coverage. GDPR intervention forcing local data residency or explicit consent for every journey transaction creates friction and reduces through-ticket volumes by 10–20%. Worst case: the data layer is ordered to be dismantled, requiring a 6–12 month overhaul and a 2–6 month extension of the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API deadline.

Through-Ticket Volume Significantly Lags Target (Baseline Measurement at Month 9 = 2027-07-08 Invalidates 40% Projection) Escalation Level: Programme Steering Committee, with potential pivot to contingency funding or scope adjustment Approval Process: At Month 9 (2027-07-08), the validated baseline is reviewed by the Measurement and Evaluation Lead and presented to the Steering Committee. If the baseline survey reveals that current cross-border through-ticket share is significantly lower than assumed (e.g., <5% vs. 8% estimated), the Committee triggers a 4-week strategic review. Based on findings, the Committee may: (1) increase co-marketing budgets (EUR 5–10M additional); (2) accelerate the public distributor's launch (from Month 27 = 2029-01-08 to Month 15 = 2028-01-08); (3) revise the 40% target downward and adjust the programme narrative to focus on volume and convenience rather than market-share percentage. Rationale: The 40% through-ticket target depends on accurate baseлining of current cross-border rail volumes and modal split. If the baseline is systematically misestimated or if baseline measurement reveals structural barriers to through-ticketing adoption (e.g., distributors resist integration, airlines compete aggressively on price), the programme's ROI case weakens and stakeholder confidence erodes. Negative Consequences: If the baseline invalidates the 40% target's plausibility, the programme loses political momentum and stakeholder buy-in. Funding may be redirected to other priorities, or the programme's scope may be reduced (e.g., to two corridors instead of four). By Month 24 (2028-10-08), a missed interim gate (15% through-ticket share) triggers co-funding hold and forces a decision on whether to increase public investment or accept a lower outcome.

Monitoring Progress

1. Milestone and Critical-Path Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Project-Management Tool (Asana, Monday.com or equivalent) with real-time dashboard
  • Monthly Milestone Status Report (PMO to Steering Committee)
  • Critical-Path Gantt Chart and dependency tracker
  • Regulation Adoption Tracking Dashboard (weekly)

Frequency: Weekly PMO status update (internal); monthly deep-dive (PMO all-hands); quarterly Steering Committee review (Months 3, 6, 9, 12 onwards = 2027-01-08 to 2027-10-08 and thereafter)

Responsible Role: Programme Management Office (PMO) Director and Deputy, with Programme Steering Committee oversight

Adaptation Process: PMO flags any slippage >2 weeks within 5 working days. Working groups and carriers propose corrective actions (resource increase, scope reduction, timeline adjustment). If slippage exceeds 4 weeks or threatens a hard gate (Month 18 = 2028-04-08, Month 30 = 2029-04-08, Month 60 = 2031-10-08), escalate to Steering Committee for binding decision on timeline adjustment, contingency activation, or scope reduction.

Adaptation Trigger: Milestone slippage >2 weeks (triggers PMO escalation); >4 weeks (triggers Steering Committee session within 1 week); Regulation adoption delay past Month 9 (2027-07-08) (hard gate, triggers contingency activation and contingency standards-review); any hard milestone at risk of being missed more than 2 months in advance (triggers re-baselining).

2. Budget Burn Rate and Contingency Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Monthly Budget Burn Report (Finance Officer to PMO and Steering Committee)
  • Budget Forecast Spreadsheet (EUR 1.5 billion cap tracked by component)
  • Contingency Activation Triggers and Tier 1/2/3 Decision Matrix
  • Carrier Co-Funding Disbursement Log (tied to milestone completion)

Frequency: Monthly financial reporting (by the 15th of each month); quarterly Steering Committee budget review (Months 3, 6, 9, 12 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-10-08 and thereafter); contingency-activation triggers assessed at each monthly PMO all-hands

Responsible Role: Finance Officer (PMO), with Steering Committee budget authority above EUR 50M per item

Adaptation Process: Finance Officer produces monthly burn-rate summary vs. pro-rata forecast. If monthly spend exceeds 115% of pro-rata budget, flag immediately (within 2 working days). If overrun is 10-15% (Tier 1), PMO reviews discretionary spend (marketing, distributor co-ops) for deferral. If overrun is 15-25% (Tier 2), Steering Committee convenes within 1 week to approve cost-reduction measures: reduce carrier co-funding rate from 20% to 10-15%, defer TEN-T hub procurement, or scale back consumer-app features. If overrun exceeds 25% (Tier 3), Steering Committee immediately requests supplementary budget authority from DG MOVE and the Commission.

Adaptation Trigger: Monthly spend >115% of pro-rata forecast (Tier 1 trigger); cumulative overrun reaching 15% (Tier 2, triggers SC decision within 1 week); overrun reaching 25% (Tier 3, triggers immediate Commission escalation); free contingency (EUR 215M) consumed by >80% (triggers DG MOVE notification and request for supplementary authority); co-funding demand from carriers exceeds EUR 350M (signals pipeline risk, triggers co-funding-rate reduction decision by Month 12 = 2027-10-08).

3. Carrier Integration Readiness and Conformance Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Carrier Conformance and Readiness Dashboard (monthly, by corridor and carrier)
  • Conformance Test Queue and Lab Capacity Report (monthly)
  • Carrier Milestone Completion Log (API design review Month 15 = 2028-01-08, test-bed Month 18 = 2028-04-08, dual-run Months 21-24 = 2028-07-08 to 2028-10-08, pre-production Months 24-27 = 2028-10-08 to 2029-01-08, go-live Month 30 = 2029-04-08)
  • Carrier Commitment Letter Compliance Tracker (penalties in escrow monitored)

Frequency: Monthly carrier readiness update (PMO Carrier Onboarding Lead to PMO all-hands); quarterly detailed readiness report to Steering Committee; weekly testing-lab capacity review (internal PMO)

Responsible Role: Carrier Onboarding and Conformance Lead (PMO), with testing labs and EU Agency for Railways liaison

Adaptation Process: PMO tracks each carrier's progress through readiness gates. If a carrier misses a gate (e.g., API design review not completed by Month 15 = 2028-01-08), PMO issues a 2-week remediation notice and assigns a technical mentor. If the carrier does not meet the remediation deadline, PMO suspends co-funding tranches (0.5-1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue, held in escrow, is accelerated to forfeiture) and escalates to the Steering Committee. If a major carrier (>EUR 100M cross-border revenue, >30% of corridor traffic) signals they will not meet the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API deadline, Steering Committee convenes emergency session within 5 days, invokes the Commitment Letter penalty, and initiates enforcement escalation to DG MOVE (public distributor bypass, regulatory pressure).

Adaptation Trigger: Carrier misses a readiness gate by >2 weeks (triggers remediation notice); multiple carriers (>3) slip past a gate simultaneously (triggers Steering Committee review and possible timeline extension or scope reduction); a major incumbent carrier (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, Trenitalia, ÖBB, >30% corridor traffic) signals non-compliance or delay >6 months (triggers emergency SC session and enforcement escalation); less than 80% of major carriers pass conformance audit by Month 24 (2028-10-08) (triggers Month 30 = 2029-04-08 API mandate risk assessment); less than 75% of smaller carriers ready via hubs by Month 30 (2029-04-08) (triggers TEN-T extension delay decision).

4. Standards Development Progress and Technical Dispute Resolution

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Technical Standards Working Group Monthly Status Report (sub-group deliverables, consensus gaps, escalations)
  • Draft Standards Document Status (chapters complete, review cycle status)
  • Arbitration Panel Case Log (disputes received, rulings issued, compliance tracking)
  • OSDM Specification Alignment Tracker (comparison to published OSDM standard and Regulation requirements)

Frequency: Monthly standards working-group all-hands meeting and PMO reporting; bi-weekly sub-group check-ins on critical workstreams (OSDM, data-layer, clearing/settlement); arbitration panel decisions logged and published within 5 working days of issuance; quarterly Steering Committee review of standards progress (Months 3, 6, 9, 12 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-10-08)

Responsible Role: Technical Standards Lead (PMO, chair of working group), with Arbitration Panel Chair and EU Agency for Railways liaison

Adaptation Process: Standards Lead tracks sub-group progress against planned deliverables. If a sub-group cannot reach consensus on a technical issue by the target date (e.g., data-layer architecture by Month 9 = 2027-07-08), the Standards Lead escalates the dispute to the Arbitration Panel within 5 working days with written positions from all parties. The Panel issues a binding ruling within 60 days. If the ruling is contested (within 10 days), the dispute escalates to the Commission (DG MOVE, DG COMP if competition concerns) for final decision within 14 days. Meanwhile, the Standards Lead proceeds with drafting on all non-disputed sections so the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards gate is not delayed by single disputed issues. If the disputed issue is resolved late (Month 12-15 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08), a 2-4 week draft-incorporation cycle is scheduled before the Month 18 (2028-04-08) approval gate.

Adaptation Trigger: Sub-group unable to reach consensus by planned date (triggers escalation to arbitration panel within 1 week); arbitration panel ruling contested (triggers Commission escalation); more than 2 major technical disputes unresolved by Month 12 (2027-10-08) (triggers Steering Committee risk assessment and possible extension of standards deadline to Month 21 = 2028-07-08, with Month 30 = 2029-04-08 API mandate at risk); draft standards not complete by Month 15 (2028-01-08) (triggers 2-week extension and expedited final review, risking Month 18 = 2028-04-08 deadline).

5. Real-Time Data Layer and API Performance Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • API Operations Centre Dashboard (latency p95, uptime %, throughput, error rates, incident log)
  • Monthly API Performance Report (by carrier and corridor)
  • Hub Performance Dashboard (uptime, latency, booking-failure rate, mapping-accuracy metrics)
  • Infrastructure Provider SLA Compliance Tracker
  • Carrier Infrastructure Assessment and Co-Funding Allocation Log

Frequency: 24/7 automated monitoring (API ops centre); daily incident summary (if any critical events >15 min downtime); weekly ops-centre meeting (Monday morning); monthly performance report (by the 5th of each month); quarterly Steering Committee review (Months 6, 9, 12 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-10-08 and thereafter)

Responsible Role: API Operations Centre Manager and Data-Layer Technical Lead (PMO), with infrastructure provider escalation protocols

Adaptation Process: API ops centre monitors latency, uptime and throughput against SLAs (p95 <2 sec, 99.95% uptime, ≥500 req/s per corridor). If latency exceeds 5 seconds p95 or uptime drops below 99.5% for >1 hour, ops centre issues a critical incident alert (within 15 minutes) to the carrier or infrastructure provider responsible. Incident must be resolved within 2 hours (target). If a carrier's infrastructure cannot meet SLAs (latency consistently >3 sec or throughput <300 req/s), the PMO triggers co-funding for infrastructure upgrades (EUR 0.5-2M per carrier, Month 6-18 = 2027-04-08 to 2028-04-08). If a hub's booking-failure rate exceeds 2% for more than 1 week, the PMO suspends new carrier onboarding to that hub and convenes a remediation task force (hub operator + carriers + PMO technical team) to debug the mapping errors. Hub downtime >12 hours triggers a postmortem review (within 48 hours) and root-cause analysis. Hub mapping errors >1% of transactions trigger liability-insurance claim and carrier reimbursement (from hub operator's E&O policy).

Adaptation Trigger: API latency p95 exceeds 3 seconds for any corridor for >4 hours (triggers infrastructure review and capacity upgrade plan); API uptime falls below 99.5% for >2 consecutive days (triggers infrastructure provider penalty and failover activation); hub booking-failure rate exceeds 2% for >1 week (triggers carrier onboarding freeze and remediation sprint); hub mapping errors >1% of transactions (triggers retest and carrier compensation from E&O insurance); API response timeout rate >1% during peak hours (triggers load-test and chaos-engineering exercise).

6. Through-Ticket Volume and Measurement Baseline Tracking

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Quarterly Through-Ticket Volume Dashboard (% of cross-border journeys sold as through-tickets, by corridor and channel)
  • Measurement Baseline Report (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 validated baseline)
  • Carrier and Distributor Reporting Template (monthly from Month 18 = 2028-04-08)
  • Independent Evaluator Counterfactual Model and Progress Report (quarterly)
  • Modal-Shift Analysis (air fares vs. through-fares, short-haul air trip trends, by corridor)

Frequency: Baseline survey and definition of 'through-ticket' (Months 0-2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08, report Month 6 = 2027-04-08); validated baseline at Month 9 (2027-07-08); mandatory carrier/distributor reporting monthly starting Month 18 (2028-04-08); quarterly measurement dashboard (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 onward); quarterly Steering Committee review of progress toward the 40% target and complaints-halved target (Months 6, 9, 12, 15 = 2027-04-08 to 2028-01-08 and thereafter)

Responsible Role: Measurement and Evaluation Lead (PMO), with independent evaluator and carriers/distributors providing data

Adaptation Process: Baseline survey (Month 9 = 2027-07-08) establishes: current cross-border through-ticket share (estimated 5-10%), current distributor complaint rate (baseline for 'halved' target), modal split (baseline for modal-shift planning range). From Month 18 (2028-04-08), carriers and accredited distributors submit monthly through-ticket volumes and complaint metrics. Independent evaluator aggregates data quarterly and applies counterfactual methodology (comparing programme corridors to non-programme control routes) to isolate programme impact from external factors (fuel prices, airline capacity, aviation taxes). If baseline measurement at Month 9 (2027-07-08) invalidates the 40% target's plausibility (e.g., baseline is <3% through-ticket share, suggesting much lower market penetration), Steering Committee triggers a 4-week strategic review and may revise the target or increase co-marketing investment. Interim gate at Month 24 (2028-10-08): if through-ticket share is <15% of cross-border journeys, Steering Committee triggers co-funding hold and determines whether to increase public investment or accept a lower outcome. Final evaluation at Month 60 (2031-10-08) will report actual through-ticket share, complaints reduction and modal-shift attribution.

Adaptation Trigger: Baseline measurement at Month 9 (2027-07-08) shows through-ticket share <3% (signals unachievability of 40% target, triggers strategic review); interim gate at Month 24 (2028-10-08) shows through-ticket share <15% (triggers co-funding review and possible contingency reallocation); quarterly through-ticket growth stalls (no increase for 2+ consecutive quarters) (triggers analysis of barriers and possible accelerated consumer-app rollout or co-marketing boost); modal-shift analysis shows through-fares not competitive with airlines on any corridor (triggers assessment of whether regulated fare ceilings or subsidies are needed); distributor complaints remain >baseline at Month 36 (2029-10-08) (triggers investigation and possible claim-resolution process redesign).

7. Governance Body Effectiveness and Risk-Register Monitoring

Monitoring Tools/Platforms:

  • Risk Register (20+ initial risks identified, updated monthly with new risks, mitigation owners, and status)
  • Steering Committee Decision Log (decisions, owners, deadlines, closure tracking)
  • Governance Body Meeting Minutes and Attendance Tracker (PMO responsibility)
  • Escalation Log (issues escalated from working groups, resolution status, closed-out items)
  • Stakeholder Satisfaction Survey (annual, starting Month 12 = 2027-10-08)

Frequency: Monthly PMO risk review (PMO Risk Officer presents top 10 risks at PMO all-hands); Steering Committee risk escalation and mitigation tracking (quarterly, Months 3, 6, 9, 12 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-10-08 and thereafter); governance-body effectiveness self-assessment (Month 6 = 2027-04-08 mid-programme review); annual stakeholder satisfaction survey (Month 12 = 2027-10-08, Month 24 = 2028-10-08, Month 36 = 2029-10-08)

Responsible Role: Governance and Risk Officer (PMO), with Programme Steering Committee oversight and Community Liaison Officer (stakeholder satisfaction)

Adaptation Process: Risk Officer maintains a living risk register with ~20 key risks (regulatory adoption, governance deadlock, budget overrun, carrier non-compliance, hub failures, GDPR/competition challenges, smaller-carrier readiness, modal-shift viability). Each risk has a mitigation owner (e.g., PMO Stakeholder Lead for political/governance risks, Technical Lead for technical risks, Finance Officer for budget risks). Monthly review assesses: has the risk materialized? Is mitigation on track? Have new risks emerged? If a risk's mitigation action is overdue or ineffective, or if the risk's probability/impact increases, the Risk Officer escalates to the Steering Committee within 5 working days with a decision request (approve revised mitigation, escalate to Commission, or accept the risk). Unmitigated critical risks (e.g., Regulation adoption slips past Month 9 = 2027-07-08) trigger a contingency-activation decision at the Steering Committee. Governance-body effectiveness self-assessment (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) reviews: Are decisions being made on schedule (target: resolve issues within 4 weeks)? Are working groups productive or becoming 'talking shops'? Is stakeholder engagement sufficient (target: >70% satisfaction among all stakeholder groups)? If satisfaction drops below 70% in any group, Community Liaison Officer triggers 4-week focused outreach. If working groups are producing re-litigated decisions (same issues debated repeatedly), Steering Committee enforces decision finality and narrows working-group scope.

Adaptation Trigger: Any critical risk (probability×impact >15/25) unmitigated (triggers Steering Committee decision within 5 days); risk mitigation action overdue by >2 weeks (escalation to action owner's manager); new critical risk identified (triggers rapid assessment and mitigation planning within 1 week); Steering Committee decision delayed >4 weeks (triggers chair escalation and simplified decision-making protocol); stakeholder satisfaction <70% in any group (triggers focused outreach; if <60%, escalation to DG MOVE); governance-body meeting cancellations or no-shows >2 in a quarter (signals disengagement, triggers restructuring or workload reduction); more than 3 decisions re-litigated in Steering Committee (signals working-group lack of clarity, triggers tighter TOR and decision-finality rule).

Governance Extra

Governance Validation Checks

  1. Completeness Confirmation: All core governance components from Stages 2–5 are generated and present: internal governance bodies (Steering Committee, PMO, working groups, arbitration panel, regulators, consumer team, ethics committee), implementation plan (step-by-step governance setup from Month 0 = 2026-10-08 to Month 60 = 2031-10-08), decision-escalation matrix (11 major issue types with approval processes and negative consequences), and monitoring progress (five approach tracks with tools, frequency, adaptation triggers). The governance framework is internally complete.
  2. Internal Consistency Check: The framework is logically aligned across stages. Implementation plan activations (e.g., Steering Committee appointment at Month 1 = 2026-11-08, arbitration panel at Month 2 = 2026-12-08) feed into decision-escalation procedures, which rely on authority delegations secured in setup phase. Monitoring tracks (budget, milestones, conformance, disputes, measurement) all feed escalation triggers to the bodies defined in Stage 2. Working-group deliverables (binding standards by Month 18 = 2028-04-08) are gated by Steering Committee decisions and supported by arbitration panel dispute resolution. Consistency confirmed with one minor note: the ethics committee's oversight of compliance is mentioned but not formally invoked as an escalation endpoint in the matrix; recommend adding ethics escalation for GDPR/accessibility/conflict-of-interest discoveries.
  3. Clarity of Roles and Authority: The programme sponsor (DG MOVE) holds ultimate authority and budget-holder role, confirmed in Stage 2 and Stage 3. Steering Committee has binding authority over standards, corridors, and budget above EUR 50M; PMO has operational authority up to EUR 10M and escalates disputes. Arbitration panel authority is explicitly scoped to technical standards only, with escalation to Commission for conflicts. Member-state regulators hold enforcement authority with lead-regulator mechanism for cross-border cases. Consumer product director owns the app and support centre. Ethics committee is advisory but can recommend suspension of participants. This structure is clear, though the Programme Director's authority during governance setup (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) before Steering Committee appointment could be explicitly stated as interim/transitional (currently implied).
  4. Process Depth and Clarity: Key operational processes are defined at moderate detail. Conformance testing (Stage 5) specifies testing labs, checklist items, and queue allocation; passenger-rights backstop (assumptions) specifies reroute timelines and refund procedures; refund dispute resolution (Stage 5 escalation matrix) specifies 5-day panel ruling targets; GDPR compliance includes DPIA, DPA consensus, and consent protocols (Stage 3). However, three areas lack granular definition: (a) Conflict-of-interest management: ethics code is drafted (Stage 3), but procedures for handling discovered conflicts during programme execution (e.g., a Steering Committee member's carrier receives co-funding) are not detailed; recommend adding a conflict-of-interest escalation procedure to the ethics committee. (b) Whistleblower investigation: confidential channel is established (Stage 3), but investigation procedures (who investigates, how findings are acted on, retaliation-protection enforcement) are not specified; recommend defining a formal investigation SOP. (c) Change control: no formal change-control board is described for mid-programme adjustments to scope, timelines, or budget allocation; recommend that major changes (scope reduction, deadline extension >4 weeks, budget reallocation >EUR 50M) require Steering Committee approval via a structured change-request process.
  5. Thresholds and Delegation Clarity: Delegation is well-defined for budget (PMO up to EUR 10M, Steering Committee EUR 50M+, Commission above cap), milestones (Steering Committee binding on standards/corridors/gates; arbitration panel on technical disputes within 60 days; Commission on regulatory conflicts). Escalation thresholds are specific: budget overrun triggers at 115% of pro-rata spend (Tier 1), 120%+ (Tier 2), 125%+ (Tier 3); milestone slippage >2 weeks triggers PMO escalation, >4 weeks triggers Steering Committee; carrier non-compliance by >2 weeks triggers remediation notice, >4 weeks triggers co-funding hold and enforcement escalation. However, one gap: the arbitration panel's decision authority ends at Month 30 (2029-04-08) per the decision-escalation matrix, but the monitoring plan (Stage 5) does not explicitly state what happens to ongoing technical disputes after Month 30 (2029-04-08) (e.g., if a carrier disputes a data-quality audit finding post-API mandate). Recommend clarifying that the panel's authority extends through Month 60 (2031-10-08) for any remaining standards disputes or that a new body takes over.
  6. Integration and Information Flow: Components are well-integrated. Budget tracking (Stage 5) informs Steering Committee decisions on contingency activation; measurement dashboard (Stage 5) feeds gate decisions (15% through-ticket share at Month 24 = 2028-10-08 gate); carrier conformance tracking informs corridor readiness gates; risk register (Stage 5) escalates unmitigated critical risks to Steering Committee within 5 days. Information flow is hierarchical (PMO to Steering Committee weekly, Steering Committee to Commission via escalation matrix as needed). One area for improvement: the flow of regulator compliance findings to the Steering Committee is mentioned in Stage 5 (Standing Regulators Committee monthly call with PMO) but not explicitly included in the Steering Committee's quarterly agenda template; recommend adding 'Member-State Regulator Enforcement Report' as a standard SC agenda item starting Month 6 (2027-04-08).

Tough Questions

  1. What is the current probability-weighted forecast for the Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services adoption by Month 9 (2027-07-08), and what credible contingency plan exists if Parliament or Council votes for material amendments (e.g., narrowed scope, weaker non-discrimination rules) that invalidate the pre-work standards? Is the 'shadow standards' team (proposed Month 0–3 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08) staffed and adequately funded to execute a 2–4 week rapid-rework cycle if final text diverges?
  2. Show evidence that the written Council/Commission delegation of binding arbitration authority to the panel will be secured by Month 2 (2026-12-08). What is the legal pathway, and which Commission and Council contacts have pre-agreed the delegation scope? If delegation slips past Month 2 (2026-12-08), what is the contingency governance model, and how does it avoid losing authority over the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards approval?
  3. Provide a detailed cost breakdown and committed funding sources for the EUR 215 million free contingency reserve. How is it held at DG MOVE, what is the release process, and who has authority to commit it (Steering Committee or Commission)? If free contingency is consumed by Month 24 (2028-10-08), does the programme have a mechanism to request supplementary budget authority, and what is the realistic timeline (6–12 months?) for Commission approval?
  4. Which 12–18 carriers have been formally identified as hub-eligible (revenue under EUR 50M, or IT staff under 10 FTE)? Have regional hub operators been pre-identified or pre-qualified to confirm they can deliver the four priority-corridor hubs operational by Month 9 (2027-07-08)? If hub procurement slips beyond Month 3 (2027-01-08) or hub operators cannot be contracted, what is the fallback (e.g., mandatory native OSDM integration for all carriers, or use a publicly hosted gateway)?
  5. What is the verified baseline measurement (Month 9 = 2027-07-08) of current cross-border through-ticket share (assumed 5–10%), and does that baseline support the plausibility of a 40% target by Month 60 (2031-10-08)? If the baseline is below 3%, what decision triggers (co-marketing surge, regulated fares, or target revision) will the Steering Committee pre-commit to at Month 12 (2027-10-08) before momentum is lost?
  6. Have the 2–3 accredited payment institutions been pre-marketed or pre-vetted to confirm they will apply for accreditation (call Month 2 = 2026-12-08, decision Month 8 = 2027-06-08)? What transaction-fee benchmarking has been done to validate the EUR 0.3–0.5% cap target? If fewer than 2 providers apply, what is the credible fallback (emergency procurement timeline, cost, and operational risk)?
  7. Provide written confirmation from Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, Trenitalia, Renfe, ÖBB, NS, SJ and SNCB (or their representatives in CER) that they commit to API integration by Month 30 (2029-04-08) and accept the penalty (0.5–1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue in escrow) for non-compliance. If any major incumbent declines to sign a Commitment Letter by Month 3 (2027-01-08), what enforcement strategy will the programme execute, and does it risk political intervention that softens the Month 30 (2029-04-08) deadline?

Summary

The governance framework for the EUR 1.5 billion, five-year EU through-ticketing programme is comprehensive and operationally grounded. It establishes a clear hierarchy (DG MOVE as sponsor, Steering Committee with binding strategic authority, PMO with operational execution, arbitration panel for technical disputes, member-state regulators for enforcement) and defines detailed procedures for standards development (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 gate), carrier integration (Month 30 = 2029-04-08 API mandate), measurement (40% through-ticket target), and budget control (contingency tiers). Key strengths are the explicit escalation matrix linking each decision type to approval bodies and timelines, the month-by-month implementation roadmap (Stages 3–5) with specific deliverables and adaptation triggers, and the risk-aware contingency planning (Tier 1–3 budget activation, regulation adoption gate, carrier non-compliance procedures). Primary dependencies are regulatory adoption by Month 9 (2027-07-08), written Council delegation of arbitration authority by Month 2 (2026-12-08), and carrier Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08). The framework is realistic for a pragmatic, non-aggressive scenario but requires early political buy-in from major member states and carriers, disciplined budget tracking with clear contingency triggers, and sustained stakeholder engagement to manage the inherent tensions between incumbent carrier resistance, smaller-operator inclusion, and fixed timelines. Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability (estimated EUR 45M/year unfunded run-cost) must be addressed by Month 48 (2030-10-08) to avoid programme collapse.

Suggestion 1 - OSDM – Open Sales and Distribution Model (UIC / OSJD-independent, with CER and EU-Rail partners)

OSDM is an open API standard for selling rail products across operators, led by the International Union of Railways (UIC) with members such as DB, SBB, ÖBB, SNCF and others. It covers offers, bookings, fulfilment, refunds and exchanges. It has been developed and maintained since about 2020 and is being adopted by several operators and distributors. It is the technical basis named in the programme brief.

Success Metrics

Live implementations by several operators and distributors (exact count not verified). Published versioned specification and open documentation. Reuse of the standard in procurement and EU-level proposals.

Risks and Challenges Faced

Uneven adoption by carriers: handled by voluntary working groups and published reference implementations, but pace remains slow. Competing national formats: addressed through mapping to existing UIC and TAP/TSI messages. No enforcement power: still unresolved; this is where the programme's panel and regulation must add force.

Where to Find More Information

https://osdm.io UIC website, OSDM pages: https://uic.org CER (Community of European Railway and Infrastructure Companies): https://www.cer.be

Actionable Steps

Contact the OSDM working group via the contact form on osdm.io and ask for the conformance-test approach and governance charter. Approach UIC's digital/distribution unit (role: OSDM programme manager) for a briefing on adoption data. Ask CER's passenger/ticketing policy officer for the carriers' view on mandatory API exposure.

Rationale for Suggestion

Direct technical match: the programme requires OSDM-compatible APIs. The OSDM community shows how a standard is governed, versioned and conformance-tested among competing carriers, which informs the Month 18 (2028-04-08) binding standards and the certification scheme. Geography matches (pan-European, Swiss and EU carriers). It lacks binding enforcement, which the programme adds.

Suggestion 2 - Alliance SwissPass / Swiss Direct Service (Nationale Direkter Verkehr) clearing

Switzerland's public transport sector runs a shared ticketing and revenue-allocation system through the Alliance SwissPass and the Direct Service (Direkter Verkehr) arrangement, in which hundreds of transport companies sell and accept each other's tickets and apportion revenue through a common allocation system. The sector association (VöV/Alliance SwissPass) operates the rules and the clearing. It has run for decades and is continuously updated.

Success Metrics

Near-universal national through-ticket coverage across operators (exact figures not verified). Stable long-run operation of allocation and clearing. Single customer account across modes.

Risks and Challenges Faced

Fair allocation between large and small operators: handled by agreed allocation keys and periodic reviews. Data protection for customer data: handled through the SwissPass account design and sector rules. Governance among many companies: addressed by a sector association with defined decision rules.

Where to Find More Information

https://www.allianceswisspass.ch VöV/UTP: https://www.voev.ch SBB: https://www.sbb.ch

Actionable Steps

Contact Alliance SwissPass through its published contact channel and request a briefing on allocation rules and dispute handling. Ask VöV/UTP (role: head of tariffs and distribution) how disputes between operators are resolved. Connect with SBB's international distribution team via its corporate contacts.

Rationale for Suggestion

It is a working example of single-ticket, multi-carrier sales with automatic revenue split, close to the programme's settlement and apportionment challenge, including small and large operators together. It supports the choice to extend shared rules rather than build a new central payment entity. Switzerland is also directly involved in the Wien–München–Zürich corridor. Limits: one country, one legal regime.

Suggestion 3 - Deutschlandticket (Germany) – nationwide flat-rate ticket with sector clearing

Launched in May 2023, the Deutschlandticket is a monthly subscription valid on regional and local public transport across Germany, sold by many operators and distributors, with revenue shared among about a thousand transport companies through a clearing arrangement and federal-state compensation funding. Distribution and clearing are coordinated by the sector (VDV and associated bodies).

Success Metrics

Several million subscribers reported shortly after launch (exact figure not verified). Participation of nearly all regional operators. Operating continuously since launch.

Risks and Challenges Faced

Funding uncertainty between federal and state governments: handled by repeated political agreements, still a recurring risk. Revenue allocation among many operators: handled by a sector clearing key and later adjustments. Fast launch on legacy IT: handled by allowing existing sales channels plus a common data format.

Where to Find More Information

https://www.vdv.de Federal Ministry for Digital and Transport: https://bmdv.bund.de Deutsche Bahn: https://www.bahn.de

Actionable Steps

Contact VDV (role: head of tariff and distribution) for lessons on clearing and interface standardisation. Ask the Federal Ministry's rail-policy unit about the co-funding mechanism. Request an interview with DB Vertrieb's product team through DB's press office.

Rationale for Suggestion

It shows a large multi-operator product launched quickly (months, not years) on existing sector structures, with standardised distribution interfaces, shared revenue split and public co-funding tied to results. This informs the milestone co-funding and no-new-entity approach. It also shows the funding-cliff risk the programme faces after Month 60 (2031-10-08). It is domestic and subscription-based, not a per-journey cross-border through-ticket.

Suggestion 4 - Secondary: Rail Baltica joint ticketing preparation (Baltic states)

Secondary suggestion. Rail Baltica is a new cross-border rail link among Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania with Poland connections, and the planning includes shared, interoperable passenger ticketing across several national operators. Details of the ticketing design are limited and not fully verified.

Success Metrics

Not yet established; ticketing is not live (not verified).

Risks and Challenges Faced

Small national operators with differing systems and budgets. Long infrastructure timelines delaying ticketing decisions.

Where to Find More Information

https://www.railbaltica.org

Actionable Steps

Contact RB Rail AS through the website to ask about the ticketing workstream and any lessons on shared back-ends.

Rationale for Suggestion

Shows early-stage multi-country ticketing planning among smaller operators with weaker IT, relevant to the hub and smaller-carrier strand and the Lisbon–Tallinn ambition. Evidence of delivered outcomes is limited.

Summary

Reference projects for the EU cross-border rail through-ticketing programme (Pragmatic Foundation: certified access, accredited payment providers, regional hubs, arbitration panel). Primary references are real and documented: the OSDM standard (UIC), the Swiss Alliance SwissPass/NRT public-transport distribution and clearing, and Germany's Deutschlandticket with its clearing and revenue-split model. A secondary reference is the Nordic/Baltic Rail Baltica ticketing effort. Figures are stated only where reasonably established; others are marked unverified. Geographic proximity is high for all of them (Europe). None is a full multi-country, multi-carrier through-ticket regime with a passenger-rights backstop, so lessons apply by component. Contacts are organisations and roles, not named individuals. Links should be checked before use (not verified).

1. Regulatory Adoption Status and Legislative Text Alignment

The programme's entire timeline and governance model depend on the Commission Regulation being adopted by Month 9 (2027-07-08) and defining non-discriminatory access, settlement, and passenger-rights obligations. If adoption slips beyond Month 10 (2027-08-08) or the final text diverges materially (e.g., stricter liability, narrower data-sharing scope, or mandatory API exemptions), the Month 18 (2028-04-08) binding standards deadline and the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate are at risk of 6–12 month delays. Early tracking and shadow standards pre-work reduce re-work downstream and enable accelerated standards finalisation if adoption is delayed.

Data to Collect

  • Final adopted text of the Commission's proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail (expected adoption Month 6–12 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-10-08)
  • Parliamentary amendments (TRAN, IMCO committees) and member-state negotiating positions on liability, data-sharing scope, mandatory API timelines, and non-discriminatory access definitions
  • Gaps between the final Regulation text and OSDM v2.1 specification, access-term templates, settlement message standards, and passenger-rights protocols
  • Timeline confirmation for Council delegation of binding technical authority to the arbitration panel (target Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23)

Simulation Steps

  • Track weekly Parliament TRAN and IMCO rapporteur briefings (Months 0–9 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-07-08) using public Parliament legislative tracking (Europarl.europa.eu legislative observatory)
  • Monitor member-state positions via Council Presidency summaries and official transport minister statements (EUR-Lex, Council website, bilateral liaison with Germany, France, Belgium, Austria, Spain transport ministers)
  • Conduct gap analysis: compare Commission's May 2026 proposed text against OSDM v2.1 (UIC specification) and draft candidate standards on access-term templates, settlement formats, and passenger-rights rules using a shadow standards pre-work team (5–8 FTE)
  • Model three adoption scenarios (Month 9 = 2027-07-08, Month 11–12 = 2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08 with text changes, blocked past Month 12 = 2027-10-08) with pre-drafted standards language for contested areas so accelerated standards-setting can begin immediately post-adoption

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage DG MOVE, Commission legal services and EU Agency for Railways to confirm the Council delegation pathway and legal feasibility of binding the arbitration panel by Month 2 (2026-12-08)
  • Consult the European Parliament's TRAN and IMCO rapporteurs monthly (Months 0–9 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-07-08) to obtain early-warning signalling of blocking amendments or adoption delays
  • Present draft standards (from shadow pre-work) to a UIC OSDM working-group representative and to a carrier technology advisory panel (CER-nominated) by Month 6 (2027-04-08) to validate technical feasibility and carrier buy-in
  • Secure written confirmation from the Commission and Council that the final Regulation text aligns with the programme's OSDM and access-term assumptions by Month 9 (2027-07-08); if material divergence is identified, trigger re-baseline decision by Month 12 (2027-10-08)

Responsible Parties

  • DG MOVE (programme owner; regulatory liaison with Parliament and member states)
  • EU Agency for Railways (technical secretariat; OSDM gap analysis)
  • Shadow standards pre-work team (5–8 FTE; OSDM specialist, legal counsel, carrier IT representative) hired by Month 0 (2026-10-08)
  • CER (carrier federation; transportation of carrier feedback on standards feasibility)

Assumptions

  • High: The Commission's proposed Regulation will be adopted by Parliament and Council by Month 9 (2027-07-08) with only minor text divergence from the May 2026 proposal (sensitivity: high). If adoption slips to Month 11–12 (2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08) or the text diverges materially on liability or data-sharing scope, the standards-setting window compresses from 9 months to 3–4 months, forcing either non-consensus or rushed standards.
  • High: The Council will grant written delegation of binding technical-decision authority to the arbitration panel by Month 2 (2026-12-08) (sensitivity: high). This is a political decision not yet confirmed; delays in Council adoption will compress the carrier-commitment timeline and risk incumbent non-compliance.
  • Medium: OSDM v2.1 specification will remain stable and compatible with the proposed Regulation's mandatory API scope (sensitivity: medium). If UIC releases OSDM v3.0 with material changes during Months 0–12 (2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08), standards work must be re-scoped.
  • Medium: DG MOVE and the Commission will publicly signal support for the programme and the arbitration panel's authority by Month 1 (2026-11-08) (sensitivity: medium). Political wavering or ambiguity undermines carrier buy-in for Commitment Letters.
  • Low: CER member carriers will provide honest feedback on standards feasibility and IT integration timelines during gap analysis (Months 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) (sensitivity: low). Carriers may downplay readiness to extract co-funding or demand exemptions.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 6 (2027-04-08), confirm that (1) Parliament and Council adoption is on track for Month 9 (2027-07-08) or identify a specific blocking issue and revised target; (2) shadow standards pre-work has completed gap analysis against OSDM v2.1 and drafted candidate access-term and settlement standards for at least two contested areas (inventory parity, refund processing timelines); (3) at least 4 of 8 major carriers (estimated) have reviewed draft standards and signalled technical feasibility for Month 30 (2029-04-08) API exposure. If any condition is not met, escalate to Steering Committee by Month 7 (2027-05-08) for re-baseline decision.

Notes

  • Regulation adoption is the critical upstream gate; every month of delay compresses the standards window (baseline 9 months, floor 3–4 months) and threatens Month 18 (2028-04-08) binding standards deadline.
  • Shadow standards pre-work (5–8 FTE from Month 0 = 2026-10-08) is essential to enable rapid post-adoption finalisation; without pre-work, standards finalisation would require 9–12 months and miss Month 18 (2028-04-08).
  • Council delegation is a political/legal prerequisite; absence of written authority undermines arbitration panel credibility and carrier Commitment Letters. Secure delegation target Month 2 (2026-12-08), target Month 1.5 (2026-11-23).
  • Material text divergence from the Commission proposal (especially on liability, data-sharing scope, or API exemptions) would require standards re-work; establish re-baseline gate by Month 7 (2027-05-08) if adoption text diverges significantly.
  • Contingency acceleration pathway: if adoption slips past Month 8 (2027-06-08), contract external standards consortium by Month 8.5 (2027-06-23) for 4–6 week compressed standards finalisation (EUR 1–2M cost from EUR 10M governance line budget).

2. Carrier Commitment and Incumbent Acceptance of Arbitration Panel Authority

Carrier commitment is the foundation of the arbitration panel's authority and the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate. Without binding Commitment Letters signed by major incumbents (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, ÖBB) by Month 3 (2027-01-08), the panel is advisory and carries no enforcement power. Large carriers can delay or contest technical rulings, fragmenting the network and missing the critical-path milestones. Incumbent non-compliance by any of the top 5 carriers would reduce through-ticket coverage to below 70% of potential corridors, undermining the 40% share target.

Data to Collect

  • Written Commitment Letters from all carriers with annual cross-border revenue above EUR 50 million, signed by Month 3 (2027-01-08), accepting arbitration panel authority, 14-day compliance deadlines, and penalties (0.5–1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue in escrow for non-compliance)
  • Individual carrier IT readiness assessments: estimated integration cost (native API vs. hub), timeline to Month 30 (2029-04-08) API exposure, and private IT investment budget per carrier
  • Incumbent carrier political positioning and signalling of non-compliance risk (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, ÖBB, Renfe, Trenitalia, ÖBB) from bilateral executive negotiation (Months 0–3 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08)
  • Smaller carriers' eligibility for hub integration (cross-border revenue under EUR 50M, booking system older than 10 years, or IT staff under 10 FTE) and their co-funding requests

Simulation Steps

  • Model carrier-by-carrier IT integration cost using baseline scenarios: native OSDM API implementation (EUR 10–20M per major carrier, EUR 2–8M per SME), hub integration (EUR 2–5M per carrier), or regional hub use without IT investment. Sensitivity: cost variance ±30% depending on legacy-system age and in-house IT capacity.
  • Conduct bilateral executive engagement with SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, ÖBB, Renfe, Trenitalia and NS leadership (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08.5 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-23) to present the arbitration panel framework, escrow penalties, and co-funding offers. Record each carrier's stated compliance commitment and any preconditions (e.g. delay, API scope exemptions, co-funding rate).
  • Use CER quarterly roundtables (December 2026, February 2027, April 2027) to publicly present Commitment Letter terms and facilitate signature-gathering; measure attendance and signatory intent as a proxy for coalition strength.
  • Model the consequence of non-compliance by any of the top 5 carriers (SNCF, DB, Trenitalia, Renfe, ÖBB) on corridor coverage: estimate what percentage of cross-border traffic remains bookable end-to-end if one major carrier refuses API exposure (estimate: 60–75% if incumbent excludes one corridor).

Expert Validation Steps

  • Have the arbitration panel secretariat and DG MOVE legal counsel review final Commitment Letter language by Month 1 (2026-11-08) to confirm enforceability of penalties under EU law and national insolvency/contract law.
  • Engage CER's legal and policy lead to validate that the proposed carrier commitment terms are realistic and enforceable under CER member-company bylaws and carrier regulatory frameworks.
  • Present the arbitration panel delegation document to three major carrier CIOs (representative sample from SNCF, DB, ÖBB) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) to assess technical and institutional feasibility of the panel's authority; flag any legal or operational blocker for escalation to DG MOVE.
  • Validate incumbent non-compliance signalling by Month 3 (2027-01-08): if any carrier above EUR 100M revenue has not signed the Commitment Letter, escalate to DG MOVE and the Commission for enforcement action (threaten EU funding suspension or antitrust investigation) by Month 4 (2027-02-08).

Responsible Parties

  • DG MOVE (programme owner; responsible for political negotiation with member states and incumbent carriers, and for escalation to Commission if carriers refuse commitment)
  • Carrier Engagement Manager / Coalition Builder (designated by Month 1 = 2026-11-08; leads bilateral negotiations with SNCF, DB, ÖBB, Renfe, Trenitalia, NS, SJ, SNCB)
  • CER (facilitates public roundtables and coordinates smaller-carrier and association input)
  • Arbitration panel secretariat (validates legal enforceability of panel authority and penalties by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23)

Assumptions

  • High: All carriers above EUR 50M annual cross-border revenue will sign binding Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08) accepting arbitration panel authority and penalties (sensitivity: high). If a major incumbent (SNCF, DB, ÖBB) refuses, the panel becomes advisory and large carriers can delay or contest rulings indefinitely.
  • High: Incumbent carriers' estimated IT integration cost (native API EUR 10–20M per major, EUR 2–8M per SME) is accurate and carriers' private IT budgets are sufficient to fund integration without requesting 100% public co-funding (sensitivity: high). If carriers demand greater than 30% co-funding for native builds, the EUR 290M co-funding allocation will be exhausted and trigger Tier 2–3 contingency cuts.
  • Medium: Smaller carriers (12–18 estimated) meeting hub-eligibility criteria (revenue <EUR 50M, legacy system >10 years, or IT staff <10 FTE) will choose hub integration over native API build, reducing their co-funding demand (sensitivity: medium). If more carriers demand full co-funding for native APIs, co-funding budget shortfall occurs.
  • Medium: The Commission will take enforcement action (EU funding suspension, antitrust investigation) against any major carrier that refuses the Commitment Letter by Month 4 (2027-02-08), signalling credible consequences for non-compliance (sensitivity: medium). Political reluctance to enforce against domestic 'champion' carriers could weaken this signal.
  • Low: CER will cooperate in facilitating public roundtables and carrier signature-gathering (sensitivity: low). CER is institutionally committed to cross-border interoperability but is also accountable to incumbent members; it may seek to water down enforcement terms.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 3 (2027-01-08), confirm that (1) at least 95% of carriers above EUR 50M revenue (estimated ~20 carriers) have signed binding Commitment Letters accepting arbitration authority and penalties; (2) all eight major carriers (SNCF, DB, Trenitalia, Renfe, ÖBB, NS, SJ, SNCB) have signed; (3) each carrier has provided an estimated IT integration cost, timeline and private investment commitment; (4) at least 10 of 12–18 hub-eligible smaller carriers have confirmed hub-integration preference or native-API co-funding request. If <95% have signed or any major incumbent refuses, escalate to DG MOVE by Month 4 (2027-02-08) for Commission enforcement action and re-baseline decision (pause programme if enforcement is not credible).

Notes

  • Incumbent resistance is the highest-risk factor for the arbitration panel's credibility; secure Commitment Letters before Month 3 (2027-01-08) is a critical gate.
  • Bilateral negotiation with SNCF, DB, ÖBB and other large carriers (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08.5 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-23) must be personally conducted by the Carrier Engagement Manager and the Programme Director; phone calls and formal letters are insufficient.
  • Non-compliance by a single major carrier on one corridor (e.g., DB refusing to expose inventory data on the Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln route) fragments the through-ticket network and undermines the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate; escalate and enforce immediately.
  • Smaller carriers' co-funding requests should be capped at EUR 2–8M per carrier (hub integration) or EUR 10–15M (native API); any request above this range should trigger cost-justification review by Month 2 (2026-12-08).
  • If cumulative carrier co-funding requests exceed EUR 350M by Month 3 (2027-01-08) (vs. EUR 290M budget), trigger Tier 2 contingency (reduce co-funding rate to 10%, limit hubs to priority corridors) by Month 6 (2027-04-08).

3. Hub Procurement, Operationalization and Carrier Integration Readiness

Regional hubs are the mechanism for enabling 12–18 smaller legacy-system carriers to meet the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate without expensive native integration (estimated EUR 10–20M per carrier). Hub readiness is on the critical path: if hub procurement slips past Month 3 (2027-01-08) or hubs are not operational by Month 9 (2027-07-08), integration window for carriers is compressed to 6–9 months, reducing Month 30 (2029-04-08) readiness from ~85% to ~60–70% and fragmenting the through-ticket network. Hub data-quality failures (mapping errors causing >2% booking-failure rate) undermine distributor and passenger trust and trigger refund disputes exceeding the EUR 10M passenger-rights reserve.

Data to Collect

  • Hub operator qualifications and bids (technical architecture, uptime SLAs, latency targets, capacity, disaster-recovery plans) for 4–6 regional hubs (Four priority corridors + 2 TEN-T hubs)
  • Integration timelines and mapping accuracy: legacy-carrier system architecture assessment, data-format compatibility, and estimated dual-run testing duration per carrier (target 2–4 weeks)
  • Hub operating costs (opex), revenue models (per-booking fees or annual subscriptions), and cost-recovery feasibility by Month 48 (2030-10-08)
  • Smaller-carrier integration readiness: IT staff capacity, network latency constraints, and commitment to participate in hub integration by Month 30 (2029-04-08)

Simulation Steps

  • Issue RFP for regional hub operators by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) specifying technical requirements (99.9% uptime, <2-second latency, <2-hour incident recovery, ≥10,000 bookings/day capacity). Request cost estimates: upfront development EUR 0.5–1M per hub, annual opex EUR 0.8–1.2M per hub, and fee revenue model (EUR 0.5–1.5 per booking or EUR 50–200K per carrier per year).
  • Model hub economics: baseline opex EUR 1.2M/year vs. fee revenue EUR 0.73M/year at capacity, leaving a EUR 0.47M/year gap (EUR 1.9M/year for 4 hubs, ~EUR 9.5M over 5 years). Sensitivity: cost variance ±20% depending on carrier-concentration and booking-volume growth; revenue variance ±30% if carrier adoption is slower than planned.
  • Conduct joint technical integration workshops pairing hub operators and 2–3 eligible legacy-system carriers per hub (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) to identify network latency, API compatibility and data-format mismatches. Estimate dual-run pilot duration per carrier: 2–4 weeks (baseline), 4–8 weeks if mapping errors are detected.
  • Simulate hub failure scenarios: if a hub serving 6 carriers fails and recovery takes 12–48 hours (vs. target 2-hour SLA), model the operational and financial impact (estimated 10,000–50,000 daily searches affected, EUR 100–500K in cascade refunds and claims per incident).

Expert Validation Steps

  • Have an independent integration consultant assess hub operator bids for technical feasibility and SLA achievability by Month 2 (2026-12-08); flag any bid with unachievable latency (<2 seconds) or uptime (99.9%) guarantees.
  • Conduct technical due diligence with 3–4 hub operator finalists (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) to validate their disaster-recovery plans, data-encryption protocols, and compliance with GDPR and payment-services regulations.
  • Engage 2–3 eligible legacy-system carriers (one per region: central Europe, southeast Europe, Iberia) in pilot integration workshops (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) and validate that their network latency and API compatibility issues can be resolved within the 2–4 week dual-run window.
  • Commission an independent hub-economics audit (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) to validate cost estimates and fee-revenue assumptions; flag any hub projected to have an annual loss above EUR 0.5M by Month 48 (2030-10-08), signalling cost-recovery risk.

Responsible Parties

  • Smaller Carriers and Regional Integration Lead (responsible for hub procurement RFP, contract negotiation, and pilot integration)
  • Regional support coordinators (3–5 FTE, hired by Month 4 = 2027-02-08; on-site integration troubleshooting)
  • Hub operator (contractor; responsible for 99.9% uptime SLA, mapping accuracy, incident response)
  • Independent integration consultant (validates hub technical feasibility and smaller-carrier readiness)

Assumptions

  • Medium: At least 4–6 qualified hub operator bidders will respond to RFP by Month 2 (2026-12-08) with competitive pricing and credible SLA commitments (sensitivity: medium). If fewer than 3 qualified bidders respond, there is limited competitive choice and cost competition is weak.
  • High: Hub data-mapping accuracy will be validated to below 0.5% booking-failure rate (target) and below 2% threshold for onboarding suspension by Month 18 (2028-04-08) (sensitivity: high). Legacy-system translation errors (missing seat allocations, incorrect pricing, duplicate bookings) could cause 2–5% failure rate post-launch, requiring 4–8 week rework per carrier.
  • Medium: Hub cost-recovery is achievable by Month 48 (2030-10-08) through carrier-subscription fees (EUR 50–200K per carrier per year or per-booking fees) combined with volume growth (sensitivity: medium). If carrier adoption is slower than planned or fee-revenue models are uncompetitive, EUR 1.9M/year gap (for 4 hubs) persists, requiring extended public subsidy.
  • Medium: Smaller carriers' network latency and API compatibility issues can be resolved within the 2–4 week dual-run pilot window (sensitivity: medium). Carriers with extremely constrained network connectivity (e.g., regional operators in southeast Europe with limited bandwidth) may require 4–8 week pilots or custom network solutions, delaying integration.
  • Medium: Hub operators will maintain 99.9% uptime SLA and <2-hour incident recovery through the 5-year programme (sensitivity: medium). A single catastrophic hub failure lasting >12 hours could affect 4–6 carriers simultaneously and trigger cascading refund claims exceeding the EUR 10M passenger-rights reserve.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 3 (2027-01-08), confirm that (1) at least 4 qualified hub operators have been awarded contracts with operational start by Month 9 (2027-07-08); (2) each hub has committed to 99.9% uptime, <2-second latency and <2-hour recovery SLAs in writing; (3) all 12–18 hub-eligible carriers have participated in technical integration workshops and provided data-format compatibility assessments; (4) at least 6–8 carriers have committed to pilot integration with assigned dual-run dates in Months 15–18 (2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08). By Month 9 (2027-07-08), confirm all hubs are operational and ready for pilot carriers. By Month 18 (2028-04-08), confirm that all hubs and assigned carriers have completed dual-run pilots with booking-failure rate below 0.5%; any hub or carrier with failure rate above 2% for >1 week shall be escalated for re-work (estimated 4–8 week delay) and suspended from new onboarding.

Notes

  • Hub procurement is the critical upstream task; delay past Month 3 (2027-01-08) cascades to Month 9 (2027-07-08) operational start and compresses carrier integration to 6–9 months (vs. planned 12 months), causing 15–25% readiness slippage by Month 30 (2029-04-08).
  • Hub economics gap (EUR 0.47M/year per hub) is an unfunded item in the budget; cost-recovery decision must be made by Month 30 (2029-04-08) (extend public subsidy vs. raise carrier fees vs. consolidate hubs). If decision is deferred, hub losses compound to EUR 5–10M by Month 48 (2030-10-08).
  • Data-mapping errors are the highest operational risk; independent validation by Month 6 (2027-04-08) and mandatory dual-run pilots (Months 15–18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08) before production go-live are essential to prevent post-launch refund disputes.
  • Hub failure stop threshold (2% booking-failure rate for >1 week) is a gate: suspend new carrier onboarding to a failed hub immediately and allocate 4–8 weeks for rework. If multiple hubs fail simultaneously, escalate to Programme Director and consider fallback to gateway or bilateral pairing (cost unestimated).
  • Smaller carriers' IT resources are limited; on-site mentoring by 3–5 regional coordinators (budget EUR 1–2M over five years) is essential to support successful integration during Months 6–30 (2027-04-08 to 2029-04-08).

4. Budget Burn Rate and Contingency Trigger Events

The EUR 1,500M cap is fixed (user constraint) and the EUR 215M free contingency (EUR 225M – EUR 10M earmarked) is the only buffer against overruns. A 20–30% overrun (EUR 300–450M) exceeds free contingency by EUR 85–235M. Early detection of overrun signals (by Month 12–18 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08) enables timely contingency-tier response (cost cuts, co-funding rate reductions) that protects critical-path items (conformance testing, capacity building, smaller-carrier support). Delayed detection leads to late-stage cuts (Month 24–30 = 2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08) that compromise Month 30 (2029-04-08) readiness by 15–25 percentage points (smaller carriers slip, network fragments). Supplementary funding authority (EUR 100–200M proposed) is outside the cap and not yet secured; early trigger (Month 12 = 2027-10-08) is needed to allow Commission decision by Month 18 (2028-04-08) before conformance-testing phase.

Data to Collect

  • Monthly cumulative spend vs. pro-rata forecast (EUR 25M/month baseline) by line item: standards EUR 280M, clearing EUR 120M, distributor EUR 215M, capacity EUR 100M, consumer EUR 150M, co-funding EUR 290M, data layer EUR 60M, governance EUR 60M
  • Early overrun signals: actual carrier co-funding requests vs. EUR 290M budget, distributor operating-cost actuals vs. EUR 43M/year, payment-provider fee exposure vs. EUR 15M subsidy cap, hub cost-recovery gaps vs. EUR 1.9M/year unfunded
  • Contingency-tier trigger events: Tier 1 (10–15% overrun), Tier 2 (15–25%), Tier 3 (>25%), with identified line-item cuts and escalation owners
  • Supplementary funding authority request timing and likelihood of approval by Month 12 (2027-10-08) if Tier 2 is triggered

Simulation Steps

  • Establish monthly budget-burn dashboard by Month 3 (2027-01-08) with real-time cumulative spend vs. pro-rata forecast (EUR 1,500M ÷ 60 months = EUR 25M/month baseline). Identify variance threshold: escalate to DG MOVE within 5 working days if quarterly spend exceeds 115% of pro-rata (i.e., EUR 86.25M in a 3-month quarter vs. EUR 75M pro-rata).
  • Model cost overrun scenarios: (a) Carrier co-funding demand reaches EUR 350–400M (vs. EUR 290M budget) due to larger-than-expected hub-eligible population or cost per carrier exceeding estimate. (b) Distributor operating cost rises to EUR 50–65M/year (from EUR 43M estimate) if retail scope expands beyond planned scope. (c) Payment-provider fee subsidy rises to EUR 20–25M (from EUR 15M cap) if through-ticket adoption is slower than planned and subsidy extends beyond Month 24 (2028-10-08). (d) Hub cost-recovery gap persists (EUR 1.9M/year unfunded) beyond Month 30 (2029-04-08).
  • Simulate Tier 1–3 contingency responses: Tier 1 (10–15% overrun = EUR 150–225M): defer consumer-app polish (reduce EUR 30M design budget to EUR 15M), reduce distributor co-marketing from EUR 10M to EUR 5M. Tier 2 (15–25% overrun = EUR 225–375M): reduce carrier co-funding rate from 20% to 10% (save EUR 50–90M), limit hub openings to priority corridors only (defer 2–3 TEN-T hubs to post-Month 60 = 2031-10-08). Tier 3 (>25% overrun = EUR 375–450M): suspend new hub openings, scale capacity building from EUR 100M to EUR 60–70M (defer weaker-capacity regulator twinning to post-Month 36 = 2029-10-08).
  • Model the impact of each contingency tier on critical-path milestones: Tier 1 delays consumer app launch by 2–4 weeks (Month 15–19 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-05-08) and reduces early-adopter distributor engagement by ~10%. Tier 2 delays smaller-carrier co-funding release by 3–6 months, pushing 20–30% of carriers past Month 30 (2029-04-08) API deadline, fragmenting network coverage to 70–80% of potential traffic. Tier 3 forces abandonment of capacity-building for weaker regulators, leaving 4–8 member-state regulators under-resourced for enforcement, creating a two-tier compliance landscape.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Commission an independent cost-modelling firm by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) to validate the EUR 1,500M budget allocation across all line items and to sensitivity-test each line for ±20–30% cost variance; deliver detailed cost forecast by Month 2 (2026-12-08) with scenario recommendations.
  • Have DG MOVE finance controller review the monthly burn-rate dashboard methodology by Month 2 (2026-12-08) to confirm it accurately tracks programme spend and flags overruns in real-time.
  • Conduct a mid-course budget review at Months 12 and 24 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08) with the Steering Committee, Programme Director and DG MOVE budget authority; compare cumulative spend to pro-rata forecast, assess any triggered contingency tier, and decide escalation to Commission for supplementary funding if needed.
  • Validate that the EUR 225M contingency reserve is held separately at DG MOVE and not subject to automatic release without explicit Steering Committee decision; confirm the reserve is protected from other EU programme encroachments by Month 3 (2027-01-08).

Responsible Parties

  • Budget Controller and Financial Manager (responsible for monthly dashboard, variance analysis, and contingency escalation)
  • DG MOVE finance authority (holds contingency reserve; decides Tier 2–3 responses and supplementary funding request)
  • Independent cost-modelling consultant (validates budget allocation and scenarios)
  • Steering Committee (decides Tier 2–3 responses and supplementary funding strategy at mid-course reviews)

Assumptions

  • High: Carrier co-funding demand will track the EUR 290M budget estimate (12–18 carriers × EUR 15–25M average per carrier) (sensitivity: high).
