If actual demand is 30% higher (EUR 350–400M), contingency is triggered at Month 12 (2027-10-08) and Tier 2 response (reduce co-funding rate to 10%) must be invoked, delaying smaller-carrier integration by 3–6 months.
  • High: Distributor operating cost will be EUR 43M/year as budgeted (based on reference-implementation scope, not full retail channel) (sensitivity: high). If retail scope expands or consumer support costs are underestimated, operating cost could rise to EUR 50–65M/year, consuming EUR 35–110M from free contingency.
  • Medium: Payment-provider fee subsidy will be EUR 15M (60% of fees Months 0–24 = 2026-10-08 to 2028-10-08) and will not extend beyond Month 24 (2028-10-08) (sensitivity: medium). If through-ticket adoption is slow or carriers demand extended subsidy, actual cost could reach EUR 20–25M, consuming EUR 5–10M from free contingency.
  • Medium: Hub cost-recovery gap (EUR 0.47M/year per hub, EUR 1.9M/year for 4 hubs) will be managed by Month 30 (2029-04-08) through carrier-fee increases or cost reduction (sensitivity: medium). If hub operators cannot achieve cost recovery and public subsidy extends beyond Month 30 (2029-04-08), cumulative deficit reaches EUR 5–10M and forces hub consolidation or extended public funding.
  • Medium: DG MOVE will seek supplementary budget authority from the Commission by Month 12 (2027-10-08) if Tier 2 is triggered, with a 60-day Commission decision gate (approval target Month 18 = 2028-04-08) (sensitivity: medium). Political reluctance or competing budget priorities could delay supplementary authority, forcing unplanned Tier 3 cuts.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 12 (2027-10-08), confirm that (1) monthly burn-rate dashboard is operational and cumulative spend through Month 11 (2027-09-08) is within 110% of pro-rata forecast (EUR 275M vs. EUR 250M pro-rata; acceptable variance); (2) no Tier 2 or Tier 3 contingency has been triggered; (3) early overrun signals from carrier co-funding requests, distributor cost actuals, or payment-fee demand have been identified and flagged to DG MOVE within 2 weeks of detection. By Month 24 (2028-10-08), reconfirm that cumulative spend is within 115% of pro-rata forecast (EUR 575M vs. EUR 500M pro-rata); if Tier 2 is triggered, escalate supplementary funding request to Commission with target EUR 100–200M and decision gate Month 30 (2029-04-08). If cumulative spend exceeds 125% of pro-rata (EUR 625M at Month 24 = 2028-10-08), trigger Tier 3 and immediately suspend new hub or capacity-building commitments.

Notes

  • Early detection of overrun signals is critical; delays of more than 2 weeks in flagging a variance reduce the window for contingency response from 6–12 months to 2–4 months, preventing orderly mitigation.
  • Contingency-tier responses have cascading effects: Tier 2 (reduce co-funding to 10%, limit hubs to priority corridors) delays smaller-carrier integration by 3–6 months and risks fragmenting the network; Tier 3 (suspend new hub openings, scale-back capacity building) compromises the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate and halved-complaints target. Escalate any trigger immediately to Steering Committee.
  • Supplementary funding (EUR 100–200M proposed) is outside the cap and not pre-approved; early triggering (Month 12 = 2027-10-08) is essential to allow Commission decision before conformance-testing phase (Month 18 = 2028-04-08).
  • Hub cost-recovery gap (EUR 1.9M/year unfunded) is a known item; decide cost-recovery strategy by Month 30 (2029-04-08) (extend public subsidy, raise carrier fees, or consolidate hubs) to avoid cumulative EUR 5–10M deficit by Month 48 (2030-10-08).
  • Reserve the EUR 225M contingency strictly for programme use; prevent other EU priorities from encroaching on the reserve. Confirm separation at DG MOVE by Month 3 (2027-01-08).

5. Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) and GDPR Consensus from National DPAs

Passenger PII flows across 5+ data controllers (distributors, carriers, payment institutions, clearing entity, national regulators), and cross-border data transfers require GDPR compliance via Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) or similar mechanisms. Unresolved GDPR governance can halt payment-institution accreditation (payment institutions will not partner without clear data-governance framework) and delay the data layer by 6–12 months if a national DPA issues a unilateral stop order on cross-border flows. Accessibility data (mobility restrictions, medical conditions) is special-category under GDPR Article 9 and requires heightened consent; if the programme requires explicit consent at booking time, it may create friction that reduces assisted-travel uptake. Early engagement with national DPAs (Months 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08) reduces the risk of a late-stage blocking challenge (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08).

Data to Collect

  • Complete Data Protection Impact Assessment mapping all passenger PII flows by transaction type (booking, payment, refund, disruption notification, accessibility assistance request) across 5+ data controllers (distributors, carriers, payment institutions, clearing entity, national regulators)
  • Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) templates for carrier-to-carrier data transfers, carrier-to-clearing transfers, and third-party distributor access to carrier inventory data
  • Data residency rules and national DPA positions from Austria, Germany, France, Netherlands, Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Spain, Sweden on whether carrier data must be stored in home member state or may be stored in a EU-wide data centre
  • Accessibility data consent regime and special-category data (GDPR Article 9) governance: whether explicit consent is required at booking time or implicit opt-in is lawful
  • Cross-border refund-dispute data sharing protocols: which member state's data-protection law applies when a German passenger disputes a refund with French and Austrian carriers

Simulation Steps

  • Commission a Data Protection Impact Assessment by Month 1 (2026-11-08) mapping all PII flows by transaction type and identifying minimum-necessary data per flow (booking: name, email, payment details, mobility attributes; payment: card details to accredited providers only; refund: booking reference, original payment method, passenger contact; disruption: passenger email/SMS only). Sensitivity: if data minimisation is too strict, distributors lack inventory detail for good through-fare offers (e.g., seat availability, loading factor); if too loose, GDPR audit will flag over-collection.
  • Model three data-governance scenarios: (a) Federated (each carrier holds authoritative data, access points route queries, no central cache): slower latency (5–10 seconds), lower residency risk, higher complexity; (b) Central cache (EU-wide availability cache, carriers feed continuously): faster latency (<2 seconds), higher residency risk, depends on DPA consensus; (c) Hybrid (federated + event-streaming for disruption data only): medium latency, medium residency risk, acceptable to most DPAs.
  • Conduct 1-on-1 pre-engagement consultations with 7–9 national DPAs (Austria, Germany, France, Netherlands, Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Spain, Sweden) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) to identify residency, consent, or data-minimisation concerns early, before formal DPIA publication.
  • Develop SCC templates for three data-flow categories (carrier-to-carrier inventory sharing, carrier-to-clearing revenue apportionment, distributor-to-carrier for booking/refund) and circulate drafts to task-force DPAs by Month 2 (2026-12-08) for pre-review and feedback.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Present the draft DPIA and SCC templates to the EDPB secretariat by Month 3 (2027-01-08) and request guidance on a single harmonised SCC template covering all multi-carrier through-ticketing data flows (target guidance Month 4 = 2027-02-08). If EDPB escalates the question to full EDPB plenary (risk: 6–9 month delay), trigger emergency procedure (propose supplementary legal instrument or Commission adequacy decision) by Month 5 (2027-03-08).
  • Obtain written sign-off from at least 8 of 27 member-state DPAs on the DPIA and SCC framework by Month 4 (2027-02-08); flag any DPA that signals a unilateral stop order on cross-border data flows as a blocking risk and escalate to Commission for emergency mediation.
  • Have an EU data-protection law specialist review the final DPIA and SCC templates for compliance with Schrems II and recent EDPB guidance on Standard Contractual Clauses (risk of invalidation by courts or regulatory challenge) by Month 3 (2027-01-08).
  • Validate accessibility-data consent regime (implicit vs. explicit) with BEUC and disability-rights organizations by Month 2 (2026-12-08) to confirm the chosen model does not create barriers to booking assistance (e.g., if explicit consent is required, will passengers refuse and thus not be able to book accessible itineraries?).

Responsible Parties

  • Data Protection Impact Assessment Lead / GDPR Compliance Specialist (hired by Month 1 = 2026-11-08; leads DPIA drafting and DPA engagement)
  • DPA Task Force (7–9 member-state DPAs: Austria, Germany, France, Netherlands, Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Spain, Sweden; provides pre-engagement feedback and signs off on DPIA and SCC framework by Month 4 = 2027-02-08)
  • EU Data Protection Law Specialist (validates DPIA and SCCs for Schrems II and EDPB guidance compliance)
  • EDPB secretariat (provides guidance on harmonised SCC template for multi-carrier through-ticketing, if needed)

Assumptions

  • High: At least 8 of 27 member-state DPAs will review and sign off on the DPIA and SCC framework by Month 4 (2027-02-08) (sensitivity: high). If fewer than 8 DPAs sign off or if a major DPA (Austria, Germany, France) refuses, the framework is rejected and must be redesigned, delaying payment-institution accreditation by 3–6 months.
  • High: The EDPB will issue guidance on a single harmonised SCC template for multi-carrier through-ticketing by Month 4 (2027-02-08) or will accept the programme's proposed SCCs without further escalation (sensitivity: high). If the EDPB escalates to full plenary or requests major revisions, the timeline extends 6–9 months and payment-institution accreditation is delayed.
  • Medium: Accessibility data (mobility attributes, medical conditions) can be handled via implicit opt-in consent (passive consent at booking time unless explicitly refused) (sensitivity: medium). If GDPR Article 9 requires explicit opt-in consent, passengers may refuse or become confused during booking, reducing assisted-travel uptake by 10–20%.
  • Medium: Data residency rules will allow EU-wide storage of carrier inventory and booking data (with encryption and access controls) rather than requiring home-member-state residency only (sensitivity: medium). If Bulgaria, Romania or Hungary demand local residency, the data layer must be redesigned to federated queries (slower latency, higher complexity).
  • Low: The recent Schrems II court ruling on Standard Contractual Clauses (and EDPB follow-up guidance) will be stable and will not require rework of SCCs during the programme (sensitivity: low). Further court challenges or DPA guidance updates in 2027–2028 could force revision of the programme's data-governance framework post-DPIA.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 4 (2027-02-08), confirm that (1) the DPIA is complete and maps all PII flows by transaction type with minimum-necessary data identified for each; (2) SCC templates for three data-flow categories (carrier-to-carrier, carrier-to-clearing, distributor-to-carrier) are drafted and have been reviewed by at least 8 national DPAs; (3) the EDPB has issued or indicated acceptance of the programme's SCC framework without requiring major revisions; (4) the accessibility-data consent regime (implicit opt-in) has been validated by BEUC and disability-rights organizations as not creating barriers to assisted-travel booking. By Month 6 (2027-04-08), if no DPA has issued a unilateral stop order or blocking challenge, escalate DPIA sign-off to Payment Provider Accreditation task force as a prerequisite for accreditation. If a DPA blocks the framework, trigger emergency escalation to Commission for dispute resolution (4-week target).

Notes

  • GDPR governance is on the critical path for payment-institution accreditation (Month 8 = 2027-06-08 decision). Unresolved DPIA or DPA consensus delays accreditation to Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08), compressing the data-layer deployment window and threatening Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate.
  • Austria, Germany, France and Poland are known to have strict data-governance regimes; early 1-on-1 engagement (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23) with these DPAs is essential to identify blocking concerns before formal DPIA publication.
  • Schrems II ruling on SCCs is already in effect (from July 2020 decision, enforcement varies by DPA); validate that the programme's SCCs comply with EDPB follow-up guidance (October 2020 and follow-ups) by Month 2 (2026-12-08) to avoid late-stage rework.
  • Accessibility data consent is a tension: GDPR Article 9 requires heightened protection of special-category data, but disability-rights advocacy demands easy assistance booking. The programme must balance these via a consent model that is lawful but not burdensome; pilot with BEUC by Month 2 (2026-12-08).
  • Data residency divergence (home-state only vs. EU-wide cache) is a major architectural choice; if residency is mandated, the data layer must be re-architected to federated queries (slower, more complex). Decision point: Month 4 (2027-02-08).

6. Killer Application Definition and Through-Ticket Valuation Hypothesis Testing

The programme targets 40% through-ticket share and 5–15% modal shift from air, yet no validated product or pricing strategy demonstrates traveller demand for these outcomes. Without a compelling killer application—a product that travellers prefer over flying or buying separate tickets—distributor incentive, carrier willingness to invest, and passenger adoption all remain weak. The programme risks hitting 40% volume through convenience alone (single booking) but missing the modal-shift and halved-complaints goals. Early customer research (Months 1–6 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-04-08) and a pilot (Months 9–12 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08) validate whether a killer application is viable before the programme commits to full-scale rollout (Month 27 = 2029-01-08).

Data to Collect

  • Customer research on traveller willingness to pay for three candidate killer applications: (1) guaranteed-connection through-ticket (4-hour reroute, 10-day refund, single contact), (2) air-rail city-pair (all-inclusive fare vs. flight competitor), (3) assisted-travel journey (pre-confirmed assistance + priority seating + platform handover)
  • Pricing elasticity and cross-elasticity: through-fare competitiveness vs. budget airlines (baseline flight price EUR 40–70, through-fare estimate EUR 70–90), vs. separate operator tickets (EUR 60–80)
  • Traveller booking intent and conversion rate: percentage of surveyed travellers willing to book each killer application vs. existing alternatives (flight, separate tickets, car)
  • Reduction-card effectiveness: cross-border reduction-card recognition value (~10–15% effective discount) and traveller response to unified reduction-card scheme

Simulation Steps

  • Commission customer research (willingness-to-pay study, conjoint analysis) on three candidate killer applications by Month 1 (2026-11-08) targeting 300–500 surveyed travellers per application, stratified by route (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon, Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin) and traveller segment (frequent business, leisure, budget-conscious). Baseline question: 'Would you choose rail over a flight if the through-fare were EUR X [vary 60, 70, 80, 90] and you could change trains for free if you missed your connection?' Sensitivity: pricing elasticity and switching behaviour vary by route (short-haul air competition is strong on Paris–Brussels; moderate on Wien–München; weaker on Copenhagen–Hamburg).
  • Model through-fare competitiveness: baseline through-fare (sum of segment prices) EUR 70–90 on priority corridors vs. low-cost airlines (EUR 40–70 on aggressive routes, EUR 50–80 on moderate competition). Estimate mode-shift elasticity (% of air passengers switching to rail per 10% fare reduction) and apply to annual short-haul air volumes on each corridor to forecast baseline modal-shift rate (5–10% without killer application, 15–25% with validated killer application).
  • Pilot one killer application on one corridor (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln or Wien–München–Zürich) by Month 9 (2027-07-08) with real traveller bookings (target 500–1,000 bookings over 3-month pilot). Track booking conversion rate, customer satisfaction (NPS, 5-star rating), and actual usage (completion rate, refund frequency). Measure: did guaranteed-connection messaging increase conversion vs. standard multi-operator tickets? Did 4-hour reroute promise and 10-day refund reduce passenger anxiety and increase loyalty?
  • Sensitivity test: if pilot conversion rate is <3% (vs. existing single-operator rail product at 5–8%), the killer application lacks valuation and demand is driven by convenience only. If conversion rate is >8%, the product has strong appeal and should be scaled to all four corridors.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage Trainline, Omio and the public reference distributor in co-design of the killer application (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) to ensure the product is technically feasible (booking interface, rerouting system integration, refund processing) and commercially viable (margin requirements). Request these distributors' historical through-ticket booking data and willingness-to-promote the product in exchange for early API access (proposed at Month 9–12 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08).
  • Present the willingness-to-pay study findings to a carrier product council (SNCF, DB, ÖBB, Renfe, Trenitalia representatives) by Month 6 (2027-04-08) to validate that the promised reroute (<4 hours) and refund (<10 days) timelines are operationally feasible and that reduction-card recognition is acceptable to carriers.
  • Commission an independent modal-shift analyst to validate the research's elasticity assumptions and to reconcile the study's stated willingness to pay against observed market pricing (e.g., current Trainline and Omio through-ticket share and pricing strategy on comparable corridors) by Month 6 (2027-04-08).
  • After the pilot (Month 12 = 2027-10-08), present conversion-rate and satisfaction results to the Steering Committee; if conversion rate is <3%, escalate and propose a contingency decision (regulated fare ceilings, modal-shift subsidy, or re-scope of the 40% target) by Month 15 (2028-01-08).

Responsible Parties

  • Consumer Product and App Development Lead (owns killer-application design and pilot rollout)
  • Independent customer-research firm (conducts willingness-to-pay study and pilot conversion/satisfaction tracking)
  • Distributor partners (Trainline, Omio, public reference distributor; co-design the killer application and provide booking and refund-processing integration)
  • Carrier product council (validates operational feasibility of promised reroute and refund timelines)

Assumptions

  • High: Customer willingness-to-pay research will show that a guaranteed-connection through-ticket with 4-hour reroute and 10-day refund, priced at EUR 70–80, is preferable to a budget flight at EUR 40–70 by at least 15–20% of surveyed travellers (sensitivity: high). If <10% prefer the through-ticket, demand is weak and the 40% target is unachievable without subsidies.
  • Medium: Reduction-card harmonisation (cross-border recognition at 10–15% effective discount) will increase through-ticket conversion by 5–10 percentage points (sensitivity: medium). If reduction-card value is lower or recognition is incomplete, the conversion uplift is smaller.
  • High: The pilot killer application will achieve conversion rate >3% (vs. existing single-operator rail at 5–8% estimate) by Month 12 (2027-10-08) (sensitivity: high). If conversion is <3%, the product lacks demand and the 40% target requires either fare subsidies, regulatory mandates, or re-scoping.
  • Medium: Carriers will agree that promised reroute (<4 hours) and refund (<10 days) timelines are operationally feasible given existing disruption-handling and refund procedures (sensitivity: medium). If operationally infeasible, promises cannot be kept and passenger dissatisfaction erodes demand.
  • Medium: Trainline and Omio will commit to early API access and co-marketing support in exchange for killer-application co-design and preferential treatment at launch (Month 15 = 2028-01-08) (sensitivity: medium). If distributors lack margin incentive or are unwilling to prioritise the programme, the product lacks distribution channels.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 6 (2027-04-08), confirm that (1) willingness-to-pay research is complete and shows that at least 15–20% of surveyed travellers prefer the killer application over budget flights or separate tickets at the target through-fare (EUR 70–90); (2) one killer application has been selected for pilot (e.g., guaranteed-connection through-ticket) and is in co-design with Trainline, Omio and carrier partners; (3) operational feasibility of promised reroute (<4 hours) and refund (<10 days) timelines has been validated by a carrier product council. By Month 12 (2027-10-08), confirm that the pilot has been live for 3 months and conversion rate is >3% (vs. benchmark 5–8% for single-operator rail); customer satisfaction is ≥4.0/5; refund and reroute timelines are being met >90% of the time. If conversion is <3% or satisfaction is <3.5/5, escalate to Steering Committee and propose contingency decision (regulate fares, subsidy, or re-scope target) by Month 15 (2028-01-08). If pilot is successful, scale to all four corridors and four-corridor consumer go-live at Month 27 (2029-01-08).

Notes

  • Killer application is the missing link in the programme's commercial strategy; without validated traveller demand, the 40% through-ticket and modal-shift targets are aspirational and unachievable via regulatory mandate alone.
  • Willingness-to-pay study should include pricing sensitivity across routes (short-haul air is competitive on Paris–Brussels, weaker on Copenhagen–Hamburg) and traveller segments (business vs. leisure); bulk findings may hide important route-level divergence.
  • Pilot conversion rate <3% signals weak demand and should trigger a re-baseline decision: either introduce regulated fare ceilings (antitrust risk), offer modal-shift subsidies (budget impact), or re-scope the 40% target to exclude air-competitive routes.
  • Reduction-card harmonisation is a secondary driver of conversion; estimate its contribution (5–10 percentage points) separately from the killer application's primary benefit (single booking, guaranteed connection).
  • Distributor buy-in is critical; without Trainline and Omio prioritising the killer application, commercial reach is limited and consumer adoption lags. Offer early API access and co-marketing budget (EUR 5–10M over Months 15–27 = 2028-01-08 to 2029-01-08) to secure commitment by Month 6 (2027-04-08).

7. Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) Funding Model for Distributor, Hubs, Data Layer and Regulator Capacity

The programme's public budget ends at Month 60 (2031-10-08), but core infrastructure dependencies (distributor, hubs, data layer, regulator capacity) have recurring costs estimated at EUR 45M/year unfunded (distributor EUR 43M + hub gap EUR 1.9M). Without a decision on post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding by Month 48 (2030-10-08), the programme risks operational collapse at Month 60 (2031-10-08), with the distributor forced to shut down, hubs abandoned, and the data layer orphaned. This would strand all prior investment and revert cross-border rail to pre-programme fragmentation. Early sustainability planning (Months 30–48 = 2029-04-08 to 2030-10-08) allows time for political negotiation, member-state commitment, and orderly transition design.

Data to Collect

  • Sustainable operating costs for core infrastructure beyond the 5-year programme: public reference distributor (estimated EUR 43M/year, post-Month 60 = 2031-10-08), hub cost-recovery gap (EUR 0.47M/year per hub, EUR 1.9M/year for 4 hubs), data-layer operations (EUR 15–30M/year estimated), regulator capacity maintenance (EUR 5–10M/year estimated)
  • Revenue models and fee-recovery scenarios: carrier subscription fees for hub use, distributor transaction fees passed to travellers/carriers, payment-provider cost recovery, data-layer access fees
  • Transition mechanisms: timeline for shifting from programme subsidy to sustainable funding (cost-recovery transition deadline Month 48 = 2030-10-08, funding model decision Month 48 = 2030-10-08, implementation Month 55 = 2031-05-08)
  • Contingency funding sources if fee-recovery is insufficient: member-state co-funding, EU structural funds, voluntary carrier contributions, or sunset/consolidation of services

Simulation Steps

  • Establish a Sustainability Task Force by Month 30 (2029-04-08) with representatives from DG MOVE, the EU Agency for Railways, hub operators, the reference distributor, carrier federation (CER) and a payment services provider. Commission a financial sustainability study: model the operating costs for each core service post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) (distributor EUR 43M/year baseline, hub EUR 1.9M/year gap, data layer EUR 20M/year estimate, regulators EUR 8M/year estimate) and estimate fee-revenue potential (hub fees EUR 50–200K per carrier per year, distributor transaction fees 0.5–1% per ticket, data-layer access fees if applicable).
  • Develop three scenarios: (a) Cost-recovery via fees: carriers and distributors pay for hub use, distributor operations, and data-layer access; revenue gap estimated at EUR 10–30M/year if through-ticket volume is 40% as targeted (spread across 1,000s of transactions, fee per transaction 1–2% may be infeasible without raising traveller fares). (b) Member-state co-funding: 27 member states commit to shared contribution (EUR 5–15M/year from collective transport budgets) to sustain regulator capacity and hub operations; feasibility depends on national political commitments by Month 48 (2030-10-08). (c) Sunset/consolidation: public distributor shuts down by Month 60 (2031-10-08), hubs transition to paid carrier consortia or private operators, data layer transferred to EU Agency for Railways with reduced feature set (federated queries only, no central cache).
  • Sensitivity test: if through-ticket volume plateaus at 25% instead of 40% by Month 60 (2031-10-08), fee-revenue potential decreases 35–40%, making cost-recovery via fees unachievable and forcing reliance on member-state co-funding or sunset.

Expert Validation Steps

  • Engage the EU Agency for Railways and DG MOVE by Month 30 (2029-04-08) to confirm willingness to absorb data-layer operations post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) under a sustainable funding model (membership fees, EU budget allocation, or carrier levies).
  • Present the sustainability study to the Steering Committee by Month 42 (2030-04-08) and request guidance on the preferred funding model (fee-recovery vs. member-state co-funding vs. sunset).
  • Secure written commitment from at least 15 of 27 member states to contribute to post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) regulator capacity funding (EUR 5–15M/year collectively) by Month 48 (2030-10-08), conditional on demonstrating the 40% through-ticket share and halved-complaints targets by Month 60 (2031-10-08).
  • Negotiate hub transition agreements with hub operators by Month 42 (2030-04-08) specifying: if cost-recovery is chosen, hub fees are raised to EUR 100–300K per carrier per year (from estimated EUR 50–200K); if member-state funding is chosen, hubs continue under programme subsidy transition; if sunset is chosen, hubs shut down by Month 60 (2031-10-08) and carriers transition to native APIs or consortia-run hubs (unplanned cost for carriers).

Responsible Parties

  • Sustainability Task Force (established by Month 30 = 2029-04-08; includes DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways, hub operators, distributor, CER, payment provider; leads financial sustainability study and scenario modelling)
  • Independent financial sustainability consultant (models operating costs, fee-revenue potential, and funding scenarios)
  • EU Agency for Railways (confirms willingness to absorb data-layer operations post-Month 60 = 2031-10-08 under sustainable funding)
  • DG MOVE (negotiates member-state commitment to post-Month 60 = 2031-10-08 regulator capacity funding)

Assumptions

  • High: Through-ticket volume will reach 40% of cross-border rail journeys by Month 60 (2031-10-08), generating sufficient fee-revenue (1–2% per transaction across millions of annual bookings) to offset some operational costs (sensitivity: high). If actual volume is 25–30%, fee-revenue potential is reduced 35–40%, making cost-recovery via fees insufficient and forcing reliance on member-state co-funding or sunset.
  • Medium: Member states will commit to EUR 5–15M/year collective contribution to post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) regulator capacity funding if the 40% through-ticket target is achieved (sensitivity: medium). If targets are missed (through-ticket share 25%, complaints not halved), member-state political commitment weakens.
  • Medium: Hub operators will accept a transition from programme subsidy to fee-revenue (EUR 100–300K per carrier per year) or will opt out and shut down hubs by Month 60 (2031-10-08) (sensitivity: medium). If hub operators demand extended public subsidy post-Month 60 (2031-10-08), the programme's cost obligation extends indefinitely.
  • Medium: The EU Agency for Railways will agree to absorb data-layer operations post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) as part of its core mandate, with dedicated budget allocation or fee-recovery via access charges (sensitivity: medium). If the Agency declines, the data layer is orphaned or transferred to a commercial operator.
  • Low: The public reference distributor can transition to either (a) cost-recovery (transaction fees to carriers/distributors/travellers), (b) hand-off to a commercial operator, or (c) orderly shutdown by Month 60 (2031-10-08) (sensitivity: low). If none of these options are viable, the distributor becomes a long-term unfunded liability.

SMART Validation Objective

By Month 42 (2030-04-08), confirm that (1) the Sustainability Task Force has completed a financial sustainability study estimating post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) operating costs for distributor, hubs, data layer and regulators; (2) three funding scenarios (fee-recovery, member-state co-funding, sunset) have been modelled with realistic cost and revenue projections; (3) the Steering Committee has recommended a preferred funding model. By Month 48 (2030-10-08), confirm that (1) the preferred funding model has been formally decided by DG MOVE and the Commission; (2) at least 15 member states have committed in writing to post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) regulator capacity funding (if member-state co-funding is chosen); (3) hub operators have been notified of the transition plan and fee schedule (if fee-recovery is chosen); (4) the public distributor has a transition plan (shutdown, hand-off, or cost-recovery) with a target implementation date (Month 55 = 2031-05-08). If no funding model is agreed by Month 48 (2030-10-08), escalate to the Commission with a contingency recommendation (e.g., sunset of distributor, consolidation of hubs, data-layer transition to Agency) to prevent programme collapse at Month 60 (2031-10-08).

Notes

  • Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding is a critical but deferred decision; early planning (Months 30–48 = 2029-04-08 to 2030-10-08) is needed to avoid operational collapse. The EUR 45M/year unfunded cost must be resolved, not assumed to continue indefinitely from EU budget allocations.
  • Through-ticket volume at Month 60 (2031-10-08) directly determines fee-revenue potential; if the 40% target is missed, fee-recovery scenarios are less viable and member-state co-funding becomes essential. Use measurement dashboard (Months 18–60 = 2028-04-08 to 2031-10-08) to forecast Month 60 (2031-10-08) volume by Month 42 (2030-04-08) and adjust sustainability plans accordingly.
  • Hub cost-recovery gap (EUR 0.47M/year per hub, EUR 1.9M/year for 4 hubs) is an unfunded item in the current budget; decision to extend public subsidy beyond Month 48 (2030-10-08) or raise carrier fees (EUR 50–300K per carrier per year) must be made by Month 30 (2029-04-08) to give carriers time to plan.
  • EU Agency for Railways' willingness to assume data-layer operations is a political decision not yet confirmed; early engagement (Month 30 = 2029-04-08) is needed to signal expectations and secure commitment.
  • If cost-recovery via fees is chosen, traveller fares may increase 1–2% (depending on volume and margin) due to distributor, hub, and data-layer fees; model the impact on through-ticket demand and fee-revenue feedback loops.

Summary

This project data-collection plan identifies 7 critical validation areas essential to the EUR 1.5 billion, five-year EU cross-border rail through-ticketing programme: (1) Regulation adoption and standards alignment (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 gate); (2) Carrier commitment to arbitration panel authority (Month 3 = 2027-01-08 gate); (3) Hub procurement and smaller-carrier integration readiness (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 operationalization); (4) Budget burn-rate monitoring and contingency triggers (monthly dashboards, Tier 2–3 decisions); (5) GDPR/DPA consensus on data governance (Month 4 = 2027-02-08 gate); (6) Killer-application validation and traveller demand testing (Months 6–12 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-10-08 pilot); and (7) Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability planning (Month 48 = 2030-10-08 decision). Immediate actionable tasks: (A) Launch regulatory adoption tracking and engagement with Parliament/member states by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); commission shadow standards pre-work and cost model by Month 1 (2026-11-08); (B) Secure Council/Commission delegation of arbitration panel authority by Month 2 (2026-12-08, target 1.5 = 2026-11-23); (C) Issue hub operator RFP by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) and award contracts by Month 3 (2027-01-08); (D) Commission DPIA and convene DPA task force by Month 1 (2026-11-08); (E) Launch customer research on killer applications and pilot one by Month 9 (2027-07-08); (F) Establish monthly budget dashboards with 115% spend trigger by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Success hinges on securing the three highest-sensitivity prerequisites: Regulation adoption by Month 9 (2027-07-08), arbitration panel delegation by Month 2 (2026-12-08), and carrier Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08). If any prerequisite slips beyond its gate, the critical path shifts downstream, threatening Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards and Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate. Contingency: if Regulation adoption slips past Month 8 (2027-06-08), contract external standards consortium by Month 8.5 (2027-06-23) for accelerated pre-work; if budget overruns exceed 115% of pro-rata by Month 12 (2027-10-08), trigger Tier 2 contingency (reduce co-funding, limit hubs); if GDPR consensus is not reached by Month 4 (2027-02-08), escalate to EDPB for expedited guidance.

Create Document 1: Project Charter and Programme Authority Framework

ID: 20bfc80f-1561-4b0f-86ab-09346e1cf583

Description: Foundational governance document establishing the programme's legal authority, scope, objectives, stakeholder roles, and decision-making structures. Specifies the arbitration panel's binding technical authority, Council delegation, member-state regulator coordination, and escalation procedures. Audience: DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways, member-state transport ministries, carriers, distributors. Approval required from the Commission and Council.

Responsible Role Type: Governance and Legal Affairs Advisor

Primary Template: EU Programme Charter Template (adapted for multi-stakeholder infrastructure)

Secondary Template: Commission Decision on Delegated Authority Framework

Steps to Create:

  • 1. Draft the charter's executive summary, scope, objectives and success criteria aligned to the user constraints (EUR 1.5B cap, Month 18/30/60 = 2028-04-08, 2029-04-08, 2031-10-08 milestones, 40% through-ticket target, halved complaints).
  • 2. Define the arbitration panel's authority: binding decision scope (technical standards, access terms, settlement formats; excluded: commercial pricing), 60-day cycles, 14-day compliance deadlines, escalation to Commission.
  • 3. Specify governance structure: PMO reporting to DG MOVE and Steering Committee; Standing Regulators Committee with lead-authority rule for cross-border disputes; twinning for capacity building.
  • 4. Include risk governance: contingency tiers (Tier 1–3 triggers at 115% spend), mid-course reviews (Months 12, 24 = 2027-10-08, 2028-10-08), decision gates for Regulation adoption, hub readiness, payment accreditation.
  • 5. Obtain legal review from DG MOVE legal services and Council Presidency (target Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23); present for formal Council adoption by Month 2 (2026-12-08).

Approval Authorities: European Council (for delegation of authority); Commission (DG MOVE); Member-state transport ministers (for regulator coordination)

Essential Information:

  • Establish the foundational legal authority and governance structure: define the arbitration panel's binding technical decision scope (standards, access terms, settlement formats), decision cycles (60 days to ruling, 14 days to comply), escalation path to the Commission, and member-state regulator coordination framework.
  • Specify the programme's scope, objectives and success criteria: EUR 1,500 million public budget cap (Months 0–60 = 2026-10-08 to 2031-10-08), binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-08), mandatory API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-08), 40% through-ticket target, halved distributor complaints, and 90%+ corridor coverage threshold at Month 30 (2029-04-08).
  • Define stakeholder roles and decision rights: DG MOVE as budget holder and programme owner; EU Agency for Railways as technical secretariat; PMO reporting structure; quarterly Steering Committee; Standing Regulators Committee with lead-authority rule for cross-border disputes; tiered engagement for carriers, distributors, national regulators and disability-rights bodies.
  • Include governance contingencies: mid-course budget reviews at Months 12 and 24 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08) with Tier 1–3 escalation (triggered at 115% pro-rata spend); gates for Regulation adoption (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 target), hub readiness (Month 9 = 2027-07-08), payment accreditation (Month 12 = 2027-10-08), and carrier Commitment Letters (Month 3 = 2027-01-08).
  • Specify risk governance: dispute-resolution procedures; conflict escalation timelines (<2 weeks); authority for mid-course corrections; contingency reserves (EUR 225 million total, EUR 215 million free); and decision criteria for programme pauses or timeline adjustments.
  • Anchor legal prerequisites: Council delegation to arbitration panel by Month 2 (2026-12-08); Regulation adoption gate by Month 9 (2027-07-08); carrier Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08) with binding penalties; GDPR and competition-law clearance by Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08).
  • Document post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability planning: decision on permanent funding for the distributor, hubs and data layer by Month 48 (2030-10-08) to avoid operational discontinuity.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous arbitration panel authority undermines governance credibility: if the Commission or Council delegation is unclear or contested, major incumbents can refuse to accept technical rulings, causing standards approval and carrier compliance to fracture and pushing the Month 18 (2028-04-08) and Month 30 (2029-04-08) milestones at risk.
  • Incomplete stakeholder role definition leads to duplicated effort, delayed decisions and stakeholder conflict: without clear ownership (who decides on access terms vs. settlement rules vs. corridor sequencing), working groups re-litigate resolved issues, and governance overhead consumes 25–30% of programme staff time, adding 3–6 month delays by Month 30 (2029-04-08).
  • Missing budget and contingency governance exposes the programme to uncontrolled overruns: without clear mid-course review gates and tier-based cut triggers, a 20–30% budget overrun is not detected until Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), at which point conformance testing or smaller-carrier co-funding must be cut retroactively, fragmenting the network.
  • Vague Regulation adoption gate results in wasted pre-work or late pivot: if the document does not specify a hard deadline for regulation adoption (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 proposed) and contingency actions (pause onboarding if missed), the programme invests in standards pre-work that may need rework, or charges ahead without legal certainty, risking non-compliance.
  • Unclear post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability plan creates operational cliff: if the charter does not commit to deciding on permanent funding by Month 48 (2030-10-08), the public distributor, hubs and data layer face discontinuity or mission creep (expanding into commercial operations to stay funded), undermining the programme's long-term credibility.

Worst Case Scenario: The charter fails to secure explicit written Council delegation to the arbitration panel by Month 2 (2026-12-08), leaving the panel's authority ambiguous. Major carriers (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF) contest a Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) technical ruling on API access terms, claiming national sovereignty and refusing compliance. Escalation to the Commission takes 8–12 weeks and yields no binding decision. Simultaneously, the Regulation is adopted late (Month 10–12 = 2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08 instead of Month 9 = 2027-07-08), compressing the standards window. Standards finalisation is rushed or incomplete by Month 18 (2028-04-08), forcing a choice: miss the binding-standards deadline or deliver standards without carrier or distributor consensus. Distributors (Trainline, Omio) withdraw from early integration, and the public reference distributor must expand beyond plan, consuming EUR 60–100M extra (exceeding the EUR 215M free contingency). By Month 30 (2029-04-08), only 70–75% of corridor traffic is bookable (below the 90% threshold), the mandate is questioned, and stakeholder confidence erodes. The programme is delayed 6–12 months to Month 36–42 (2029-10-08 to 2030-04-08) or faces restructuring, with estimated EUR 200–500M in additional costs and reputational damage to the EU's regulatory authority.

Best Case Scenario: The charter is approved by Council by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) and secured in writing by Month 2 (2026-12-08), establishing unambiguous arbitration-panel authority and escalation procedures. Carriers above EUR 50M cross-border revenue sign Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08), accepting binding arbitration and escrow penalties. The Regulation is adopted by Parliament and Council by Month 7 (2027-05-08), allowing 11 months for standards-setting (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 deadline is comfortably met). The charter's clear governance structure enables faster dispute resolution (60-day cycle, no re-litigation), and working-group overhead is kept to 15–20% of staff time. The Standing Regulators Committee harmonises enforcement, and twinning for weaker regulators builds capacity early. Budget mid-course reviews at Months 12 and 24 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08) detect a 12% projected overrun by Month 15 (2028-01-08), triggering a Tier 1 response (reduction in distributor marketing, not cutting core programmes). By Month 30 (2029-04-08), 95%+ of corridor traffic is bookable, the API mandate is achieved with carrier buy-in, and the arbitration panel has issued 5–8 binding rulings with 100% compliance rate, establishing governance credibility. The charter's post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) decision gate (Month 48 = 2030-10-08) ensures that permanent funding is secured for the distributor, hubs and data layer, avoiding operational discontinuity. The programme enters Month 60 (2031-10-08) with 38–42% through-ticket share (within reach of 40%), halved complaints, and momentum for TEN-T extension.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If Council delegation cannot be secured by Month 2 (2026-12-08): escalate to the highest political level (EU Commission President, Council Presidency) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) and seek explicit commitment within 2 weeks. If political commitment is still uncertain by Month 3 (2027-01-08), pause carrier Commitment-Letter signature and engage an external governance counsel to draft an alternative arbitration framework (e.g., joint undertaking or independent arbitral tribunal) that can be stood up rapidly if formal delegation fails.
  • If Regulation adoption is delayed beyond Month 8 (2027-06-08): activate the 'shadow standards' pre-work stream (Month 0–3 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08 already underway) and contract an external standards consortium by Month 4 (2027-02-08) to produce standards within 6 weeks of adoption, using accelerated working-group cycles (twice-weekly vs. weekly). This risks consensus-quality loss but protects the Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline.
  • If budget projections show a 20%+ overrun by Month 9 (2027-07-08): immediately trigger Tier 2 contingency cuts (reduce carrier co-funding from 20–25% to 10–15%, prioritise the top 5 corridors by traffic volume, defer TEN-T hub openings to Month 42 = 2030-04-08 instead of Month 36 = 2029-10-08). Simultaneously, commission a supplementary budget request to the Council/Commission for EUR 100–200M; if declined, trigger Tier 3 (suspend new hub onboarding, scale back consumer-app features to MVP only, reduce capacity building to top-3 member states).
  • If fewer than 2 payment providers apply for accreditation by Month 6 (2027-04-08): immediately pivot to Plan B (bilateral carrier settlement via existing arrangements plus an emergency procurement of a custom settlement service from a qualified fintech provider), accepting slightly longer settlement cycles (48–72 hours instead of 24–36 hours). This reduces the competitive benefit but avoids a single-provider monopoly and protects the Month 30 (2029-04-08) milestone.
  • If a major carrier (>30% of cross-border traffic) signals non-compliance in Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08): immediately convene an escalation meeting with the Commission, the carrier's home-country transport ministry and the EU Agency for Railways. Offer time-limited co-funding uplift (up to EUR 10M additional per carrier) in exchange for commitment to Month 30 (2029-04-08). If the carrier still refuses, invoke enforcement: hold co-funding, public distributor competes on that carrier's routes, and escalate to Commission for potential regulatory action. This signals consequences and may stiffen resolve among other carriers to comply.

Create Document 2: OSDM-Compatible API Specification and Binding Standards Document

ID: 87b09b1b-9803-4d4d-ab98-e04a1fe62a2c

Description: Comprehensive technical standards binding on all participating carriers and distributors, aligned to OSDM v2.1 and the (final) EU Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing. Covers access-term templates (non-discriminatory inventory, fare and post-sale API exposure), data-quality SLAs (latency, uptime, inventory freshness, disruption timeliness), settlement message formats, ticket validation protocols, GDPR compliance rules, accessibility requirements, and certification conformance criteria. Audience: carriers, distributors, test labs, national regulators. Due Month 18 (2028-04-08); locked and non-negotiable thereafter.

Responsible Role Type: Chief Technical Standards Officer / OSDM and API Architecture Lead

Primary Template: OSDM v2.1 Specification (extended)

Secondary Template: EU Technical Standards Framework (CEN/CENELEC model)

Steps to Create:

  • 1. Conduct a gap analysis Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) between the Commission's final Regulation text (adopted by Month 9 = 2027-07-08 target) and OSDM v2.1, identifying areas requiring specification or clarification.
  • 2. Draft candidate access-term templates (inventory API, fare API, post-sale API) specifying fields, response times, error handling, retry logic.
  • 3. Define data-quality SLAs: API p95 latency under 2 seconds, uptime 99.95%, throughput at least 500 requests/second per corridor, inventory freshness under 5 minutes, disruption-event latency under 2 minutes.
  • 4. Embed GDPR compliance rules (from the DPIA and DPA consensus by Month 4 = 2027-02-08), accessibility requirements (24-hour assistance confirmation, 90%+ confirmation rate, 95%+ delivery), and liability-allocation framework for passenger rights.
  • 5. Define conformance-test criteria (test harnesses, successful API calls, data-quality samples, performance benchmarks) to be validated by independent testing labs starting Month 9 (2027-07-08).
  • 6. Hold stakeholder consultation rounds (Months 7–17 = 2027-05-08 to 2028-03-08), with formal technical dispute resolution by the arbitration panel for contested items.
  • 7. Publish the binding standards document by Month 18 (2028-04-08) with signatures from DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways, CER, and major carriers acknowledging adoption.

Approval Authorities: Arbitration Panel (technical validation); Commission (final approval); Member-state regulators (enforcement authority)

Essential Information:

  • Define the complete OSDM v2.1 API specification covering three mandatory interfaces: inventory API (real-time seat availability, fare tiers, ancillary services), fare API (through-fare calculation logic, reduction-card harmonisation, dynamic pricing rules), and post-sale API (disruption notifications, rerouting logic, refund processing workflows).
  • Specify access-term templates that all carriers must publish by Month 18 (2028-04-08): non-discriminatory inventory parity (no preferential delay for third-party distributors vs. own channels), API response latency SLAs (<2 seconds p95), uptime guarantees (99.95%), throughput minimums (≥500 requests/second per corridor).
  • Detail data-quality SLAs: inventory freshness <5 minutes, disruption-event latency <2 minutes (for real-time missed-connection detection and passenger notification), settlement message format standards (ISO 20022 or equivalent multi-currency multi-carrier revenue apportionment).
  • Embed GDPR compliance rules derived from the Month 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) DPIA and Month 4 (2027-02-08) DPA consensus: PII data fields permitted per transaction (name, booking reference, payment details for accredited providers only), retention (90 days post-journey, 12 months if refund/complaint pending), cross-border transfer via Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) or Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs).
  • Define passenger-rights integration: continuity-of-journey obligations (guaranteed rerouting or refund if connection missed), accessibility assistance confirmation (≤24 hours, ≥90% confirmation rate), liability allocation (distributor single contact, cost recovery from liable carrier via clearing mechanism).
  • Specify accessibility requirements: booking interface WCAG 2.1 AA standard compliance, assistance-request turnaround ≤24 hours, platform and vehicle accessibility data (lift availability, staff assistance capability, accessible seating), assistance delivery verification (≥95% of confirmed assistance actually delivered), assistance-related complaint rate <2%.
  • Detail conformance-test criteria and certification thresholds: test harnesses (successful API calls to all three interfaces under load, error-handling scenarios), data-quality validation (sample journeys from each carrier across 30–50 test cases per carrier), performance benchmarking (p95 latency, uptime measurement, throughput sustained at ≥400 req/s), accessibility checklist (WCAG audit, assistance-confirmation mock-ups), GDPR audit trail.
  • Establish dispute-resolution procedures: contested technical items escalated to the arbitration panel by Month 16 (2028-02-08) with a 14-day decision target; tie-breaking authority on access-term fairness, SLA stringency and conformance thresholds.
  • Specify the document's binding nature: signatures required from DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways, CER and at least 70% of major carriers (by cross-border revenue) by Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline; non-negotiable thereafter (only amendments via formal standards-revision process with Commission approval, to occur no more than annually).
  • Define compliance enforcement: quarterly conformance-test results reported by all carriers; carriers failing conformance by Month 24 (2028-10-08) are ineligible for Month 30 (2029-04-08) API go-live and must use hub/gateway; carriers non-compliant with access-term templates by Month 30 (2029-04-08) face regulatory penalties (0.5–1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue, escalation to Commission).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or ambiguous API specification (e.g., missing error codes, unclear field definitions, vague response-time thresholds) forces carriers to make conflicting implementation choices, causing interoperability failures; distributors cannot reliably book multi-carrier journeys, and the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate fails or launches with <70% compliance.
  • Weak or unenforceable access-term templates allow incumbents to publish terms that look non-discriminatory but contain hidden delays (e.g., '48-hour API key provisioning,' 'priority query routing for own inventory'), defeating the programme's anti-discrimination goal; distributors cannot achieve inventory parity, and smaller carriers' market access is undermined.
  • Vague data-quality SLAs (e.g., 'availability should be fresh' without latency numbers) lead to inventory stale by 15–30 minutes in production; 5–10% of bookings fail at confirmation, triggering refund disputes and passenger complaints that damage programme credibility.
  • GDPR rules unclear or not pre-consulted with DPAs risk a national authority challenge in Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08), forcing a data-architecture redesign or halt to standards approval and delaying the Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline by 4–8 weeks.
  • Passenger-rights and accessibility requirements not tightly specified or without measurable thresholds (e.g., assistance 'should' be confirmed vs. 'must be confirmed within 24 hours') allow carriers to provide substandard service, excluding persons with reduced mobility and inviting disability-rights complaints and regulatory intervention.
  • Conformance-test criteria too lenient or under-resourced (e.g., test lab capacity insufficient for 20+ carriers) delays carrier certification by 4–12 weeks per carrier; smaller operators slip past Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate, fragmenting the network to 60–75% coverage instead of 90%+.
  • Dispute-resolution process not time-boxed or gives the arbitration panel unclear authority results in standards disputes being re-litigated across multiple forums (working groups, Steering Committee, Commission), consuming 2–6 months per issue and jeopardising the Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline.
  • Document not signed or endorsed by major carriers and regulators, or signed with caveats ('subject to national law review'), undermines the document's binding status and leaves carriers able to non-comply without clear consequence.
  • Enforcement mechanisms absent or toothless (e.g., non-compliance noted but no penalty) results in 20–30% of carriers ignoring access-term or data-quality requirements by Month 30 (2029-04-08), and the mandatory API mandate becomes advisory; the programme's legal and regulatory credibility collapses.

Worst Case Scenario: The standards document is delayed beyond Month 18 (2028-04-08) or delivered without consensus from major carriers (70%+ buy-in not secured). Concurrently, a national DPA (e.g., Austria or Poland) challenges the GDPR compliance rules in Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08), claiming data flows violate Article 5 (data minimisation) or require explicit consent per Article 9 (special category). The arbitration panel's authority is questioned by a large incumbent (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF) over an access-term dispute; escalation to the Commission takes 8–12 weeks. By Month 24 (2028-10-08), the standards document is six months overdue, is unsigned by 30%+ of carriers, and is being re-negotiated. Conformance testing backlogs build due to incomplete test harnesses. The Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate is no longer credible, and carriers announce phased 18–24 month compliance timelines. Distributors, seeing no firm standards or enforcement, reduce investment in integration; the public reference distributor is forced to expand coverage and consume EUR 50–100M in extra operating costs. The 40% through-ticket target becomes unachievable by Month 60 (2031-10-08), and the programme's return on investment is questioned in Parliament. Environmental and modal-shift benefits are not realised, and the Commission may propose to suspend or drastically scale back the programme by Month 36–48 (2029-10-08 to 2030-10-08), representing a loss of EUR 400–600M in unrecovered investment.

Best Case Scenario: The standards document is finalised and signed by DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways, CER and 85%+ of major carriers by Month 18 (2028-04-08), incorporating feedback from the Month 4–17 (2027-02-08 to 2028-03-08) stakeholder consultation and arbitration panel dispute resolution. GDPR consensus is reached with the EDPB and national DPAs by Month 4 (2027-02-08), enabling the standards to include agreed data-flow rules without later legal challenges. Conformance testing labs are fully operational by Month 9 (2027-07-08) and complete pilot testing of all carriers by Month 24 (2028-10-08), with 90%+ of carriers certified compliant by Month 28 (2029-02-08). The document's binding status is enforced: by Month 30 (2029-04-08), 95%+ of carrier APIs are live and compliant, 90%+ of corridor traffic is bookable end-to-end, and distributors report high integration confidence. This enables accelerated distributor onboarding (Months 24–30 = 2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08), through-ticket volumes reach 20% of cross-border rail journeys by Month 30 (2029-04-08) and 35–40% by Month 60 (2031-10-08), meeting the programme's headline target. Passenger satisfaction with through-tickets exceeds expectations (ratings >4.2/5 stars), distributor complaints drop 50%+ below baseline, and accessibility assistance is reliably delivered (>95% success rate). The programme becomes a regulatory and political success story, attracting investment for TEN-T extension and scaling to other EU modal-shift corridors.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the full Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards document cannot be finalised due to regulatory or technical disputes, issue a 'Minimum Viable Standards' (MVS) document by Month 18 (2028-04-08) covering only the three mandatory APIs (inventory, fare, post-sale) with core SLAs (p95 latency <3 seconds, uptime 99.9%, 500 req/s), deferring settlement message formats, accessibility detail and dispute procedures to a 'Phase 2 Standards' update by Month 24 (2028-10-08). This maintains the Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline while preserving quality and avoiding compressed final negotiations.
  • If carrier consensus on access-term fairness cannot be reached, establish an independent Access Fairness Reviewer (external audit body, perhaps a Big Four consulting firm under contract) that certifies each carrier's published terms as compliant with non-discrimination principles by Month 20 (2028-06-08), rather than embedding detailed access rules in the standards. This shifts dispute resolution to an auditor rather than the arbitration panel, reducing timing risk.
  • If GDPR/DPA consensus cannot be reached by Month 4 (2027-02-08), issue the standards with a 'GDPR Compliance Conditional' clause: carriers and distributors must comply with the standards' operational logic, but PII handling and cross-border-transfer mechanisms are subject to each carrier's national-regulator guidance (issued by Month 12 = 2027-10-08). This allows technical standards to move forward while GDPR alignment is conducted in parallel, accepting higher residual legal risk but protecting the Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline.
  • If conformance testing backlogs develop (test labs cannot accommodate 20+ carriers by Month 24 = 2028-10-08), expedite testing via parallel test-lab networks in 3–4 regions (EU-West, EU-Central, EU-East, southern Europe) and allow carriers to test in parallel in Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), rather than sequentially. Reserve EUR 5–8M from contingency for additional lab capacity and staffing.
  • If a major carrier (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF) refuses to sign the standards or disputes the binding nature, escalate immediately to the Commission (Month 16 = 2028-02-08 for early warning, formal escalation by Month 18 = 2028-04-08) and invoke contingency: conditionally approve the standards with a note that carrier's compliance is pending Commission arbitration; if unresolved by Month 24 (2028-10-08), invoke regulatory enforcement (mandatory audit, co-funding hold, public communication of non-compliance). Proceed with 70%+ signatory coalition rather than seeking 100% consensus.
  • If the arbitration panel's dispute-resolution authority is challenged in court or by a member state, seek an emergency expedited EU Court of Justice advisory opinion (Month 16–18 = 2028-02-08 to 2028-04-08) confirming the panel's legal standing under the Regulation and the Commission's delegation. If court review is not feasible in time, issue the standards under a 'subject to judicial review' caveat, accepting legal risk but protecting operational progress.

Create Document 3: Clearing and Settlement Architecture Design and Accredited Payment Provider Specification

ID: 0634d9ee-b437-4f8a-9151-b1603b008392

Description: Detailed specification of the clearing and settlement mechanism using 2–3 accredited payment institutions (not a central clearing entity). Defines revenue apportionment rules (how multi-carrier fares are split), refund reversal protocols, dispute resolution within 5 business days, settlement cycle under 48 hours, SLA guarantees (99.95% uptime), and transaction-fee management. Includes accreditation criteria (PSD2 licensing, multi-currency support, SLAs), applicant evaluation framework, and fallback procurement if fewer than 2 providers apply. Audience: payment institutions, carriers, distributors, clearing-entity operators, regulators.

Responsible Role Type: Clearing and Settlement Mechanism Designer / Payment Systems Specialist

Primary Template: PSD2 Accreditation Framework (EU Central Bank guidance)

Secondary Template: Settlement Architecture Standards (ISO 20022, SEPA specifications)

Steps to Create:

  • 1. Conduct market sounding (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) identifying potential accredited providers and their capacity.
  • 2. Draft the accreditation criteria document (Month 1 = 2026-11-08): PSD2 compliance, multi-currency support (EUR, DKK, SEK, CHF, PLN, CZK, HUF, BGN, RON), settlement cycle under 48 hours, refund processing under 10 days, error handling and dispute resolution within 5 business days, SLA guarantees (99.95% uptime).
  • 3. Issue a formal call for applicants (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) with detailed RFP specifying technical, operational and financial requirements.
  • 4. Define the apportionment logic (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08): which carrier receives what share of the passenger fare based on segment distance, time or agreed allocation keys; specify rounding and residual handling.
  • 5. Design the refund-reversal protocol (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08): when a distributor refunds a passenger, how the cost flows back to the responsible carrier via the accredited provider; dispute escalation if the carrier contests the refund.
  • 6. Evaluate applications and make accreditation decisions (Month 8 = 2027-06-08); target at least 2 accredited providers operational by Month 12 (2027-10-08).
  • 7. Define the fallback: if fewer than 2 providers qualify by Month 6 (2027-04-08), activate contingency procurement or bilateral carrier settlement by Month 8 (2027-06-08).

Approval Authorities: European Central Bank (PSD2 oversight); DG MOVE (settlement governance); Commission (final framework approval)

Essential Information:

  • Define the accreditation criteria for payment institutions: PSD2 licensing, multi-currency support (EUR, DKK, SEK, CHF, PLN, CZK, HUF, BGN, RON), settlement cycle <48 hours, refund processing <10 days, error resolution <5 business days, and SLA guarantees (99.95% uptime).
  • Specify the revenue-apportionment logic: which carrier receives what share of multi-carrier through-fares based on segment distance, segment time, or agreed allocation keys; define rounding rules and residual-fee handling.
  • Detail the refund-reversal protocol: how distributor refunds flow back to the liable carrier via accredited providers, including escalation procedures if a carrier contests a refund.
  • Establish the RFP framework for accreditation: evaluation criteria for applicant suitability, financial stability checks, SLA verification, and redundancy/failover requirements.
  • Define settlement timelines and dispute resolution: settlement cycle commitment (<48 hours), monthly reconciliation windows, and a 5-business-day dispute-resolution window with escalation to a Dispute Resolution Panel.
  • Quantify transaction-fee exposure and subsidy model: estimate costs at EUR 80–120 million over five years; specify fee caps (0.3–0.5% per transaction) and subsidy coverage (60% of fees in Months 0–24 = 2026-10-08 to 2028-10-08, capped at EUR 15 million).
  • Identify fallback scenarios: if fewer than 2 accredited providers apply by Month 6 (2027-04-08), specify contingency procurement or bilateral carrier settlement; define switching costs (up to EUR 1 million per incident) and insurance/liability requirements.
  • Specify payment-institution liability and insurance: require errors-and-omissions (E&O) insurance covering settlement failures, overpayments and disputes, with minimum policy limits of EUR 2–5 million per provider.
  • Outline governance and oversight: define the Programme's dispute-escalation path (payment provider → Programme Dispute Panel → Commission), monthly performance dashboards, and enforcement triggers (e.g., if uptime falls below 99.95% for one week, fees are withheld).
  • Address data governance for split payments: specify what PII flows between the distributor, carriers, and payment institutions; confirm GDPR compliance (Standard Contractual Clauses, 90-day PII deletion, consent protocols).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Insufficient accreditation criteria or weak SLA enforcement: if accredited providers do not meet uptime (99.95%) or settlement-cycle (<48 hours) commitments, settlement delays cascade to carriers, distributors and passengers, creating refund backlogs and eroding confidence in the through-ticket system.
  • Flawed revenue-apportionment logic: ambiguous or incorrect allocation of fares among carriers leads to systematic underpayment or overpayment, creating carrier disputes, delayed payouts (months of reconciliation), and financial liability exposure for the Programme (estimated EUR 5–20 million per year in disputes).
  • Unclear refund-reversal protocol: if the process for reversing a distributor refund back to a liable carrier is not clearly specified, refund disputes accumulate, dispute-resolution times exceed the 5-business-day target by 200–300%, and passengers experience weeks-long refund delays that generate complaints and regulator intervention.
  • Weak or absent SLA enforcement: if uptime, latency or settlement-cycle failures are not monitored or penalised, providers have no incentive to invest in reliability, and system outages (e.g., 4–8 hour payment processing failures) affect 10,000–100,000 daily transactions, generating cascading refund obligations and operational disruptions.
  • Inadequate liability and insurance coverage: if accredited providers do not carry sufficient E&O insurance (e.g., only EUR 500K instead of EUR 2–5M), a single major settlement failure (e.g., overpayment of EUR 5M due to rounding errors or duplicate posting) exhausts insurance and becomes a Programme liability, consuming EUR 5–10 million of the contingency reserve.
  • Incomplete data-governance specification: if the document does not clarify how PII flows among distributors, carriers and payment institutions, GDPR compliance is ambiguous, and a data protection authority can challenge the architecture, forcing a 6–12 month redesign and halting Month 30 (2029-04-08) settlement integration.
  • Absent or poorly designed fallback scenarios: if the document does not specify what happens if a sole accredited provider withdraws or if fewer than 2 providers apply, the Programme lacks contingency, and an unplanned provider loss during Months 18–30 (2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08) forces carriers to roll back to bilateral settlement, derailing the through-ticket launch.
  • Missing transaction-fee and subsidy rules: if the cost of split-payment orchestration is not budgeted, actual fees (EUR 80–120 million) can consume 5–8% of the public budget, triggering 10–20% cuts to conformance testing or distributor operations, slowing smaller-carrier adoption by 4–12 weeks per carrier.

Worst Case Scenario: An accredited payment provider fails or withdraws mid-deployment (Month 18–30 = 2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08), and the specification does not define clear fallback procedures. Carriers are forced to revert to bilateral settlement, and a 2–4 week switchover period creates settlement delays affecting 50,000–500,000 daily through-ticket transactions. Passengers experience 2–4 week refund delays, distributors face liability disputes with carriers over settlement accuracy, and the Programme's credibility is damaged. The through-ticket launch is delayed by 4–8 weeks, threatening the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate. Additionally, if the specification's revenue-apportionment logic is flawed and discovered in live operation, systematic under/overpayments accumulate EUR 10–50 million in carrier claims, forcing reconciliation and rework lasting 2–6 months. Estimated total impact: Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate at risk, EUR 20–80 million in unplanned refund/liability reserves consumed, and reputational damage requiring 6–12 month reputation repair.

Best Case Scenario: The document specifies clear, benchmarked accreditation criteria (PSD2 compliance, <48-hour settlement, <5-day dispute resolution, 99.95% uptime) and defines 2–3 accredited payment providers operational by Month 12 (2027-10-08). The revenue-apportionment logic is unambiguous, tested against 50+ live scenarios before Month 18 (2028-04-08), and carrier settlement disputes drop to <2% of transactions. SLAs are monitored in real-time, and enforcement triggers (fee withholds for uptime breaches) create strong provider incentives. The refund-reversal protocol is clear and automated, achieving <5-business-day resolution for 98%+ of cases. Fallback scenarios (e.g., provider switchover cost EUR 1 million per incident, bilateral settlement as last resort) are pre-authorised and funded. This enables the Programme to launch the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate on schedule with 90%+ of through-tickets settled correctly within 48 hours, passenger refunds resolved in <10 days, and zero settlement-related delays to carrier onboarding or distributor operations. The document thus enables the core promise of through-ticketing (reliable, single-payment, continuous journeys) and removes a major risk to the 40% and Month 60 (2031-10-08) targets.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If accreditation of 2+ private payment institutions takes longer than Month 8 (2027-06-08) or fewer than 2 qualified providers apply, activate contingency procurement by Month 6–8 (2027-04-08 to 2027-06-08): engage a pre-identified Tier-2 provider (e.g., a central bank payments service or a large carrier consortium) to operate a custom settlement service under interim governance. This delays settlement infrastructure readiness by 2–4 months but avoids the critical-path risk of zero accredited providers.
  • If accredited payment institutions' fees exceed the EUR 80–120 million budget (e.g., providers demand 1.0%+ per transaction instead of 0.3–0.5%), negotiate a tiered fee structure: full subsidy for the first 12 months (Months 0–12 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-10-08), 60% subsidy Months 12–24 (2027-10-08 to 2028-10-08), and 30% subsidy thereafter, conditional on through-ticket volumes hitting 15% by Month 24 (2028-10-08). This spreads fees over a longer period and creates volume-based financial incentives.
  • If dispute resolution within 5 business days is infeasible due to carrier-side delays (e.g., legacy systems cannot audit refunds quickly), establish a temporary two-tier protocol: automated disputes (<EUR 1,000) resolved in 5 business days; manual disputes (>EUR 1,000) resolved in 10 business days by Month 18 (2028-04-08), and tighten to 5 business days by Month 24 (2028-10-08) once carriers' legacy systems are upgraded.
  • If the Programme's Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) surfaces major GDPR compliance gaps (e.g., member states demand data residency), redesign the payment-data flow to minimise PII exposure: adopt a 'data minimisation' protocol where distributors hold passenger PII, and payment institutions receive only booking reference + amount + carrier ID (not passenger name or contact). This reduces GDPR risk by 40–60% and may accelerate EDPB consensus by Month 4 (2027-02-08).
  • If accredited payment institutions cannot support the full multi-currency and cross-border settlement model by Month 12 (2027-10-08), use a phased approach: launch settlement in EUR-only on the four priority corridors (Months 18–30 = 2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08), then extend to non-EUR currencies (DKK, SEK, CHF, PLN) by Month 36 (2029-10-08). This compresses technical complexity and allows provider ramp-up time.
  • If a sole accredited provider fails or withdraws during Months 18–30 (2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08), activate emergency bilateral settlement: carriers agree to a temporary 'multi-bilateral' arrangement in which each carrier pair settles directly using a common message standard (ISO 20022) and an independent dispute-resolution body (not the payment institution). Transition back to accredited providers within 4 weeks once replacement provider is operational.

Create Document 4: Regulation Adoption Tracking and Shadow Standards Pre-Work Plan

ID: 9efb0ff1-7161-49c8-b445-c7fb2f3b4709

Description: Strategic plan for tracking the Commission's proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail through Parliament and Council, identifying blocking amendments, and conducting pre-work on binding standards (Month 0–18 = 2026-10-08 to 2028-04-08) without formally binding the programme until adoption. Includes weekly adoption-status updates, scenario planning (adoption Month 9, 11–12, or blocked post-Month 12 = 2027-10-08, 2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08, or 2027-10-08+), contingency standards-acceleration pathways, and decision gates. Audience: DG MOVE, Parliament TRAN/IMCO rapporteurs, member-state transport ministers, arbitration panel, working groups.

Responsible Role Type: Governance and Legal Affairs Advisor; Strategy and Programme Director (co-owners)

Primary Template: EU Legislative Tracking and Contingency Planning Framework

Secondary Template: None

Steps to Create:

  • 1. Establish weekly liaison with Parliament TRAN and IMCO rapporteurs and key member-state ministers (Germany, France, Belgium, Austria, Spain) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23).
  • 2. Map the Parliament and Council legislative timeline: identify likely debate windows, amendment deadlines, rapporteur positions, and member-state consensus blockers.
  • 3. Conduct a gap analysis (Month 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) comparing the Commission's proposed text (May 2026) to OSDM v2.1 and the Pragmatic Foundation scenario, identifying any material divergences on liability, access-term scope, data-sharing rules, or API mandates.
  • 4. Commission a shadow standards pre-work team (5–8 FTE, Month 0 = 2026-10-08 onwards) to draft candidate standards on access-term templates, settlement message formats and passenger-rights protocols without formally binding the programme until adoption is confirmed.
  • 5. Define three adoption scenarios: (a) adoption by Month 9 (2027-07-08) as proposed, (b) adoption by Month 11–12 (2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08) with text changes, (c) adoption blocked or deferred beyond Month 12 (2027-10-08). For each, specify standards-finalisation timeline and escalation actions.
  • 6. Establish decision gates: (a) Month 6 (2027-04-08): if adoption probability drops below 60%, escalate to Commission and assess whether to pause carrier onboarding; (b) Month 8 (2027-06-08): if adoption is not imminent, contract external standards-review consortium for accelerated pre-work; (c) Month 10 (2027-08-08): if adoption is not secured, pause carrier commitments and re-baseline the critical path.
  • 7. Prepare a 2-week rapid-deployment standards-finalisation sequence (detailed specs, stakeholder validation, formal vote) for immediate activation post-adoption.

Approval Authorities: DG MOVE (tracking and scenario decisions); Commission (liaison authority)

Essential Information:

  • Define the weekly and monthly liaison protocol with Parliament TRAN/IMCO rapporteurs and key member-state transport ministers to monitor legislative progress toward Regulation adoption (target: Month 9 = 2027-07-08).
  • Map the Parliament and Council legislative timeline, identifying likely amendment windows, rapporteur positions, blocking-issue clusters, and member-state consensus risks by Month 1 (2026-11-08).
  • Conduct a gap analysis comparing the Commission's proposed Regulation text (May 2026) to OSDM v2.1 standard and the Pragmatic Foundation scenario, flagging material divergences on liability allocation, access-term definitions, data-sharing rules, or mandatory API scope by Month 2 (2026-12-08).
  • Establish a shadow standards pre-work team (5–8 FTE, active from Month 0 = 2026-10-08 onward) to draft candidate standards on: (1) non-discriminatory access terms and audit protocols, (2) clearing and settlement message formats, (3) passenger-rights refund and rerouting procedures—without formally binding the programme until Regulation adoption is confirmed.
  • Define three adoption scenarios with corresponding standards-finalisation timelines: (a) adoption by Month 9 (2027-07-08) as proposed (9-month standards window), (b) adoption by Month 11–12 (2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08) with material text changes (6-month window, compressed), (c) adoption blocked or deferred beyond Month 12 (2027-10-08) (contingency pathways invoked).
