  • Establish decision gates and escalation actions: Month 6 (2027-04-08)—if adoption probability drops below 60%, escalate to Commission and assess whether to pause carrier onboarding; Month 8 (2027-06-08)—if adoption is not imminent, contract external standards-review consortium for accelerated pre-work; Month 10 (2027-08-08)—if adoption is not secured, pause carrier Commitment Letters and re-baseline the critical path.
  • Prepare a 2-week rapid-deployment standards-finalisation sequence to be activated immediately post-adoption: detailed specifications (Week 1), stakeholder validation and amendment incorporation (Week 1), formal steering committee vote and approval (Week 2), enabling carrier integration work to begin within 7 days of Regulation entry into force.
  • Document all blocking amendments, rapporteur positions, and member-state concerns in a weekly adoption-status dashboard (accessible to DG MOVE, arbitration panel, working groups, steering committee) with colour-coded risk signals (green: adoption on track, yellow: risk factors emerging, red: adoption at risk).
  • Specify roles and decision rights: DG MOVE owns adoption tracking and scenario decisions; Commission liaison authority; arbitration panel and working groups are notified of scenarios and are consulted on technical implications; Steering Committee (quarterly) ratifies scenario decisions and escalation triggers.
  • Define success metrics: (1) Regulation adopted by Month 9 (2027-07-08) with no material divergence from proposed text; (2) shadow pre-work produces testable draft standards within 2 weeks of adoption; (3) carrier onboarding commitments proceed on the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate timeline; (4) no unplanned standards rework required due to legislative surprises.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Delayed or absent adoption tracking allows the legislative process to drift: rapporteur amendments or member-state reservations are not surfaced until Month 8–10 (2027-06-08 to 2027-08-08), leaving insufficient time to engage negotiators and resulting in either a weakened Regulation (non-discrimination rules diluted, exemptions for incumbents) or a missed adoption deadline.
  • Incomplete gap analysis between the proposed Regulation and OSDM fails to identify technical incompatibilities or scope gaps: standards-setting work (Months 4–18 = 2027-02-08 to 2028-04-08) proceeds on false assumptions and requires rework after adoption, adding 4–8 weeks delay to the Month 18 (2028-04-08) milestone.
  • Under-resourced shadow pre-work team (fewer than 5 FTE, or unfocused scope) produces superficial draft standards that require substantial revision post-adoption: instead of a 2-week finalisation sprint, remedial work takes 6–10 weeks, compressing the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards window and delaying carrier integration gates.
  • Ill-defined or missing decision gates result in delayed escalation: adoption risk is not surfaced until Month 9–10 (2027-07-08 to 2027-08-08) when contingency acceleration is no longer feasible, forcing either a missed Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards deadline or a decision to proceed with incomplete or non-consensus standards (low carrier and distributor buy-in).
  • Unclear role assignments and communication protocols cause decision paralysis: if DG MOVE, the arbitration panel, and working groups have conflicting views on adoption scenarios, or if escalation authority is ambiguous, competing recommendations fragment programme momentum and delay critical decisions by 2–4 weeks per cycle.
  • Weak stakeholder alignment on scenarios creates implementation friction: if the Commission privately expects Month 11–12 (2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08) adoption but DG MOVE and carriers plan for Month 9 (2027-07-08), the mismatch results in either premature commitments (carrier demobilisation if timeline slips) or wasted contingency spending (accelerated contracting that may not be needed).

Worst Case Scenario: A material divergence emerges in the Regulation text (e.g., Parliament votes to exempt dominant carriers from the API mandate, or the Council insists on national regulatory optionality) and is not detected until Month 10–11 (2027-08-08 to 2027-09-08). By then, the shadow pre-work team has drafted standards incompatible with the adopted text, and 4–6 weeks of rework are needed. Simultaneously, adoption is delayed beyond Month 9 (2027-07-08), compressing the standards-finalisation window from 9 months to 4 months. Standards finalisation slips from Month 18 (2028-04-08) to Month 22–24 (2028-08-08 to 2028-10-08), and carrier integration cannot begin until Month 24–30 (2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08), risking the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate. Carriers signal non-compliance by Month 18 (2028-04-08), claiming unrealistic integration timelines, and the programme loses political credibility. The through-ticket system is perceived as undeliverable, commercial distributors reduce investment, and the 40% target becomes unachievable.

Best Case Scenario: The adoption-tracking protocol surfaces a blocking amendment by Month 5 (2027-03-08), enabling early negotiation and resolution. The Commission, Parliament and Council reach consensus by Month 9 (2027-07-08) with text matching the Pragmatic Foundation assumptions (no material divergence). The shadow pre-work team delivers testable draft standards within 2 weeks of adoption. Standards finalisation proceeds on schedule (Month 18 = 2028-04-08), carriers sign Commitment Letters confident in the regulatory timeline, and integration work begins immediately. Carrier compliance reaches 90%+ by Month 30 (2029-04-08), and the first through-tickets go live on Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln by Month 24 (2028-10-08) on pilot basis. The 40% target becomes achievable, programme credibility is established, and TEN-T extension planning is accelerated.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If adoption slips beyond Month 8 (2027-06-08) but seems likely by Month 11–12 (2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08), do not pause carrier commitments; instead, proceed with conditional Commitment Letters that are contingent on Regulation adoption by Month 12 (2027-10-08). Activate contingency standards-acceleration: contract an external consortium to produce final standards in 4 weeks post-adoption (instead of 9 weeks), using the shadow pre-work as a foundation.
  • If adoption is unlikely by Month 10 (2027-08-08) or faces material rework, pause new carrier onboarding commitments and conduct a programme-viability review: assess whether a narrower scope (fewer corridors, phased rollout, non-binding initial phase) can proceed pending final Regulation adoption. Commission a legal opinion on whether the programme can be launched under the existing EU regulatory framework (rail passenger rights rules, competition law, payment services directives) without a specific Digital Booking Regulation.
  • If the Regulation text diverges materially on a critical point (e.g., API mandate is optional instead of mandatory), trigger an immediate strategic decision: either (1) advocate for a legislative correction via the Commission's amendment power before Council final vote, or (2) redesign the programme to achieve the same outcomes using voluntary industry standards and non-binding commitments (slower adoption but avoids a missed legislative window).
  • If the shadow pre-work team is under-resourced or produces low-quality drafts, engage external standards consultants (OSDM Alliance, industry working groups) from Month 2 (2026-12-08) onward to supplement the team and validate outputs. Use an independent external review (Month 6–8 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-06-08) to assess draft standards quality; if validation fails, ramp up consulting team to 12–15 FTE and extend finalisation timeline by 2–4 weeks (within the Month 18 = 2028-04-08 buffer).
  • If adoption is delayed to Month 12 (2027-10-08) or beyond and the 9-month standards window is lost, implement a 'compressed standards protocol': deliver binding technical standards on a rolling basis (access terms by Month 20 = 2028-06-08, settlement by Month 22 = 2028-08-08, passenger rights by Month 24 = 2028-10-08), allowing carrier integration to begin in parallel with later standards finalisation. Accept higher integration risk and require carriers to commit to rapid re-integration if standards change.
  • If the Commission liaison signal indicates adoption is at risk (probability <40% by Month 8 = 2027-06-08), prepare a 'regulatory-delay contingency scenario': design a voluntary industry-led standards process (OSDM Alliance as the standards body, arbitration panel as dispute resolver) that is decoupled from the formal Regulation and can proceed under existing law (competition clearance sought upfront). This is slower and less enforceable but allows work to continue without waiting for legislative completion.

Create Document 5: Carrier Commitment Letter and Non-Compliance Consequences Protocol

ID: e3138ca0-02ae-4064-89f6-c2ba5d0b45a8

Description: Binding commitment from each participating carrier above EUR 50 million annual cross-border revenue, specifying acceptance of arbitration panel authority, compliance with technical standards and access-term requirements by Month 30 (2029-04-08), and agreement to penalties for non-compliance. Includes the Non-Compliance Consequences Protocol detailing graduated penalties (first violation: written notice and 48-hour cure; second: 0.5% of quarterly through-ticket revenue in escrow; third: 1% of annual cross-border revenue withheld, escalated to Commission). Audience: major carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, Trenitalia, ÖBB, Renfe, NS, SJ, SNCB and others), DG MOVE, arbitration panel.

Responsible Role Type: Carrier Engagement and Stakeholder Manager / Coalition Builder

Primary Template: EU Service Agreement Template (adapted for rail sector)

Secondary Template: CER Standard Terms and Conditions for Cooperative Initiatives

Steps to Create:

  • 1. Define the commitment scope: carriers accept arbitration panel rulings as binding, commit to API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-08), meet data-quality SLAs (inventory freshness, latency, uptime), comply with non-discriminatory access duties, and participate in conformance testing.
  • 2. Draft the Non-Compliance Consequences Protocol (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08): specify the three violation levels, penalties in escrow, and escalation to the Commission.
  • 3. Conduct bilateral negotiations with carriers above EUR 50M cross-border revenue (Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23, target): address carrier-specific concerns (IT cost sharing, integration timelines, API design input), offer early API-design participation or co-funding in exchange for signatures.
  • 4. Prepare executive-summary talking points for DG MOVE negotiators: emphasise the carrier's role in the through-ticket ecosystem, the competitive advantage of early adoption, the enforcement risk if they refuse.
  • 5. Collect signatures by Month 3 (2027-01-08); escalate any major carrier refusing to sign to the Commission for political intervention by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23).
  • 6. Publish a summary of signatories (names, dates) to signal broad coalition buy-in and deter holdouts from contesting standards later.

Approval Authorities: Carriers themselves (signatories); DG MOVE (witness); Commission (enforcement authority for non-compliance)

Essential Information:

  • Define binding carrier acceptance of arbitration panel authority as a legal precondition for programme participation (target: carriers above EUR 50M annual cross-border revenue).
  • Specify technical and operational compliance commitments: API exposure by Month 30 (2029-04-08), data-quality SLAs (inventory freshness <5 min, latency <2 sec p95, uptime 99.95%), non-discriminatory access duties, and participation in conformance testing.
  • Detail the graduated Non-Compliance Consequences Protocol: (1) First violation—written notice with 48-hour cure window; (2) Second violation—0.5% of quarterly through-ticket revenue held in escrow until compliance; (3) Third violation—1% of annual cross-border revenue withheld, escalated to Commission for enforcement action.
  • Establish baseline commitment date: signatures required by Month 3 (2027-01-08); list signatories publicly to signal coalition strength and deter holdouts.
  • Include explicit acceptance clauses: signatories agree to binding arbitration panel rulings, accept SLA penalties (withheld from co-funding or through-ticket revenue), and waive re-litigation of closed technical disputes.
  • Quantify co-funding incentives by carrier size and integration pathway (native API build, hub use, gateway): specify the EUR 290M carrier co-funding envelope and how signature unlocks early co-funding disbursal.
  • Define escalation path: non-compliance by Month 9 (2027-07-08) triggers escalation to DG MOVE and Commission; persistent non-compliance (after third violation) invokes regulatory enforcement and potential exclusion from the through-ticket system.
  • Address carrier-specific concerns collected in bilateral negotiations (Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23): IT cost-sharing mechanisms, integration-timeline flexibility for legacy-system operators, API design-input seats for signatories, and exemptions or timelines for operators under EUR 50M (if negotiated separately).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If the letter lacks binding arbitration acceptance or contains ambiguous SLA definitions, major carriers (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF) can contest technical rulings retroactively, unraveling the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards and delaying the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate by 6–12 months.
  • Unclear or unenforceable penalty clauses (e.g., escrow language not tied to measurable compliance metrics) render the protocol toothless; carriers ignore non-discrimination duties or skip SLA targets, and the programme has no credible leverage to force compliance.
  • If the letter does not clearly delineate which carriers must sign by Month 3 (2027-01-08) (threshold: EUR 50M cross-border revenue), smaller operators claim ambiguity, sign late or refuse, fragmenting the coalition and leaving gaps in corridor coverage (e.g., if a regional operator on one corridor refuses, through-ticketing on that route is incomplete).
  • Failure to specify co-funding conditions tied to signature (e.g., 'signatories unlock 10% early co-funding disbursement at Month 6 = 2027-04-08') reduces incentive for carriers to sign; holdouts proceed with slower private-spend integration, and the programme loses negotiating leverage by Month 3–6 (2027-01-08 to 2027-04-08).
  • If the letter does not address IT cost-sharing details (e.g., co-funding rates, eligible integration costs, reimbursement timeline), carriers negotiate separately for each cost category post-signature, consuming 2–4 months of programme time and creating disputes over what is 'eligible' (e.g., is legacy-system decommissioning an eligible cost?).
  • Vague escalation language (e.g., 'non-compliance will be escalated') without a defined timeline or Commission decision path leaves enforcement discretionary; a major carrier can delay or contest escalation indefinitely, and the Commission lacks clear authority to act.
  • If signatories are not published prominently (Steering Committee meeting, public press release, European Parliament notification by Month 3 = 2027-01-08), the coalition signal is lost, and late signers (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) are viewed as reluctant, weakening political support and distributor confidence.

Worst Case Scenario: A major carrier (40–50% of cross-border traffic, e.g., Deutsche Bahn or SNCF) refuses to sign the Commitment Letter by Month 3 (2027-01-08), citing ambiguity in the arbitration-panel authority or demanding exemptions from SLA penalties for legacy-system costs. The programme lacks credible enforcement (no signed commitment), and when the arbitration panel issues its Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards ruling, the holdout carrier contests it, claiming it was not bound. Escalation to the Commission takes 4–8 weeks; meanwhile, smaller carriers and distributors lose confidence in the regime's enforceability and defer investments. Other major carriers follow the holdout's lead and either refuse to sign or demand renegotiation of penalty terms. By Month 9 (2027-07-08), fewer than 50% of targeted carriers have signed, the coalition fractures, and the programme is forced to weaken the Commitment Letter (e.g., removing penalties or arbitration-binding language) to secure signatures. This weakening cascades: by Month 18 (2028-04-08), standards are approved but viewed as non-binding; carriers adopt selectively, and by Month 30 (2029-04-08), only 60–70% of the mandatory target (90% of corridor traffic) is API-ready, falling short of the legal threshold. The programme's credibility is permanently damaged, distributors pull back investment, and through-ticket targets (40% share, halved complaints) become unachievable.

Best Case Scenario: The Commitment Letter is finalized by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) with clear, binding arbitration-panel authority, graduated penalties tied to measurable SLA compliance, and transparent co-funding eligibility. Bilateral negotiations with major carriers (Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23) resolve IT cost-sharing and integration-timeline concerns; all carriers above EUR 50M cross-border revenue sign by the Month 3 (2027-01-08) deadline, with a public ceremony or press release announcing >90% coalition coverage (est. 18–22 of 25+ major operators). Early signers unlock 10% co-funding disbursement advance (Month 6 = 2027-04-08), signalling programme commitment to DG MOVE. By Month 9 (2027-07-08), even smaller carriers (under EUR 50M) submit conditional commitment letters acknowledging the protocol and the arbitration panel's authority, though with timeline flexibility. When arbitration-panel technical rulings are issued (Month 18 = 2028-04-08), all signatories accept them as binding; non-compliant carriers face escrow penalties, and the Commission escalates one or two minor violations (e.g., a carrier misses data-quality SLAs by 2 weeks) by Month 19–20 (2028-05-08 to 2028-06-08), but the carrier corrects course within the cure window. By Month 30 (2029-04-08), 95%+ of corridor traffic is API-ready, exceeding the 90% threshold; distributors invest confidently in integration and marketing; through-ticket volumes hit 25%+ by Month 30 (2029-04-08), enabling early acceleration toward the 40% target; and the programme's credibility is anchored by visible carrier buy-in and enforceable compliance.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If major carriers resist binding commitment letters by Month 2 (2026-12-08), pivot to a 'tiered commitment framework': Stage 1 (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08): secure non-binding Letters of Intent from carriers (acknowledging arbitration-panel authority and committing to Month 30 = 2029-04-08 API exposure in principle); Stage 2 (Month 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08): follow up with binding Commitment Letters once regulatory adoption clarifies the legal basis; Stage 3 (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08): carriers that have not signed face conditional co-funding holds (access to co-funding is withheld until signature). This preserves flexibility while maintaining momentum.
  • If a major carrier signals non-compliance by Month 6 (2027-04-08) and refuses to sign, escalate immediately to DG MOVE and the Commission (not waiting until Month 9 = 2027-07-08 gate): Commission engages the carrier's political leadership (transport minister, CEO) directly, offering face-saving compromises (e.g., extended timeline for legacy-system migration, reduced SLA penalties for the first 6 months) in exchange for commitment. Document the negotiation as a 'Confidential Compliance Agreement' rather than a public letter to preserve carrier dignity.
  • If a smaller carrier (under EUR 50M) cannot meet the full Commitment Letter requirements due to IT constraints, offer a 'Conditional Participation Agreement' (Month 3–6 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-04-08) that: (1) acknowledges the operator's intention to comply by Month 36–42 (2029-10-08 to 2030-04-08) (not Month 30 = 2029-04-08), (2) ties fuller co-funding to a phased integration plan (gateway use from Month 30 = 2029-04-08 onwards, native API by Month 36 = 2029-10-08), and (3) applies lighter penalty terms (no escrow, only milestone-based funding holds). This avoids fragmenting the coalition while accommodating weaker operators.
  • If the Commission or DG MOVE signals that explicit binding authority for the arbitration panel cannot be secured by Month 2 (2026-12-08), redesign the Commitment Letter as a 'Memorandum of Understanding' (MOU) that carriers sign voluntarily, accepting arbitration and penalties as contractual obligations (not legal directives). Frame the MOU as a 'carrier-to-programme commitment' managed by CER rather than a government instrument, reducing sovereignty concerns. Pair this with a carrier-consortium governance structure (e.g., 'Rail Through-Ticket Alliance') that endorses the arbitration panel's rulings, providing peer-level enforcement pressure on holdouts.
  • If a carrier refuses to sign and cannot be brought into compliance by Month 12 (2027-10-08), invoke a 'Selective Exclusion' protocol: (1) the non-compliant carrier is excluded from the shared data layer, access to accredited payment providers and participation in the arbitration panel; (2) passengers and distributors are notified that the carrier does not participate in through-ticketing; (3) the programme designates a 'hub operator' or gateway to bridge the non-compliant carrier's inventory for read-only access (allowing passengers to book via the hub but not directly with the carrier), effectively sidelining the holdout until it signs. This approach preserves corridor continuity while creating strong reputational and commercial incentive for the holdout to join.
  • If co-funding eligibility and IT cost-sharing details create bottlenecks in bilateral negotiations (Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23), establish a 'Co-Funding Eligibility Committee' (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) with representatives from 2–3 major carriers and smaller-carrier groups, tasked with pre-negotiating a standard co-funding menu (e.g., 'up to EUR 2M for legacy-gateway integration', 'up to EUR 5M for hub-operator fees', 'up to EUR 1M for staff training'). Publish this menu by Month 2 (2026-12-08); carriers then negotiate only over their individual allocation within the pre-agreed framework, reducing negotiation time from 4–6 weeks to 1–2 weeks per carrier.

Create Document 6: Data Protection Impact Assessment and GDPR Compliance Framework

ID: 3c79f33b-24be-43b5-a0b7-cd61a637248d

Description: Comprehensive Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) mapping all passenger personally identifiable information (PII) flows among distributors, carriers, payment institutions, clearing entities, and national regulators. Specifies minimum-necessary PII per transaction type (search, booking, refund, dispute), data-residency rules, Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) for cross-border transfers, consent and special-category data governance (accessibility attributes), and breach-response protocols. Includes EDPB and national DPA engagement plan to achieve written consensus by Month 4 (2027-02-08). Audience: national DPAs, EDPB, payment institutions, clearing entity, carriers, distributors, legal counsel.

Responsible Role Type: Data Protection Impact Assessment and GDPR Compliance Lead

Primary Template: GDPR Article 35 Data Protection Impact Assessment Template (European Data Protection Board)

Secondary Template: Standard Contractual Clauses Module (EU Commission-approved templates)

Steps to Create:

  • 1. Map all PII flows (Month 1 = 2026-11-08): identify each transaction type (search, booking, payment, refund, dispute), which data controllers are involved, what PII is transferred, and the legal basis (contract, legitimate interest, consent).
  • 2. Identify minimum-necessary PII per flow (Month 1 = 2026-11-08): baseline (name, contact, booking reference, seat/assistance notes) vs. extended (payment details to payment institution only, carrier PII for refund communication only).
  • 3. Define data-residency rules (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08): can carrier data be stored in an EU-wide data centre or must it stay in the carrier's home member state? Propose: any EU member state if encrypted and access-controlled.
  • 4. Draft SCC templates (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08) for carrier-to-carrier data transfers (e.g., Austrian carrier sharing passenger name with Italian carrier for disruption notification) and carrier-to-clearing transfers (booking and revenue data).
  • 5. Specify consent and special-category governance (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08): accessibility data (mobility, health-related assistance) is special-category under GDPR Article 9; propose passive opt-in consent at booking time (if passenger does not explicitly refuse, deemed consented); document in booking confirmation.
  • 6. Engage EDPB and 7–9 national DPAs (Austria, Germany, France, Netherlands, Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Spain, Sweden) by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); conduct joint review of draft SCC and consent models (Months 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08); seek written sign-off from at least 8 DPAs by Month 4 (2027-02-08).
  • 7. If fewer than 8 DPAs sign off by Month 4 (2027-02-08), escalate to EDPB for expedited guidance (target 4 weeks) and reserve EUR 3–5M from GDPR line for emergency SCC negotiation or re-architecture.
  • 8. Embed resolved GDPR rules and SCC details in the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08).

Approval Authorities: European Data Protection Board; National DPAs (written consensus required); Commission (if additional legal instruments needed)

Essential Information:

  • Map all passenger personally identifiable information (PII) flows across the programme: identify transaction types (search, booking, payment, refund, dispute handling), data controllers involved, PII transferred per flow, and legal basis (contract, legitimate interest, consent) for each transfer by Month 2 (2026-12-08)
  • Define minimum-necessary PII per transaction type: baseline set (name, contact, booking reference, seat/assistance notes) and extended set (payment details to accredited payment institutions only; carrier PII for refund/disruption communication only); identify which fields are essential vs. optional
  • Specify data-residency rules: confirm whether carrier data can be stored in any EU member state (with encryption and access controls) or must remain in the carrier's home jurisdiction; resolve early differences among Austria, Poland and Hungary on data localisation preferences
  • Draft Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) templates for cross-border transfers: carrier-to-carrier (e.g., Austrian carrier sharing passenger name with Italian carrier for disruption notification); carrier-to-clearing entity (booking and revenue data); payment institution-to-carrier (refund communication)
  • Define consent and special-category data governance: classify accessibility data (mobility, health-related assistance attributes) as GDPR Article 9 special category; specify consent model (passive opt-in at booking time, documented in confirmation); identify any heightened consent needed for assistance-request data
  • Conduct structured engagement with European Data Protection Board (EDPB) and 7–9 national DPAs (Austria, Germany, France, Netherlands, Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Spain, Sweden) to achieve written sign-off on SCCs and data-flow model by Month 4 (2027-02-08)
  • Specify breach-response and incident-notification protocols: define internal breach detection and escalation steps, notification timelines to affected data subjects (under 72 hours per GDPR Article 33), authority notification requirements, and containment procedures for each type of data loss or unauthorised access
  • Establish data-deletion and retention rules: PII deleted 90 days post-journey unless a refund or complaint is pending (extend to 12 months for pending cases); specify which system holds retention records and audit logs (proposed: clearing entity or independent auditor)
  • Detail GDPR compliance verification in conformance checklist: audits of carriers' and payment institutions' consent documentation, data-handling practices, breach-response readiness, and SCC compliance starting Month 12 (2027-10-08); quarterly compliance reviews thereafter
  • Quantify GDPR implementation costs: estimated budget line EUR 5–10 million over Months 0–60 (2026-10-08 to 2031-10-08) covering DPIA, SCC negotiation, legal review, compliance audits, training and breach-response infrastructure; request approval by Month 3 (2027-01-08)

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • A vague or incomplete DPIA fails to identify all PII flows or misses a data-transfer scenario, leaving the programme exposed to unreviewed (potentially non-compliant) data handling; a national DPA challenge to an unassessed flow could halt the entire programme during critical deployment phases (Months 12–30 = 2027-10-08 to 2029-04-08)
  • Disputed or unaligned SCC terms between member states cause carriers to refuse cross-border data sharing, fragmenting the through-ticket system and blocking the continuity-of-journey promise that requires real-time passenger information transfer across carriers
  • Lack of consensus from at least 7–8 national DPAs by Month 4 (2027-02-08) leaves data-governance rules uncertain, forcing either a costly emergency renegotiation (6–12 weeks, consuming EUR 3–5M and delaying standards) or operation under provisional terms that invite later regulatory intervention
  • Accessibility data consent model is ambiguous or non-compliant, creating friction at booking time (passengers confused by lengthy consent flows) and reducing accessibility-assisted journey uptake by 15–25%, undermining the programme's inclusion commitments and attracting disability-rights complaints
  • Data-retention and deletion rules are not operationalised in the clearing entity's systems, leading to accidental non-compliance (data kept longer than 90/12 days), breach-response delays (>72-hour notification), and audit findings that damage carrier and passenger trust and invite DPA enforcement action
  • GDPR compliance is not embedded in the conformance checklist; carriers certify as 'OSDM-compliant' without proving they handle PII correctly, allowing non-compliant operators to go live, creating liability exposure and privacy risk for passengers
  • Insufficient budget (EUR <5M allocated instead of EUR 5–10M) for GDPR implementation results in incomplete DPIA, no external legal review, and ad-hoc compliance auditing, leaving the programme exposed to costly DPA investigations and potential fines (up to 4% of annual revenue per GDPR Article 83)

Worst Case Scenario: A national DPA (Austria, Poland or Germany) opens an investigation into the programme's data-sharing architecture in Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08), alleging that SCC terms were not properly reviewed and that passenger data is being transferred without adequate safeguards or explicit consent. The investigation stalls carrier integration and standards approval until Month 15–18 (2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08), pushing the Month 18 (2028-04-08) binding standards deadline at risk. In a worst case, the DPA issues a preliminary ban on cross-border data flows without a redesigned GDPR framework, forcing a 6–12 month rework of the data-layer architecture and the through-ticket clearing mechanism, delaying the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate by 6+ months. Estimated cost: EUR 5–10M in emergency legal and technical rework; reputational damage to the programme and reduced stakeholder trust; and potential EU fines for systematic data-handling non-compliance reaching EUR 20–50M if negligence is found.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 4 (2027-02-08), the EDPB and at least 8 national DPAs formally endorse the programme's SCC templates, data-flow minimisation design and consent model in writing. This provides legal certainty: payment institutions and carriers sign on with confidence, knowing their data-handling is compliant and auditable. The resolved GDPR rules are embedded in the Month 18 (2028-04-08) binding standards, eliminating the risk of later reinterpretation or challenge. Conformance testing from Month 12 (2027-10-08) onward includes GDPR compliance audits, so all go-live carriers have proven data-handling practices. The programme operates with transparent, auditable consent and deletion procedures, building passenger trust in through-tickets. By Month 30 (2029-04-08), no DPA investigations or data-handling disputes have emerged, and the programme advances to full deployment without GDPR-related delays or budget pressure.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Conduct an expedited DPIA focused on the highest-risk flows (payment data, accessibility attributes, cross-border carrier-to-carrier transfers) rather than exhaustive mapping of every possible scenario; prioritise consensus from the 3–4 largest member-state DPAs (Germany, France, Austria, Netherlands) plus the EDPB by Month 3 (2027-01-08), with a commitment to extend consensus to other member states in a second phase (Month 6–9 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08)
  • Use EU Commission template SCCs rather than negotiating custom templates; rely on the Commission's pre-negotiated Standard Contractual Clauses that are already recognised by most DPAs, reducing negotiation time from 6 weeks to 2 weeks, and allocate saved time to DPA engagement on the specific data minimisation and consent design (novel aspect unique to through-ticketing)
  • Adopt a 'privacy by design' phased approach: launch with minimal PII flows in Months 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08) (booking reference, seat number, payment—no passenger health or mobility data initially), then expand to accessibility data in Phase 2 (Months 24–30 = 2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08) once GDPR consensus is fully secured; this reduces initial compliance risk while allowing time for DPA engagement
  • Engage an independent, DPA-certified data-protection officer (external firm) to conduct the DPIA and lead DPA negotiations, rather than relying on in-house legal counsel; external credibility often accelerates DPA sign-off by 2–4 weeks and reduces the risk of later challenge (cost: EUR 200–400K for 6-month engagement, but justified if it prevents a Month 9–12 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08 regulatory investigation)
  • If DPA consensus is not achieved by Month 4 (2027-02-08), invoke a fallback: request a formal EDPB guidance or expedited emergency opinion (target 4 weeks under GDPR Article 36) on the specific data flows, rather than waiting for individual member-state buy-in; escalate to the Commission and request diplomatic intervention if a single DPA blocks consensus (sovereignty concern, but justified if delay exceeds 4 weeks)

Create Document 7: Budget and Financial Management Framework, Including Contingency Tiers and Mid-Course Review Gates

ID: 81ae85a7-b43a-4301-9940-e11ea5fd843f

Description: Detailed activity-based cost model specifying EUR 1.5 billion public budget allocation across eight major cost lines (standards/conformance EUR 280M, clearing/settlement EUR 120M, reference distributor EUR 215M, capacity building EUR 100M, consumer rollout EUR 150M, carrier co-funding EUR 290M, data layer EUR 60M, governance/measurement EUR 60M), with EUR 225 million contingency (EUR 215M free). Monthly burn-rate dashboards, Tier 1–3 contingency actions (triggered at 115% of pro-rata spend), mid-course reviews (Months 12, 24 = 2027-10-08, 2028-10-08), and decision gates for supplementary budget authority. Includes sensitivity analysis for hub economics, distributor operating cost, payment-fee exposure, and carrier co-funding demand.

Responsible Role Type: Budget Controller and Financial Manager / Contingency Steward

Primary Template: EU Programme Budget Framework (multi-year financial planning model)

Secondary Template: Activity-Based Budgeting Template (Commission)

Steps to Create:

  • 1. Commission an independent cost-modelling firm (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23); deliver detailed forecast by Month 2 (2026-12-08) specifying: carrier co-funding per carrier size (EUR 2–8M per SME, EUR 10–15M per mid-size, EUR 0.5–2M per major), hub opex per hub (EUR 1.2M/year vs. fee revenue EUR 0.73M/year = gap EUR 0.47M/year), reference distributor annual opex (EUR 50–65M/year for full retail, EUR 20–30M/year for reference-implementation only), and payment-institution fee exposure (EUR 80–160M over five years at 0.5–1.0% per transaction).
  • 2. Allocate the EUR 1.5 billion cap to the eight cost lines per the canonical facts (standards EUR 280M, clearing EUR 120M, distributor EUR 215M, capacity EUR 100M, consumer EUR 150M, co-funding EUR 290M, data EUR 60M, governance EUR 60M).
  • 3. Establish monthly burn-rate dashboards (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) showing cumulative spend vs. pro-rata forecast (EUR 25M/month baseline), with automatic escalation if quarterly spend exceeds 115% of budget line.
  • 4. Define contingency tiers and responses: Tier 1 (10–15% overrun): defer consumer-app polish, reduce co-marketing by 20%; Tier 2 (15–25% overrun): reduce carrier co-funding from 20% to 10%, limit hub openings to priority corridors; Tier 3 (>25% overrun): suspend new hub openings, scale capacity building to 3–4 priority member states.
  • 5. Schedule mid-course reviews at Months 12 and 24 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08) to assess cumulative spend, trigger contingency actions, and request supplementary authority from the Commission if needed.
  • 6. Secure DG MOVE commitment (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) to seek supplementary budget authority (EUR 100–200M) from the Commission by Month 12 (2027-10-08) if Tier 2 is triggered.
  • 7. Include sensitivity analyses: impact on contingency if hub opex is 30% higher, distributor cost runs EUR 60M/year instead of EUR 43M/year, or payment-fee subsidy demand is EUR 25M instead of EUR 15M.

Approval Authorities: DG MOVE (budget approval and mid-course decisions); Commission (supplementary authority requests)

Essential Information:

  • Define the canonical EUR 1,500 million public budget allocation across eight cost lines (standards EUR 280M, clearing EUR 120M, reference distributor EUR 215M, capacity building EUR 100M, consumer rollout EUR 150M, carrier co-funding EUR 290M, data layer EUR 60M, governance/measurement EUR 60M) with EUR 225 million contingency reserve (EUR 215M free).
  • Specify monthly burn-rate forecasts (EUR 25M/month baseline) and quarterly cost-tracking dashboards that flag overruns at 115% of pro-rata spend per cost line, enabling early escalation before budget exhaustion.
  • Detail the three contingency tiers and automatic response triggers: Tier 1 (10–15% overrun, defer app polish and reduce co-marketing); Tier 2 (15–25% overrun, cut carrier co-funding from 20% to 10% and limit hub openings); Tier 3 (>25% overrun, suspend new hubs and scale capacity building to priority member states).
  • Establish mid-course review gates at Months 12 and 24 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08) to assess actual spend vs. forecast, trigger contingency actions, and request supplementary budget authority (EUR 100–200M target from the Commission if needed).
  • Conduct sensitivity analyses quantifying budget impact of: hub operating-cost variance (±30%), reference-distributor annual cost (EUR 50–65M/year vs. EUR 20–30M/year), payment-institution fee exposure (EUR 80–120M over five years at 0.5–1.0% per transaction), and carrier co-funding demand (EUR 150–300M for 12–18 smaller operators).
  • Identify EUR 10 million earmarked contingency (passenger-rights backstop residual liability) and EUR 215 million free contingency; specify which cost lines and unforeseen risks each can absorb.
  • Define the decision point (Month 48 = 2030-10-08) for securing post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainable funding (~EUR 45M/year for ongoing distributor, hub operations and data-layer maintenance not covered by the cap).
  • Specify supplementary budget-authority trigger and escalation path: if Tier 2 is triggered at Month 12 (2027-10-08), DG MOVE seeks Commission authorization by Month 12 (2027-10-08) for emergency funding; document the approval process and any conditions (e.g., programme scope reduction, timeline extension).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Inadequate cost model leads to budget surprises: if carrier co-funding demand is underestimated by 30% (actual EUR 300M vs. plan EUR 290M), a EUR 10M shortfall forces cuts to conformance testing (delaying certification by weeks) or capacity building (weakening regulator enforcement), fragmenting smaller-carrier adoption and pushing Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate at risk.
  • Lack of real-time cost tracking and escalation triggers causes budget overruns to accumulate unnoticed until Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), when corrective action is too late and either critical work is cancelled (standards work postponed, distributor launch delayed) or the budget cap is breached with political consequences.
  • Unclear contingency tier definitions and decision authority delay responses to overruns: if the budget controller is ambiguous about when Tier 2 is triggered or who approves co-funding cuts, disputes arise, decisions slip by 2–4 weeks per incident, and the programme drifts over budget.
  • Inadequate sensitivity analysis misses high-impact budget risks: if hub economics is 30% worse than estimated (gap EUR 2.8M/year instead of EUR 1.9M/year) or distributor cost doubles (EUR 86M/year instead of EUR 43M/year), the free contingency is consumed faster, leaving no reserve for payment-provider switching or accessibility delivery failures.
  • Missing post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability planning leaves EUR 45M/year in recurring costs unfunded; if no decision is made by Month 48 (2030-10-08), the programme either collapses at Month 60 (2031-10-08) (abandoning the digital infrastructure after five years) or lurches into crisis mode, forcing ad-hoc fundraising or scope cuts that undermine stakeholder trust.
  • Failure to document and communicate the budget framework to carriers and distributors creates expectations of unlimited co-funding; when cuts are imposed (Tier 2), recipients feel betrayed and withdraw support (e.g., distributors delay integration, smaller carriers demand exemptions), fracturing the coalition.

Worst Case Scenario: A budget and financial management framework is created but lacks granular cost visibility and real-time tracking. By Month 18 (2028-04-08), cumulative programme spend is EUR 450M (30% overrun vs. EUR 346M pro-rata forecast) due to hub operating costs 40% higher than estimated and distributor operations at EUR 55M/year instead of EUR 43M/year. The overrun is discovered only in a Month 18 (2028-04-08) review, too late to adjust standards work or carrier integration. The EUR 215M free contingency is depleted by Month 30 (2029-04-08), forcing suspension of carrier co-funding mid-programme. Smaller carriers unable to complete hub integration slip past the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate. Payment-institution accreditation is delayed to Month 15 (2028-01-08) due to insufficient budget for accreditation oversight. The programme fails to deliver on the Month 30 (2029-04-08) binding API milestone, national regulators declare non-compliance, and the Commission is forced to renegotiate the Regulation or grant exemptions. By Month 48 (2030-10-08), the programme is EUR 200–300M over budget, no decision exists for post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding, and stakeholder confidence collapses. The 40% through-ticket target and the full corridor deployment (Month 60 = 2031-10-08) are abandoned or substantially scaled back.

Best Case Scenario: A detailed activity-based cost model and financial-management framework is in place by Month 2 (2026-12-08), with monthly burn-rate dashboards and automated escalation at 115% of pro-rata spend. Quarterly mid-course reviews at Months 12 and 24 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08) detect early cost pressures (hub opex 20% higher, carrier co-funding demand EUR 310M) and trigger Tier 1 cost controls immediately. Contingency actions (defer app features, reduce distributor co-marketing) are applied swiftly, holding cumulative spend to EUR 370M by Month 24 (2028-10-08) (within plan). By Month 36 (2029-10-08), through-ticket volumes are tracking to 35% share (on pace for 40% by Month 60 = 2031-10-08); carrier compliance is 85%+ and trending toward 90% by Month 30 (2029-04-08); and the budget is within 10% of forecast. The EUR 100M supplementary-authority request to the Commission (filed at Month 12 = 2027-10-08) is approved by Month 15 (2028-01-08), enabling full funding of hub resilience, accessibility delivery and payment-provider redundancy. By Month 48 (2030-10-08), a post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainable-funding model is agreed (transition to cost-recovery clearing, host agency for data layer, member-state regulator co-funding). Programme credibility is maintained, stakeholder buy-in remains strong, and the Month 60 (2031-10-08) corridor deployment is on track with confidence that operations will continue beyond the cap-funded period.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Adopt a simplified activity-based budget without detailed sensitivity analysis: allocate the EUR 1.5 billion across the eight lines using high-level estimates, then focus all contingency management on real-time tracking and escalation. This reduces upfront modelling time (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08 instead of Month 2 = 2026-12-08) and is faster, but increases risk of budget surprises; use this only if detailed cost data are unavailable by Month 1 (2026-11-08), with plan to upgrade to full sensitivity analysis by Month 6 (2027-04-08).
  • Implement a rolling 12-month cash-flow forecast instead of a five-year budget: update quarterly projections of spend, contingency depletion and funding needs based on actual delivery progress, enabling more nimble rebaselining but reducing visibility into structural cost risks (hub persistence, distributor expansion). Reserve a larger contingency (EUR 300M, 20% of cap) to absorb forecasting error. Suitable if programme complexity makes five-year prediction unreliable.
  • Establish a cost-sharing mechanism with carriers and distributors: instead of absorbing co-funding and hub operating costs entirely from the public budget, negotiate contribution agreements (carriers fund 10–20% of hub opex, distributors co-fund marketing campaigns). This reduces public budget pressure but requires complex negotiations and creates equity concerns (smaller carriers cannot afford their share). Document agreements by Month 4 (2027-02-08) if pursuing this approach.
  • Defer sustainability-funding decisions until Month 54 (2031-04-08) (two months before Month 60 = 2031-10-08 end): instead of planning post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) operations by Month 48 (2030-10-08), maintain all options open and let the Commission decide continuity based on programme performance and fiscal conditions at the time. This reduces planning overhead now but increases risk of abrupt service shutdown or emergency funding scrambles; only acceptable if political commitment to continuation is very high.
  • Use an independent third-party budget controller/financial manager to oversee cost tracking, escalation and contingency release: hire a professional financial audit and PMO firm (€5–8M over five years) to maintain cost discipline, conduct monthly reviews, and recommend tier-trigger decisions. This reduces dependency on DG MOVE staff capacity but adds cost and governance complexity; suitable if internal DG MOVE PMO staffing is constrained.

Create Document 8: Regional Shared Booking Hub Specification, Procurement and Operational Plan

ID: 1d5e829c-f56a-40b9-8785-1cec5d7662f6

Description: Specification for 4–6 regional shared booking hubs serving legacy-IT carriers (estimated 12–18 carriers with annual revenue under EUR 50M, booking systems older than 10 years, or IT staff under 10 FTE). Defines hub technology (OSDM translation layer, inventory mapping, API gateway), operational SLAs (99.9% uptime, <2-second latency, <2-hour incident recovery, 10,000+ bookings/day capacity), governance (hub operators, data governance, security), and cost model (EUR 5–8M per hub over five years, with annual opex EUR 1.2M vs. fee revenue EUR 0.73M/year, creating EUR 0.47M/year gap per hub). Includes hub-eligibility criteria, procurement RFP timeline (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23, awards by Month 3 = 2027-01-08, operational Month 9 = 2027-07-08), pilot testing (Months 15–18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08), and sunset/cost-recovery gate (Month 48 = 2030-10-08). Audience: hub operators, smaller carriers, regional coordinators, national regulators.

Responsible Role Type: Smaller Carriers and Regional Integration Lead / Digital Inclusion Specialist

Primary Template: EU Service Provider Agreement Template (IT infrastructure provision)

Secondary Template: OSDM Hub Technical Specification (UIC guidance adapted)

Steps to Create:

  • 1. Define hub eligibility (Month 1 = 2026-11-08): annual cross-border revenue under EUR 50M, or booking system older than 10 years, or IT staff under 10 FTE; estimate 12–18 carriers.
  • 2. Specify hub technology (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08): OSDM-translation layer mapping legacy inventory and business rules to OSDM standards, API gateway, secure data transfer, redundancy (dual data centres per hub).
  • 3. Define hub SLAs (Month 2 = 2026-12-08): 99.9% uptime, <2-second latency for distributor queries, <2-hour incident recovery, capacity 10,000+ bookings/day without degradation.
  • 4. Establish cost model (Month 2 = 2026-12-08): opex EUR 1.2M/year per hub (staffing, infrastructure, vendor fees), fee revenue EUR 0.73M/year at capacity (EUR 0.1–0.3 per booking), creating EUR 0.47M/year gap; hubs are programme-financed (EUR 5–8M per hub over five years).
  • 5. Issue RFP (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23): 4 priority hubs (one per corridor) + 2 TEN-T hubs reserved; operational start by Month 9 (2027-07-08).
  • 6. Award contracts (Month 3 = 2027-01-08); establish technical integration workshops with eligible carriers (Month 4 = 2027-02-08).
  • 7. Schedule pilot tests (Months 15–18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08): 2–3 eligible carriers per hub, 2–4 week dual-run (hub + native), resolve mapping errors before production cutover.
  • 8. Establish hub stop threshold: suspend new carrier onboarding to a hub if booking-failure rate exceeds 2% for more than 1 week.
  • 9. Define sunset clause: hub operation expires Month 48 (2030-10-08); all carriers must migrate to native OSDM or alternative hub by that date; fee-recovery transition begins Month 36 (2029-10-08) (from programme subsidy toward carrier-paid fees).

Approval Authorities: DG MOVE (procurement approval); EU Agency for Railways (technical oversight); Hub operators (implementation)

Essential Information:

  • Define hub eligibility criteria operationally: which carrier types qualify (annual cross-border revenue threshold, booking-system age, IT-staff size), estimated carrier count (12–18), and regional distribution across four priority corridors.
  • Specify hub technology architecture: OSDM translation layer design, legacy-system inventory mapping logic, API gateway specification, data-security protocols, redundancy/failover design (dual data centres per hub), and integration testing requirements.
  • Establish hub operational SLAs and performance metrics: uptime (99.9% target), query latency (<2 seconds p95), incident recovery (<2 hours), capacity (≥10,000 bookings/day without degradation), booking-failure rate threshold (stop expansion if >2% for >1 week).
  • Detail the cost model: annual opex per hub (~EUR 1.2M: staffing, infrastructure, vendor fees), projected fee revenue (~EUR 0.73M at capacity), resulting subsidy gap (~EUR 0.47M/year per hub), and five-year total cost (EUR 5–8M per hub programme-financed, EUR 44M for 4 launch + 2 TEN-T hubs).
  • Specify procurement timeline and RFP scope: issue dates (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23), application deadline, technical evaluation criteria, contract awards (Month 3 = 2027-01-08), and hub operational start date (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 for four priority, with TEN-T hubs contingent on Month 30 = 2029-04-08 gate).
  • Define hub pilot and cutover process: dual-run duration (2–4 weeks per carrier), mapping-error detection and resolution protocols, external validation by independent test lab (Months 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08), and pilot testing schedule (Months 15–18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08 with 2–3 carriers per hub).
  • Establish governance and data controls: hub operator responsibilities (SLA compliance, incident response, data minimisation), data-flow security (GDPR compliance, PII retention rules, breach notification), inventory-mapping correctness accountability, and insurance requirements (E&O liability EUR 2–5M).
  • Specify hub sunset and cost-recovery transition: operation expiry at Month 48 (2030-10-08), migration requirement for all carriers to native OSDM or alternative hub by that date, fee-recovery rate increase from Month 36 (2029-10-08) onward (programme subsidy declines, carrier-paid fees increase from ~EUR 0.10–0.30 per booking toward full opex recovery).
  • Define escalation and contingency paths: hub performance thresholds (booking-failure >2%, latency >3 seconds, uptime <99.8%), escalation to Steering Committee and DG MOVE within 1 week, contingency actions (capacity surge funding, external support, carrier re-routing to alternative hub), and fallback to bilateral settlement or native OSDM acceleration for at-risk carriers.
  • Address hub failure and disaster-recovery scenarios: single hub failure affecting 4–6 carriers, estimated recovery time (<48 hours), refund exposure and liability (estimated EUR 100K–500K per incident), redundancy and backup operator protocols, and programme contingency reserve allocation for incident costs (from EUR 10M passenger-rights reserve or EUR 215M free contingency).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or ambiguous hub-eligibility criteria result in disputes over which carriers qualify for hub access, creating unfair allocation, missed onboarding targets and 4–8 week delays per contested carrier.
  • Under-specified hub technology and data-mapping logic lead to integration failures (legacy-system rules incorrectly translated), causing 2–5% booking-failure rate post-launch, passenger refunds, distributor liability disputes and revenue losses of EUR 5–15M over years 2–3.
  • Vague operational SLAs enable hub operators to under-invest in reliability, resulting in latency >5 seconds during peak hours, uptime <99%, and cascading failures that strand 50,000+ passengers and trigger EUR 100K–500K refund claims per incident.
  • Incorrect cost model underestimates opex (actual EUR 1.5–2M/year) or overestimates fee revenue, creating unexpected budget pressure and forcing programme-funded hubs to operate beyond Month 48 (2030-10-08) cost-recovery gate, consuming an extra EUR 5–10M from contingency.
  • Delayed or unclear procurement process results in hub-operator contracts not awarded until Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), compression of integration and testing timelines from 12 months to 6–9 months, and hubs not operational by Month 9 (2027-07-08), pushing smaller-carrier readiness to Month 36–42 (2029-10-08 to 2030-04-08) and missing the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate.
  • Inadequate pilot and dual-run testing allows mapping errors to slip into production, causing 10–20% of through-tickets on hub-dependent carriers to fail at booking confirmation, generating disputes, refund waves (EUR 20–50M over months 18–30 = 2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08) and reputation damage that reduces distributor confidence and through-ticket volumes by 10–20 percentage points.
  • Weak data-governance and security specifications expose passenger PII to breach risk, trigger GDPR enforcement action by national DPAs, halt hub operations during investigation (2–4 week delay) and carry EUR 5–20M liability exposure under GDPR Articles 82/83.
  • Unclear hub-failure and disaster-recovery protocols result in a single hub outage (4–6 dependent carriers affected) lasting 24–72 hours without clear escalation, creating operational paralysis, passenger stranding, refund liability of EUR 200K–1M per outage and loss of distributor trust.
  • Ambiguous sunset and cost-recovery clause at Month 48 (2030-10-08) leads to extended hub operation beyond plan (cost overrun EUR 10–20M), or abrupt hub closure stranding carriers without native-OSDM migration path, forcing fall-back to bilateral settlement and network fragmentation.
  • Missing contingency-trigger thresholds and escalation paths delay response to hub under-performance by 4–12 weeks, allowing service degradation to accumulate and affecting 20–50% of through-tickets on impacted corridors before remediation is triggered.

Worst Case Scenario: If the hub specification is incomplete or operationally vague, hub-operator procurement is delayed to Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), integration testing is compressed to 4–6 months, and hubs are not reliably operational by Month 9 (2027-07-08). Mapping errors in legacy-system translation and insufficient validation allow 5–10% booking-failure rates to persist into live operation (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08). A cascade of failures follows: (1) 50,000–100,000 passengers per month experience failed bookings and refund disputes, consuming EUR 30–60M in unplanned refunds and carrier liability claims; (2) distributors lose confidence and reduce co-marketing investment by 30–50%; (3) 8–12 smaller carriers, unable to complete hub integration by Month 30 (2029-04-08) or experiencing repeated failures, either miss the API mandate or revert to bilateral settlement, fragmenting the network; (4) media coverage of booking failures and unresolved refunds damages programme credibility; (5) by Month 36 (2029-10-08), the programme has missed the through-ticket volume gate (15% target at Month 24 = 2028-10-08), and political pressure mounts for programme suspension or major re-scoping. The TEN-T extension beyond the four priority corridors is indefinitely delayed, and the full-network through-ticketing timeline slips from Month 60 (2031-10-08) to Month 72+ (2032-10-08+), eliminating environmental and capacity benefits. Total estimated cost: EUR 50–100M in unplanned refunds, litigation and reputation repair, plus loss of 3–6 months of programme timeline and distributor/carrier confidence recovery.

Best Case Scenario: A clear, operationally detailed hub specification with precise eligibility criteria, technology requirements, SLAs and pilot protocols enables rapid, high-confidence procurement (RFP issued Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23, awards Month 3 = 2027-01-08). Hub operators are contracted and resourced; integration workshops with eligible carriers begin Month 4 (2027-02-08); external validation of legacy-system mapping by an independent test lab (Months 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) catches and resolves mapping errors before pilot testing. Pilot and dual-run testing (Months 15–18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08) confirms booking-failure rates are <0.5% and API performance meets SLAs. All four priority-corridor hubs are operational by Month 9 (2027-07-08) with high reliability (>99.9% uptime, <2-second latency). By Month 30 (2029-04-08), 85–95% of 12–18 hub-eligible smaller carriers are integrated and passing conformance, enabling 90%+ corridor traffic coverage and full API mandate compliance. The hub ecosystem becomes a trusted onboarding pathway for smaller operators; TEN-T extension (Month 36 = 2029-10-08) is fully resourced with operational hub templates; by Month 60 (2031-10-08), through-ticketing reaches 40% of cross-border rail volumes, smaller carriers are sustainably integrated, and the cost-recovery transition (Month 48 = 2030-10-08 onward) is on track. Total value realized: EUR 44M programme investment in hubs generates EUR 100M+ in through-ticket revenue uplift (via increased distributor integration, smoother carrier adoption, and avoided fragmentation), enabling the programme to meet its 40% target and supporting 5–15% modal shift from air on priority corridors.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If hub procurement slips past Month 6 (2027-04-08) or fewer than 2 qualified hub-operator bids are received: activate bilateral-pairing contingency, pairing each eligible smaller carrier with a larger carrier in the same region for data-sharing and booking-gateway access (lower integration cost for smaller carriers, higher operational dependency on bilateral governance), with a fast-track procurement of a single backup hub operator by Month 9 (2027-07-08) if viability is confirmed.
  • If external hub-mapping validation (Months 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) identifies >3 critical mapping errors per hub or >5% booking-failure rate in test scenarios: execute a 4–8 week mapping-rework cycle, potentially delay pilot testing by one month (to Month 19–22 = 2028-05-08 to 2028-08-08), or hand off detailed mapping validation to the hub operator's dedicated data-quality team with enhanced programme oversight (biweekly audits vs. standard quarterly).
  • If hub operational start slips to Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08) due to infrastructure delays or carrier readiness: launch a 'staged hub go-live' approach in which the first 3–4 eligible carriers per hub begin dual-run in Month 15–18 (2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08), while remaining carriers use temporary bilateral settlement or a lightweight API-gateway layer (lower SLA initially, 2–3 second latency acceptable) until the hub stabilises.
  • If a hub's booking-failure rate remains >1.5% at Month 21 (2028-07-08) after the pilot phase: implement a 'hub performance improvement plan' with increased staffing (data-quality engineers), external vendor support (contract a specialised legacy-system integration firm), and temporary carrier re-routing to a backup hub or bilateral channel, with a 4–6 week remediation window before escalation to Steering Committee and potential hub operator replacement.
  • If hub cost-recovery at Month 48 (2030-10-08) proves infeasible (fee revenue is <60% of opex, carriers resist fee increases above EUR 0.20/booking): shift hubs to a 'break-even' model in which the programme funds the EUR 0.47M/year gap in perpetuity (beyond Month 60 = 2031-10-08), redesign hubs as permanent infrastructure rather than temporary bridges, or merge hubs into a single federated European hub operated by a multi-carrier consortium or the EU Agency for Railways (long-term sustainability decision, separate governance change).
  • If by Month 24 (2028-10-08) <12 smaller carriers have committed to hub integration due to concerns about cost, technology risk, or operational dependency: launch an 'accelerated co-funding and support surge' for Months 24–30 (2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08) with 2x co-funding grants (EUR 4–16M per carrier instead of EUR 2–8M), on-site carrier mentoring by a regional coordinator full-time at the carrier's office, and simplified contractual terms (shorter commitment periods, easier exit clauses), targeting 15+ carrier adoption by Month 30 (2029-04-08).
  • If hub infrastructure or data-centre availability in a particular region (e.g., southeast Europe) is constrained: procure a cloud-hosted hub alternative (AWS, Azure, GCP) operated by a third-party managed-services provider, with the programme retaining data-sovereignty and security oversight via Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs); this trades higher quarterly opex costs (~15–20% premium) for faster deployment (3–4 month deployment vs. 6–9 months for on-premises hub).
  • If a critical hub operator (covering 4–6 carriers) signals withdrawal or bankruptcy during Months 12–48 (2027-10-08 to 2030-10-08): activate an 'emergency hub transition' protocol: (1) the programme assumes hub operation directly or procures emergency replacement operator within 2 weeks (contingency budget EUR 2–3M); (2) affected carriers are rerouted to a backup hub or bilateral settlement within 48 hours; (3) performance data and carrier configurations are transferred to the replacement operator within 5 business days; (4) if no replacement is available within 30 days, affected carriers accelerate migration to native OSDM (co-funded at 50% of integration cost, EUR 5–10M surge funding from contingency) or revert to bilateral booking for up to 6 months pending hub restoration.
  • If by Month 30 (2029-04-08), hub-dependent carriers represent <60% of the needed carrier coverage for the 90% corridor-traffic gate: activate 'contingency native-OSDM acceleration' for Months 30–36 (2029-04-08 to 2029-10-08) with emergency co-funding (EUR 10–20M surge) for 2–4 smaller carriers to build native OSDM interfaces in parallel with hub use, enabling fallback to distributed native implementations if hubs do not scale or have insufficient coverage by Month 30 (2029-04-08).

Create Document 9: Passenger-Rights Backstop and Liability Allocation Framework

ID: 72109965-2674-42da-b09e-c99766f9ced1

Description: Operational design for rerouting, care, and refund obligations when a through-ticket's connection is missed due to carrier delay or infrastructure failure. Specifies single point of contact (selling distributor), decision and payment timelines (<4 hours reroute decision, <10 days refund), fault-allocation protocol (which carrier is responsible when multiple carriers are involved), cost recovery via accredited payment providers, and a pooled guarantee fund (EUR 30–40M reserve, or 8–12% of tickets estimated at EUR 10–40M over five years). Includes dispute-resolution panel (5-day ruling), insurance requirements (EUR 2–10M errors-and-omissions per entity), and audit/compliance procedures. Aligns with revised EU Regulation 1371/2007 and the programme's non-discrimination goals. Audience: distributors, carriers, payment institutions, regulators, passengers.

Responsible Role Type: Cross-Border Rail Passenger Rights and Liability Framework Specialist

Primary Template: EU Rail Passenger Rights Operational Procedures (Regulation 1371/2007 adapted)

Secondary Template: Multi-Operator Liability Allocation Template (ICC Incoterms model adapted)

Steps to Create:

  • 1. Commission an actuarial study (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) estimating claim rate (baseline 3–5%, stress case 8–12%), average claim cost (EUR 50–200), and total exposure (EUR 10–40M over five years).
  • 2. Draft the Fault-Allocation Protocol (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08): specify who makes the fault decision (e.g. independent arbiter or the responsible carrier initially with appeal to dispute panel), timeline (24–48 hours), and the cost-allocation logic (which carrier reimburses the distributor's refund advance).
  • 3. Define single-point-of-contact procedures (Month 3 = 2027-01-08): the selling distributor is the passenger-facing contact for rerouting and refund; the distributor advances cost and recovers from liable carrier(s) via accredited payment providers.
  • 4. Specify response timelines: rerouting decision within 4 hours of notification (automatic for missed connections due to the programme's API integration); refund decision within 10 days.
  • 5. Design dispute-resolution panel (Month 3 = 2027-01-08): 5–7 members (rotating carrier and distributor representatives), empowered to rule on contested claims within 5 business days.
  • 6. Define the pooled guarantee fund (Month 3 = 2027-01-08): EUR 30–40M reserve (or 8–12% claim-rate estimate) to cover unrecovered first-level refunds if a liable carrier is insolvent or disputes the refund; administer via the clearing entity.
  • 7. Require all operational entities (distributors, hubs, payment institutions, clearing entity) to carry errors-and-omissions liability insurance (EUR 2–10M minimum, EUR 5M target) by Month 4 (2027-02-08); verify coverage before go-live.
  • 8. Pilot the refund process on one corridor (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam) by Month 15 (2028-01-08): measure claim volume, resolution time, dispute rate; if resolution time exceeds 10 days for >5% of claims or dispute rate exceeds 3%, increase the guarantee fund by EUR 10–20M by Month 18 (2028-04-08).
  • 9. Embed the framework and SLAs in the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08); include compliance audits in quarterly regulator reviews (starting Month 12 = 2027-10-08).

Approval Authorities: Commission (through binding standards Month 18 = 2028-04-08); Member-state regulators (enforcement); Steering Committee (guarantee-fund adjustments)

Essential Information:

  • Specify the single point of contact (selling distributor) and confirm that distributors advance refund/rerouting costs and recover from liable carriers via accredited payment providers, with clear timelines: reroute decision <4 hours, refund decision <10 days.
  • Define the fault-allocation protocol: which carrier is responsible when a through-ticket's connection is missed due to delay, infrastructure failure, or missed assistance; criteria for fault determination and dispute escalation.
  • Establish the pooled guarantee fund mechanics: EUR 30–40M reserve (8–12% of estimated claim volume EUR 10–40M over five years), trigger conditions for draw-down, and administration via the clearing entity.
  • Quantify expected claim rates and costs: baseline 3–5% of through-tickets result in claims; average claim cost EUR 50–200 (rerouting, care, refund); estimate total five-year exposure and annual burn.
  • Design the dispute-resolution panel: 5–7 rotating members (carrier and distributor seats), decision authority on contested claims, 5-day ruling timeline, escalation path for unresolved disputes.
  • Specify insurance requirements: minimum EUR 2–10M errors-and-omissions liability per operational entity (distributors, hubs, payment institutions, clearing entity); verification and enforcement mechanism.
  • Detail the pilot on one corridor (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam): Month 15–18 (2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08); measure claim volume, resolution time, dispute rate; decision gate for guarantee-fund adjustment if resolution time exceeds 10 days for >5% of claims or dispute rate exceeds 3%.
  • Align the framework with revised EU Regulation 1371/2007 (rail passenger rights), the programme's non-discrimination commitments, and payment-services and liability law across member states.
  • Identify the responsible parties for different failure modes: distributor liable for booking errors and false promises; carriers liable for operational failures (missed connections, accessibility delivery); payment institutions liable for settlement errors; hub operators liable for mapping errors.
  • Establish audit and compliance procedures: quarterly review of claim metrics (volume, resolution time, dispute rate) starting Month 12 (2027-10-08); escalation triggers; integration into conformance testing checklist.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Ambiguous fault-allocation logic leads to carrier-distributor disputes over who pays for rerouting, delaying passenger refunds by weeks and generating liability claims against the programme (estimated EUR 10–50M exposure if unresolved).
  • Missing or weak guarantee-fund provisions: if the pooled reserve (EUR 30–40M) is underfunded or trigger conditions are unclear, carriers become insolvent mid-journey and passengers are left without recourse, damaging the programme's credibility and inviting regulatory intervention.
  • Inadequate insurance requirements: if distributors or hubs carry insufficient errors-and-omissions coverage (e.g., EUR 500K instead of EUR 2–10M), a single incident (mapping error causing 5,000 booking failures) exhausts reserves and leaves gaps unfunded by the pooled fund.
  • Slow dispute resolution (e.g., 20–30 days instead of 5–10 days) creates a complaint backlog of 1,000+ by Month 21 (2028-07-08), eroding distributor confidence and reducing through-ticket volumes by 5–10 percentage points.
  • Misalignment with national passenger-rights rules: if the backstop contradicts interpretation of rerouting or care obligations under Regulation 1371/2007 in a member state, that state's regulator may prohibit through-ticket sales until clarified, fragmenting the network.
  • Vague or unenforceable timelines for rerouting decision (<4 hours) or refund (<10 days) permit carriers to delay compliance, and without enforcement teeth (e.g., penalties or escrow), the timeline becomes advisory and passenger experience deteriorates.
  • Unplanned refund volumes exceed 8–10% of through-tickets (e.g., due to tight connections or high-demand corridors), consuming EUR 20–40M of the EUR 215M free contingency by Month 24 (2028-10-08) and forcing budget cuts to conformance testing or capacity building.
  • Missing accessibility-specific refund procedures: if a through-ticket passenger with reduced mobility is stranded due to missed assistance, no clear path for escalated compensation is defined, inviting BEUC and disability-rights complaints and reputational damage.

Worst Case Scenario: A high claim rate (8–12% of through-tickets) emerges in the pilot corridor (Month 15–18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08), and a cascade of distributor-carrier disputes over fault allocation overwhelms the dispute panel (designed for 5-day rulings but facing 200+ contested claims monthly). Average resolution time stretches to 30+ days; passenger refunds are delayed; and Trainline and Omio announce they are reducing through-ticket promotion. Simultaneously, a regional hub suffers a mapping error affecting 10,000 bookings (2–5% failure rate), and the hub operator's EUR 2M insurance is exhausted by litigation costs, leaving EUR 3M gap unfunded. By Month 24 (2028-10-08), the guarantee fund (EUR 30–40M) is depleted 80%, and the programme must draw EUR 20–40M from the EUR 215M free contingency. Momentum collapses; through-ticket volumes drop 15–20%, missing the 15% interim target at Month 24 (2028-10-08). The Commission is forced to halt corridor expansion (TEN-T extension delayed from Month 36 = 2029-10-08 to Month 48 = 2030-10-08) and initiates a review of the programme's sustainability, threatening the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate and requiring 6–12 months of remediation and policy rework.

Best Case Scenario: The framework is finalised and pilot-tested by Month 18 (2028-04-08) with clear fault allocation, sub-10-day average refund resolution, and claim rates tracking at 3–5% baseline. The dispute panel establishes credible precedents and resolves 90%+ of contested claims within 5 days; carriers trust the process and comply with rerouting timelines. Insurance requirements are met by all entities; no individual incident exceeds reserve limits. By Month 24 (2028-10-08), the guarantee fund has consumed only EUR 3–5M (well within EUR 30–40M budget), and the framework is embedded in the conformance checklist without friction. Distributors report high passenger satisfaction (95%+ say refunds/rerouting were resolved fairly), and through-ticket volumes achieve 18–22% by Month 24 (2028-10-08), exceeding the 15% interim gate and signalling strong uptake. Passenger trust in through-tickets rises, enabling confident expansion to the TEN-T network (Month 36 = 2029-10-08), and the 40% target becomes credibly achievable by Month 60 (2031-10-08) with no need for contingency reserve drawdown and demonstrable cost-effectiveness.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If full framework development is delayed beyond Month 4 (2027-02-08), adopt a simplified 'fast-track' version for the pilot corridor (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam): distributor liability is unconditional (no fault determination); claims are processed by a single independent arbiter (not a rotating panel) with 7-day decision timeline; guarantee fund is fixed at EUR 50M (higher reserve, lower dispute overhead) and deployed only at Month 27 (2029-01-08) after pilot results are known.
  • If the dispute-resolution panel cannot be staffed or operational by Month 6 (2027-04-08), defer formal panel creation to Month 9 (2027-07-08) and use an interim binding arbitration service (contract an external firm for EUR 500K–1M annually) to rule on claims during Months 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08); transition to the in-house panel once staffed.
  • If insurance requirements cannot be met by all entities by Month 4 (2027-02-08), implement a tiered insurance approach: large entities (Trainline, SNCF) required to carry EUR 5–10M by Month 4 (2027-02-08); smaller entities (regional hubs, payment providers) required EUR 2–5M by Month 6 (2027-04-08); verification deferred to Month 9 (2027-07-08) with go-live conditional on 90%+ coverage.
  • If actuarial study reveals claim costs significantly exceed EUR 40M (five-year estimate), activate contingency early: (1) increase the guarantee fund from EUR 30–40M to EUR 50–60M funded from the EUR 215M free contingency (consuming EUR 20–30M by Month 6 = 2027-04-08), and (2) reduce the expected through-ticket volumes or shorten the timeline for reaching 40% (extending to Month 66–72 = 2032-04-08 to 2032-10-08).
  • If the pilot corridor (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam) experiences >8% claim rates or >30% dispute rate during Month 15–18 (2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08), pause the rollout of other corridors and conduct a 4–8 week framework remediation: strengthen fault-allocation rules, add expedited tracks for low-value claims (<EUR 100), and increase the dispute panel from 5–7 members to 9–11 to handle capacity surge.
  • If member-state regulators diverge on interpreting rerouting or care obligations under Regulation 1371/2007 (creating conflicting national requirements), establish a Standing Regulators Committee ruling (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) harmonising interpretation across borders; if consensus cannot be reached, defer non-consensus rules to bilateral carrier-distributor agreements and allow 12-month transition (Month 12–24 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-10-08) before enforcement.

Create Document 10: Measurement Baseline, Through-Ticket Definition and Evaluation Methodology

ID: 2648beee-5f21-41d1-b18a-d06f1414aa1a

Description: Operational definition of 'through-ticket' (single booking reference + single payment + continuity-of-journey rights on a multi-carrier journey), baseline survey methodology (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08), and independent counterfactual evaluation design to separate programme effects from fuel prices and aviation-tax policy. Specifies mandatory monthly reporting by carriers and distributors (starting Month 18 = 2028-04-08), quarterly aggregated dashboards, interim gates (15% through-ticket share by Month 24 = 2028-10-08), and attribution analysis for the three headline targets (40% through-ticket share, halved complaints, modal shift 5–15%). Budget EUR 5–10M over five years for baseline, evaluator contract, and analytics. Audience: Steering Committee, carriers, distributors, Parliament, Commission.

Responsible Role Type: Measurement, Evaluation and Evidence Lead / Impact Analytics Director

Primary Template: EU Evaluation Framework (Regulation (EU) 1303/2013 adapted)

Secondary Template: Counterfactual Evaluation Design Template (World Bank guidance)

Steps to Create:

  • 1. Define 'through-ticket' operationally (Month 2 = 2026-12-08): single booking reference + single payment + continuity-of-journey rights (rerouting/refund if connection missed) on a multi-carrier journey, sold via any distributor or operator platform.
