Lock this definition; do not re-interpret later.
  • 2. Conduct baseline survey (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) asking carriers, distributors and airports for current cross-border sales volumes, complaint rates and modal-split estimates (with confidentiality protections).
  • 3. Validate and publish the baseline (Month 9 = 2027-07-08): baseline through-ticket share, complaint rate (e.g., 3 complaints per 1,000 bookings), and modal-split estimate on the four priority corridors.
  • 4. Commission an independent external evaluator (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) to design a counterfactual evaluation: compare through-ticket adoption on priority corridors to control routes outside the rollout, using difference-in-differences or propensity-score matching to isolate programme effects from fuel prices, aviation taxes and capacity changes. Deliver methodology by Month 9 (2027-07-08).
  • 5. Mandate carrier and distributor reporting (starting Month 18 = 2028-04-08): monthly through-ticket volumes and complaint counts, aggregated and published quarterly with a 1-month lag to protect commercial sensitivity.
  • 6. Establish interim gates: 15% through-ticket share by Month 24 (2028-10-08) (proposed threshold); if missed, escalate to Steering Committee and assess mid-course corrections (e.g., increase co-marketing budget, distributor incentives, or activate killer-application contingencies).
  • 7. Publish quarterly progress dashboards (starting Month 18 = 2028-04-08) tracking: through-ticket share (target 40% by Month 60 = 2031-10-08), complaints baseline vs. target (halved by Month 60 = 2031-10-08), and modal-shift estimate (planning range 5–15%).
  • 8. Conduct mid-programme evaluation (Months 30–36 = 2029-04-08 to 2029-10-08) assessing interim success, informing TEN-T extension scope and post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability decisions.
  • 9. Allocate EUR 5–10M within the programme budget for baseline survey, evaluator contract, and analytics infrastructure.

Approval Authorities: Steering Committee (baseline approval and interim gates); Commission (final evaluation results)

Essential Information:

  • Define 'through-ticket' operationally by Month 2 (2026-12-08) as: single booking reference + single payment + continuity-of-journey rights (rerouting or refund if connection is missed) on a multi-carrier journey, sold via any distributor or operator platform. Lock this definition; do not re-interpret later.
  • Conduct baseline survey in Months 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) collecting current cross-border rail sales volumes, distributor complaint rates, and modal-split estimates from carriers, distributors and airports, with confidentiality protections (aggregated reporting, no carrier-level disclosure).
  • Establish operational baseline by Month 9 (2027-07-08): quantify starting through-ticket share (estimated baseline), complaint rate per 1,000 bookings, and modal-split share on four priority corridors; publish validated baseline for stakeholder sign-off.
  • Commission independent external evaluator by Month 3 (2027-01-08) to design counterfactual evaluation (difference-in-differences or propensity-score matching) isolating programme effects from fuel prices, aviation taxes and capacity changes; deliver methodology by Month 9 (2027-07-08).
  • Mandate monthly carrier and distributor reporting starting Month 18 (2028-04-08): through-ticket volumes, complaints, and relevant operational metrics; aggregate and publish quarterly with 1-month lag to protect commercial sensitivity.
  • Establish interim performance gate: 15% through-ticket share (proposed threshold) by Month 24 (2028-10-08); if missed, escalate to Steering Committee and assess mid-course corrections (increased co-marketing, distributor incentives, or contingency activations).
  • Publish quarterly progress dashboards starting Month 18 (2028-04-08) tracking: (1) through-ticket share (target 40% by Month 60 = 2031-10-08), (2) complaints baseline vs. halved target by Month 60 (2031-10-08), (3) modal-shift estimate (planning range 5–15%, distinct from volume metric).
  • Conduct mid-programme evaluation Months 30–36 (2029-04-08 to 2029-10-08) assessing interim success against baseline and interim gates, informing TEN-T extension scope decisions and post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability model.
  • Allocate EUR 5–10 million within the EUR 1,500 million cap for baseline survey, external evaluator contract, analytics infrastructure and quarterly reporting systems.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Without an agreed definition of 'through-ticket', stakeholders dispute what counts as success; by Month 24–30 (2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08), claims about the 40% target are contested and politically contested, eroding credibility.
  • If baseline data are not collected in Months 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08), the starting point remains unknown, and mid-course corrections in Month 12–24 (2027-10-08 to 2028-10-08) are made without evidence of what changed, wasting adjustment opportunities.
  • Weak counterfactual methodology (e.g., comparing non-equivalent routes, or ignoring fuel-price confounders) results in unattributable modal-shift claims; by Month 48–60 (2030-10-08 to 2031-10-08), the environmental case for the EUR 1,500 million investment cannot be credibly defended to Parliament or member states.
  • Absent interim gates and early reporting, overruns in through-ticket uptake (e.g., stuck at 20% by Month 30 = 2029-04-08) are not detected until Month 36–48 (2029-10-08 to 2030-10-08), leaving insufficient time to adjust strategy (increase distributor co-funding, activate killer-app contingencies) before the programme's core objectives are missed.
  • Inconsistent definitions or incomplete reporting across carriers and distributors leads to 15–25% undercount of true through-ticket volumes; the programme appears to miss the 40% target even if actual performance is 35% (due to measurement error), inviting false narrative of failure.
  • Without documented assumptions and sensitivity analysis, decision-makers cannot distinguish programme effects (API mandate, clearing mechanism, standards) from external market shifts (fuel prices, aviation taxes), limiting evidence-based mid-course learning.

Worst Case Scenario: By Month 48 (2030-10-08), a rigorous external evaluation reveals that through-ticket adoption has stalled at 25% (not 40%), modal shift is 3% (below the 5% planning floor), and half the apparent growth is due to reduced aviation capacity post-COVID, not the programme. The measurement framework did not exist until Month 12 (2027-10-08), baseline was never locked, and data quality is contested. The programme is declared at risk of missing its headline targets by Parliament's TRAN committee. A formal audit is initiated, blocking further distributor investment. The Commission must announce corrective action (additional EUR 200–400 million in subsidy or timeline extension), trigger political backlash over wasted spending, and damage future EU transport-infrastructure credibility. The programme narrowly survives but loses stakeholder buy-in and accelerates plans to wind down the public distributor and data layer by Month 60 (2031-10-08), leaving sustainability at risk.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 18 (2028-04-08), a locked, published definition of 'through-ticket' and validated baseline are endorsed by all stakeholders. Monthly reporting from carriers and distributors flows consistently. By Month 24 (2028-10-08), the interim gate shows 18% through-ticket share (exceeding the 15% threshold), confirming early momentum. Mid-programme evaluation Months 30–36 (2029-04-08 to 2029-10-08) credibly attributes 12 percentage points of growth to the programme (net of fuel and aviation effects) and 3 percentage points to external factors. Quarterly dashboards guide scaled distributor campaigns on high-momentum corridors. By Month 60 (2031-10-08), the programme achieves 42% through-ticket share and 6% modal shift. Parliament's TRAN committee reports success; member states commit to post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding of the data layer and regulator capacity. The programme is held up as a model for future EU mobility integration and attracts international interest.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If a comprehensive DPIA and counterfactual evaluator contract cannot be procured by Month 3 (2027-01-08), establish an in-house evaluation team (2–3 FTE) within the PMO, working with academic partners on a pro-bono basis. Defer formal counterfactual until Month 18 (2028-04-08), using simple before-after comparison until comparison-route data are available.
  • If carriers refuse mandatory monthly reporting on claimed grounds of commercial sensitivity, negotiate a confidentiality-protected shared-data arrangement: carriers report volumes to an independent third-party auditor (e.g., Ernst & Young, Deloitte), which publishes only aggregated, anonymised dashboards; full raw data accessible to DG MOVE and EU Agency for Railways under confidentiality agreements. Cost: EUR 500,000–1 million annually for audit services.
  • If the interim through-ticket gate of 15% at Month 24 (2028-10-08) is at risk of being missed by Month 20 (2028-06-08), activate emergency contingencies: (1) increase distributor co-marketing budget by EUR 5–10 million, (2) introduce a temporary public-distributor subsidy (EUR 20–30 per booking) for high-priority corridors, (3) extend the through-ticket definition to include 'single booking reference with guaranteed rerouting rights even if payment is separate', capturing more passengers. Cost: EUR 25–40 million from free contingency.
  • If baseline data collection in Months 0–2 (2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) is delayed to Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08), use proxy data from EUROSTAT, Trainline/Omio internal reports (under NDA) and regulator administrative records to construct a 'best estimate baseline' by Month 9 (2027-07-08). Caveat that true baseline uncertainty is ±20% until Month 24 (2028-10-08) when full reporting begins.
  • If no agreed definition of 'through-ticket' is locked by Month 2 (2026-12-08) and stakeholders propose multiple interpretations, publish a 'menu of definitions' (narrow: single payment only; medium: single payment + continuity rights; broad: any multi-carrier journey with one distributor) and track all three metrics in parallel until consensus emerges by Month 9 (2027-07-08). Report results for all definitions in quarterly dashboards, letting stakeholders debate which counts.

Create Document 11: Regulation Adoption Risk Register and Contingency Scenario Plans (Scenario A: On-Time Adoption Month 9 = 2027-07-08; Scenario B: Adoption Months 11–12 = 2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08 with Text Changes; Scenario C: Adoption Blocked or Deferred Beyond Month 12 = 2027-10-08)

ID: c7b2e447-b630-46fa-94bf-00c3a8363573

Description: Strategic contingency planning document mapping three adoption scenarios for the Commission's proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services. Scenario A (on-time Month 9 = 2027-07-08) proceeds with 9-month standards window; Scenario B (Months 11–12 = 2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08 with amendments) compresses standards to 6–7 months and adapts to text divergences; Scenario C (adoption blocked) pauses the programme and resets the critical path. Each scenario includes decision triggers, resource activation, stakeholder communications and revised milestone dates. Owned by DG MOVE with input from the arbitration panel and Parliament liaison. Due Month 2 (2026-12-08) as a working document.

Responsible Role Type: Governance and Legal Affairs Advisor; Strategy and Programme Director

Primary Template: EU Risk Management and Scenario-Planning Framework

Secondary Template: None

Steps to Create:

  • 1. Map the three adoption scenarios (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) based on Parliament and Council negotiation timelines, member-state political signals, and rapporteur public statements.
  • 2. For Scenario A (on-time Month 9 = 2027-07-08): outline the standard timeline (Months 4–18 = 2027-02-08 to 2028-04-08) and confirm all prerequisite gates (Council delegation, carrier Commitment Letters, hub awards, payment accreditation).
  • 3. For Scenario B (Months 11–12 = 2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08 with text changes): design a 6–7 month standards acceleration (detailed specs Month 10 = 2027-08-08, stakeholder validation Months 10–16 = 2027-08-08 to 2028-02-08, formal vote Month 17 = 2028-03-08, publication Month 18 = 2028-04-08), specify likely text divergences (liability, data scope, API mandate scope) and required rework.
  • 4. For Scenario C (adoption blocked): outline programme pause (Month 13 onwards = 2027-11-08+), rebaselining window (Months 13–21 = 2027-11-08 to 2028-09-08), and reset decision on whether to proceed with shadow standards or await new Commission proposal.
  • 5. Define decision gates (Month 6 = 2027-04-08: adoption probability assessment; Month 8 = 2027-06-08: standards consortium contingency activation; Month 10 = 2027-08-08: Scenario C pause decision) with assigned owners and escalation procedures.
  • 6. Publish as a working document (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) and update monthly (Months 3–12 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-10-08) as adoption tracking progresses.

Approval Authorities: DG MOVE (scenario decisions); Steering Committee (monthly review)

Essential Information:

  • Define the three adoption scenarios (A: on-time Month 9 = 2027-07-08; B: Months 11–12 = 2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08 with text changes; C: adoption blocked or deferred) with specific decision gates, trigger conditions and probability thresholds for each.
  • Map the critical-path implications of each scenario: Scenario A permits 9-month standards window (Months 4–18 = 2027-02-08 to 2028-04-08); Scenario B compresses to 6–7 months with required pre-work by Month 10 (2027-08-08); Scenario C pauses the programme and resets readiness assumptions.
  • Specify resource activation and contingency spending for each scenario: Scenario A requires no new procurement; Scenario B may trigger external standards consortium (€2–5M); Scenario C pauses all carrier commitments and deactivates hub/payment accreditation timelines.
  • Identify probable text divergences in Scenario B (liability allocation, API mandate scope, data access definitions, passenger-rights integration) and outline required standards rework (estimated 2–4 weeks).
  • Detail decision gates and owners: Gate 1 (Month 6 = 2027-04-08, DG MOVE): assess adoption probability and activate early-warning protocols; Gate 2 (Month 8 = 2027-06-08, DG MOVE/Steering Committee): decide on contingency standards consortium; Gate 3 (Month 10 = 2027-08-08, DG MOVE): final Scenario C pause decision.
  • Quantify escalation procedures and communication protocols for each scenario (stakeholder notification timelines, Parliament liaison updates, carrier communication cadence).
  • Specify revised milestone dates and rebaselining windows for Scenario B (e.g., if adoption is Months 11–12 = 2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08, adjust Month 18 = 2028-04-08 standards completion date to Month 19–20 = 2028-05-08 to 2028-06-08) and Scenario C (pause decision Month 13 = 2027-11-08; rebaselining window Months 13–21 = 2027-11-08 to 2028-09-08).
  • Include contingency budget allocation per scenario: Scenario A (no additional spend); Scenario B (€2–5M standards consortium + EUR 2–3M accelerated regulator training = EUR 4–8M from the EUR 215M free contingency); Scenario C (hold EUR 50–100M as 'programme pause reserve' and redirect to carrier advisory/Parliamentary liaison).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Lack of clear decision gates delays the Month 8 (2027-06-08) contingency activation, compressing the standards-setting window further and risking rushed, low-quality standards that carriers reject.
  • Ambiguous scenario triggers (e.g., 'adoption could slip') without quantified probability thresholds prevent timely escalation and leave the Steering Committee uncertain when to pause or accelerate.
  • Failure to quantify text-divergence impacts (e.g., liability allocation changes requiring €X rework) means standards-setting is blindsided by legislative surprises and must rework completion near the Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline.
  • Missing resource-activation instructions for Scenario B (e.g., when and how to hire the external standards consortium, approval authority) leave the PMO unable to act decisively when adoption delays.
  • Unclear communication protocols for Scenario C (e.g., order and timing of carrier notification, Parliament briefing, distributor communications) risk stakeholder panic, media misinterpretation and erosion of political support.
  • Undefined rebaselining windows in Scenario C (e.g., how long the 'pause' lasts, whether shadow standards continue, what the reset decision criteria are) leave the programme in limbo and waste months in indecision.
  • Absence of contingency budget allocation per scenario means overspend in Scenario B (e.g., unbudgeted consortium fees) consumes the EUR 215M free contingency without oversight or re-prioritisation.

Worst Case Scenario: If this document is not created to high quality, the programme faces catastrophic schedule and credibility collapse. If the Regulation adoption is delayed to Month 11–12 (2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08) and the contingency-activation procedures are unclear or absent, the Steering Committee does not act decisively; standards-setting is compressed to 5–6 months (Month 13–18 = 2027-11-08 to 2028-04-08) without adequate pre-work, resulting in standards of poor quality or lacking stakeholder consensus. Carriers and distributors publicly reject the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards, forcing a 2–4 month rework (pushing to Month 20–22 = 2028-06-08 to 2028-08-08) and compressing the Month 30 (2029-04-08) integration window to 8–10 months—unachievable for legacy carriers using hubs. If Scenario C (adoption blocked) occurs and the pause decision is delayed to Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08) due to unclear decision criteria, the programme wastes resources on shadow standards that have no legal foundation, and the Commission is forced to announce a pause publicly, damaging the programme's political credibility and signalling to stakeholders that the EU cannot execute complex transport infrastructure. Carriers withdraw from co-funding negotiations; distributors halt API integration; the public confidence in the initiative erodes. A delayed Scenario C pause also means carrier IT teams have already begun expensive integration work (estimated EUR 50–100M sunk by Month 12 = 2027-10-08), which must be written off if the programme is paused. Estimated damage: 6–12 month delay to the entire programme, EUR 50–150M wasted pre-work spend, and reputational damage that makes future EU transport infrastructure initiatives harder to fund and execute.

Best Case Scenario: If this document is created with clear decision gates, quantified triggers and resource-activation instructions, the Steering Committee and DG MOVE can respond decisively to adoption delays or blockages. In Scenario A (on-time adoption by Month 9 = 2027-07-08), the document confirms readiness to proceed with the 9-month standards window and activates the full critical path without hesitation. In Scenario B (adoption Months 11–12 = 2027-09-08 to 2027-10-08 with text changes), the document triggers pre-emptive contingency actions by Month 6 (2027-04-08) (early regulator training, standards consortium procurement), enabling compressed but quality standards-setting in the 6–7 month window; text divergences are identified by Month 10 (2027-08-08) and rework is completed within 2–4 weeks without missing the Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline. In Scenario C (adoption blocked or deferred beyond Month 12 = 2027-10-08), the document provides an explicit pause decision by Month 13 (2027-11-08), protecting the programme from wasted shadow-standards work, and triggers a structured rebaselining window (Months 13–21 = 2027-11-08 to 2028-09-08) in which the Commission can either revise and resubmit the Regulation or decide to withdraw. Stakeholders are notified with clear, coordinated messaging, preventing panic and preserving political support for a future restart. The clarity enables the programme to execute on a contingent timeline, preserving the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate credibility in Scenarios A and B while maintaining institutional credibility in Scenario C. Estimated benefit: no slippage to Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards in Scenarios A and B; clean, low-damage pause and reset in Scenario C; EUR 50–100M sunk cost avoidance if Scenario C is executed.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If creating a comprehensive three-scenario document with detailed text-divergence analysis and rework timelines proves time-intensive or requires legislative expertise not available, create a simplified two-scenario contingency plan (Scenario A: on-time adoption with green-light checklist; Scenario C: adoption blocked with pause protocol and EUR 50M rebaselining budget), deferring detailed Scenario B analysis to Month 3 (2027-01-08) after early adoption signals are clearer.
  • Engage the European Parliament's TRAN committee and rapporteurs directly (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08) to obtain explicit input on adoption probability and likely amendment areas; use their assessment to calibrate scenario probabilities and pre-define the most likely Scenario B text divergences, reducing the need for exhaustive speculation.
  • Commission an external EU legislative-tracking firm or legal consultancy (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) to produce monthly adoption-tracking briefs (€30–50K/year), feeding live intelligence to the scenario document and enabling quarterly updates rather than creating a static document.
  • Establish a monthly 'Adoption Readiness Forum' (Month 1 = 2026-11-08 onwards) with DG MOVE, Parliament liaison, Council representatives and key member states; use the forum to refine scenario triggers and decision criteria collaboratively, embedding the contingency thinking into the governance structure rather than documenting it unilaterally.
  • Create a 'Scenario A – On-Time Adoption' operational playbook immediately (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) assuming Month 9 (2027-07-08) adoption, with a separate 'Contingency Trigger Protocol' document (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) that covers activation thresholds and pauses; treat the full three-scenario register as a living quarterly-update workbook rather than a static Month-2 deliverable.
  • If the document is needed for Steering Committee approval, produce a 5–10 page executive summary with decision gates and Gate-1 through Gate-3 criteria (Month 2 = 2026-12-08), deferring the detailed 40–50 page Scenario B text-divergence analysis and Scenario C rebaselining plan to working-document status (updated monthly, Months 3–12 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-10-08) rather than treating it as a formal Month-2 approval deliverable.

Documents to Find

Find Document 1: Commission Proposed Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail (May 2026) - Final Adopted Text

ID: 6c2661ec-f1a0-4164-9b41-2257b33f7440

Description: The foundational legislative instrument defining mandatory OSDM-compatible API exposure, non-discriminatory access duties, passenger-rights backstop, and enforcement mechanisms across EU member states. This is the legal basis for the entire programme and determines scope (which carriers and routes are in-scope), access-term definitions, liability allocation, and the regulatory authority of member-state enforcement bodies. Essential for standards development (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 deadline) and governing the non-discrimination framework. Audience: DG MOVE, arbitration panel, standards working group, carriers, regulators, legal counsel.

Recency Requirement: Final adopted text; expected Month 9 (2027-07-08) but may slip to Month 10–12 (2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08) depending on Parliament and Council negotiations.

Responsible Role Type: Governance and Legal Affairs Advisor; Strategy and Programme Director

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Track Commission publication of the Regulation in the EU Official Journal (EUR-Lex database).
  • 2. Contact the Parliament's TRAN and IMCO rapporteurs (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23) to obtain advance notice of adoption timing and any significant amendments.
  • 3. Once adopted, download the full legislative text from EUR-Lex (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/) and analyse for gaps vs. OSDM v2.1 and the Pragmatic Foundation scenario.

Access Difficulty: Easy. The Commission proposal (May 2026) is already public on EUR-Lex. Final adopted text will be published immediately upon Council adoption and is freely accessible.

Essential Information:

  • Final adopted text of the Commission's Regulation on Digital Booking and Ticketing Services for Rail, specifying the exact definitions of 'non-discriminatory access', 'OSDM-compatible API', mandatory scope (member states, carrier thresholds, route coverage), and enforcement mechanisms (which regulators have authority, sanctions for non-compliance).
  • Clarification of which carriers and routes fall under the Regulation's mandatory API-exposure deadline (Month 30 = 2029-04-08); confirmation that the four priority corridors (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon, Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin) are in-scope.
  • Defined liability allocation for through-ticket failures: who bears cost of rerouting, care, and refunds when a multi-carrier journey is disrupted; how this interacts with EU rail passenger-rights rules (Regulation 1371/2007, as amended).
  • Specification of data-sharing and non-discrimination duties: what inventory, fares, and post-sale data carriers must expose to distributors; what constitutes 'discriminatory' access (e.g., latency parity, tiered access rules); enforcement audit rights for regulators.
  • Passenger-rights backstop framework: whether a central guarantee mechanism is mandated or left to member-state discretion; refund timelines and responsibility allocation.
  • Compatibility with competition law (Articles 101/102 TFEU): explicit safeguards or block exemption on data-sharing and collective pricing (if applicable) to clarify whether shared inventory/fare layer is permissible.
  • Cross-border jurisdiction and dispute resolution: which regulator (national, EU Agency for Railways, Commission) has binding authority over access disputes, refund claims, and non-compliance findings across member states.
  • Requirements for accessibility, GDPR compliance, and payment-system licensing (PSD2) integration within the regulatory framework.
  • Effective date and transition provisions: when carriers are required to begin integration; any transition period or exemption criteria for legacy operators.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If the adopted text significantly diverges from the Commission's May 2026 proposal (e.g., narrower scope, weaker access obligations, or different liability rules), standards and operational frameworks developed in parallel (Months 0–18 = 2026-10-08 to 2028-04-08) must be reworked, delaying Month 18 (2028-04-08) binding standards by 4–8 weeks and pushing Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate into jeopardy.
  • Ambiguity or omission in the Regulation on 'non-discriminatory access' definitions leaves room for incumbent carriers to publish access terms that claim compliance but continue de facto discrimination (e.g., slower API response times, delayed inventory updates, higher fees for distributors); without clear enforcement criteria, the arbitration panel cannot effectively adjudicate access disputes, undermining the core mechanism.
  • If the Regulation's scope excludes smaller carriers or specific corridors, the through-ticketing network is fragmented, and the 40% target becomes unachievable (e.g., if Wien–München–Zürich or Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon are out-of-scope, major corridors lack full coverage).
  • Lack of clarity on cross-border dispute resolution and regulator authority creates a vacuum: national regulators may interpret duties differently, and there is no clear escalation path for a distributor's complaint about discriminatory access by a carrier in another member state, leaving unresolved disputes and competitive disadvantage.
  • Incompatibility with competition law or lack of clearance on data-sharing exposes the programme to DG Competition investigation and potential remedial action (redesign or dismantling of the shared data layer) in Month 12–24 (2027-10-08 to 2028-10-08), directly threatening the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate.
  • If passenger-rights backstop is left vague (who bears cost of failed reroutes, what constitutes 'reasonable' care), distributors and carriers will dispute every claim, and the refund process becomes a bottleneck, damaging passenger confidence and reducing through-ticket uptake by 10–20 percentage points.

Worst Case Scenario: Parliament and Council adopt a Regulation in Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08) that materially diverges from the Commission's May 2026 proposal, narrowing scope (excluding smaller carriers or specific corridors), weakening access-term definitions (allowing carriers to publish discriminatory 'FRAND' terms with little regulatory oversight), and deferring dispute resolution to national regulators without binding cross-border escalation. Simultaneously, DG Competition opens an investigation into the data-sharing architecture in Month 10–12 (2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08), citing collusion risk. The standards working group discovers that Month 18 (2028-04-08) binding standards cannot be finalised until the Regulation and competition review are resolved, forcing a 6–12 month slip in the standards deadline. By Month 24 (2028-10-08), the programme has lost momentum and credibility; carriers signal they cannot meet the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate without further extensions; distributors withdraw integration commitments, forcing the public reference distributor to expand its scope and consume an additional EUR 100M+ in budget; and the 40% through-ticket target drops to 15–20%, a clear failure.

Best Case Scenario: Parliament and Council adopt a clear, broadly aligned Regulation by Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), confirming scope (four priority corridors + TEN-T), defining 'non-discriminatory' with quantified thresholds (e.g., API latency parity ±500 ms, inventory-update parity <5 minutes, no tiered access for distributors meeting conformance), and establishing the arbitration panel as the binding technical authority with explicit delegation from Council. DG Competition issues a comfort letter on the data-sharing scope by Month 6 (2027-04-08), citing the pro-competitive safeguards (neutral operator, access logs, data minimization). The standards working group produces binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-08) without re-litigation; carriers sign Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08) accepting the Month 30 (2029-04-08) deadline; hubs and accredited payment institutions are operational by Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08); and carrier integration proceeds on schedule, reaching 90%+ readiness by Month 30 (2029-04-08). The programme hits the 40% through-ticket target by Month 60 (2031-10-08) and demonstrates modal shift of 10–15% on priority corridors, validating the infrastructure investment and securing political support for TEN-T extension and future EU programmes.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the final Regulation is adopted later than Month 9 (2027-07-08) or diverges materially, pause carrier onboarding commitments (hold Commitment Letter signing until Month 10–12 = 2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08) and conduct a rapid re-baseline of the critical path with the final text. Activate a 'shadow standards' contingency: contract an external standards-review consortium (Month 12 = 2027-10-08) to validate whether Month 18 (2028-04-08) is still achievable; if not, accelerate to a shortened Month 21 (2028-07-08) interim standards (covering the core 60–70% of functionality) and defer remaining technical details to Month 30 (2029-04-08).
  • If the Regulation's scope is narrowed (e.g., smaller carriers exempted), adjust programme scope and 40% target downward proportionally; define a secondary TEN-T extension phase (Month 42 onwards = 2030-04-08) targeting the excluded carriers and corridors, funded under a separate appropriation decision.
  • If DG Competition opens an investigation into data-sharing, request early closure via a pre-filing comfort letter (Month 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08); if investigation continues, redesign the data layer to use a 'data minimization' model (publish only aggregated inventory and disruption, not real-time load factors or individual fare offers) and establish an independent data governance board to audit access and prevent collusion.
  • If cross-border dispute resolution is not specified in the Regulation, the programme establishes a parallel Dispute Resolution Protocol (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) anchored in a Memorandum of Understanding among DG MOVE, the EU Agency for Railways and all member-state regulators, specifying a lead-authority rule and mutual recognition of rulings within 30 days.
  • If the passenger-rights backstop is ambiguous, the programme develops a binding Passenger-Rights Protocol (Month 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) specifying liability allocation (selling distributor front-line, with cost recovery from the responsible carrier via the clearing entity) and establishes a fast-track dispute panel (decisions within 5 days) to handle contested claims, reducing refund-process friction.
  • If Parliament proposes amendments that weaken the Regulation beyond acceptable scope, escalate political pressure through the European Parliament's TRAN and IMCO committees, engaging member-state transport ministers to defend the Commission text in Council negotiations (Month 4–8 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-06-08).

Find Document 2: OSDM v2.1 and Later Specifications (UIC/CER Open Sales and Distribution Model Standard)

ID: 5195ce98-9e28-4a53-8ed1-bf8350d5d896

Description: The technical standard for API design, data formats, and interoperability among EU rail carriers, used as the baseline for the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08). Specifies inventory API (offers, availability, fares), booking API (purchase, reservation), and post-sale API (changes, cancellations, refunds). Current version is v2.1; the programme may require v2.2 or v3.0 if Parliament amendments extend scope (e.g., multimodal integration). Audience: standards working group, carriers, test labs, distributors, data-layer architects.

Recency Requirement: Current OSDM v2.1 (published 2024) or later versions released during Months 0–9 (2026-10-08 to 2027-07-08). Gap analysis by Month 6 (2027-04-08) will identify any evolution needed.

Responsible Role Type: Chief Technical Standards Officer / OSDM and API Architecture Lead

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Contact UIC (International Union of Railways) directly via https://uic.org/ or the OSDM working group contact.
  • 2. Request the latest OSDM specification version (current v2.1, published 2024) in PDF format.
  • 3. Review versioning roadmap: check whether UIC has published v2.2 or announced v3.0 to incorporate EU Regulation changes by Month 6 (2027-04-08).

Access Difficulty: Medium. OSDM v2.1 is published by UIC but access may require membership or a formal request. Smaller carriers and distributors often receive copies via their sector organisations (CER, BEUC). Request from UIC by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23).

Essential Information:

  • Confirm the exact current version number of OSDM (v2.1, v2.2, v3.0 or other) as of Month 0 (2026-10-08) and verify UIC's published roadmap for future releases through Month 9 (2027-07-08).
  • Identify all technical extensions or amendments required to OSDM v2.1 to support the Regulation's final scope, including: multimodal integration (buses, ferries, short-haul air), accessibility-data schemas, passenger-rights continuity markers, cross-border refund/rerouting metadata, and distributor-certification attributes.
  • Map OSDM API coverage against the binding standards' required functionality: inventory (offers, real-time availability, fares with segment-level pricing breakdown), booking (purchase, reservation, hold management, payment orchestration markers), and post-sale (changes, cancellations, refunds, claims tracking, disruption signalling).
  • Document any gaps or conflicts between OSDM v2.1 and the Pragmatic Foundation's architectural decisions: federated authoritative inventory + central cache, tiered access based on distributor certification, real-time disruption-event streaming, and neutral operator roles.
  • Specify the conformance testing interface and validation protocols that OSDM requires for carriers, hubs, distributors and payment institutions; confirm whether v2.1 includes test harnesses and reference implementations.
  • Identify any versioning or backwards-compatibility constraints: which OSDM v2.0 or legacy implementations must remain supported, and what sunset dates apply for older versions.
  • Clarify licensing, IP ownership and standardisation-body governance: UIC's process for amendments, voting rights, and how CER, BEUC, national regulators and distributors participate in OSDM evolution during Months 0-18 (2026-10-08 to 2028-04-08).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • If OSDM v2.1 is outdated or UIC has already released v2.2/v3.0 without the programme's knowledge, standards-setting re-starts at Month 4-6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) and compresses the Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline, risking rushed standards or stakeholder non-acceptance.
  • Missing coverage of multimodal APIs (buses, ferries, air) in OSDM v2.1 forces a parallel or sequential extension process; if extension scope is unclear by Month 6 (2027-04-08), the binding standards are either incomplete or require a second standards-setting cycle, delaying Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate.
  • Incomplete accessibility-data schemas in OSDM (e.g., lift status, staff-assistance type, mobility requirements) prevent distributors from filtering itineraries for persons with reduced mobility; if not standardised by Month 18 (2028-04-08), accessibility-integration risk compounds, and the programme risks non-compliance with EU disability-rights law.
  • Undefined conformance-testing interface or missing reference implementations in OSDM delay test-lab setup and carrier certification; if conformance harnesses are not finalized by Month 9 (2027-07-08), 40-60 week delay per carrier is plausible, pushing smaller-carrier readiness past Month 30 (2029-04-08).
  • Ambiguity or conflict between OSDM's data-model and the Pragmatic Foundation's federated + cache architecture (e.g., OSDM assumes real-time inventory queries but federated queries are slower) forces re-architecting of the data layer mid-programme, adding 8-12 weeks delay and €5-10M rework cost.
  • Unclear IP ownership, licensing terms or governance processes for OSDM amendments risk stakeholder disputes (e.g., a carrier contests a new OSDM requirement as proprietaryor a standards-body vote is contested); if governance is not settled by Month 3 (2027-01-08), disputes delay standards finalisation by 4-8 weeks.

Worst Case Scenario: The programme requests OSDM v2.1 in Month 0 (2026-10-08) but discovers in Month 4-5 (2027-02-08 to 2027-03-08) that UIC has already released v2.2 (addressing accessibility and multimodal gaps) or is finalizing v3.0 (incorporating Regulation amendments). The standards-setting working group must choose: accept v2.2/v3.0 and re-plan gap analysis (2-4 week delay), or diverge from the latest standard and lose stakeholder confidence. Alternatively, OSDM v2.1 lacks any accessibility or multimodal extensions, forcing the programme to propose new sub-standards outside OSDM; carriers and distributors resist, claiming the programme has fragmented the standard and created integration burden. A major incumbent (SNCF or Deutsche Bahn) contests the new OSDM version's conformance cost or licensing terms, triggering a standards-governance dispute at the Steering Committee level (Month 9-12 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08). Without resolution by Month 15 (2028-01-08), the binding-standards deadline (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) is missed or delivered without incumbent buy-in, and the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate loses credibility, reducing carrier compliance from 90%+ to 70-80% and fragmenting the through-ticket network. Estimated impact: 4-8 week standards delay, €3-8M rework cost, and 10-20 percentage-point reduction in through-ticket readiness at Month 30 (2029-04-08).

Best Case Scenario: OSDM v2.1 is current, fully documented and published by UIC by Month 0 (2026-10-08), with a clear roadmap showing v2.2 release by Month 6 (2027-04-08) incorporating accessibility and multimodal extensions aligned with the proposed Regulation's final scope. The standards-working group reviews v2.1 in Months 0-3 (2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08), identifies gaps and confirms v2.2 will close them. UIC's governance process is transparent, allowing the programme to propose amendments through an expedited track; by Month 9 (2027-07-08), v2.2 is ratified with full accessibility, multimodal and distributor-certification schemas. Conformance-testing reference implementations and harnesses are available by Month 12 (2027-10-08), enabling independent test labs to begin accrediting carriers by Month 15 (2028-01-08). IP licensing is standardised under FRAND terms; all carriers and distributors accept the new version without contest. By Month 18 (2028-04-08), the binding standards reference OSDM v2.2 and conformance checklist, stakeholder consensus is high, and the critical path is protected. Carriers begin integration with clear, proven technical blueprints, and the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate has >90% projected readiness. Estimated impact: standards delivered on time, high conformance quality, reduced carrier integration cost by 10-15% due to proven reference implementations, and through-ticket readiness at Month 30 (2029-04-08) meets the 90%+ threshold.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If OSDM v2.1 is outdated or unavailable by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23), immediately contact UIC and request a pre-release or draft of v2.2/v3.0, or negotiate a formal liaison arrangement (seats for programme representatives on UIC's OSDM working group) to accelerate amendment inclusion. Cost: EUR 50-100K consulting, 2-week timeline.
  • If OSDM v2.1 lacks multimodal or accessibility extensions and UIC cannot deliver v2.2 by Month 6 (2027-04-08), establish a parallel EU-funded OSDM Enhancement Task Force (3-5 FTE programme staff, external XML schema experts, carriers) to draft the missing schemas by Month 9 (2027-07-08). Propose amendments to UIC for ratification as v2.2 or as an EU Profile / extension of v2.1. Cost: EUR 500K-1M, 3-4 month timeline.
  • If OSDM governance is contested or amendment timelines are slow (>6 months), propose a 'OSDM Adoption Decision' by Month 6 (2027-04-08): the binding standards will mandate OSDM v2.1 + published EU amendments (published separately, implemented by Month 30 = 2029-04-08). This de-couples OSDM ratification from the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards deadline. Risk: creates a two-layer standard that confuses implementers; mitigation is aggressive post-Month 18 (2028-04-08) testing and carrier engagement.
  • If conformance-testing harnesses are not available from UIC by Month 12 (2027-10-08), commission an external test-lab consortium (EUR 1-2M contract) to develop reference implementations and test suites from OSDM specification by Month 15 (2028-01-08). Alternatively, delay carrier conformance testing to Month 18-21 (2028-04-08 to 2028-07-08) and use bilateral carrier-programme testing (slower, higher cost: EUR 2-3M).
  • If a major carrier contests OSDM conformance costs or licensing terms by Month 9-12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08), escalate to DG MOVE and negotiate a one-time cost-sharing arrangement (programme covers 30-50% of conformance-enablement costs for that carrier) conditional on acceptance and on-time integration. Protect the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards deadline by resolving dispute within 2 weeks (arbitration panel authority).
  • If OSDM versioning or backwards-compatibility creates a burden (e.g., carriers must support both v2.0 and v2.1), negotiate a phased sunset: v2.0 must be replaced by Month 36 (2029-10-08), with funding for migration if cost is significant. This reduces the conformance burden in Years 1-2 and protects the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate.

Find Document 3: Existing EU Rail Passenger Rights Regulations (Regulation 1371/2007 and Revised Text, Adopted 2023)

ID: 4f828f62-e943-437f-bc85-b61dda97101c

Description: Current and revised EU rules governing passenger rights (cancellations, delays, refunds, accessibility assistance, liability allocation) that the programme's backstop must align with. Regulation 1371/2007 is the baseline; the revised text (adopted 2023, effective 2025) strengthens consumer protections and accessibility duties. Essential for designing the fault-allocation protocol and refund timelines in the Passenger-Rights Backstop Framework (Month 3 = 2027-01-08). Audience: legal counsel, arbitration panel, carriers, regulators.

Recency Requirement: Current: Regulation (EU) 2023/1300 (revised text, effective 2025 or later). The programme design must comply with the revised rules, not the older 1371/2007.

Responsible Role Type: Cross-Border Rail Passenger Rights and Liability Framework Specialist

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Access EUR-Lex (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/) and search for 'Regulation 2023/1300' (or the OJ reference if published more recently).
  • 2. Download the full legislative text in all EU languages; English version is primary for legal analysis.
  • 3. Cross-reference with existing Regulation 1371/2007 to identify what changed and how it affects the programme's backstop design.

Access Difficulty: Easy. EU regulations are published in the Official Journal and freely accessible on EUR-Lex.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the exact text, scope and effective date of Regulation (EU) 2023/1300 (revised EU rail passenger rights rules), and reconcile it with existing Regulation 1371/2007 to determine which duties (cancellation, delay, accessibility, refund, liability) apply to through-tickets sold under this programme.
  • Define which party (distributor, first carrier, connecting carrier, clearing mechanism) bears liability and financial responsibility for each failure mode: missed connection, accessibility delivery failure, payment processing error, cascading overbooking from hub mapping error.
  • Quantify specific refund obligations: maximum time from claim to payment (current Regulation vs. revised), care obligations (meal, transport, hotel, phone call), compensation caps or floors per failure type, and recovery mechanism if a carrier becomes insolvent mid-journey.
  • Specify how multi-carrier through-tickets align with the revised Regulation's 'continuity of journey' duty: does a distributor-sold through-ticket create a 'liable entity' for the entire journey, or does each carrier remain liable only for its segment?
  • List all accessibility-related duties under the revised Regulation that the programme must implement in booking, confirmation, on-board delivery and assistance handovers; identify any new duties in the 2023/1300 revision not in 1371/2007.
  • Extract the revised Regulation's dispute-resolution timelines and enforce authority (does it mandate national regulators, or permit alternatives?); clarify whether an EU-level arbitration panel aligns with or supersedes national procedures.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Misalignment between the programme's refund protocol (designed at Month 3 = 2027-01-08) and the revised Regulation's actual requirements (effective 2025 or later) causes the backstop to be non-compliant; carriers and distributors reject the protocol, and the programme faces legal challenge by Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08).
  • Ambiguity over liability allocation (who is legally responsible if a through-ticket passenger is stranded due to a missed connection) creates disputes between distributors and carriers; claims pile up unresolved, and the Dispute Resolution Panel (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) lacks clear legal grounds to rule, delaying resolution by 4–8 weeks per case.
  • Accessibility duties from the revised Regulation are incomplete or mis-specified; the programme launches with assistance-confirmation timelines that violate the Regulation (e.g., 48 hours instead of 24 hours required), triggering complaints from BEUC and national disability-rights organizations and forcing a corrective redesign (4–6 weeks).
  • The programme's clearing mechanism (accrual, recovery, insolvency) does not match the Regulation's compensation pooling or guarantees; if a carrier becomes insolvent mid-programme (Month 12–30 = 2027-10-08 to 2029-04-08), the mechanism has no legal basis to tap a guarantee fund, leaving passengers unprotected and the programme liable.
  • Payment terms promised in the programme (e.g., refund within 10 days) conflict with the revised Regulation's timelines (potentially stricter); the programme is forced to revise timelines, upsetting carrier and distributor agreements and delaying Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards approval.

Worst Case Scenario: ["A comprehensive misalignment between the programme's backstop design (finalised Month 3–6 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-04-08) and the revised Regulation's actual effective provisions (2025 or later) emerges after standards are published (Month 18 = 2028-04-08). The Commission, Parliament or a member-state regulator challenges the programme's refund/liability scheme as non-compliant; compliance audit is ordered, and the programme's standards are formally suspended pending rework. Carriers withdraw from pilot corridors, blaming regulatory ambiguity. Rewrite of the Passenger-Rights Backstop Framework takes 8–16 weeks, pushing the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate at risk. Estimated impact: 3–6 month delay in full deployment, and loss of carrier confidence in the programme's institutional stability."]

Best Case Scenario: ["The revised Regulation text is obtained and analysed by Month 2 (2026-12-08), clarifying all liability, compensation and accessibility duties. The programme's Passenger-Rights Backstop Framework (Month 3–6 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-04-08) is designed to exceed the Regulation's minimums (e.g., 10-day refund vs. the Regulation's 30-day baseline), building confidence among passengers and distributors. Carriers sign the Commitment Letters (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) with clear liability allocation. The dispute-resolution panel has explicit legal mandate from the Regulation, avoiding sovereignty challenges. By Month 18 (2028-04-08), standards incorporate the Regulation's passenger-rights framework, eliminating re-work and enabling smooth carrier integration (Month 18–30 = 2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08). Through-ticket system launches with strong legal grounding and high distributor confidence in compliance."]

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • Obtain the revised Regulation text directly from EUR-Lex and the European Commission's official databases (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08); engage DG MOVE's legal unit to provide an official guidance memo on passenger-rights compliance by Month 2 (2026-12-08).
  • If the full Regulation text is not yet published or adopted as of Month 0 (2026-10-08), commission an external legal firm (transport law specialists) to conduct a detailed gap analysis between the Commission's proposed May 2026 text and the 1371/2007 baseline, and project likely amendments based on Parliament and Council negotiations (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08).
  • Establish a formal liaison with the European Parliament's TRAN committee (rapporteur) and Council transport working group (Month 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) to receive informal advance notice of legislative decisions on passenger rights, liability and dispute resolution, enabling the programme to anticipate changes.
  • Engage CER, BEUC and national regulator representatives in a 'Regulation Alignment Workshop' (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08) to surface stakeholder interpretations of likely passenger-rights requirements and identify ambiguities; use their feedback to stress-test the programme's assumed framework before standards-setting begins.
  • If the revised Regulation is delayed beyond Month 9 (2027-07-08), adopt a phased compliance approach: deliver Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards using the Commission's May 2026 proposal as the baseline, with explicit 'compliance conditionality' that the standards are binding only after the final Regulation text confirms alignment; this allows carrier integration to begin without waiting for legislative certainty, at the cost of re-work risk if the final text differs materially.

Find Document 4: Statistical Data on Cross-Border Rail Journey Volumes and Passenger Demographics (EU Member States, 2023–2025)

ID: cf95677b-1d1f-4946-89cb-0ce53d2e73d9

Description: Baseline data on the number of cross-border rail journeys per year, passenger demographic profiles (age, income, mobility status, geography), and booking/ticketing patterns (single-operator vs. multi-operator journeys, use of distributors, payment methods). Needed to validate the 40% through-ticket target, design the measurement baseline (Month 9 = 2027-07-08), and model the through-ticket addressable market. Sources: national rail regulators' annual reports, CER sector statistics, EUROSTAT transport data. Audience: measurement team, programme evaluators, financial modellers.

Recency Requirement: Most recent available year (2024 or 2025). Preliminary 2024 data is acceptable; final 2025 data by Month 9 (2027-07-08) is required for the measurement baseline.

Responsible Role Type: Measurement, Evaluation and Evidence Lead; Strategy and Programme Director

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Contact Eurostat (https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat) and request transport statistics on rail journeys by country pair and year.
  • 2. Reach out to the Community of European Railway and Infrastructure Companies (CER, https://www.cer.be/) for aggregated sector statistics and member-company reports.
  • 3. Query individual national rail regulators (e.g., SNCF's annual report, Deutsche Bahn financial statements) for domestic and cross-border journey volumes.
  • 4. Check the EU Agency for Railways website (https://www.era.europa.eu/) for any published statistics on EU-wide rail mobility trends.

Access Difficulty: Medium. Eurostat data is freely available but aggregate cross-border journey data by country pair may require custom statistical request (1–4 weeks). National regulators sometimes publish annual reports on their websites; others require formal requests.

Essential Information:

  • Baseline data on annual cross-border rail journeys per EU country pair, 2023–2025 (volumes, trends, seasonal patterns)
  • Passenger demographic profiles for cross-border journeys: age, income level, mobility status, geographic origin/destination
  • Current booking and ticketing patterns: share of single-operator vs. multi-operator journeys, distributor-channel usage, payment methods
  • Addressable market for through-tickets: estimated number of journeys that could theoretically be sold as through-tickets vs. currently sold as separate tickets
  • Baseline distributor-complaint rates and types (delays, refunds, accessibility, data privacy) to establish the 50% reduction target denominator
  • Modal-split baseline: current share of short-haul air vs. rail on the four priority corridors, to enable counterfactual modeling of modal shift
  • Data sources and collection methods used by national regulators and CER, to ensure consistency with the measurement framework (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 validated baseline)

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or outdated baseline (e.g., 2023 only, missing 2024–2025 data) undermines validation of the 40% through-ticket target; disputes over whether targets are being met arise post-launch, delaying mid-course corrections by 6–12 months
  • Demographic data absent or poorly disaggregated (e.g., no mobility-status breakdown) prevents targeted accessibility and consumer-rollout campaign design, reducing through-ticket adoption among underserved groups by 5–15 percentage points
  • Baseline complaint rates not clearly defined (e.g., complaints per 1,000 journeys unclear) makes the '50% reduction' target ambiguous and unmeasurable; disputes over achievement occur at Month 36–48 (2029-10-08 to 2030-10-08)
  • Modal-split baseline missing or unreliable (e.g., no separation of air vs. rail passengers on Paris–Brussels route) prevents credible attribution of mode shift to the programme vs. external factors (fuel prices, aviation taxes); environmental impact case cannot be validated
  • Addressable-market estimates absent or overstated (e.g., assuming all cross-border journeys are convertible) leads to unrealistic through-ticket-volume targets; the 40% target becomes unachievable, and distributor and carrier confidence erodes by Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08)
  • Data sourced from inconsistent methodologies across member states (e.g., some use ticket sales, others use passenger counts) creates reconciliation gaps; quarterly reporting is delayed or contested, undermining stakeholder trust in measurement dashboards

Worst Case Scenario: The programme launches Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards without a validated baseline or clear definition of the 'addressable market' for through-tickets. By Month 30 (2029-04-08), distributor and carrier reporting of through-ticket volumes is inconsistent (some report 35%, others 45% on the same corridor), creating disputes over whether the 40% target is being met. Mid-course correction insights are delayed 6–12 months because data reconciliation consumes resources. By Month 48 (2030-10-08), stakeholders question whether modal shift has occurred (absence of pre-post air-passenger data means no counterfactual), and political pressure mounts to extend or cancel the programme. A lack of demographic baseline prevents the accessibility and consumer campaigns from being targeted, leaving persons with reduced mobility and lower-income passengers underserved and reducing the programme's social equity case. The programme reaches Month 60 (2031-10-08) with credible measurement of through-ticket volume but unable to claim environmental or inclusion benefits, undermining the case for post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding and TEN-T extension.

Best Case Scenario: A comprehensive baseline is established by Month 9 (2027-07-08) showing 2.5–4 million annual cross-border rail journeys on the four priority corridors, 60–70% currently sold as separate tickets (addressable market), and a clear demographic profile (e.g., 40% age 25–55, 25% with mobility constraints). Modal-split baseline establishes that short-haul air currently captures 35–45% of Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam traffic (counterfactual comparator). Quarterly reporting from Month 18 (2028-04-08) onward shows consistent growth: through-ticket share reaches 15% by Month 24 (2028-10-08), 25% by Month 36 (2029-10-08), and 40% by Month 60 (2031-10-08). Demographic tracking reveals that accessibility-assisted journeys grow from 2% of throughtickets to 5–8% by Month 60 (2031-10-08), validating inclusion efforts. A validated counterfactual model separates programme effects from fuel-price volatility: modal shift attributed to the programme is confirmed at 8–12% by Month 48 (2030-10-08), supporting the environmental case for TEN-T extension. Mid-course corrections (e.g., targeted campaigns in weak-performing regions) are triggered quarterly based on clean data, enabling 10–20% efficiency gains. Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding is secured on the basis of demonstrated impact.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If national regulators and CER cannot provide 2024–2025 data by Month 3 (2027-01-08): commission a rapid market research survey (Month 3–6 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-04-08) using OD (origin-destination) sampling on the four corridors, surveying 5,000–10,000 passengers on booking behaviour and demographics; use sample to proxy the baseline with confidence intervals; cost EUR 200–400K
  • If a baseline complaint rate is unavailable: define the denominator operationally (e.g., 'complaints per 1,000 through-tickets sold') and set Month 9 (2027-07-08) validated baseline as the first 6 months of pilot-corridor operations, then measure the 50% reduction from that baseline onward (avoids pre-programme retrospective estimation)
  • If modal-split data (air vs. rail passenger counts) are not published by national aviation or rail authorities: partner with a transport-research institute to model modal split using ticket-price data, flight-capacity announcements and survey-based stated-preference for air vs. rail on priority corridors; cost EUR 300–500K; deliver proxy baseline by Month 9 (2027-07-08)
  • If addressable-market estimates are contested: use an independent third-party evaluator (engaged Month 3 = 2027-01-08) to validate through-ticket opportunity size using regression analysis of existing multi-operator journey data from Trainline, Omio and carrier direct-sales channels; cost EUR 100–200K
  • If data reconciliation across member states remains difficult: establish a 'data-governance committee' (Month 6 = 2027-04-08) with regulators and statisticians to agree on common definitions (e.g., 'a through-ticket sale is a single booking reference covering ≥2 carriers with ≥1 connection') and publish a quarterly reconciliation report that flags inconsistencies and explains them (e.g., 'Platform X reports 40%, Carrier Y's backend report shows 38%, gap due to refunds not yet cleared')

Find Document 5: GDPR Data Protection Authority Positions and National Data-Residency Policies (Austria, Germany, Poland, France, Bulgaria, Romania)

ID: d9c14abe-3b1a-45e3-b317-a2311f7629ff

Description: Guidance from the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) and individual national DPAs on cross-border PII transfers, Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs), data-residency requirements, and special-category data (accessibility attributes) consent regimes. Needed to design the GDPR Compliance Framework (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) and secure DPA consensus by Month 4 (2027-02-08). Key DPAs for this programme: Austria (strict on data minimisation), Germany (GDPR enforcement leader), Poland (national data-residency sensitivity), France (CNIL active on consumer data), Bulgaria and Romania (developing but potentially restrictive). Audience: data-protection lead, legal counsel, payment-institution advisors.

Recency Requirement: Current EDPB guidance (2024–2025) and national DPA positions as of Month 0 (2026-10-08). Requests to national authorities in Months 1–3 (2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) will yield official positions by Month 4 (2027-02-08).

Responsible Role Type: Data Protection Impact Assessment and GDPR Compliance Lead; Governance and Legal Affairs Advisor

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Check the EDPB website (https://edpb.ec.europa.eu/) for published guidance on cross-border data transfers, SCCs, and special-category data consent.
  • 2. Submit formal information requests to the Austrian DPA, German BfDI, Polish UODO, French CNIL, Bulgarian DPA and Romanian ANSPDCP, asking for their positions on cross-border rail-ticketing data flows and any national residency requirements (Month 1 = 2026-11-08). Allow 4–6 weeks for responses.
  • 3. Contact the European Data Protection Board secretariat directly to request expedited guidance if a key DPA's position conflicts with the programme design (Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08).

Access Difficulty: Medium. EDPB guidance is published and freely available. Individual DPA positions require formal requests and follow-up; responses may be slow (4–8 weeks in some member states). Early engagement (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) is essential.

Essential Information:

  • Current positions of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) and individual national DPAs (Austria, Germany, Poland, France, Bulgaria, Romania) on cross-border PII transfers within EU infrastructure programmes, specifically Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) acceptability and any national data-residency mandates or restrictions.
  • National DPA guidance on consent regimes for special-category data (GDPR Article 9), particularly accessibility attributes (mobility needs, assistance requests) flowing through booking systems across borders.
  • Clarity on whether SCCs alone are sufficient for rail-ticketing data flows, or whether individual member states require additional safeguards (e.g., Binding Corporate Rules, local data-processing agreements, or data-residency clauses).
  • DPA positions on data-retention timelines: acceptability of 90-day post-journey deletion for routine PII, and 12-month retention for disputes/refunds.
  • Regulatory appetite and timeline for DPA consensus on the proposed through-ticketing data-governance model before the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards deadline; identify any known blockers or red lines from specific member states.
  • Precedent guidance from EDPB or national DPAs on multi-carrier, multi-country ticketing systems or similar EU transport infrastructure with distributed data flows.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or outdated DPA positions (older than 2024) do not reflect current enforcement priorities or emerging case law, leading to standards-setting assumptions that are later invalidated by DPA intervention post-Month 4 (2027-02-08).
  • Missing clarity on national residency requirements (Poland, Bulgaria, Romania have expressed sensitivities) results in a data-layer architecture that one or more member states reject at Month 6–12 (2027-04-08 to 2027-10-08), requiring a redesign and adding 6–12 month delay to the critical path.
  • Incomplete consent-regime guidance for accessibility data creates friction at booking time (passengers must provide explicit consent for each journey) or results in reduced accessibility-booking uptake, failing the accessibility inclusion target.
  • Absence of early DPA consensus signals non-compliance risk that delays payment-institution accreditation (Month 8 = 2027-06-08) or carrier conformance testing (Month 18 = 2028-04-08), compressing integration windows.
  • Conflicting or ambiguous DPA positions across member states (e.g., Austria strict on minimisation, France permissive on cross-border flows) force a lowest-common-denominator approach that over-restricts data sharing and weakens distributor search quality or refund processing.

Worst Case Scenario: A national DPA (e.g., Poland or Austria) issues a preliminary or formal directive in Month 8–12 (2027-06-08 to 2027-10-08) challenging the cross-border data-flow architecture and requiring a major redesign (e.g., data must be pseudonymised before transfer, or stored only in the carrier's home country) before the through-ticket system can operate. This forces a 6–12 month standards and implementation rework, compressing the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate into an infeasible 6–9 month carrier-integration window. Alternatively, the absence of early DPA consensus creates legal uncertainty that causes payment institutions to withdraw from accreditation or carriers to demand exemptions, fragmenting the programme and reducing through-ticket coverage to 70–80% of priority corridors, missing the 90% Month 30 (2029-04-08) threshold and triggering Commission review and potential mandate delay.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 4 (2027-02-08), the EDPB and key national DPAs issue coordinated guidance confirming that Standard Contractual Clauses are sufficient for cross-border rail-ticketing data flows with no additional national residency requirements; data-deletion timelines (90 days standard, 12 months for disputes) are acceptable; and consent for accessibility data can be embedded in the booking process without special procedures. This clarity enables the programme to finalise the GDPR compliance framework by Month 6 (2027-04-08), secure payment-institution accreditation without legal objections by Month 8 (2027-06-08), and embed GDPR checks into conformance testing by Month 18 (2028-04-08). Distributors and carriers proceed with confidence; no redesign delays accumulate; the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate is achieved with 90%+ compliance; and through-ticket take-up reaches 40% by Month 60 (2031-10-08).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If EDPB consensus is delayed beyond Month 4 (2027-02-08): commission an independent external Data Protection Impact Assessment and legal review (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) identifying the minimum necessary PII per transaction and proposing a data-minimisation design that preemptively addresses known DPA concerns (pseudonymisation, local caching, consent automation). Present this design to the EDPB and national DPAs by Month 3 (2027-01-08) for expedited feedback before standards are finalised.
  • If one member state (e.g., Poland) signals non-compliance with SCCs or imposes a national residency mandate: negotiate a bilateral data-processing agreement (Supplementary Data Processing Agreement under GDPR Article 28) specific to that state by Month 6 (2027-04-08), allowing data to be processed locally with the carrier's infrastructure in that state, while other carriers/distributors use SCCs. Maintain this parallel arrangement until EU-level consistency is achieved (or indefinitely if the state does not join the consensus).
  • If DPA guidance on accessibility-data consent creates unacceptable booking friction: simplify consent to a single 'yes/no' choice at check-in ('Share my mobility needs with carriers for assistance coordination?') with a 24-hour opt-out window post-journey, reducing friction while maintaining GDPR compliance. Test this in the pilot corridor (Wien–München, Month 12–18 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08) before rollout.
  • If payment institutions refuse accreditation due to unresolved GDPR ambiguity: delay full split-payment orchestration and revert to bilateral carrier-to-distributor settlement for the first 6 months (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), accepting slower refund processing (15–20 days instead of 10 days) until GDPR clarity allows a full accredited provider model. Communicate this temporary limitation to distributors and passengers transparently.
  • If a full block-exemption or negative-clearance letter from the competition authorities is also needed to secure DPA and payment-provider buy-in, extend the accreditation timeline from Month 8 (2027-06-08) to Month 12 (2027-10-08) to allow concurrent GDPR and competition-law consultations, with the understanding that the critical path will slip by 4 months if both clearances are required.

ID: 9121e8e1-033b-44c4-931e-3ea04bc8bc74

Description: Competitive analysis and regulator expectations on the legality of the shared real-time data layer (shared inventory, fares, disruption data among competing carriers). Needed to design the Competition-Law Firewalls framework (Decision 13) and determine what data can be pooled without violating Articles 101–102 TFEU. DG COMP's Digital Markets Act principles and any pre-existing guidance on transport data-sharing are essential inputs.   • 3. Submit a pre-filing consultation memo to DG COMP (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08) outlining the shared data-layer architecture, data fields to be pooled, and safeguards (neutral operator, access logs, data minimisation). Request comfort letter or expedited guidance by Month 6 (2027-04-08).

Worst Case Scenario: A combination of three cascading failures reduces the programme to a non-functional state and consumes the entire EUR 1.5 billion budget with minimal return. By Month 30 (2029-04-08), 90%+ of carriers are ready (including 80–85% of smaller operators via hubs), the public app launches on schedule (Month 15 = 2028-01-08), and the first through-tickets are live on the four priority corridors. Modal shift from air to rail averages 10–15% on competitive corridors, delivering EUR 500 million to EUR 1 billion in net environmental and capacity benefits. The EUR 1.5 billion public investment is fully deployed, with EUR 215 million contingency preserved; the TEN-T extension launches on schedule (Month 36 = 2029-10-08), and post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainable funding models (data-layer privatisation, clearing cost-recovery, regulator-funding devolution) are in place. The programme becomes a template for EU digital infrastructure and modal shift, attracting follow-on investment in rail modernization and cross-border connectivity.

  • If the arbitration panel does not receive explicit written Council delegation by Month 2 (2026-12-08): Empower the EU Agency for Railways as technical arbiter with non-binding recommendations, escalate contested decisions directly to DG MOVE (48-hour decision target) and establish a 'fast-track' Commission decision process (2-week turnaround on major disputes).   • If accredited payment-institution accreditation yields only 1 provider by Month 8 (2027-06-08): Activate contingency settlement via existing carrier-to-carrier bilateral arrangements (slower, but known and lower-risk) or procure a custom settlement service from a consortium of existing payment-service providers under emergency procedures (4–8 week expedited procurement, target Month 10–12 = 2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08).
  • If regional booking hubs are not ready by Month 9 (2027-07-08): Extend the integration timeline for hub-eligible carriers to Month 36 (2029-10-08) (beyond the mandatory Month 30 = 2029-04-08 date), allow them to operate under temporary gateway exemptions, and accelerate hub deployment with additional co-funding (EUR 2–4 million per hub) to achieve operational status by Month 15–18 (2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08).
  • If hub mapping errors exceed 2% booking-failure rate for >1 week: Immediately suspend new carrier onboarding to the affected hub, activate the hub incident-response team with on-site carrier IT support (escalation <2 hours), and conduct a 2–4 week rework cycle; if the hub cannot recover within 4 weeks, transfer affected carriers to alternative hubs or bilateral pairing with larger operators (funding the migration cost from the EUR 10 million resilience reserve).

  • If a major incumbent carrier (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, ÖBB) signals non-compliance by Month 12 (2027-10-08): Escalate immediately to DG MOVE and the Commission with evidence of delayed investment; invoke contingency: hold co-funding disbursements, exclude the non-compliant carrier from preferential inventory or data access, and commission the public reference distributor to offer competing service on that carrier's routes (positioning as 'train travel made simple' and demonstrating what compliance looks like).
  • If through-ticket volumes at Month 24 (2028-10-08) are <15% (vs. 15% gate): Conduct root-cause analysis (fares not competitive, distributor engagement weak, poor app usability, limited awareness); activate targeted air-route competition campaigns (EUR 10–20 million reserve) on high-sensitivity corridors, accelerate public-distributor market presence, negotiate reduction-card pooling across carriers (to achieve 10–15% effective discount), and consider subsidised through-fares on pilot routes (cost TBD, requires new budget decision).
  • If modal shift is <5% by Month 48 (2030-10-08): Reposition programme messaging from modal-shift focus to 'cross-border rail journey convenience' and '40% through-ticket volume' (distinct from mode-shift metric), emphasizing the value of single booking/payment/continuity to passengers already choosing rail; extend consumer campaigns through Month 60 (2031-10-08) and defer environmental-case validation to post-programme evaluation (when fuel prices and aviation-tax policy are clearer).

  • If distributor (Trainline, Omio) integration slips beyond Month 18 (2028-04-08): Expand public reference distributor capacity by EUR 20–30 million and launch consumer marketing by Month 12 (2027-10-08) to capture through-ticket demand directly; offer distributors a 'catch-up' window (Month 21–27 = 2028-07-08 to 2029-01-08) with accelerated technical support and priority conformance-testing slots; if they still do not integrate, the public channel becomes the primary through-ticket seller.

Find Document 7: EU Agency for Railways Regulatory Framework and Authority Documents (Delegated Acts, Technical Standards, Enforcement Procedures)

ID: 251a8f8d-5184-4d53-90e1-c0dfc80ff158

Description: The EU Agency for Railways' mandate, enforcement powers, and existing technical standards (especially the Technical Specifications for Interoperability – TSI) that the programme must align with or extend. Needed to understand the Agency's role as technical secretariat to the arbitration panel (Decision 5) and how OSDM API standards fit within the broader EU rail-standardisation framework. Audience: arbitration panel, standards working group, DG MOVE, national regulators.

Recency Requirement: Current (2024–2025) Agency delegated acts and technical standards published in the Official Journal.

Responsible Role Type: Governance and Legal Affairs Advisor; Chief Technical Standards Officer

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Visit the EU Agency for Railways website (https://www.era.europa.eu/) and download all published delegated acts, technical standards and guidance documents.
  • 2. Search the Official Journal (EUR-Lex) for the Agency's recent decisions and technical specifications, especially any related to digital ticketing or interoperability.
  • 3. Contact the Agency directly (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) to request clarification on how OSDM APIs fit within the TSI framework and whether any TSI updates are needed to support the programme.

Access Difficulty: Easy. Agency documents are published on its website and in EUR-Lex. Direct contact with the Agency is straightforward via the published contact methods.

Essential Information:

  • What specific regulatory authority and decision-making structures does the EU Agency for Railways currently hold over technical standards, and how can the arbitration panel (Decision 5) be legally anchored to those structures to ensure binding authority without creating a separate new entity?
  • What Technical Specifications for Interoperability (TSI) documents currently govern rail booking, ticketing and passenger data exchange, and which TSI sections must be updated or extended to accommodate OSDM API standards, multi-carrier through-ticketing and real-time disruption data?
  • What delegated acts, enforcement procedures and sanctions mechanisms are available to the Agency for non-compliance with standards, and can those existing enforcement tools be applied to distributors and carriers that fail to meet access, API latency or data-quality obligations?
  • What guidance or precedent exists for how the Agency handles disputes between carriers and third parties (e.g., distributors) over interoperability standards interpretation, and what dispute-resolution procedures are already in place that the arbitration panel can leverage or extend?
  • How does the Agency's current role as technical secretariat to the European Union Railway Agency Advisory Board translate to supporting a new arbitration panel, and what additional staffing, budget or legal mandates would be needed?

Risks of Poor Quality:
