  • If the Agency's mandate and authority are not clearly mapped to the arbitration panel's scope, contested technical decisions may be re-litigated by member-state regulators or incumbents, delaying standards by 4–8 weeks per dispute and threatening the Month 18 (2028-04-08) milestone.
  • Without a clear inventory of which TSI documents require updating, standards work duplicates effort or leaves gaps (e.g., TSI fails to cover OSDM data formats), forcing rework in Months 6–12 (2027-04-08 to 2027-10-08) and delaying conformance testing.
  • If the Agency lacks adequate enforcement tools or cannot delegate authority to the arbitration panel, non-compliant carriers and distributors face no credible consequences, undermining the non-discrimination access obligations and the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate.
  • Absence of a working dispute-resolution framework within the Agency creates governance vacuum; each major dispute requires ad-hoc escalation to the Commission (2–4 month resolution), slowing decision cycles and blocking milestone progress.
  • If the Agency's existing governance and advisory structures are not redesigned to support the arbitration panel and the programme's governance vehicle, parallel decision-making bodies create confusion, conflicting authority and stakeholder frustration, eroding buy-in.

Worst Case Scenario: The EU Agency for Railways is consulted late (Month 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08 instead of Month 0 = 2026-10-08), and its leadership signals that extending the Agency's authority to bind the arbitration panel requires a formal Council decision and amendment to the Agency's founding regulation (necessitating 12–18 months of legal process). Simultaneously, a technical dispute over inventory-parity thresholds escalates to the Commission in Month 12 (2027-10-08), which lacks the expertise to arbitrate quickly, and the decision drags on 8–12 weeks. As a result, the standards finalisation (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 target) is delayed to Month 21–24 (2028-07-08 to 2028-10-08), compressing carrier integration time and pushing the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate into jeopardy. A major carrier (Deutsche Bahn) contests the final standards, claiming they conflict with its national safety regulations, and without the Agency's backing, the carrier's objection carries weight and fractures stakeholder consensus. The programme's credibility is damaged, and the through-ticket target is revised downward from 40% to 25–30%.

Best Case Scenario: The Agency is engaged from Month 0 (2026-10-08) and, by Month 2 (2026-12-08), publishes a Delegated Act or formal opinion clarifying that the arbitration panel operates as an extension of the Agency's technical secretariat function, with binding authority over TSI interpretation and implementation. The Agency conducts a comprehensive TSI gap analysis (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) identifying 3–5 TSI sections that require updates for OSDM and multi-carrier through-ticketing; those updates are fast-tracked and incorporated into the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) without rework. The Agency's existing dispute-resolution and enforcement mechanisms are clarified and applied to the programme, so contested technical decisions are resolved within 60 days by the arbitration panel, with confidence that the Agency's authority backs compliance. Carrier and regulator buy-in is strong, standards are finalised on schedule, and the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate is achieved with >90% corridor readiness. The Agency becomes a recognised centre of excellence for EU rail interoperability, and the programme's technical credibility is reinforced.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the Agency cannot be legally empowered to back the arbitration panel by Month 2 (2026-12-08), escalate immediately to the Commission and seek an emergency Council decision (target Month 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) granting the panel explicit binding authority via a Commission decision or a temporary delegated act, avoiding the need for a full regulatory amendment.
  • If a major technical dispute arises in Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08) and the Agency cannot resolve it internally, engage an independent external technical arbitrator (e.g., a consortium of rail-standards experts) to issue a binding opinion within 14 days, with the Commission endorsing the opinion so it carries legal weight.
  • If the TSI gap analysis reveals that multiple TSI updates are needed and the standard TSI-update timeline (12–18 months) is too long, fast-track the updates through a dedicated Agency technical working group (Month 2–6 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-04-08) and publish interim guidance ('Interpretative Guidance on OSDM Implementation within TSI') that carriers and distributors accept as binding until formal TSI amendments are published.
  • If the Agency's existing dispute-resolution procedures are too slow (>60 days), establish a dedicated 'OSDM Dispatch Board' within the Agency with expedited decision authority (48-hour turnaround on urgent issues) and empowered to issue interim technical guidance that is recognised by all member-state regulators pending formal standards approval.
  • If the Agency lacks the staffing or budget to support the arbitration panel and broader standards work, negotiate a temporary co-staffing arrangement with DG MOVE (assign 2–4 DG MOVE staff to the Agency during Months 1–30 = 2026-11-08 to 2029-04-08) to augment the Agency's capacity without requiring a formal budget reallocation.

Find Document 8: Payment Services Directive (PSD2) and Electronic Money Directive (EMD2) Regulatory Framework and Competent-Authority Guidance

ID: eb88554c-3add-4cea-b7be-3836777532ee

Description: EU rules governing licensed payment institutions, settlement procedures, multi-currency handling, fraud liability and SLA requirements. Needed to design the accreditation criteria for payment providers (Clearing and Settlement Architecture document, Month 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08) and to understand member-state regulators' expectations for through-ticket settlement. Audience: clearing-mechanism designer, payment-institution applicants, competent authorities (national banking regulators).

Recency Requirement: Current PSD2 (Directive (EU) 2015/2366) and any amendments or EDPB guidance on multi-currency settlement and through-ticketing scenarios (2024–2025).

Responsible Role Type: Clearing and Settlement Mechanism Designer / Payment Systems Specialist; Governance and Legal Affairs Advisor

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Download PSD2 from EUR-Lex (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/) and the European Banking Authority (EBA) regulatory technical standards (RTS) on payment security and data protection.
  • 2. Contact the EBA (https://www.eba.europa.eu/) to request guidance on through-ticket settlement as a novel use case under PSD2.
  • 3. Engage the European Central Bank (ECB, https://www.ecb.europa.eu/) on multi-currency settlement and FX exposure management (Month 1–2 = 2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08).

Access Difficulty: Easy. PSD2 and EBA guidance are published and freely available. ECB consultation requires a formal request but is straightforward (2–4 weeks response time).

Essential Information:

  • Specify the exact scope of PSD2 and EMD2 requirements applicable to multi-currency, multi-carrier through-ticket settlement (e.g., which payment institution licenses are mandatory, what SLAs and liability caps apply, which member-state regulators must approve the settlement design).
  • Clarify the technical and operational requirements for split-payment orchestration under PSD2: who holds passenger funds during the settlement cycle, how refunds are reversed across multiple carriers, and what fraud-liability allocation applies to the clearing entity vs. accredited providers.
  • Detail the process and timeline for accrediting payment institutions under PSD2; identify which competent authorities (national banking regulators, EBA) must approve accreditation criteria and confirm whether accreditation can be expedited for the proposed Months 2–8 (2026-12-08 to 2027-06-08) timeline.
  • Quantify the compliance costs and operational requirements for accredited payment providers to meet through-ticket settlement SLAs (latency, settlement cycle, multi-currency FX handling, dispute resolution, audit trails) and confirm which cost items are permitted under PSD2 pricing rules.
  • Identify EDPB or EBA guidance on cross-border data flows for passenger PII during split-payment settlement and confirm whether Standard Contractual Clauses suffice or if additional member-state consent/approval is needed.
  • List the specific anti-fraud, anti-money-laundering (AML) and know-your-customer (KYC) requirements that accredited providers must implement for through-ticket transactions, especially for small-value bookings (EUR 50–200).
  • Confirm whether the proposed 'accredited payment providers compete' model (2–3 providers, carriers choose) is permissible under PSD2 or if it triggers competition-law or data-access concerns that require regulatory pre-clearance.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete or misinterpreted PSD2 requirements delay payment-institution accreditation beyond Month 8 (2027-06-08), preventing the 2 accredited providers from being operational by Month 12 (2027-10-08) and compressing carrier integration timelines to 6 months (Months 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08) instead of 12, increasing non-compliance risk.
  • Missing clarity on split-payment liability (which entity bears loss if a carrier defaults or a refund reversal fails) causes disputes with accredited providers, deterring applicants and leaving fewer than 2 qualified providers, triggering expensive fallback to bilateral settlement (slower, weaker).
  • Overlooked AML/KYC requirements for through-ticket transactions force accredited providers to implement heavy compliance infrastructure post-accreditation, adding EUR 1–3M per provider in unanticipated costs and potentially making 0.3–0.5% fee caps unviable.
  • Ambiguity on cross-border data flows and consent delays GDPR and data-protection approval, pushing through-ticket settlement design into Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) instead of Month 4 (2027-02-08), cascading into standards-finalisation delays (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 at risk).
  • Failure to confirm competition-law permissibility of the competitive provider model triggers a DG Comp investigation (Month 12–18 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08), causing 6–12 month legal uncertainty and deterring provider applicants.

Worst Case Scenario: Accreditation criteria and PSD2 compliance scope are finalised without input from competent authorities and EBA, and when the call for applicants is issued (Month 2 = 2026-12-08), only 1 provider applies and 2 others decline due to unforeseen compliance costs or regulatory uncertainty. The sole provider demands pricing concessions (1.0–1.5% per transaction instead of 0.5% cap) and refuses SLA commitments, making the fee subsidy budget (EUR 15M) insufficient. Fallback to bilateral carrier settlement is activated, adding 2–4 week delay in each carrier's go-live and reducing settlement reliability; the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate is at risk due to 20–30% of carriers being unprepared for bilateral settlement complexity. Legal review in Month 10–12 (2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08) uncovers competition-law exposure, forcing a redesign and pushing decision to Month 18 (2028-04-08) or beyond. Final impact: EUR 5–10M in additional compliance costs, 3–6 month delay in payment-layer readiness, and 10–20% reduction in through-ticket volumes due to settlement friction.

Best Case Scenario: PSD2 and EMD2 regulatory requirements are fully documented and aligned with the arbitration panel's settlement rules by Month 4 (2027-02-08). Accreditation criteria are clear, lean and pre-approved by the EBA and national banking regulators; competition authorities confirm that the competitive provider model is permissible; and cross-border data-flow rules are clarified in advance of the applicant call. Three qualified payment institutions apply by Month 6 (2027-04-08) and are accredited by Month 8 (2027-06-08), with fee caps at 0.4% and strong SLA commitments (99.95% uptime, 48-hour settlement, <5-day dispute resolution). By Month 12 (2027-10-08), at least 2 providers are live and processing test transactions; carriers and distributors have high confidence in settlement reliability. PSD2 compliance costs are predictable and absorbed within the accreditation budget; no legal challenges emerge. Settlement becomes a non-blocker for the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate, and through-ticket volumes scale to 20–30% by Month 36 (2029-10-08).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If accreditation of independent payment institutions cannot yield 2+ qualified providers by Month 8 (2027-06-08), contract a bespoke settlement service from an established payments infrastructure provider (e.g., a central bank settlement system or a SWIFT subsidiary) on a time-and-materials basis; expect higher cost (EUR 20–40M vs. EUR 15M subsidy) and longer build time (9–12 months), but avoids accreditation delay.
  • If competition-law clarity on multi-provider data sharing cannot be obtained by Month 6 (2027-04-08), pivot to a single neutral-operator settlement model in which a publicly or jointly owned entity (not a commercial payment institution) runs settlement; this avoids competitive data-sharing concerns but requires new governance and licensing, adding 4–8 weeks legal setup.
  • If PSD2 compliance costs for accredited providers exceed EUR 5M per provider (making the 0.5% fee cap unsustainable), negotiate a hybrid fee model: carriers pay 0.3–0.4% directly to providers, and the programme covers EUR 5–10M of compliance/operational costs directly (reducing the fee subsidy from EUR 15M to EUR 5–10M).
  • If EBA guidance on through-ticket settlement under PSD2 is not forthcoming by Month 3 (2027-01-08), engage a specialist payments-law advisory firm (EUR 0.5–1M) to produce a detailed legal opinion on PSD2 permissibility and share it with national banking regulators for informal pre-approval; this accelerates confidence without formal guidance.
  • If fallback to bilateral carrier settlement is activated, establish a dedicated settlement message-standard working group (Month 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) to define OSDM-compatible bilateral settlement formats and a neutral dispute-resolution body (separate from the arbitration panel, focused on settlement only) to unblock carrier-to-carrier deadlocks; expect slower settlement (72–96 hours instead of 48 hours) and EUR 10–20M in additional IT integration costs for carriers.

Find Document 9: Current Cross-Border Rail Booking and Ticketing Practices, Including Carrier IT Systems Assessment and Distributor Capabilities

ID: e02934d1-a4a0-4be0-b65a-946a1c3af9e7

Description: Technical and operational audit of the 25+ participating carriers' current booking systems, APIs, data maturity, and integration readiness. Needed for the Legacy Carrier IT Migration Pathway (Decision 4), hub eligibility assessment (identify which 12–18 carriers need hub access), and budget forecasting for carrier co-funding (Month 2 = 2026-12-08 cost model). Includes legacy-system inventory (mainframe vs. cloud), API maturity assessment (OSDM readiness, security, performance), and distributor integration capabilities (Trainline, Omio). Audience: smaller-carriers support team, cost modellers, hub programme lead.

Recency Requirement: Surveys and assessments conducted Months 0–3 (2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08) with carriers and distributors directly. Self-assessment templates issued by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); responses due Month 2 (2026-12-08).

Responsible Role Type: Smaller Carriers and Regional Integration Lead; Large Enterprise IT Legacy System Migration Program Director

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Prepare a standardised carrier IT-readiness questionnaire (Month 0 = 2026-10-08) covering: current booking-system age and architecture, API maturity, current distributor integrations, IT staff capacity, and timeline for OSDM readiness.
  • 2. Issue the questionnaire to all CER member carriers (via CER, https://www.cer.be/) by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); collect responses by Month 2 (2026-12-08).
  • 3. Conduct follow-up calls with carriers showing legacy systems or low OSDM readiness (identified as hub-eligible in Month 1 = 2026-11-08) to refine the assessment.
  • 4. Engage major distributors (Trainline, Omio, others) separately to assess their integration timeline and API-development roadmap.

Access Difficulty: Medium. Carriers may be reluctant to disclose system details for competitive reasons. CER can help as a trusted intermediary. Expect 40–60% response rate on initial questionnaire; follow-up calls are essential to fill gaps. Plan 4–6 weeks for the full assessment.

Essential Information:

  • Detailed inventory of all 25+ participating carriers' current booking systems: age, architecture (mainframe/cloud/hybrid), API maturity (current OSDM alignment level), authentication/security mechanisms, and per-carrier integration timeline to OSDM compliance by Month 30 (2029-04-08).
  • Breakdown of hub-eligible carriers: identification of which 12–18 carriers meet hub-eligibility criteria (cross-border revenue <EUR 50M, booking system >10 years old, or IT staff <10 FTE) and their distribution by region (for hub resource planning).
  • Carrier-by-carrier IT integration cost estimate (disaggregated from the private-sector EUR 500M–2B estimate): baseline cost per carrier for native OSDM build, hub-assisted integration, or gateway use; sensitivity to legacy-system age and complexity.
  • Distributor integration readiness: current API capabilities of Trainline, Omio and other major platforms; their planned OSDM integration timelines; gaps between planned timelines and the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards deadline.
  • Data quality assessment: current data maturity (inventory, fares, disruption notifications) across carriers; gaps in real-time capability, multi-carrier coordination, and distributor data access; baseline for the shared real-time data layer design.
  • API security and performance baseline: current latency, uptime, and throughput for each carrier's booking system (where available); identification of carriers unable to meet the proposed technical SLAs (p95 latency <2s, 99.95% uptime, ≥500 req/s per corridor).
  • Assessment of existing bilateral settlement arrangements: current message standards (ISO 20022 or proprietary), settlement cycle times, and reconciliation practices among the four priority corridors' carriers; mapping of which arrangements can be extended vs. which require redesign for single-payment through-tickets.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Inaccurate hub-eligibility assessment: if the document misidentifies carriers that can achieve native OSDM vs. those requiring hub access, co-funding allocations are misaligned, and 5–15% of carriers slip past the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate, fragmenting the through-ticket network and reducing end-to-end bookability below the 90% (proposed) threshold.
  • Underestimated carrier IT integration costs: if private-sector costs exceed the EUR 500M–2B range, carriers lobby for larger public co-funding; the EUR 290M co-funding allocation becomes insufficient, forcing 20–30% budget reallocation from conformance testing or capacity building, delaying smaller-carrier certification by 4–8 weeks.
  • Distributor integration timeline misalignment: if Trainline or Omio's actual OSDM integration timeline slips beyond Month 18 (2028-04-08), the programme lacks major distribution channels at the standards deadline; through-ticket volumes depend on the public reference distributor, consuming EUR 60–90M in unplanned operating costs and reducing market reach by 10–20 percentage points.
  • Data quality baseline incomplete: if the current state of multi-carrier disruption data, inventory accuracy, and distributor API access is not documented, the shared real-time data layer's design (federated vs. central) is based on incomplete information; wrong architecture choice leads to either overselling (central cache stale data) or latency (federated queries slow), causing 5–10% booking failures and refund disputes.
  • Missing API performance gaps: if the document does not identify carriers whose systems cannot support the proposed technical SLAs (p95 <2s latency, 500 req/s throughput), infrastructure co-funding is insufficient; those carriers become de facto ineligible for Month 30 (2029-04-08), requiring hub or gateway routing and reducing network reliability by 15–25%.
  • Incorrect settlement arrangement assessment: if existing bilateral settlement practices are not accurately mapped, the accredited payment-institution design (assuming integration of multi-carrier split payments) is infeasible; fallback to slow bilateral settlement delays refunds by 2–5 days, violating the <10-day target and eroding distributor and passenger confidence.

Worst Case Scenario: The document is not completed by Month 2 (2026-12-08) or is based on incomplete carrier responses (sub-40% survey return). As a result: (1) hub-eligibility criteria are applied incorrectly at Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), allocating co-funding to carriers that could achieve native integration and denying it to those that genuinely need hub access; (2) distributor integration timelines are misjudged, and Trainline or Omio signals non-compliance in Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08), forcing the public reference distributor to expand from EUR 43M/year to EUR 60–100M/year, consuming EUR 60–150M from the free contingency by Month 24 (2028-10-08); (3) API infrastructure gaps are not identified, and by Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), carriers' systems are overloaded during peak searches, causing 5–10% of searches to timeout and damaging the programme's reputation before the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate; (4) the cost model is off by 30–50%, and by Month 12 (2027-10-08), budget pressure forces 40% cuts to conformance testing, delaying 50% of smaller-carrier certifications by 8–12 weeks, rendering the Month 30 (2029-04-08) 90% readiness gate unachievable. The programme enters Month 24 (2028-10-08) with no clear picture of who is ready, free contingency is depleted by Month 24–30 (2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08), and the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate becomes legally binding but operationally unmet (50–70% compliance instead of 90%), triggering Commission enforcement action and reputational damage.

Best Case Scenario: The document is completed by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) based on 65–75% carrier response rate and 2–3 follow-up rounds of calls, providing a precise, disaggregated picture of each carrier's OSDM readiness, IT investment plan, and hub eligibility. As a result: (1) co-funding allocation is accurate and fair; 12–18 hub-eligible carriers are identified and prioritised, reducing their integration cost by 50–70% vs. native build; (2) distributor commitments are locked in by Month 3–4 (2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08) with clear timelines (Trainline, Omio live by Month 15–18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08), removing distribution risk; (3) the cost model has <10% variance from actual spend, allowing budget discipline and enabling a realistic mid-course review at Month 12 (2027-10-08) without major surprises; (4) API infrastructure co-funding is targeted to the 3–5 carriers that need upgrades, completed by Month 15 (2028-01-08), and the technical SLAs are met on schedule; (5) settlement baseline is clear, accredited payment-institution design is validated, and EUR 120M clearing allocation is sufficient. By Month 30 (2029-04-08), 92–95% of corridor traffic is bookable end-to-end, exceeding the 90% (proposed) gate; through-ticket volumes reach 20–25% on the four priority corridors (tracked accurately from Month 18 = 2028-04-08 onward); and carrier satisfaction with the programme remains high (>75%), enabling TEN-T extension to proceed on schedule at Month 36 (2029-10-08).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If <40% of carriers respond to the initial self-assessment survey by Month 2 (2026-12-08): commission an external audit firm to conduct 1-on-1 calls with non-respondents in Month 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08); prioritise large carriers (top 10 by traffic) and hub-eligible operators; use publicly available information (annual reports, regulator filings, tech-news sources) to fill gaps for smaller operators.
  • If carrier IT integration costs cannot be disaggregated per carrier: use a benchmarking approach—identify 3–4 'reference carriers' across small/medium/large segments and different legacy-system ages; conduct detailed cost-breakdown interviews with each; model the remaining carriers based on similarity scoring (traffic size, system age, current API maturity); validate the model against top-10 carriers.
  • If distributors (Trainline, Omio) refuse to participate in a formal readiness assessment: engage them through CER, IATA distributor affiliates or bilateral meetings with business development leads (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08); offer early API access and co-marketing funds (EUR 5–10M) as incentive to share integration roadmaps; if they still decline, assume conservative 6-month integration timeline (live by Month 24 = 2028-10-08, not Month 18 = 2028-04-08) and plan distributor contingency (expand public channel by EUR 30–50M).
  • If data quality baseline is incomplete (carriers do not report disruption-event timeliness or inventory freshness): conduct a 2-week live pilot (Month 3–4 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08) on one high-traffic corridor (e.g., Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln) measuring actual search latency, inventory staleness and disruption-notification lag; extrapolate findings to the other corridors; use the pilot results to inform data-layer architecture design (federated vs. central trade-off).
  • If settlement arrangements are proprietary and carriers are unwilling to disclose: meet with clearing houses (e.g., Equens, SIA, national settlement operators) that operate existing bilateral schemes; understand their message standards and capabilities; model a settlement design based on their existing infrastructure rather than re-engineering from scratch; this reduces the likelihood of rejection by carriers already using those systems.
  • If the cost model indicates a >25% variance after Month 2 (2026-12-08): trigger a mid-course review by Month 4 (2027-02-08); re-baseline co-funding allocation using a more conservative scenario (assume 20% fewer carriers can afford native integration); revise the EUR 290M co-funding pool to prioritise the top 3–5 smaller carriers most at-risk of non-compliance; use the freed funds (if any) for additional hub or gateway capacity as a fallback.

Find Document 10: Member-State National Rail Regulatory Capacity and Enforcement Capability Assessment (All 27 Member States)

ID: 1ad74e82-df4e-498a-a81c-8247c3eb86ec

Description: Audit of the 27 member-state rail regulators' staffing, expertise, IT systems, enforcement experience, and capacity to enforce non-discrimination, passenger rights and data-quality duties under the programme. Needed to design the regulator capacity-building plan (Member-State Regulator Capacity-Building and Enforcement-Alignment Programme, Month 2 = 2026-12-08) and to identify priority targets for twinning support (estimated 8–12 weaker-capacity regulators). Includes assessment of each regulator's GDPR and competition-law expertise, dispute-resolution procedures, and cross-border coordination mechanisms. Audience: regulator-capacity lead, Standing Regulators Committee, twinning coordinators.

Recency Requirement: Assessments conducted Months 1–3 (2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) with direct engagement of national regulators. Self-assessment templates issued Month 1 (2026-11-08); responses due Month 3 (2027-01-08).

Responsible Role Type: Member-State Regulator Capacity and Cross-Border Enforcement Lead

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Prepare a standardised regulator capacity-assessment template (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) covering: number of staff, expertise areas (access enforcement, passenger rights, GDPR, competition law), IT systems, current dispute-resolution procedures, and cross-border coordination experience.
  • 2. Issue the template to all 27 member-state national rail regulators via the EU Agency for Railways (https://www.era.europa.eu/) by Month 1 (2026-11-08); collect responses by Month 3 (2027-01-08).
  • 3. Conduct bilateral calls with regulators identified as lower-capacity (expected: Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia, Malta) to understand specific needs and design targeted twinning support.
  • 4. Aggregate findings in a capacity report due Month 4 (2027-02-08) to inform the Standing Regulators Committee and twinning partnerships.

Access Difficulty: Medium. National regulators are often cooperative with EU-level capacity initiatives but may take time to respond (6–8 weeks is typical). Direct contact via the EU Agency for Railways helps. Some regulators have limited English proficiency; consider offering assessment in national languages.

Essential Information:

  • Identify the specific staffing, expertise gaps and enforcement capacity constraints (e.g., number of staff, expertise areas, IT systems maturity, dispute-resolution capability) for each of the 27 member-state national rail regulators.
  • Quantify which national regulators are classified as 'lower-capacity' (proposed criterion: fewer than 5 dedicated staff, limited access-enforcement or GDPR expertise, or no cross-border dispute-resolution experience) and prioritise 8–12 regulators for targeted twinning support.
  • Assess each regulator's current authority and resources to enforce non-discrimination duties, passenger-rights claims, and data-quality obligations under the proposed Regulation and the programme's standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 onward).
  • Evaluate regulatory readiness for GDPR compliance audits, competition-law coordination (data-sharing safeguards), and cross-border dispute handling (lead-authority model).
  • Define regulator-specific capacity-building needs (training in OSDM standards, access enforcement, GDPR, accessibility compliance) and estimate the number of person-days required per regulator.
  • Specify each regulator's current dispute-resolution procedures and timelines (current target, e.g., 60+ days for access complaints) vs. the programme's proposed 30-day cross-border dispute-resolution target.
  • List any data-protection or sovereignty concerns expressed by individual regulators (e.g., data-residency preferences, resistance to EU Agency for Railways mediation) that could affect the Standing Regulators Committee's effectiveness.
  • Identify regulators with existing bilateral or multilateral coordination mechanisms (e.g., within the EU Agency for Railways or CER networks) and assess whether these can be leveraged for the programme's cross-border enforcement model.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Capacity assessment conducted too late (after Month 3 = 2027-01-08) delays twinning partnerships, leaving weaker regulators unprepared for Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards or Month 30 (2029-04-08) enforcement duties; estimated 2–4 month delay in regulator readiness.
  • Underestimating capacity gaps for 3–5 regulators results in inconsistent enforcement of non-discrimination duties post-Month 30 (2029-04-08); carriers in weak-capacity member states exploit enforcement laxity, and distributors face uneven access conditions across borders, fragmenting the through-ticket network.
  • Failing to identify data-protection or sovereignty red-lines from individual regulators early allows them to surface as blockers to the Standing Regulators Committee or the arbitration panel in Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08), delaying the consensus needed for standards adoption.
  • Misclassifying a regulator as 'high-capacity' when it lacks cross-border dispute experience leads to slow complaint resolution (90+ days instead of 30 days), damaging distributor confidence and delaying smaller-carrier onboarding.
  • Insufficient detail on regulator IT systems (e.g., no digital filing, paper-based complaint handling) underestimates the cost and timeline for deploying shared complaint-handling platforms and automated enforcement tools, adding EUR 5–10M to the capacity-building budget and delaying readiness by 6–12 months.
  • Assessment document fails to recommend specific regulator pairs for twinning (e.g., no proposal to pair France or Germany with Poland, Bulgaria, or Romania), leaving the Regulator Capacity Lead without actionable guidance for Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) twinning-partnership setup.

Worst Case Scenario: Regulator capacity assessment is either not conducted or completed too late (Month 9–12 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08 instead of Month 3 = 2027-01-08). Twinning partnerships are not established, and weaker regulators in Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Croatia, and Malta remain under-resourced at Month 30 (2029-04-08). By Month 24–30 (2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08), disputes over API access discrimination, passenger-refund obligations and data-quality violations in weak-capacity member states accumulate; national regulators take 60–120 days to respond (vs. the 30-day target). Carriers in low-enforcement jurisdictions begin denying distributor API access without consequence; smaller distributors and foreign operators withdraw from those markets. The Standing Regulators Committee collapses due to inconsistent enforcement rulings; the Commission is forced to intervene in Month 30–36 (2029-04-08 to 2029-10-08), issuing compliance directives that trigger national appeals and further delay. By Month 36 (2029-10-08), cross-border through-ticket reliability is questioned, and distributor confidence erodes; throughticket volumes fall to 20–25% instead of the 40% target, and the programme's credibility is severely damaged.

Best Case Scenario: Regulator assessment is completed by Month 3 (2027-01-08) with full engagement from all 27 member states. Twinning partnerships are formally established by Month 6 (2027-04-08), pairing stronger regulators (France, Germany, Netherlands, Austria) with weaker ones (8–12 identified). Capacity-building training is delivered in Months 6–12 (2027-04-08 to 2027-10-08), and weaker regulators achieve documented competency in access enforcement, GDPR compliance audits, and cross-border dispute handling by Month 18 (2028-04-08). The Standing Regulators Committee convenes monthly from Month 3 (2027-01-08) onward with high attendance and clear decision logs. By Month 30 (2029-04-08), all 27 regulators are operationally ready to enforce non-discrimination and passenger-rights duties; cross-border disputes are resolved within 30 days with consistent outcomes; carriers and distributors report confidence in the enforcement framework. Smaller carriers in all member states are willing to commit to the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate, knowing enforcement will be fair and timely. The programme achieves 90%+ compliance at Month 30 (2029-04-08) and the 40% through-ticket target by Month 60 (2031-10-08).

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If regulator capacity assessment is delayed beyond Month 4 (2027-02-08), activate an emergency procurement of an independent capacity-assessment consultant by Month 2 (2026-12-08) to conduct a rapid 4–6 week audit of all 27 regulators in parallel, with structured interviews and desktop review; prioritise the 12 regulators identified as likely lower-capacity based on available data (staff budgets, prior EU programme participation, regulatory-maturity indicators).
  • If weaker regulators resist twinning or capacity-building engagement, use conditionality: tie EU transport-infrastructure funding (e.g., Rail Connecting Europe Facility grants) to regulator participation in the programme's training and cross-border coordination mechanisms; set a 'regulator-readiness gate' at Month 18 (2028-04-08), with non-compliant member states required to cede primary enforcement authority to the EU Agency for Railways.
  • If individual regulators express data-protection or sovereignty red-lines, negotiate bilateral Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) by Month 6 (2027-04-08) specifying opt-in or opt-out terms (e.g., some regulators may not participate in cross-border mediation but will enforce standards in their own member states); document these variations in the Standing Regulators Committee charter and communicate them to carriers and distributors to manage expectations.
  • If regulator IT systems are found to be obsolete (e.g., paper-based complaint filing, no digital systems), use EU technical-assistance funding (e.g., European Structural and Investment Funds) to co-finance a shared digital complaint-management platform (EUR 5–10M estimate); procure this by Month 6 (2027-04-08) and deploy to all 27 regulators by Month 18 (2028-04-08).
  • If establishing a Standing Regulators Committee with binding consensus is infeasible due to political friction, create a 'Lead Authority' model: designate 3–4 strong regulators (France, Germany, Netherlands, Austria) as leads for specific dispute types (access discrimination, refund disputes, data quality); their rulings are recognised across all member states, with weaker regulators providing implementation support in their territories; validate this model through a Steering Committee vote by Month 6 (2027-04-08).
  • If capacity-building timelines slip, use rotation-based prioritisation: focus intensive twinning on the 4–6 regulators covering the four priority corridors (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon, Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin) first by Month 12 (2027-10-08), then extend to TEN-T extension regulators in Months 18–30 (2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08); stagger regulator readiness gates accordingly.

Find Document 11: Distributor Market Research: Trainline, Omio and Other Commercial Platforms' Margin Requirements, Integration Capacity and Co-Marketing Preferences

ID: dff2502f-f5a0-466e-a715-904906ee843c

Description: Detailed market research on the three largest rail-ticketing distributors (Trainline, Omio, others) to understand their business models, margin expectations (typically 5–10% of booking value for rail, lower for through-tickets), current IT investment capacity, likely timeline for OSDM API integration, and co-marketing incentive requirements. Needed to design the distributor engagement and incentive strategy (Carrier Engagement and Stakeholder Manager) and to forecast whether early API access and co-marketing support (EUR 5–10M budget proposed) will be sufficient to secure integration by Month 18 (2028-04-08). Audience: distributor engagement lead, budget planner, consumer product lead.

Recency Requirement: Market research conducted Months 1–3 (2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) via interviews and questionnaires to platform leadership. Collect responses by Month 2 (2026-12-08).

Responsible Role Type: Carrier Engagement and Stakeholder Manager / Coalition Builder

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Schedule bilateral meetings with Trainline (Group Chief Technology Officer or VP Partnerships), Omio (Chief Product Officer or VP Partnerships), and 2–3 smaller platforms (Month 1 = 2026-11-08).
  • 2. Ask each platform: (a) current gross margin on rail bookings; (b) estimated cost of OSDM API integration (development, testing, operations); (c) timeline for live integration if early API access is offered; (d) marketing budget and co-marketing discount expectations; (e) data-access requirements (e.g., real-time inventory, competitor pricing visibility).
  • 3. Document responses in a distributor-readiness matrix (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) and use findings to tailor the distributor engagement strategy and incentive package.

Access Difficulty: Medium. Major distributors are reachable via public contacts and usually willing to meet for strategic dialogue. Expect preliminary answers in Months 1–2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08); detailed financial and timeline estimates may require follow-up (Months 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08).

Essential Information:

  • Identify current gross margin on rail bookings for Trainline, Omio and 2–3 smaller platforms (typically reported as percentage of booking value; baseline estimate 5–10% for rail, potentially lower for through-tickets).
  • Quantify estimated development cost and timeline for each platform to integrate OSDM API (Month 12–18 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08 baseline; identify any platform signalling Month 24+ = 2028-10-08+ slippage).
  • Document co-marketing budget and co-funding expectations per platform (e.g., request for cost-sharing on distributor campaigns, performance bonuses tied to through-ticket volumes, or transaction-fee waivers).
  • Map data-access requirements unique to each platform (real-time inventory detail, competitor pricing, accessibility information, disruption feeds) and compatibility with the certification-based tiered access model.
  • Assess each platform's capacity to promote through-tickets: marketing resource allocation, integration with existing rail/multimodal offerings, and likelihood of prioritising through-ticketing if margins are compressed.
  • Document non-integration or partial-integration risks per platform (e.g., 'Trainline will not fully integrate until Month 27 = 2029-01-08' or 'Omio demands exclusive early access to high-demand city pairs').
  • Establish a distributor-readiness matrix (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) quantifying each platform's integration timeline, cost expectations and co-funding demand to inform final engagement strategy and budget allocation.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Incomplete margin data leads to undersized co-funding offers; platforms reject the incentive package and delay integration, pushing Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards deadline at risk.
  • Underestimated integration costs per platform prevent realistic budget planning for co-funding (proposed EUR 5–10M); actual demand exceeds EUR 215 million free contingency, triggering Tier 2 or Tier 3 cost cuts.
  • Delayed or absent market research leaves engagement strategy undirected; programme proceeds with ad-hoc negotiations in Months 4–9 (2027-02-08 to 2027-07-08), missing early buy-in window and allowing platforms to set demanding terms in Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08).
  • Undetected non-compliance signals (e.g., Trainline's stated Month 24 = 2028-10-08 integration date) are discovered late; programme lacks time to escalate or activate fallback distributor-expansion strategy before the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards and Month 30 (2029-04-08) API milestones.
  • Data-access demands are not mapped; programme constructs the tiered access and data-layer architecture without knowing platform requirements, leading to rework and distributor rejection at Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08).
  • Missing competitive-positioning intelligence: if a major platform signals preference for a competing through-ticketing scheme (e.g., voluntary carrier agreements outside the regulation) or demands exclusivity on inventory, the programme's 40% target and distributor coalition fracture.

Worst Case Scenario: Two major platforms (Trainline and Omio, representing ~60% of anticipated through-ticket volume) signal in Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08) that full OSDM API integration is not feasible by the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards deadline or requires co-funding exceeding the EUR 215 million free contingency. In response, the programme must either (1) extend the API integration timeline past Month 30 (2029-04-08), breaking the legal mandate and triggering Commission enforcement risk, or (2) expand the public reference distributor into a full retail competitor to capture the 40% target, consuming an estimated EUR 200–400 million of additional operating costs that trigger a Tier 3 budget overrun and force across-the-board cuts to standards, conformance testing, and capacity building. By Month 24 (2028-10-08), smaller carriers lack certified compliance support, the through-ticket network is incomplete, and the 40% target becomes unachievable within the original timeline.

Best Case Scenario: Market research completed by Month 2 (2026-12-08) shows that Trainline and Omio require EUR 3–5M each for full OSDM integration by Month 18 (2028-04-08) and are willing to commit to integration and co-marketing in return for early API access (Month 9–12 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08) and a co-funding package (EUR 5–10M over 24 months, shared among platforms). Both platforms confirm >20% margin on through-tickets and plan dedicated promotional campaigns. Commitment Letters are signed by Month 4 (2027-02-08). Programme constructs the tiered access model and data layer with platform input by Month 6 (2027-04-08). Both platforms go live by Month 18 (2028-04-08), driving distributor-side adoption and increasing through-ticket volumes to 25–30% by Month 24 (2028-10-08), providing momentum for the 40% target and enabling TEN-T extension without further distributor renegotiation.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If market research reveals non-compliance signals or prohibitive integration costs from Trainline and Omio, escalate immediately to the Carrier Engagement and Stakeholder Manager in Month 3–4 (2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08) and trigger bilateral negotiations with individual platform executives (CTO, VP Partnerships) to understand technical blockers and cost drivers.
  • If co-funding demand from all platforms exceeds EUR 20M (vs. the proposed EUR 5–10M allocation), conduct a comparative analysis of public-distributor expansion costs (estimated EUR 200–400M for full retail operation) vs. increasing platform co-funding (EUR 30–50M), and escalate to the Budget Planner for a mid-course decision on whether to reduce co-funding rates or expand the public channel.
  • If Trainline or Omio refuses integration by Month 18 (2028-04-08) but signals willingness by Month 24–27 (2028-10-08 to 2029-01-08), activate a phased integration model: public distributor handles the initial through-ticket volume (Months 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), then transitions traffic to commercial platforms as they come online, reducing long-term public-distributor cost and avoiding a distributed-channel fragmentation.
  • If platforms demand exclusive early access to premium inventory (e.g., first access to new fares on high-demand routes) in return for integration, engage the Data Governance and Competition teams (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) to assess whether such exclusive access violates the non-discrimination rules in the proposed Regulation; if yes, deny the demand and use refusal as a negotiation trigger to accelerate other platforms' integration.
  • If market research indicates that a small-scale distributor aggregator or a carrier-owned direct-sales channel could capture significant through-ticket volume without the major commercial platforms, commission a breakeven analysis (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) of whether the programme should reduce reliance on Trainline and Omio and instead invest in alternative distribution channels (estimated EUR 50–100M additional spend, offset by reduced co-funding demand).
  • If margin data show that through-ticket margins are 2–3% (not the assumed 5–10%), indicating distributor-profitability risk, recommend a 'distributor revenue guarantee' pilot (Month 6–24 = 2027-04-08 to 2028-10-08): the programme subsidises the margin difference for early adopters (Months 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), creating financial certainty and accelerating integration, with the subsidy tapering as volumes grow.

Find Document 12: Carrier Financial Benchmarking and Willingness-to-Pay Analysis for Through-Ticket Integration and Co-Funding (Major and Smaller Carriers)

ID: 58a58352-8eed-4fca-bbd8-2c63a8fc2d8b

Description: Financial analysis of the 25+ participating carriers' likely tolerance for integration costs, their expected return on investment from increased through-ticket volumes, and the co-funding rates that would incentivise adoption. Needed for the Funding Allocation and Carrier Incentives framework (Decision 3) and the cost model (Month 2 = 2026-12-08). Includes assessment of each carrier's integration cost (hub use EUR 2–5M, native build EUR 10–20M) and expected revenue uplift from through-ticket sales. Audience: financial modeller, carrier engagement lead, budget planner.

Recency Requirement: Analysis conducted Months 1–3 (2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) via surveys and interviews. Estimates due Month 2 (2026-12-08).

Responsible Role Type: Budget Controller and Financial Manager; Carrier Engagement and Stakeholder Manager

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Prepare a carrier financial-assessment template (Month 1 = 2026-11-08) requesting: estimated IT integration cost (hub or native), expected revenue from through-tickets as % of total cross-border revenue, and acceptable co-funding rate (10%, 20%, 50%).
  • 2. Issue the template to carriers above EUR 10M annual cross-border revenue via CER (Month 1 = 2026-11-08); collect responses by Month 2 (2026-12-08).
  • 3. Conduct follow-up calls with carriers that initially indicate low willingness-to-pay to understand cost barriers and alternative incentive structures.
  • 4. Aggregate findings in a cost-model input document (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) to inform the budget framework.

Access Difficulty: Medium. Carriers are often willing to share cost estimates with the Commission but may be coy about expected revenue uplifts (competitive sensitivity). CER coordination helps; expect 50–70% response rate initially and 80%+ after follow-up.

Essential Information:

  • Quantify each carrier's estimated IT integration cost: distinguish hub-use costs (EUR 2–5M) vs. native-build costs (EUR 10–20M) by carrier size, legacy-system age and geography.
  • Identify expected revenue uplift from through-ticket sales as a % of each carrier's total cross-border revenue, segment by carrier size and corridor (baseline assumption: 5–15% of cross-border revenue uplift).
  • Determine the co-funding rate each carrier type would accept: small operators (< EUR 50M cross-border revenue), medium operators (EUR 50–200M), and incumbents (> EUR 200M), to incentivise adoption by Month 30 (2029-04-08).
  • Map the 12–18 hub-eligible carriers (criteria: cross-border revenue under EUR 50M, OR booking system older than 10 years, OR IT staff under 10 FTE) and assess their willingness to use hubs vs. native integration.
  • Estimate the funding gap: sum of expected co-funding demand vs. the EUR 290 million allocated for carrier grants, hubs and accessibility—quantify shortfall or surplus by carrier cohort.
  • Identify cost-control levers: which carrier segments are most price-sensitive and would respond to co-funding reductions; which would resist integration if co-funding falls below a threshold.
  • Assess the opportunity cost of co-funding to carriers: would private investment occur without subsidy? (additionality question); estimate the share of EUR 290M that would duplicate carriers' planned IT spend.
  • Specify the conditionality for co-funding disbursement: which milestones (API exposure, data-quality attestation, conformance testing) must carriers pass before each funding tranche is released?

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Underestimated integration costs (e.g., hub fees are EUR 5–8M, not EUR 2–5M) reduce willingness-to-pay and force higher co-funding rates, consuming contingency earlier than planned and leaving less for conformance testing or capacity building.
  • Overestimated revenue uplifts (e.g., carriers expect 20%+ uplift but achieve 5%) will disappoint participants and erode their incentive to invest, leading to post-commitment delays or demands for renegotiation in Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08).
  • Incomplete carrier participation (< 80% of cross-border traffic volume commits to integration) will fragment the network, prevent the 90% bookability target at Month 30 (2029-04-08), and force costly alternative provisions (expanded hubs, gateway fallback).
  • Ambiguous additionality assessment (not distinguishing public co-funding from planned private investment) risks subsidising work that carriers would do anyway, wasting EUR 50–100M of public money and inviting audit criticism.
  • Poor conditionality design (milestone triggers that are vague, unmeasurable or unenforced) allows carriers to claim funds without delivering integration, leaving key milestones unmet.
  • Low response rate (<50%) to the financial-assessment template or reluctance to share revenue expectations leaves the cost model underpowered, forcing Month 2 (2026-12-08) decisions on EUR 290M allocation with incomplete data.

Worst Case Scenario: By Month 3–4 (2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08), the cost analysis reveals that actual carrier co-funding demand is EUR 450–550M (30–50% higher than the EUR 290M allocation), driven by underestimated hub operational costs, higher integration expenses for legacy systems, or broader hub-eligibility criteria. The programme is forced to cut carrier co-funding from the planned 20–25% to 10–15%, triggering resistance from smaller operators and member-state representatives. Adoption commitments from 5–8 smaller carriers are withdrawn, and their readiness at Month 30 (2029-04-08) slips to Month 36–42 (2029-10-08 to 2030-04-08). Simultaneously, the contingency reserve is depleted by EUR 100–150M to fund the shortfall, leaving no buffer for unplanned costs (GDPR intervention, payment-provider switching, passenger-rights claims). The EUR 40–60M cut to conformance testing slows certification timelines by 8–12 weeks, and several carriers miss the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate. The programme's credibility is damaged by unmet commitments, and distributor confidence erodes.

Best Case Scenario: The financial benchmarking is completed by Month 2 (2026-12-08) with >80% carrier response and clear, validated cost profiles. Integration costs are confirmed at EUR 10–15M for native builds and EUR 3–5M for hub use, with additionality clearly separated (EUR 100–150M of the EUR 290M is new investment, the remainder matches existing plans). Smaller carriers' willingness-to-pay analysis reveals that a 20% co-funding rate is sufficient to secure adoption commitments from 16–18 hub-eligible operators. The EUR 290M allocation is validated as sufficient with EUR 50–70M margin. Conditionality is designed as specific, measurable milestones: API conformance testing passed (Month 15–18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08), data-quality attestation completed (Month 18 = 2028-04-08), and booking integration tested in dual-run (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08). By Month 3 (2027-01-08), Commitment Letters from 22–24 carriers are signed with clear funding schedules. The programme achieves 85–90% of cross-border traffic ready by Month 30 (2029-04-08), contingency remains intact, and budget discipline is established.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If carrier response to the financial-assessment template is low (< 50%) by Month 2 (2026-12-08): conduct targeted phone interviews with CER and the largest 8 carriers (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, Trenitalia, Renfe, ÖBB, NS, SJ, SNCB) by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23) to extract cost and revenue estimates; use an industry cost model (based on published IT-modernisation benchmarks for rail operators) to fill gaps for smaller carriers.
  • If integration costs are significantly underestimated (e.g., EUR 15–20M for native, EUR 5–8M for hub use): immediately trigger a Tier 2 budget review (Month 6 = 2027-04-08); reduce co-funding from 20% to 10–15%; focus subsidy on the top 8–10 carriers and make smaller operators choose between hubs or delayed integration.
  • If additionality is unclear (carriers claim all costs as 'new' but some are planned): conduct a counterfactual analysis using CER survey data on carriers' baseline IT roadmaps (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08); separate 'attributable to the programme' from 'would happen anyway'; cap co-funding to the attributable share.
  • If carriers resist committing by Month 3 (2027-01-08): escalate to CER and DG MOVE for formal negotiation; use Commitment Letters as a negotiating tool, with public communication of non-compliance to signal consequences; consider holding back co-funding commitments and releasing them only after a major carrier's signed commitment is public.
  • If hub-eligible carriers are fewer than 12 (e.g., only 8–10 meet criteria): reduce the hub network from 4 launch hubs to 2–3 and redeploy the saved EUR 12–18M to increase co-funding for the remaining eligible carriers, ensuring they all reach Month 30 (2029-04-08).
  • If the EUR 290M allocation is insufficient and cannot be increased: trigger Tier 3 contingency cuts (suspend new hub openings, reduce distributor operations by 10–20%, defer TEN-T hub planning to Month 48 = 2030-10-08 instead of Month 30 = 2029-04-08); communicate trade-offs transparently to the Steering Committee and seek supplementary budget authority from DG MOVE by Month 12 (2027-10-08).

Find Document 13: Existing EU Accessibility Standards and Guidelines (WCAG 2.1 AA, EU Accessibility Directive 2019/882, UN Convention on Rights of Persons with Disabilities)

ID: f90ede28-8172-4606-8956-a6b6f4107ad0

Description: Technical and legal standards for digital booking accessibility, assistance for persons with reduced mobility, and cross-border accessibility data sharing. Needed for the Accessibility Integration and Assistance-Delivery Framework and for embedding accessibility requirements in the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08). Includes WCAG 2.1 AA technical specifications, the EU Accessibility Directive's requirements for public transport booking, and the UN Convention's principles on equal access. Audience: accessibility specialist, standards working group, consumer-product team.

Recency Requirement: Current standards: WCAG 2.1 (published 2018, stable); EU Directive 2019/882 (effective 2025+); UN Convention (adopted 2006, ongoing). Use versions current as of Month 0 (2026-10-08).

Responsible Role Type: Assistance Booking and Accessibility Integration Lead

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Download WCAG 2.1 AA specification from the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C, https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/quickref/).
  • 2. Access EU Directive 2019/882 from EUR-Lex and review Title II (Public Transport) requirements for booking and real-time information.
  • 3. Consult the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (https://www.un.org/development/desa/disabilities/) for principles on accessibility to information and transportation.

Access Difficulty: Easy. All three sources are published online and freely accessible. WCAG technical specifications are detailed; allow time for study and interpretation (2–4 weeks).

Essential Information:

  • Identify the specific scope and technical requirements of EU Accessibility Directive 2019/882 (Title II, Public Transport) for digital booking systems and real-time information provision; clarify which requirements apply to through-ticket booking vs. station/vehicle operations.
  • List WCAG 2.1 AA technical success criteria applicable to the through-ticket booking interface (e.g., keyboard navigation, screen-reader compatibility, colour contrast, form labelling, error identification); specify conformance testing procedures and audit tools.
  • Detail UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities principles relevant to transportation access, with particular focus on non-discrimination in service design, reasonable accommodation, and procedural access to information and complaint mechanisms.
  • Quantify current accessibility compliance gaps in European rail booking systems (baseline state at Month 0 = 2026-10-08): existing WCAG conformance rates, assistance-request confirmation timelines, real-time accessibility data availability on stations and rolling stock.
  • Specify accessibility data standards and APIs needed for through-ticket systems: platform lift availability, accessible toilet locations, accessible seating inventory, staff assistance capability, real-time status updates (e.g., lift out of order), and cross-border data exchange protocols.
  • Define accessible design requirements for the public reference distributor's booking app and consumer support channels: chatbot accessibility, multilingual support for accessibility queries, video relay services, TTY/relay integration, and alternative booking methods (phone, email, in-person assistance).
  • Clarify interpretation of 'reasonable accommodation' and 'significant and proportionate burden' (EU Directive Article 5) as they apply to carrier obligations for assistance confirmation within 24 hours and cross-border handover of assistance.
  • Identify existing accessibility certification schemes for digital services (e.g., IAAP, AccessAbility, EN 301 549) and recommend which to embed in the through-ticket conformance testing framework.
  • Provide accessibility impact-assessment methodology for evaluating through-ticket service design changes, with templates and metrics for measuring accessibility outcomes (e.g., assisted-journey booking rate, assistance-delivery success rate, accessibility-related complaint rate).

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Booking interface non-conformance to WCAG 2.1 AA (e.g., missing alt text, poor colour contrast, non-keyboard-navigable forms) excludes persons with visual and motor disabilities; estimated 5–10% of potential passengers cannot use the system without workarounds, undermining the 40% through-ticket target and inviting regulatory intervention by national disability authorities.
  • Vague or unenforceable assistance-confirmation requirements (e.g., 'reasonable time' instead of 24-hour SLA) lead to inconsistent carrier practices; some carriers confirm within 12 hours, others 48+ hours, creating confusion and unreliable travel planning for persons with reduced mobility; estimated 10–20% of assistance requests are unconfirmed at booking time, deterring adoption.
  • Incomplete accessibility-data APIs (e.g., lift status not updated in real-time, accessible seating not visible in search) force distributors to exclude inaccessible itineraries from results, leaving assisted-journey passengers with fewer options than non-disabled travellers and breaching non-discrimination principles in the EU Directive.
  • Cross-border assistance-handover procedures undefined or not operationally enforced; a passenger arrives at a connecting station in another member state and confirmed assistance (e.g., platform lift, staff support) is not available, stranding the passenger and creating liability; estimated 5–15% of cross-border assisted journeys fail at the handover point.
  • Public distributor's consumer support (phone, chat, email) not accessible for deaf, blind or non-native speakers (e.g., no video relay, no plain-language scripts, no multilingual support for accessibility queries); estimated 10–15% of accessibility-related support requests are unresolved or resolved poorly, generating complaints to BEUC and national disability authorities.
  • Conformance testing of carrier systems omits accessibility checks (WCAG, assistance-confirmation latency, cross-border handover protocols); carriers launch with accessibility gaps undetected until live operation, requiring costly rework and delaying smaller-carrier onboarding by 4–8 weeks per carrier.
  • Accessibility requirements omitted from the binding standards document (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) or relegated to 'best practice' status rather than legal obligation; carriers argue accessibility is optional or too costly, and enforcement is weak; accessibility outcomes lag other service attributes by 20–30 percentage points.
  • Inconsistent interpretation of UN Convention principles across member states; some regulators enforce strict reasonable-accommodation duties (e.g., on-call staff for every journey), others interpret narrowly; carriers in weak-enforcement states underinvest in accessibility, creating a two-tier service across the EU.

Worst Case Scenario: By Month 18 (2028-04-08), the binding standards document omits enforceable accessibility requirements, or accessibility is present but vague and non-testable. The through-ticket booking interface launches with WCAG 2.1 AA non-conformance (estimated 30–50% of success criteria unmet), excluding 5–10% of potential passengers with disabilities. Assistance-confirmation timelines are undefined or undefined (no SLA), and carriers confirm assistance within 48–72 hours if at all, making last-minute travel planning impossible for persons with reduced mobility. Cross-border assistance handovers are not operationally coordinated; a passenger booking Wien–Munich–Zurich assistance is told at Wien station that Munich will handle handover, but Munich has no record and the passenger arrives in Munich with no assistance available. By Month 30 (2029-04-08), disability-rights organizations (BEUC, national advocates) file formal complaints to the EU Agency for Railways and national regulators, alleging discrimination. A DPA or competition authority launches an investigation into whether the programme violates the EU Accessibility Directive or the UN Convention. The Commission is forced to issue a corrective order requiring the standards to be reworked (6–12 month delay) and accessibility to be retrofitted into all systems (€20–50M additional cost). Media coverage of accessibility failures damages the programme's reputation; through-ticket adoption by all passengers drops by 10–20 percentage points, and adoption by persons with reduced mobility is near zero. The programme's credibility with vulnerable populations is destroyed, and post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) political support for scaling to the TEN-T network is undermined.

Best Case Scenario: By Month 4 (2027-02-08), a comprehensive Accessibility Requirements and Testing Framework is completed and agreed by carriers, regulators, BEUC and disability-rights organizations, specifying WCAG 2.1 AA conformance for the booking interface, 24-hour assistance-confirmation SLAs, real-time accessibility-data APIs, and cross-border assistance-coordination protocols. The framework is embedded in the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) as a non-negotiable requirement with defined penalties for non-compliance. Conformance testing includes accessibility audits (WCAG, assistance-latency, cross-border handover simulation) starting Month 12 (2027-10-08). Carriers' booking systems and the public distributor's app are tested and certified to WCAG 2.1 AA by Month 18 (2028-04-08); estimated 95%+ conformance to accessibility success criteria. By Month 27 (2029-01-08), the public distributor launches with a fully accessible booking app (keyboard navigation, screen-reader compatible, multilingual support, accessible error messages), accessible phone support (TTY/relay, multilingual staff), and email support with plain-language responses. Assistance confirmation is automated and confirmed within 12–18 hours for 90%+ of requests by Month 30 (2029-04-08); real-time accessibility data (lift status, accessible seating, staff availability) is visible in the booking interface and updates occur within 2–5 minutes of any change. Cross-border assistance handovers are coordinated via an EU assistance-coordination desk that receives all requests from all distributors and confirms handovers between carriers and stations before the passenger books (estimated 95%+ confirmation success rate). Accessibility-related complaint rates are below 2% by Month 60 (2031-10-08), and assisted-journey booking volumes grow in line with the overall through-ticket target (40% share). Disability-rights organizations endorse the programme publicly, and the EU Accessibility Directive compliance is demonstrated through independent audits. The programme becomes a model for inclusive transport in the EU, and post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) political support for TEN-T extension includes strong accessibility commitments.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If the Accessibility Requirements and Testing Framework cannot be completed by Month 4 (2027-02-08) due to stakeholder disagreement on assistance-confirmation timelines or cross-border liability: appoint an independent accessibility mediator (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) with authority to issue binding recommendations within 4 weeks; use the mediator's proposal as the baseline for the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards if stakeholders cannot agree.
  • If carriers resist WCAG 2.1 AA conformance due to high costs for legacy systems: implement a tiered conformance model—major carriers (>EUR 100M cross-border revenue) must be 100% WCAG 2.1 AA by Month 18 (2028-04-08); smaller carriers and hub-using operators can use a gateway that translates their non-accessible interface into an accessible wrapper (estimated 70–80% conformance), with a deadline to reach 100% by Month 36 (2029-10-08). Co-fund gateway development (EUR 5–10M) from the accessibility programme budget.
  • If real-time accessibility-data APIs cannot be implemented by Month 30 (2029-04-08) due to fragmented station management systems: publish a static accessibility registry (lift, accessible toilet, accessible seating capacity per vehicle) updated daily and exposed via a simple API; distributors can filter itineraries by declared accessibility features; live status updates are deferred to Month 36–42 (2029-10-08 to 2030-04-08). Allocate EUR 5–10M for registry development and station-data aggregation.
  • If cross-border assistance handovers fail at a rate >5% (estimated 10–15% of assisted journeys) by Month 36 (2029-10-08): establish a fallback assistance-coordination service (EU call centre, available Months 6–12 = 2027-04-08 to 2027-10-08, 7–19) funded by the programme (EUR 2–3M/year) that receives all assistance requests from distributors and manually coordinates handovers between carriers and stations; automate handover data exchange when technically ready (target Month 42–48 = 2030-04-08 to 2030-10-08).
  • If the public distributor's accessibility support (phone, chat, email) is not fully operational by Month 21 (2028-07-08): contract a third-party accessible customer-support provider (specialising in multilingual, disability-accessible support) for Months 21–36 (2028-07-08 to 2029-10-08) while the distributor builds in-house capacity; retain the provider on standby if support demand exceeds in-house capacity post-Month 36 (2029-10-08). Budget EUR 1–2M annually.
  • If national regulators lack capacity to enforce accessibility requirements consistently across member states by Month 18 (2028-04-08): establish an EU Accessibility Compliance Panel (6–8 experts, hosted by the EU Agency for Railways) with authority to audit carrier accessibility practices quarterly and issue binding compliance directives; member-state regulators enforce the panel's findings under a lead-authority model (one regulator per non-EU member state issue, all others recognise the decision).
  • If accessibility impact on through-ticket adoption is worse than expected (e.g., assisted-journey booking <5% of total by Month 36 = 2029-10-08, vs. target 10%): commission an accessibility-barrier study (Month 30 = 2029-04-08) to identify whether barriers are booking-interface design, assistance-confirmation unreliability, cross-border handover failure, or insufficient marketing to accessibility audiences; allocate EUR 5–10M for targeted fix (e.g., app redesign, assistance-SLA improvement, accessibility campaign).

Find Document 14: Financial Data on Carrier Profitability, IT Investment Trends and Digital Transformation Roadmaps (Annual Reports, Sustainability Reports, Investor Presentations)

ID: 563640cd-a87a-4189-b4a3-a1065cbd73c4

Description: Financial and strategic data on the 25+ participating carriers' revenue trends, operating margins, capital expenditure on IT and digital systems, and published digital-transformation roadmaps. Needed to validate the assumption that carriers can afford and will prioritise OSDM integration and to design the co-funding incentive structure. Sources: carriers' public financial reports (annual reports, investor presentations, sustainability reports), CER aggregated sector data, transport-ministry data on carrier health and strategic funding.

Recency Requirement: Most recent published data (2024–2025 financial year reports, expected to be published early 2025 or mid-2025). Investor presentations updated quarterly.

Responsible Role Type: Budget Controller and Financial Manager; Strategy and Programme Director

Steps to Find:

  • 1. Download annual financial reports from publicly listed carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, ÖBB, Renfe, Trenitalia, NS, SJ, SNCB – most file on their investor relations websites or via stock-exchange filings).
  • 2. Request publicly available investor presentations covering digital-transformation strategies and capital plans from each carrier (or access via stock-exchange databases like Refinitiv, Bloomberg).
  • 3. Obtain CER sectoral financial data (https://www.cer.be/) for aggregated trends in rail-operator profitability and IT investment.
  • 4. Check national transport ministries for strategic funding plans and state-aid data on carriers (especially state-owned operators like SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, ÖBB).
  • 5. Compile a carrier financial-health scorecard (Months 2–3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08) to inform co-funding allocation and readiness assessment.

Access Difficulty: Easy to Medium. Publicly listed carriers publish annual reports (free on investor websites). CER data is publicly available. State-aid and ministry funding information requires government website searches and formal requests. Allow 4–6 weeks to compile initial dataset from public sources; supplement with 2–3 weeks of direct carrier outreach if needed.

Essential Information:

  • Detailed breakdown of the 25+ participating carriers' 2024–2025 financial statements: revenue trends, operating margins, capital expenditure (CapEx) on IT systems, and debt/leverage ratios, by carrier size (major incumbents >€5B cross-border revenue, mid-tier €1–5B, smaller <€1B).
  • Published digital-transformation roadmaps and IT investment plans from each carrier, covering booking-system modernisation timelines, legacy-system retirement dates, and planned OSDM or API adoption (if any).
  • Aggregated CER sectoral data on rail-operator financial health, profitability trends 2020–2025, and average IT capital intensity (IT spend as % of revenue) by carrier size and geography.
  • State-aid and public-funding data from national transport ministries for state-owned carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, ÖBB, Renfe, SNCB, Trenitalia, etc.), identifying subsidy dependency and available co-funding capacity.
  • Validated carrier IT integration cost estimates by size and legacy-system age: baseline for major operators (native OSDM builds), mid-tier (gateway or hub use), and smaller operators (hub-dependent).
  • Quarterly investor presentations (latest Q3/Q4 2024 or Q1 2025) disclosing management guidance on digital investment and capital allocation priorities for the next 3–5 years.

Risks of Poor Quality:

  • Underestimation of carrier IT integration costs: if actual costs are EUR 500M–2B (vs. EUR 1.25B planning value), and co-funding is capped at EUR 290M, smaller carriers cannot afford integration, slipping past Month 30 (2029-04-08) deadline and fragmenting the network by 10–20 percentage points.
  • Misalignment of co-funding allocation: if carrier financial health data is stale or aggregated, co-funding is mis-targeted (funding carriers that are already investing heavily, or under-funding those that cannot self-fund), reducing adoption among the long tail of smaller operators and leaving 15–25% of cross-border traffic unintegrated.
  • Overstating carrier digital-transformation momentum: if published roadmaps do not reflect realistic IT investment or if carriers have deprioritised OSDM in favour of competing projects (e.g., internal modernisation), the programme cannot rely on carriers' stated timelines, causing Month 30 (2029-04-08) readiness to slip by 4–8 weeks per carrier.
  • Insufficient state-aid and subsidy data: if state-owned carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn) cannot access co-funding due to budget constraints, they delay integration, creating a two-tier network in which well-funded carriers meet the deadline but state-owned operators do not.
  • Failure to identify IT integration cost variance by legacy-system age: if cost estimates do not account for extreme cases (e.g., some carriers with 20+ year-old mainframes may face EUR 5–15M integration costs vs. EUR 1–3M for mid-age systems), hub-versus-native decisions are misinformed, leading to overruns or under-resourcing of hubs.

Worst Case Scenario: The programme commissions a cost model in Month 2–3 (2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08) based on incomplete or outdated financial data: carrier revenue figures from 2023, IT budgets that do not reflect 2025 repriorisation, and state-aid data that misses recent subsidies. Co-funding is allocated proportionally by carrier size without accounting for actual financial distress or IT maturity. By Month 12–18 (2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08), when carriers begin integration, 8–12 smaller operators signal they cannot afford native builds or hub fees and lobby for 100% public funding or timeline extensions. The programme's contingency reserve is exhausted by Month 24 (2028-10-08) attempting to retain these operators, leaving no buffer for infrastructure failures, overruns or distributor expansion. By Month 30 (2029-04-08), only 75–80% of corridors meet the 90% traffic-bookable threshold, and the mandatory API deadline is either missed or implemented with low-quality outcomes, undermining passenger and distributor confidence.

Best Case Scenario: Financial data is collected from current (2024–2025) annual reports and quarterly investor presentations by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Cost model accounts for carrier size, legacy-system age, state subsidy dependency, and existing IT roadmaps. Co-funding is precisely allocated: major carriers receive EUR 5–10M each (gap-fill for integration bottlenecks), mid-tier carriers EUR 2–5M, and smaller carriers EUR 300K–1M plus guaranteed hub access. State-owned operators receive targeted support (EUR 10–20M from capacity-building budget) to meet the deadline. By Month 18 (2028-04-08), 90%+ of carriers have signed integration plans, and cost tracking shows actual spend within 10–15% of forecast. By Month 30 (2029-04-08), 92–95% of corridor traffic is bookable end-to-end, exceeding the 90% threshold, and early distributor feedback is positive. By Month 60 (2031-10-08), the 40% through-ticket target is on track or exceeded, and the programme has credibility for TEN-T extension.

Fallback Alternative Approaches:

  • If carrier financial data is incomplete or delayed beyond Month 4 (2027-02-08): commission a rapid carrier survey (2–3 week questionnaire to CER and major carriers) asking for self-reported 2025 IT budgets, digital-roadmap summaries and integration cost estimates; use CER sectoral benchmarks to back-fill missing data for smaller carriers, accepting ±20% uncertainty in cost estimates.
