  • If state-aid data is fragmented across 27 member-state sources: engage national transport ministries and EU State Aid Monitoring Unit directly (Month 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) to obtain centralised state-subsidy and co-funding availability data; prepare a member-state co-funding capacity matrix to inform the budget allocation.
  • If carrier IT roadmaps do not explicitly address OSDM: conduct targeted interviews (Month 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) with 8–10 strategic carriers (major and mid-tier) on their digital priorities, OSDM readiness and IT investment plans; use findings to validate cost estimates and identify carriers at risk of slipping the deadline.
  • If cost estimates prove unachievable after Month 8 (2027-06-08): trigger a 'cost-reduction workshop' with CER and hub operators to explore phased integration pathways (e.g., reduced data-set in Year 1, full parity in Year 2) that defer some costs, keeping total integration CapEx within the EUR 1.25B estimate.
  • If carrier financial health is weaker than expected (e.g., state-owned carriers in southern/eastern Europe cannot co-fund): escalate to the Steering Committee by Month 12 (2027-10-08) with a revised co-funding allocation that prioritises public money toward operators at greatest risk of missing the deadline, and consider trade-offs (e.g., reduce public-distributor operating costs to free up co-funding, or defer TEN-T extension to preserve Month 30 = 2029-04-08 focus).

Strengths

  • Clear scenario (Pragmatic Foundation): certified access, accredited payment institutions, milestone co-funding, regional hubs and an arbitration panel avoid new legal entities and early price-fixing.
  • OSDM is an existing, versioned standard with live implementations, so the programme builds on proven technical foundations.
  • Public budget of EUR 1,500 million (user constraint) with a EUR 225 million contingency (15%) held at DG MOVE, and defined Tier 1-3 overrun responses.
  • Specific milestones (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 standards, Month 30 = 2029-04-08 API, Month 60 = 2031-10-08 corridors) and a fixed through-ticket definition give measurable direction.
  • Reference models exist: Swiss Direct Service clearing and the Deutschlandticket show multi-operator revenue split without a new central payment entity.
  • Strong stakeholder architecture: working groups, Steering Committee, Standing Regulators Committee, accessibility and consumer groups.

Weaknesses

  • KILLER APPLICATION MISSING: no single flagship use-case is defined that makes through-tickets compelling on their own. The plan relies on broad convenience (sum-of-segment fares, no price ceilings), which is a weak pull against low-cost flights.
  • Panel rulings depend on Council/Commission delegation not yet secured; the panel has no direct enforcement power over large incumbents.
  • Fixed budget is fragile: a 20-30% overrun (EUR 300-450M) exceeds the EUR 215M free contingency (estimate).
  • Legacy carrier IT: 12-18 carriers (estimate) need hubs, which carry mapping-error and single-point-of-failure risk.
  • No consolidated baseline for cross-border sales, complaints or modal split until Month 9 (2027-07-08).
  • Consumer rollout and communication are only lightly covered; the app launches at Month 15 (2028-01-08) and four-corridor consumer go-live is at Month 27 (2029-01-08).
  • Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) run costs of about EUR 45M/year (estimate) are unfunded.

Opportunities

  • KILLER APPLICATION CAN BE DEVELOPED: a flagship 'one ticket, guaranteed connection' product on a single high-demand corridor (e.g. Paris-Brussels-Amsterdam-Koln). One booking, one payment, a 4-hour reroute decision and a 10-day refund, with reduction cards honoured (about 10-15% effective discount). Pilot it first, then scale it. Variants: an air-rail city-pair offer where rail competes with short-haul flights, or an assisted-travel journey for persons with reduced mobility.
  • Obstacles to the killer application: through-fares may not beat budget airlines; the Regulation is not yet adopted; Trainline and Omio may lack margin incentive; weakest-carrier readiness limits end-to-end coverage; liability for missed connections is not fully funded; and mixed pilot corridors could confuse travellers.
  • Regulation adoption gives a legal base for mandatory API exposure and non-discriminatory access.
  • Distributors (Trainline, Omio) can supply large existing audiences if given early API access and co-marketing support.
  • Environmental positioning and rising aviation taxes or fuel prices could improve rail competitiveness.
  • Multimodal hooks (bus, ferry, short-haul air) extend the product beyond rail.
  • Lessons from OSDM, SwissPass and the Deutschlandticket can speed design and reduce risk.

Threats

  • Regulation adoption slips past Month 9 (2027-07-08), compressing the standards window and threatening Month 18 (2028-04-08).
  • Incumbents (DB, SNCF, OBB) signal non-compliance or seek exemptions, turning the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate advisory.
  • GDPR challenges from national data protection authorities, or a competition-law investigation into shared fare and inventory data, could force redesign.
  • Airlines respond with lower fares and more frequency; fuel-price falls weaken modal shift (planning range 5-15%, estimate).
  • Fewer than 2 payment providers apply, or one withdraws.
  • Uneven national regulator capacity and sovereignty objections undermine consistent enforcement.
  • Peak-load API failures or hub outages, and poor consumer-app quality, could damage trust early.
  • Non-EU participation (e.g. Swiss SBB) is uncertain on the Wien-Munchen-Zurich corridor.

Recommendations

  • Define and pilot the killer application (guaranteed-connection through-ticket on one corridor) by Month 9 (2027-07-08) and launch it with the public app at Month 15 (2028-01-08). Owner: PMO with the consumer product team and corridor carriers.
  • Secure written Council/Commission delegation to the arbitration panel by Month 2 (2026-12-08) (target Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23), and Commitment Letters from carriers above EUR 50M cross-border revenue by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Owner: DG MOVE.
  • Track Regulation adoption weekly from Month 0 (2026-10-08) and run shadow standards pre-work; if adoption slips past Month 8 (2027-06-08), contract an external standards consortium. Owner: DG MOVE with the EU Agency for Railways.
  • Complete the cost model by Month 2 (2026-12-08), apply the 115% trigger and Tier 1-3 responses, and hold reviews at Months 12 and 24 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08). Owner: DG MOVE finance lead.
  • Contract hubs by Month 3 (2027-01-08), run 2-4 week dual-runs in Months 15-18 (2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08), and suspend onboarding if failures exceed 2% for a week. Owner: Hub programme lead with the smaller-carrier coordinators.
  • Run payment accreditation (call Month 2 = 2026-12-08, decision Month 8 = 2027-06-08, at least 2 providers live at Month 12 = 2027-10-08), and agree distributor margin support and early API access by Month 6 (2027-04-08). Owner: Clearing workstream lead and distributor advisory council.

Strategic Objectives

  • Fix the through-ticket definition by Month 2 (2026-12-08) and validate the measurement baseline by Month 9 (2027-07-08), with monthly reporting from Month 18 (2028-04-08).
  • Adopt binding standards (including accessibility and GDPR rules) by Month 18 (2028-04-08), and make at least 90% of corridor traffic bookable end-to-end by Month 30 (2029-04-08) (proposed threshold).
  • Reach at least 15% through-ticket share by Month 24 (2028-10-08) (proposed threshold) and 40% of cross-border rail journeys by Month 60 (2031-10-08), with the killer-application product live on at least one corridor by Month 15 (2028-01-08).
  • Cut distributor complaints to 50% or less of the Month 9 (2027-07-08) baseline by Month 60 (2031-10-08).
  • Keep spend within the EUR 1,500 million cap and agree the post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding model for the distributor, hubs and data layer by Month 48 (2030-10-08).

Assumptions

  • The Regulation is adopted by Month 9 (2027-07-08) with only minor changes to the Commission proposal.
  • The Council/Commission delegation to the arbitration panel is granted by Month 2 (2026-12-08).
  • Private carrier IT spend of EUR 0.5-2.0 billion (estimate, planning value EUR 1.25 billion) stays outside the cap.
  • Through-fares are the sum of segment prices with no regulated ceilings, so modal shift is a planning range of 5-15% (estimate), not a commitment.
  • Trainline and Omio take part given early API access and co-marketing support.
  • Switzerland participates in the Wien-Munchen-Zurich corridor.

Missing Information

  • Which flagship use-case travellers value most (customer research and willingness to pay versus flights).
  • Baseline cross-border sales, complaint volumes and modal split.
  • Per-carrier IT readiness and actual integration cost.
  • Final text of the Regulation, especially on liability and the meaning of non-discriminatory access.
  • Distributor margin requirements and integration timelines.
  • Competition authority and data protection authority positions.
  • Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding and operating model, and the UK and Swiss scope.

Questions

  • Which single journey or product would make a traveller choose a through-ticket over buying separate tickets or flying, and what evidence supports that?
  • What would the programme do if the Regulation is adopted after Month 9 (2027-07-08) or the final text differs materially?
  • Can the arbitration panel realistically bind Deutsche Bahn or SNCF, and what happens if a major carrier refuses?
  • Is the 40% through-ticket target meaningful without competitive fares, and should modal shift be tracked as a separate target?
  • Which budget lines would be cut first in a 20-30% overrun, and who decides on supplementary funding?

Roles Needed & Example People

Roles

1. Programme Director / Senior Project Executive

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Programme Director requires continuous accountability for EUR 1.5 billion budget, five-year critical path (Months 0–60 = 2026-10-08 to 2031-10-08), and binding authority over milestone escalations. This is a permanent, core governance role with ongoing responsibility from project initiation through sustainability handover at Month 60+. Full-time employment ensures dedicated focus, institutional knowledge and executive presence within DG MOVE.

Explanation: Provides overall leadership, strategic decision-making, and accountability for the EUR 1.5 billion budget and five-year critical path (Months 0–60 = 2026-10-08 to 2031-10-08). Manages the Programme Management Office, reports to DG MOVE and the Steering Committee, and ensures governance clarity with binding authority over milestone escalation, budget release, and mid-course corrections. Essential throughout all phases from planning to sustainability handover.

Consequences: Without clear executive leadership, decision-making slows, accountability fragments across DG MOVE and national bodies, escalations to the Commission lengthen from 4 weeks to 8+ weeks, and critical gates (Months 18, 30, 60 = 2028-04-08, 2029-04-08, 2031-10-08) slip by 4–8 weeks. Budget oversight is lost, permitting unplanned overruns to consume contingency before mid-course correction is possible.

People Count: 1 full-time executive director from Month 0 (2026-10-08) onward; backfill with deputy programme director by Month 6 (2027-04-08) to ensure continuity during critical governance and standards windows.

Typical Activities: Helena chairs the monthly Steering Committee with representatives from DG MOVE, the EU Agency for Railways, CER, national regulators and major carriers, setting priorities and unblocking governance deadlocks within 2-week response targets. She maintains executive liaisons with member-state transport ministers (quarterly calls minimum) and carriers above EUR 50M cross-border revenue to signal consequences for non-compliance and build political cover. She reviews monthly budget-burn reports (prepared by the Finance Controller) and approves all major contracts (payment-institution accreditation, hub operators, data-layer infrastructure procurement). When disputes escalate from working groups to the Steering Committee (e.g., a carrier contests a technical standard or a regulator raises sovereignty concerns), Helena facilitates resolution and decides escalation to the Commission if internal negotiation fails. She also represents the programme publicly: quarterly progress reports to the European Parliament's TRAN committee, annual results summaries to the Council, and media engagement during milestone announcements.

Background Story: Dr. Helena Kozlov, 58, from Belgium, is a senior EU programme director with 22 years of experience in DG MOVE transport-policy coordination. She holds a PhD in transport economics from the University of Brussels and has led three previous large-scale EU infrastructure programmes (TEN-T corridor funding 2014–2020, rail interoperability standards 2015–2020, and modal-shift sustainability initiatives 2018–2023). Helena is fluent in five languages and has established credibility with member-state transport ministers and carrier leadership. She was recruited specifically for this through-ticketing programme because of her track record closing technical disputes under political pressure and her deep familiarity with both Brussels institutional procedures and rail-sector dynamics. Her role as Programme Director grants her binding authority over milestone escalations, budget release and mid-course corrections—authority explicitly needed to prevent fragmentation if major carriers signal non-compliance.

Equipment Needs: Executive workspace with secure video-conferencing capability (for quarterly member-state and carrier roundtables, plus monthly Steering Committee meetings). Access to real-time budget dashboards and milestone-tracking tools (e.g., Asana, Monday.com). High-security encrypted communications for sensitive escalations to DG MOVE and the Commission. Liaison tools for coordinating with EU institutions, national transport ministries and carrier leadership across multiple time zones.

Facility Needs: Office in Brussels, European Quarter, near DG MOVE and EU Agency for Railways. Meeting space for monthly Steering Committee (12–15 participants). Direct access to Commission and Council meeting infrastructure for political engagement. Secure facilities for classified governance documents and decision logs. Videoconference-equipped office supporting 24/7 escalation availability during critical windows (Months 18, 30, 60 = 2028-04-08, 2029-04-08, 2031-10-08).

2. Chief Technical Standards Officer / OSDM and API Architecture Lead

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Chief Technical Standards Officer owns binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 deadline) and OSDM API architecture—a foundational, continuous responsibility spanning Months 4–30 (2027-02-08 to 2029-04-08)+ with peak intensity Months 4–18 (2027-02-08 to 2028-04-08). This core technical leadership role requires deep institutional knowledge, continuity across standards disputes, and authority to make binding decisions. Full-time employment ensures the technical credibility and decision authority needed to resolve contested standards issues.

Explanation: Owns binding standards development (Month 18 = 2028-04-08 deadline), OSDM-compatible API specifications, data-layer design (federated inventory + event-streaming disruption model), ticket format and validation protocols. Leads the working groups on standards, coordinates with UIC/OSDM community, manages conformance-testing scope and laboratory accreditation. Critical during Months 4–18 (2027-02-08 to 2028-04-08) standards finalisation and Months 18–30 (2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08) carrier integration. Ensures alignment with competition-law data-sharing safeguards.

Consequences: Standards are delayed or incomplete by Month 18 (2028-04-08), or produced without consensus, inviting carrier rejection and non-compliance. Conformance testing is poorly scoped, leaving security and interoperability gaps. API performance SLAs are not defined or enforced, causing latency and data-quality issues that reduce through-ticket reliability (estimated 5–10% booking-failure rate post-launch). Competition-law risks (data-sharing collusion) are not mitigated, inviting DG Comp investigation and forcing a 6–12 month data-layer redesign.

People Count: 1 senior lead (chief standards officer) from Month 1 (2026-11-08) onward; min 2, max 5 technical specialists (OSDM/API architects, data modellers, test designers) depending on standards complexity and working-group load (scaling up Month 2–6 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-04-08, peak during Months 4–18 = 2027-02-08 to 2028-04-08).

Typical Activities: Alexander leads the monthly technical standards working group (12–15 participants from carriers, distributors, UIC and testing labs) that designs OSDM-compatible API specifications, ticket formats and data-layer protocols. He owns the binding standards document due Month 18 (2028-04-08), managing a detailed specification process: Month 4–6 (2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) baseline design, Month 7–14 (2027-05-08 to 2027-12-08) stakeholder consultation and conflict resolution, Month 15–18 (2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08) final drafting and formal vote. When carrier CIOs contest a proposed standard (e.g., arguing that inventory-parity SLAs are too tight), Alexander chairs a technical dispute panel to evaluate feasibility and cost, then presents recommendations to the Programme Director for decision. He conducts quarterly conformance-testing planning: reviewing laboratory capabilities, approving test harnesses for API correctness, and setting certification milestones for carriers (target: major carriers certified by Month 24 = 2028-10-08, smaller operators by Month 30 = 2029-04-08, 2029-04-08). He also manages the OSDM version roadmap, balancing immediate programme needs (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) against longer-term extensibility for multimodal integration and post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability.

Background Story: Dr. Alexander Grosz, 51, from Austria, is a senior systems architect and standards engineer with 25 years' experience in rail IT and interoperability standards. He holds a PhD in computer science from the Vienna University of Technology and has led the OSDM working group at UIC since 2019, where he gained deep familiarity with the challenges of multi-carrier API standardisation. Alexander was involved in Switzerland's Alliance SwissPass standardisation project (2012–2018) and has consulted on ticket-validation protocols for several European carriers. His expertise in OSDM and his standing in the rail-IT community position him as the natural Chief Technical Standards Officer. Alexander is known for his ability to navigate complex technical disputes by focusing on interoperability outcomes rather than vendor preferences, and for his patience in achieving consensus among competing carriers with differing legacy systems.

Equipment Needs: High-performance workstations for standards engineers (CAD/simulation tools not required; primarily document collaboration and API design tools). OSDM specification repository and version-control access (GitHub, GitLab or equivalent). Conformance-testing lab access (remote and on-site) to validate API correctness and interoperability. Real-time collaboration tools (video, screen-sharing, whiteboarding) for distributed working-group sessions across EU carriers and testing labs. Secure document management for binding standards versions and audit trails.

Facility Needs: Office in Brussels or Vienna (proximity to UIC, EU Agency for Railways and carrier IT centres). Dedicated conference room for monthly technical standards working group (12–15 participants) and dispute-resolution panels. Access to external conformance-testing laboratories (4–6 locations across Europe) for hands-on API and data-layer validation. Testing environment with carrier sandbox systems (stage/pre-prod) accessible for integration work. High-speed internet and low-latency connectivity to distributed carrier data centres for real-time protocol testing (Months 4–18 = 2027-02-08 to 2028-04-08, peak).

3. Governance and Legal Affairs Advisor / Regulatory Liaison

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Governance and Legal Affairs Advisor secures written Council delegation (Month 2 = 2026-12-08 deadline) and manages ongoing legal exposure (GDPR, competition law, liability frameworks) throughout Months 0–60 (2026-10-08 to 2031-10-08). This foundational role requires continuous presence in governance forums, escalation authority and deep familiarity with EU institutional procedures. Full-time employment ensures legal continuity and prevents critical deadlines from slipping due to part-time availability.

Explanation: Secures written Council/Commission delegation of arbitration-panel authority by Month 2 (2026-12-08); drafts the arbitration panel's mandate, MOU with DG MOVE and the EU Agency for Railways, and ensures legal clarity. Navigates Competition Law firewalls (GDPR, Article 101/102 TFEU), coordinates with EDPB and national DPAs on data-flow rules (DPA consensus by Month 4 = 2027-02-08), and manages non-EU participation (Switzerland SBB, post-Brexit UK). Attends all governance forums and escalates legal blockers. Ensures through-ticket liability framework and passenger-rights backstop are legally sound.

Consequences: Arbitration-panel authority is not formally delegated or is ambiguous, allowing major incumbents to contest rulings and delay compliance. GDPR challenges from national DPAs go unmanaged, halting payment-institution accreditation by Month 12 (2027-10-08) and pushing API mandate 6–12 months past Month 30 (2029-04-08). Competition-law risk materialises (DG Comp investigation), forcing a 6–12 month data-layer redesign. Hub contracts lack liability and SLA clarity, leading to disputes and operational failures during Months 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08).

People Count: 1 senior legal counsel (regulation and governance) from Month 0 (2026-10-08) onward; plus min 1, max 2 legal specialists for GDPR, competition law and transactional support (data-sharing agreements, hub SoWs, payment-institution contracts) from Month 1 (2026-11-08), scaling to 2–3 during Months 2–6 (2026-12-08 to 2027-04-08) when contracts are executed.

Typical Activities: Margit secures written Council and Commission Delegation of Authority for the arbitration panel by Month 2 (2026-12-08), drafting the delegation document with detailed scope (binding technical decisions with 60-day cycles, 14-day compliance windows), authority limits (technical only, not commercial terms), and escalation procedures (14 days to comply, then Commission enforcement). She drafts the Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) among DG MOVE, the EU Agency for Railways and the panel by Month 1 (2026-11-08), specifying governance, staffing and budget. She prepares competition-law guidance: by Month 6 (2027-04-08), she seeks pre-filing consultation with DG COMP (DG Competition) on the data-layer design (federated inventory + central cache + event-streaming disruption data), obtaining either a formal comfort letter or guidance on data-minimisation safeguards to prevent collusion. She manages GDPR compliance: commissions the Data Protection Impact Assessment (Month 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08), conducts early engagement with the EDPB and national DPAs to reach consensus on Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) for cross-border data flows by Month 4 (2027-02-08), and embeds GDPR compliance rules in the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08). She also negotiates non-EU participation agreements (Switzerland's SBB for the Wien–München–Zürich corridor, UK carriers post-Brexit if applicable), ensuring bilateral legal frameworks align with the programme's through-ticket and data-sharing model.

Background Story: Margit Johannsen, 49, from Germany, is a senior legal counsel specialising in EU transport regulation and competition law. She holds a law degree from Humboldt University Berlin and an LL.M. from the College of Europe, and has served as a legal advisor to the European Commission's transport directorate for 18 years, including work on the revised EU passenger-rights regulation and trans-European transport network (TEN-T) directives. Margit has published articles on competition-law safeguards in shared transport infrastructure and has been called to testify before the European Parliament on digital-ticketing regulation. She was recruited for this programme because she understands both the policy intent of the proposed Regulation (expected adoption Month 9 = 2027-07-08) and the detailed legal machinery required to make it operational. Her role is to ensure that the programme's governance, data-sharing and liability frameworks are legally robust and that member-state regulators and competition authorities view the design as compliant rather than risky.

Equipment Needs: Secure email and document-collaboration platform for legal drafts and regulatory correspondence (classified handling). Access to EU legal databases (EUR-Lex, CURIA, EDPB guidance repositories). Subscription to competition-law and payment-services regulatory updates (PSD2, GDPR enforcement actions, antitrust guidance). High-security communications for negotiations with the Commission, national DPAs and payment-services authorities. Contract-management and signature-capture software (DocuSign or equivalent) for binding agreements (Council delegation, MOUs, payment-institution accreditation).

Facility Needs: Law office or Brussels EU institutional campus with secure meeting facilities for confidential negotiations with DG MOVE, DG Competition, EDPB and national DPAs. Proximity to Commission legal services and EU Agency for Railways. Access to videoconference infrastructure for remote engagement with non-EU stakeholders (Switzerland's State Secretariat for Mobility, UK post-Brexit transport authorities). Secure document vault for retaining drafts of Council delegation, MOU and competition-law filings (audit trail required for transparency). Teleconference facilities for cross-timezone engagement with Swiss and UK regulators.

4. Carrier Engagement and Stakeholder Manager / Coalition Builder

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Carrier Engagement Manager negotiates Commitment Letters (Month 3 = 2027-01-08 deadline) and maintains a coalition across 25+ heterogeneous carriers and political stakeholders throughout Months 1–36 (2026-11-08 to 2029-10-08)+. This role requires continuous relationship management, diplomatic skill and authority to represent the programme in high-stakes negotiations. Full-time employment ensures consistent messaging and prevents carrier non-compliance signals from cascading into network fragmentation.

Explanation: Negotiates binding Commitment Letters from carriers above EUR 50 million cross-border revenue by Month 3 (2027-01-08); conducts quarterly roundtables with major carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, Trenitalia, ÖBB, Renfe, NS, SJ, SNCB), manages smaller-carrier representation in working groups, and addresses political pressure from member states. Builds and maintains the coalition, identifying and resolving conflicts early (within 2 weeks of surfacing). Engaged from Month 1 (2026-11-08) through Month 36 (2029-10-08) to secure compliance at Months 18, 30 (2028-04-08, 2029-04-08) and corridor gates.

Consequences: Carriers fail to sign Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08), or sign with weak non-compliance clauses. Major incumbents (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn) signal non-compliance or demand exemptions by Month 12–15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08), fragmenting the coalition and forcing renegotiation. Smaller carriers feel marginalised and push back against co-funding conditions, delaying hub integration and reducing Month 30 (2029-04-08) readiness to 60–70% (vs. target 90%+). Political pressure from member states forces weaker standards by Month 18 (2028-04-08), undermining non-discrimination enforcement.

People Count: 1 senior manager (chief negotiator) + min 1, max 3 regional coordinators (one per major region: western/Benelux, central Europe, southern Europe) for direct engagement with carriers and regulators, from Month 1 (2026-11-08) onward; scale up to 3–4 during critical windows (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08 for Commitment Letters, Month 12–18 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08 during standards finalisation).

Typical Activities: Philippe conducts quarterly roundtables with major carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, Trenitalia, ÖBB, Renfe, NS, SJ, SNCB), using these forums to: (1) understand their IT cost concerns and timeline constraints; (2) air technical disputes early before they harden into political demands; (3) offer co-funding and timeline flexibility in return for binding commitments. He negotiates Commitment Letters (Month 1–3 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) with each carrier above EUR 50M cross-border revenue, specifying compliance timeline, API readiness date (no later than Month 30 = 2029-04-08), and acceptance of arbitration outcomes, with penalties (0.5–1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue held in escrow) for non-compliance. He manages a dedicated SME (small/medium carrier) working group, rotating leadership to ensure smaller carriers' concerns are heard and co-funding allocations are perceived as fair. He also maintains political cover by securing visible member-state support (Belgium, Netherlands, Austria, Spain) and regularly reporting programme progress to the European Parliament's TRAN committee, managing narrative and deflating carrier resistance before it becomes public political friction.

Background Story: Philippe Leclerc, 56, from France, is a senior stakeholder and coalition manager with 20 years' experience in multicarrier rail operations and governance. He previously served as a senior officer at the Community of European Railway and Infrastructure Companies (CER) and has direct relationships with all major European carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, Trenitalia, ÖBB, Renfe, NS, SJ, SNCB) built through quarterly policy roundtables and strategic partnerships. Philippe speaks six languages and is known for his diplomatic skill in negotiating between incumbent carriers' self-interest and the EU's pro-competitive policy goals. He was recruited for this programme because the coalition's success hinges on carriers above EUR 50M cross-border revenue signing binding Commitment Letters (Month 3 = 2027-01-08 deadline) that accept arbitration outcomes and agree to penalties for non-compliance. Without his credibility and networks, major carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn) would likely signal non-compliance or demand exemptions, fragmenting the programme.

Equipment Needs: Secure communication platforms for confidential carrier negotiations (encrypted email, Slack/Teams with enterprise security). Relationship-management system (Salesforce or equivalent) tracking carrier engagement history, commitment status and escalation flags. Travel tools and budgets for quarterly on-site visits to major carriers (SNCF HQ Paris, DB HQ Berlin, ÖBB Vienna, etc.) and to priority-corridor regions for smaller-carrier outreach. Presentation and workshop-facilitation tools for coalition meetings.

Facility Needs: Office in Brussels with access to quarterly meeting venues in Paris, Berlin, Vienna, Amsterdam and Madrid (major carrier hubs and corridor cities). Secure meeting rooms in each carrier's location for confidential Commitment Letter negotiations (Months 1–3 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08). Access to CER offices and member-state transport ministries for political stakeholder engagement. Flexible workspace in multiple corridors to support smaller-carrier regional coordinators (Budapest, Warsaw, Sofia, Bucharest) with regular on-site presence (1–2 weeks per quarter per region). Videoconference-equipped offices for distributed working groups (12–15 carriers, 5 distributors, regulators across 27 member states).

5. Budget Controller and Financial Manager / Contingency Steward

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Budget Controller manages the EUR 1.5 billion cap, designs contingency tiers, and oversees mid-course budget reviews (Months 12, 24 = 2027-10-08, 2028-10-08). This financial stewardship role is continuous and mission-critical: uncontrolled overruns consume contingency within Months 12–24 (2027-10-08 to 2028-10-08) without mitigation. Full-time employment ensures daily burn-rate monitoring, timely escalation and budget discipline that protects conformance testing and capacity-building allocations.

Explanation: Owns the EUR 1.5 billion budget cap and the EUR 215 million free contingency; establishes monthly burn-rate dashboards and triggers contingency tiers when quarterly spend exceeds 115% of pro-rata budget. Commissions the detailed cost model by Month 2 (2026-12-08), defines co-funding allocation (EUR 290 million for smaller carriers and hubs), and approves all major contracts (hub operators, payment institutions, data-layer infrastructure). Manages mid-course budget reviews at Months 12 and 24 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08) and escalates shortfalls to DG MOVE for supplementary authority. Ensures no unplanned overrun consumes the contingency before senior leadership can decide mid-course corrections.

Consequences: Unplanned costs (extended distributor operation, hub resilience, refund exposure) consume the EUR 215 million free contingency within Months 12–24 (2027-10-08 to 2028-10-08) without triggering corrective action. By Month 24 (2028-10-08), a 20–30% budget overrun (EUR 300–450 million) forces cuts to conformance testing or capacity building, delaying smaller-carrier certification by 4–8 weeks per carrier and pushing 20–30% of carriers past the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate. The full-network timeline slips to Month 36–42 (2029-10-08 to 2030-04-08), and environmental/infrastructure benefits are deferred.

People Count: 1 senior financial controller + min 1, max 2 budget analysts for contract execution and expense tracking, from Month 1 (2026-11-08) onward; full team operational by Month 3 (2027-01-08) for the cost model and first budget dashboard.

Typical Activities: Roberto commissions a detailed activity-based cost model by Month 2 (2026-12-08) specifying: (1) carrier co-funding need per operator (EUR 2–8M per SME, EUR 10–15M per medium operator); (2) hub operating costs per region (EUR 5–8M per hub over 5 years); (3) public distributor annual operating cost (EUR 43M/year on average); (4) payment-institution transaction fees (EUR 80–120M over 5 years); (5) data-layer infrastructure (EUR 60M). He establishes monthly budget-burn dashboards by Month 3 (2027-01-08) showing cumulative spend vs. pro-rata forecast for each cost line, with automatic escalation triggers if quarterly spend exceeds 115% of budget. When a trigger fires, he escalates to the Programme Director and Steering Committee within 5 working days with options: Tier 1 contingency (10–15% overrun: defer app polish, reduce distributor co-marketing by 20%), Tier 2 (15–25% overrun: reduce carrier co-funding from 20% to 10%, limit hubs to priority corridors), Tier 3 (>25% overrun: suspend new hub openings, scale capacity building to 3–4 priority member states). He conducts mid-course budget reviews at Months 12 and 24 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08), reforecasting spend and requesting supplementary budget authority from DG MOVE if a Tier 2+ contingency is triggered.

Background Story: Roberto Moretti, 47, from Italy, is a senior financial controller and budget manager with 19 years' experience in EU programme finance. He holds a degree in accounting and an MBA in programme management and has managed budgets for three previous large-scale EU infrastructure programmes (each EUR 500M+). Roberto is known for his rigorous cost tracking, early-warning systems for overruns and his ability to design contingency-tier frameworks that preserve decision authority at senior levels rather than forcing automatic cuts. He was recruited for this programme because the EUR 1.5 billion public budget is fixed and the critical path depends on conformance testing and capacity building being protected from cuts: if carrier co-funding demand (EUR 290M) exceeds budget, or if the public reference distributor's operating costs are underestimated, unplanned overruns must be caught within weeks, not months, to trigger timely mid-course corrections.

Equipment Needs: Enterprise financial-management and budget-tracking software (SAP, Oracle or equivalent) with real-time spend dashboards, variance analysis and contingency-tier automations. Cost-modelling tools (Excel, Anaplan or purpose-built platform) for activity-based cost forecasting (standard scenario + stress tests for carrier co-funding overrun, hub delays, extended distributor operations). Contract-execution and approval workflows (document-management and e-signature). Monthly expense-tracking and reconciliation tools integrating across all programme cost lines (standards, conformance, clearing, distributor, capacity building, hubs, consumer app).

Facility Needs: Finance office in Brussels, integrated with DG MOVE budget-management systems (access to the EU budget execution portal for EUR 1.5 billion cap monitoring). Secure meeting space for monthly budget-review meetings with the Programme Director and Steering Committee. Access to contract-approval authority and DG MOVE's financial-processing systems (invoicing, payment authorisation, contingency-reserve release). High-speed connectivity to carrier cost-reporting systems (if carriers provide live IT spend forecasts). Data-storage facilities for archiving cost models, budget decisions and audit trails (7-year retention minimum for EU audit compliance).

6. Smaller Carriers and Regional Integration Lead / Digital Inclusion Specialist

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Smaller Carriers and Regional Integration Lead manages hub procurement (Month 3 = 2027-01-08 deadline), operations and 12–18 smaller-operator onboarding throughout Months 6–30 (2027-04-08 to 2029-04-08). This frontline delivery role requires continuous hands-on engagement with legacy-IT operators, hub operators and regional coordinators. Full-time employment ensures technical mentoring is sustained and hub data-quality gates (booking-failure rate <0.5%) are enforced consistently.

Explanation: Manages hub procurement, operation and smaller-carrier onboarding (12–18 legacy-IT operators). Establishes hub eligibility criteria by Month 1 (2026-11-08), contracts hub operators by Month 3 (2027-01-08), and ensures hubs are operational by Month 9 (2027-07-08). Leads 5-FTE regional coordinator team (based in Budapest, Warsaw, Sofia, Bucharest) providing hands-on mentoring for smaller carriers during Months 6–30 (2027-04-08 to 2029-04-08). Monitors hub data quality (booking-failure rate <0.5%) and suspends onboarding if a hub's failure rate exceeds 2% for a week. Ensures smaller carriers meet Month 30 (2029-04-08) through technical support and co-funding (EUR 290 million allocation).

Consequences: Hub procurement slips to Month 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08), compressing integration to 9 months for 12–18 carriers and reducing Month 30 (2029-04-08) readiness to 60–70%. Regional coordinators are absent; smaller carriers receive no hands-on support, increasing integration failure rate and booking-failure rates from 0.5% to 2–5%, forcing 4–8 week hub rework and cascading delays. 20–30% of smaller carriers miss the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate, fragmenting the network across corridors and undermining through-ticket reliability for passengers. TEN-T extension (Month 36 = 2029-10-08) is delayed 6–12 months.

People Count: 1 senior manager (hub and regional coordination lead) from Month 1 (2026-11-08) onward; plus 5 regional coordinators (1 per hub region) from Month 6 (2027-04-08), scaling to 8 if additional TEN-T hubs launch at Month 36 (2029-10-08). Peak staffing Month 12–30 (2027-10-08 to 2029-04-08) during migration wave.

Typical Activities: Katarina defines hub eligibility criteria (Month 1 = 2026-11-08): cross-border revenue under EUR 50M, booking system older than 10 years, or IT staff under 10 FTE. She issues the RFP for hub operators (Month 0.5 = 2026-10-23) and leads hub procurement (Months 0–3 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-01-08), awarding contracts to 4–6 hub operators covering the four priority corridors and 2–3 additional hubs for TEN-T extension. She conducts joint technical integration workshops (Month 4 = 2027-02-08) pairing hub operators and eligible carriers, identifying integration blockers (network latency, API compatibility, data-format mismatch). She hires and manages 5 regional coordinators (based in Budapest, Warsaw, Sofia, Bucharest) who provide on-site mentoring to smaller carriers during the integration wave (Months 6–30 = 2027-04-08 to 2029-04-08), troubleshooting mapping errors, assisting with data quality, and escalating technical blockers. She monitors hub data quality (booking-failure rate target <0.5%, threshold 2% per week for onboarding suspension) and ensures smaller carriers receive co-funding grants (EUR 234M total) on a milestone basis: funding tranches released upon completion of testing, API readiness, and data-quality compliance gates.

Background Story: Dr. Katarina Novak, 44, from Hungary, is a senior programme manager and regional development specialist with 16 years' experience supporting smaller carriers and regional transport operators in central and southern Europe. She holds a PhD in transport systems from the Budapest University of Technology and has led the EU Agency for Railways' capacity-building initiatives for weaker member-state regulators (2015–2023). Katarina is fluent in Hungarian, Polish, Bulgarian, Romanian and Czech, and has deep networks among smaller, legacy-IT operators in central and southeast Europe. She was recruited for this programme because the 12–18 hub-eligible carriers are concentrated in weaker-capacity member states, and their success in meeting the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate depends on hands-on technical mentoring, co-funding coordination and hub troubleshooting that cannot be done from Brussels.

Equipment Needs: Regional coordination and integration tools (Slack, Teams or equivalent) for 5 distributed coordinators in Budapest, Warsaw, Sofia and Bucharest. Hub-operation monitoring software (uptime, latency, booking-failure rates) with real-time dashboards and escalation alerting. Carrier IT-system assessment tools and integration checklists (shared spreadsheets, configuration-management databases). Travel and site-visit logistics tools for regional coordinators to schedule on-site mentoring and troubleshooting (1–2 weeks per quarter per carrier group). Accessibility assessment and compliance-checking tools (WCAG 2.1 validation, station/rolling-stock accessibility databases).

Facility Needs: Regional offices in Budapest, Warsaw, Sofia and Bucharest (one per region, supporting 2–4 hubs and 3–6 smaller carriers per region). Each office requires secure meeting space for carrier integration workshops and technical troubleshooting sessions. On-site presence at regional hub operators' facilities (1–2 weeks per quarter) for hands-on integration support and data-quality audits. Access to carrier legacy IT systems (remote or on-site) for testing hub data mappings and booking-failure diagnosis (expect network latency challenges in southeast Europe). Videoconference facilities for escalation to central Brussels programme team and to hub operators' IT teams. Travel budgets for quarterly regional visits and unplanned incident response (if hub outages or booking failures require urgent on-site deployment).

7. Data Layer and Real-Time Systems Architect / Infrastructure Operations Lead

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Data Layer and Real-Time Systems Architect designs and procures critical infrastructure (API hosting, cache, operations centre) by Month 6 (2027-04-08) and operates it through Month 60 (2031-10-08). This technical core role spans architecture (Months 1–6 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-04-08), procurement (Months 3–6 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-04-08), testing (Months 9–18 = 2027-07-08 to 2028-04-08) and production management (Months 18–60 = 2028-04-08 to 2031-10-08+). Full-time employment ensures performance SLAs are met and incident response is available 24/7 without latency.

Explanation: Designs and procures the shared real-time data layer (federated inventory + central availability cache + event-streamed disruption data), OSDM-compatible APIs and the 24/7 operations centre. Defines data-quality SLAs (inventory freshness <5 min, disruption latency <2 min, API p95 latency <2s, uptime 99.95%, throughput ≥500 req/s per corridor). Procures European API hosting and data-centre redundancy across ≥3 regions by Month 6 (2027-04-08), conducts monthly load testing from Month 9 (2027-07-08), and manages 24/7 incident response with escalation to carriers within 15 minutes. Establishes the neutral operator role for the data layer and manages performance monitoring through Month 60 (2031-10-08).

Consequences: Data-layer architecture decisions are deferred or contested; API latency exceeds 5 seconds during peak hours (Month 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), causing 10–20% of searches to timeout. Overbooking (inventory stale by 20–30 minutes) causes 5–10% booking-failure rate, generating refund disputes (estimated EUR 5–15 million unplanned exposure). Hub or cache failure has no incident-response protocol; recovery takes 12–48 hours, stranding 10,000–50,000 daily searches and cascading refund obligations. Distributors lose confidence and scale back marketing; through-ticket volumes drop 10–20 percentage points below target. Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate is questioned for feasibility.

People Count: 1 senior architect (data-layer and infrastructure) from Month 1 (2026-11-08) onward; plus min 2, max 5 systems engineers (API, caching, resilience, monitoring) from Month 3 (2027-01-08), scaling to 4–5 during Months 6–18 (2027-04-08 to 2028-04-08) for procurement and load testing, then 2–3 permanent ops staff from Month 18 (2028-04-08) for production management.

Typical Activities: Mikael designs the shared data-layer architecture (Months 1–4 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-02-08): federated authoritative inventory held by each carrier, with a programme-procured availability cache for the four priority corridors (launched Month 18 = 2028-04-08), plus event-streaming for disruption data (Month 21–24 = 2028-07-08 to 2028-10-08). He procures European API hosting and data-centre infrastructure by Month 6 (2027-04-08), specifying guaranteed SLAs (latency, uptime, throughput ≥500 req/s per corridor), redundancy across ≥3 data-centre regions, and automatic failover (<30 seconds). He conducts carrier infrastructure assessment (Months 3–4 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-02-08) to identify legacy systems that cannot meet API performance targets, then co-funds infrastructure upgrades (EUR 500K–2M per carrier) for those unable to meet SLAs natively. He establishes a 24/7 API operations centre by Month 6 (2027-04-08), staffed by 2–3 permanent ops engineers with escalation to carriers within 15 minutes of any incident. He conducts monthly load testing and quarterly chaos-engineering exercises (starting Month 9 = 2027-07-08) to identify weak points before they affect production. He also manages the neutral operator role for the data layer: defining governance, access logs, and data-minimisation safeguards to satisfy competition authorities that the shared layer does not enable collusion.

Background Story: Dr. Mikael Bergström, 52, from Sweden, is a senior systems architect and infrastructure operations specialist with 24 years' experience designing and operating large-scale distributed systems. He holds a PhD in computer systems from the Royal Institute of Technology (KTH) Stockholm and has led infrastructure and data-centre operations for Spotify (2012–2018) and the Nordic e-health authority (2018–2023). Mikael brings expertise in high-availability systems design, API performance optimisation and 24/7 operations centres. He was recruited for this programme because the shared real-time data layer (federated inventory + central availability cache + event-streamed disruption data) is mission-critical: any API latency >5 seconds or outage >2 hours cascades into booking failures and passenger disruptions that undermine distributor confidence and through-ticket adoption. His role is to ensure the data layer meets aggressive SLAs (p95 latency <2s, uptime 99.95%, disruption-event latency <2 min) despite carriers' heterogeneous legacy systems.

Equipment Needs: High-performance servers and workstations for API design, data-modelling and load-testing. Distributed API hosting and data-centre infrastructure: procurement contracts with at least 2 cloud providers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud or equivalent) across ≥3 EU data-centre regions (EU-West, EU-Central, EU-East) with guaranteed SLAs (99.95% uptime, <2-second p95 latency, ≥500 req/s throughput per corridor). Data-caching software (Redis, Memcached or equivalent) and distributed database systems (PostgreSQL with replication, or managed database services). Monitoring and observability tools (Prometheus, ELK stack, DataDog or equivalent) for 24/7 API and cache performance tracking. Load-testing tools (JMeter, Gatling, Locust) for monthly capacity validation and chaos-engineering exercises.

Facility Needs: Technical hub in Brussels or Frankfurt (proximity to major EU data centres and carrier IT operations) with 24/7 operations-centre workspace for API and data-layer monitoring. Secure facilities for hosting the neutral operator role (data-governance oversight, access logging, breach-response protocols). On-site access to carrier data centres (SNCF Paris, DB Frankfurt, ÖBB Vienna, SBB Bern, etc.) for integration testing of federated inventory queries and event-streaming disruption data (expect 4–6 week integration per carrier, Months 12–24 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-10-08). Telecom backbone and low-latency connectivity across all four priority corridors and TEN-T extension regions. Co-location facilities or vendor partnerships with multiple cloud providers to ensure redundancy and failover capability. Meeting space for architecture review boards and quarterly performance-optimization sessions with carrier CIOs and distributor technology leads.

8. Clearing and Settlement Mechanism Designer / Payment Systems Specialist

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Clearing and Settlement Mechanism Designer manages payment-institution accreditation (Months 0–8 = 2026-10-08 to 2027-06-08 decision deadline), defines settlement architecture and oversees ongoing compliance through Month 60 (2031-10-08). This foundational role requires continuous engagement with financial regulators, payment providers and carriers. Full-time employment ensures accreditation deadlines are met and settlement SLAs (cycle <48 hours, refund <10 days) are enforced continuously.

Explanation: Designs the clearing and settlement architecture using accredited payment institutions (2–3 providers) rather than a central payment entity, minimising legal setup delays. Manages payment-institution accreditation (market sounding Month 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08, call Month 2 = 2026-12-08, decision Month 8 = 2027-06-08). Defines common settlement message standards, apportionment rules for multi-carrier revenue split, refund reversal protocols, and dispute resolution procedures. Establishes SLAs for settlement cycle time (<48 hours) and refund turnaround (<10 days). Monitors FX exposure (EUR 10–20 million annually) and manages fee caps (0.3–0.5% per transaction). Serves as liaison with financial regulators (ECB, national competent authorities) on payment-services compliance.

Consequences: Accreditation is delayed or attracts <2 qualified providers, leaving no competitive choice. If the sole provider fails, switching costs EUR 5–10 million and forces temporary fallback to bilateral settlement (slow, unreliable, undermining through-ticket confidence). Fee negotiations fail; transaction fees average 1.0% instead of 0.5%, consuming 10–16% of the public budget (EUR 160–240 million over 5 years) and forcing cuts to conformance testing or distributor operations. Refund reversal disputes accumulate; 15–25% of claims are unresolved within SLA, damaging distributor and passenger confidence. Settlement cycle extends beyond 48 hours, straining carrier cash flow and deterring participation by smaller operators.

People Count: 1 senior specialist (clearing and settlement architecture) from Month 0 (2026-10-08) onward; plus 1–2 payment-systems engineers (settlement algorithms, message formats, dispute automation) from Month 2 (2026-12-08), scaling to 2 during accreditation (Months 2–8 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-06-08) and operations setup (Months 8–12 = 2027-06-08 to 2027-10-08).

Typical Activities: Jean-Claude manages payment-institution accreditation: market sounding (Months 0–1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08), RFP issuance (Month 2 = 2026-12-08), evaluation (Months 3–7 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-05-08), and decision (Month 8 = 2027-06-08). He defines the accreditation criteria (PSD2 licensing, multi-currency support, settlement cycle <48 hours, refund processing <10 days, SLAs 99.95% uptime, error handling with 5-day dispute resolution, and financial stability checks). He designs common settlement message standards by Month 6 (2027-04-08): the apportionment logic (which carrier receives what share of the passenger fare based on segment distance, time or agreed allocation keys), the refund reversal protocol (how a distributor refunds a passenger and recovers the cost from the responsible carrier), and the dispute resolution procedure (how carriers contest refund decisions, with DG-mediated arbitration). He monitors FX exposure for non-EUR corridors (target: cap at 5–10% of quarterly disbursements using EUR-denominated forwards) and negotiates fee caps (target 0.3–0.5% per transaction, subsidised 50–70% by the programme for Months 0–24 = 2026-10-08 to 2028-10-08). He also manages accredited-provider continuity: requiring at least 2 providers operational (Month 12 = 2027-10-08), with contractual redundancy provisions (if one provider fails, carriers failover automatically, EUR 1–2M switching reserve).

Background Story: Jean-Claude Pépin, 53, from France, is a senior payment systems architect and clearing specialist with 21 years' experience in financial settlement and multi-party transaction processing. He previously worked for Euroclear (2001–2010), managing cross-border securities settlement, and for a consortium clearing house serving European freight railways (2010–2023). Jean-Claude holds a degree in mathematics and an MBA in financial systems, and is fluent in payment-industry regulation (PSD2, SEPA, correspondent banking). He was recruited for this programme because the clearing and settlement mechanism is a financial bottleneck: using accredited payment institutions (rather than building a central clearing entity) avoids licensing delays but requires careful design of apportionment rules, refund reversal protocols, and dispute resolution. His role is to design a system that splits passenger revenue fairly across carriers, handles refunds within <10 days, and avoids the settlement delays that would undermine carrier trust.

Equipment Needs: Payment-services regulatory-compliance software (PSD2 license-tracking, SLA monitoring, settlement reconciliation). Settlement-algorithm design and testing tools (Python, Java or equivalent) for apportionment logic and refund-reversal protocols. Multi-currency handling and FX-exposure management tools (Bloomberg Terminal or equivalent for currency rates and hedging). Secure communication platforms for engagement with payment institutions, the ECB and national competent authorities (encrypted email, high-security videoconference). Contract-management systems for payment-institution accreditation agreements and SLA enforcement. Dispute-resolution case-management software (Salesforce, Jira or equivalent) for tracking settlement claims and refund disputes with 5-day resolution SLAs.

Facility Needs: Office in Brussels, integrated with DG MOVE and EU Agency for Railways. Access to ECB offices and payment-services regulatory bodies (national competent authorities in major EU member states: Germany, France, Netherlands, Austria, Spain, Italy). Meeting space for quarterly payment-provider steering committee (2–3 accredited providers + settlement-dispute panel representatives). Secure videoconference facilities for confidential negotiations with payment-institution CIOs and compliance teams. High-speed connectivity to participating banks' settlement systems (for real-time testing of transaction routing and refund reversal protocols, Months 8–12 = 2027-06-08 to 2027-10-08). Data-secure facilities for storing accreditation contracts, performance audits and dispute archives (7-year retention for EU audit and PSD2 compliance).

9. Consumer Product and App Development Lead / Digital User Experience Director

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Consumer Product and App Development Lead directs a 20–30 FTE team delivering the public distributor app on a tight timeline (MVP Month 9 = 2027-07-08, launch Month 15 = 2028-01-08, four-corridor go-live Month 27 = 2029-01-08). This product ownership role requires continuous executive oversight of design, development and launch, with escalation authority to pause rollout if user satisfaction falls below 4.0/5 stars. Full-time employment ensures product leadership and release discipline.

Explanation: Owns design, development and launch of the public reference distributor app and multilingual booking interface. Leads a 20–30 FTE consumer product team (product managers, UX designers, engineers, localization specialists, customer support). Conducts user research (Months 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08), builds MVP for one-corridor pilot by Month 9 (2027-07-08), iterates on feedback (Months 10–12 = 2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08), and launches public app by Month 15 (2028-01-08) with phased rollout to four corridors by Month 27 (2029-01-08). Establishes customer-support operations (<1 hour response time for critical issues) and manages app ratings (target ≥4.0/5 stars at Month 18 = 2028-04-08). Pauses rollout and redesigns if satisfaction falls below 4.0/5.

Consequences: App launch slips from Month 15 (2028-01-08) to Month 21–24 (2028-07-08 to 2028-10-08), missing early-corridor momentum. Initial user satisfaction is poor (3.5/5 stars) due to confusing search flows, missing accessibility features, or slow performance; media coverage is negative, damaging programme credibility. Support queue times exceed 4 hours; complaints backlog reaches 2,000+ within 3 months, taking 4–8 weeks to resolve. Distributor confidence erodes; commercial platforms reduce co-marketing investment by 20–30%. Through-ticket volumes drop 10–20 percentage points below target. Public reference distributor must expand operating costs by 20–30% (EUR 60–90 million) to compensate, consuming free contingency and crowding out capacity building or smaller-carrier co-funding.

People Count: 1 senior product director from Month 1 (2026-11-08); plus 20–30 FTE team (scaling gradually from Month 2 = 2026-12-08, peak during Months 12–27 = 2027-10-08 to 2029-01-08 for development and launch, then 10–15 FTE for ongoing operations and support from Month 27 = 2029-01-08 onward).

Typical Activities: Sarah leads the 20–30 FTE consumer product team (scaling from Month 1 = 2026-11-08 onward). She conducts user research and personas (Months 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08), then wireframes and prototypes (Months 4–6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08). She builds an MVP for one-corridor pilot by Month 9 (2027-07-08), then iterates on feedback (Months 10–12 = 2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08). She manages full-scale localization and platform scaling (Months 12–15 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08), targeting public app launch by Month 15 (2028-01-08) with phased rollout to four corridors by Month 27 (2029-01-08). She establishes customer-support operations: staffing targets of <1-hour response time for critical issues, tiered escalation (level-1 FAQs, level-2 human support in 24+ languages, level-3 dispute resolution), and a SLA of <2,000 unresolved complaints in the backlog. She monitors app ratings quarterly (target >4.0/5 stars at Month 18 = 2028-04-08 onwards), and if satisfaction falls below 4.0, she pauses rollout and conducts a 4–6 week redesign cycle before resuming. She also manages accessibility integration (WCAG 2.1 AA compliance, real-time assistance-request tracking, multi-language support) as a core feature, not an afterthought, embedding accessibility in the MVP and user research from Months 2–4 (2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08).

Background Story: Sarah Chen, 41, from the United Kingdom, is a senior product director and digital consumer specialist with 18 years' experience building consumer-facing applications and mobile platforms. She previously led product at Booking.com (2012–2018) and founded and scaled a mobility-app startup (2018–2022) before joining the EU public sector. Sarah holds a degree in computer science and an MBA from INSEAD, and is known for her user-centred design approach, rapid iteration methodology and ability to scale products from MVP to millions of users. She was recruited for this programme because the public reference distributor's consumer app is mission-critical for adoption: if the app is poorly designed (confusing refund flows, missing accessibility), launches 3–6 months late, or has low user satisfaction (<4.0/5 stars), through-ticket volumes drop 10–20 percentage points, and the 40% target becomes unachievable.

Equipment Needs: Software-development workstations (IDE, version control, continuous integration/deployment tools) for 20–30 FTE product team (front-end engineers, back-end engineers, UX designers, QA). Cloud-based app-hosting infrastructure (AWS, Azure or equivalent) with auto-scaling for user-load testing and production deployment. Mobile device testing labs (iOS, Android) for app validation across screen sizes and OS versions. User-testing and analytics tools (Figma for design, Mixpanel or Amplitude for usage analytics, UserTesting or equivalent for qualitative feedback). Localization and multilingual-support tools (translation management system, language-specific testing for 24+ languages). Customer-support platform (Zendesk, Intercom or equivalent) with ticketing, queue management and escalation workflows. A/B testing and feature-flag management tools (LaunchDarkly or equivalent) for phased rollout and rapid iteration.

Facility Needs: Consumer-product development office in Brussels or a EU tech hub (Amsterdam, Berlin). User-research and testing lab with observation and recording facilities for usability sessions (Months 2–4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08 for persona development, Months 10–12 = 2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08 for MVP iteration). Call-centre infrastructure or partnership with a multilingual customer-support vendor for <1-hour response-time SLAs across 24+ languages (Months 15+ = 2028-01-08 onwards). Meeting and demo space for quarterly distributor feedback sessions and stakeholder previews. High-speed internet and collaborative workspaces (open office, quiet focus areas, video-conferencing) supporting distributed team across Months 1–27 (2026-11-08 to 2029-01-08, with sustained operations team post-launch). Accessibility-testing facilities and tools (screen readers, voice-control software, physical accessibility simulators) to validate WCAG 2.1 AA compliance throughout development.

10. Measurement, Evaluation and Evidence Lead / Impact Analytics Director

Contract Type: full_time_employee

Contract Type Justification: Measurement, Evaluation and Evidence Lead establishes the measurement framework and baseline by Month 9 (2027-07-08), then oversees mandatory monthly reporting and quarterly dashboards from Month 18–60 (2028-04-08 to 2031-10-08). This evidence role is continuous and gatekeeping: mid-course corrections at Months 12, 24, 36 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08, 2029-10-08) depend on reliable measurement. Full-time employment ensures data quality and timely escalation of underperformance.

Explanation: Establishes the measurement framework, baseline survey and evaluation methodology for the three headline targets (40% through-ticket share, halved distributor complaints, modal shift from air). Commissions an independent evaluator by Month 3 (2027-01-08) to build a counterfactual model using comparison routes (non-rollout corridors) to separate programme effects from fuel-price and aviation-policy changes. Defines 'through-ticket' operationally by Month 2 (2026-12-08), conducts baseline survey (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08), validates baseline by Month 9 (2027-07-08), and establishes mandatory monthly carrier/distributor reporting from Month 18 (2028-04-08). Publishes quarterly progress dashboards and uses measurement to trigger mid-course corrections (e.g., if through-ticket share is 25% at Month 24 = 2028-10-08 vs. 40% target, escalate to Steering Committee).

Consequences: Baseline is not established until Month 9–12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08), delaying mid-course insights until Year 2. Without a clear baseline, stakeholder disputes over whether targets are being met undermine programme credibility by Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08). If carriers refuse to report volumes, true through-ticket share is undercounted by 15–25%, making it impossible to verify whether 40% target is met. Modal-shift attribution is weak; the case for the infrastructure investment's environmental benefit is contested and politically vulnerable. By Month 48 (2030-10-08), inability to demonstrate progress or support corrective decisions invites Commission review and possible scaling-back or defunding.

People Count: 1 senior evaluation director from Month 2 (2026-12-08); plus 1–2 data analysts (baseline survey, reporting automation, dashboard design) from Month 3 (2027-01-08), scaling to 1–2 for an independent external evaluator contract from Month 3 (2027-01-08) through Month 60 (2031-10-08) (budget EUR 5–10 million for comprehensive evaluation).

Typical Activities: Marcus establishes the measurement framework: baseline survey (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) asking carriers, distributors and airports for current cross-border sales volumes, complaint rates and modal-split estimates (with confidentiality protections). He defines 'through-ticket' operationally by Month 2 (2026-12-08): 'single booking reference + single payment + continuity-of-journey rights.' He hires an independent external evaluator (contract Month 3 = 2027-01-08, EUR 5–10M over 5 years) to build a counterfactual model: comparing through-ticket adoption on priority corridors to control routes (non-rollout corridors), separating programme effects from fuel prices, aviation taxes and capacity changes. He validates the baseline by Month 9 (2027-07-08) and establishes mandatory monthly reporting from all participating carriers and distributors, starting Month 18 (2028-04-08), with data aggregated and published quarterly with a 1-month lag (to protect commercial sensitivity). He publishes quarterly progress dashboards tracking the three targets: 40% through-ticket share, complaint baseline vs. Month 9 (2027-07-08) divided by 2 (by Month 60 = 2031-10-08), and modal-shift estimate (5–15% planning range). He uses measurement to trigger mid-course corrections: if through-ticket share is 25% at Month 24 (2028-10-08) vs. 40% target, he escalates to the Steering Committee with analysis of which corridors are lagging and what interventions (pricing support, distributor incentives, campaign intensity) might accelerate adoption. He also manages mid-programme evaluation (Month 30–36 = 2029-04-08 to 2029-10-08) assessing interim success and informing the decision on TEN-T extension scope and post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability.

Background Story: Prof. Marcus Andersen, 58, from Denmark, is a senior evaluation researcher and impact-assessment specialist with 22 years' experience in transport and infrastructure programme evaluation. He holds a PhD in econometrics from Copenhagen Business School and has led independent evaluations of the TEN-T programme (2010–2015), the EU mobility scheme (2015–2020), and several member-state transport initiatives. Marcus is known for his rigorous counterfactual methodology, stakeholder engagement in measurement design and transparent communication of results and limitations. He was recruited for this programme because the three headline targets (40% through-ticket share, halved complaints, modal shift from air) cannot be verified without a pre-planned measurement framework and baseline: without rigorous evaluation, by Month 60 (2031-10-08), claims about success are contested, the environmental case for the infrastructure investment is questioned, and the political support for scaling to the full TEN-T network erodes.

Equipment Needs: Data-analytics and statistical software (R, Python, SAS or equivalent) for counterfactual modelling and causal-inference analysis. Baseline-survey platform and tools (Qualtrics, SurveyMonkey or equivalent) for administering the baseline questionnaire to carriers, distributors and airports (Months 0–2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08). Data-visualization tools (Tableau, Power BI or equivalent) for quarterly progress dashboards and stakeholder reporting. Database infrastructure for mandatory monthly reporting from carriers and distributors (starting Month 18 = 2028-04-08) with data aggregation, confidentiality protection and lag-time automation (publish with 1-month delay to protect commercial sensitivity). Evaluation-methodology tools and templates for collaborative work with an independent external evaluator (shared document repositories, secure data-exchange protocols).

Facility Needs: Dedicated analytics office in Brussels with secure data-storage facilities (classified data handling for carrier and distributor proprietary information, 7-year retention). Meeting space for quarterly evaluation-steering-group sessions (evaluation director, external evaluator, Programme Director, Steering Committee representatives). Co-location or videoconference access to independent external evaluator's facilities (external firm or research institute, Months 3–60 = 2027-01-08 to 2031-10-08). High-speed internet and encrypted data-exchange protocols for confidential carrier and distributor reporting (monthly data feeds starting Month 18 = 2028-04-08). Database servers or secure cloud storage (encrypted, with audit trails) for managing the measurement baseline, counterfactual comparison-route data, and monthly through-ticket-volume and complaint reports. Access to EUROSTAT and aviation-data repositories for modal-shift modelling and comparison against fuel-price and aviation-policy scenarios.

Omissions

1. Crisis Communication and Reputational Risk Management Plan

The programme involves 27 member states, 25+ carriers, disability-rights organizations and millions of passengers. High-visibility milestones (Months 18, 30, 60 = 2028-04-08, 2029-04-08, 2031-10-08) attract media scrutiny and political attention. No dedicated crisis-communication protocol exists for handling booking failures, passenger incidents, accessibility delivery failures, or non-compliance by major carriers. Absent clear communication governance, negative incidents (e.g., a through-ticket passenger injured in a missed-connection incident, or an API outage affecting 50,000+ bookings) risk cascading reputational damage, eroded stakeholder confidence and political withdrawal of support before corrective action is possible.

Recommendation: Establish a Crisis Communication and Reputational Risk Management Team (1-2 FTE from Month 1 = 2026-11-08) integrated with the Programme Director's office. Define a communication protocol specifying: (1) incident triage (booking failure, passenger safety, API outage, carrier non-compliance) within 30 minutes of detection; (2) internal escalation to Programme Director and Steering Committee within 2 hours; (3) public communication within 4 hours for critical incidents (passenger safety, major outages), within 24 hours for operational issues (booking failures, complaint backlogs); (4) quarterly communication strategy reviews and annual narrative refresh with the European Parliament TRAN committee. Pre-draft response templates for each incident class in Month 2 (2026-12-08) and activate them within the 4-hour window post-incident.

2. Sustainability Transition and Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) Operating Model Ambiguity

The programme's public-coordination budget ends at Month 60 (2031-10-08), but the operational dependencies (shared data layer, clearing mechanism, public reference distributor, regulator capacity-building, hub operations) do not end. No formal decision exists on how these systems transition to sustainable funding or operational governance post-Month 60 (2031-10-08). The post-programme run-cost is estimated at ~EUR 45M/year (distributor ~EUR 43M + hub gap ~EUR 1.9M), plus data-layer and regulator costs not quantified. Member states may be unwilling to fund regulator capacity building; payment institutions may exit if volumes are insufficient; the public distributor may be unable to operate commercially. If no transition plan is agreed and executed by Month 48 (2030-10-08), the programme risks operational collapse at Month 60 (2031-10-08), undermining all prior investment.

Recommendation: Establish a Sustainability Transition Working Group by Month 30 (2029-04-08) to design post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) operating models for each core component: (1) Data layer: identify permanent operational host (e.g., EU Agency for Railways or a multi-carrier consortium) and transition governance/financing by Month 48 (2030-10-08); (2) Clearing mechanism: shift to operational cost-recovery (transaction-fee revenue covers ops costs) or secure permanent public-funding commitment; (3) Public reference distributor: define post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) model (shutdown with orderly wind-down, hand-off to commercial operator, or downsizing to niche service); (4) Regulator capacity: secure member-state written commitment to maintain funding via national budgets or EU framework. Obtain written commitment from the Commission, Council and member states by Month 48 (2030-10-08) confirming post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding arrangements. If no commitment is secured, activate contingency: consolidate regulator roles at EU Agency for Railways level with cost recovery via carrier license-fee revenue. Budget EUR 5-10M within the EUR 225M contingency for sustainability-transition planning and interim funding gaps (Months 54-72 = 2031-04-08 to 2032-10-08).

3. Unvalidated Demand for Regional Hub Capacity and Hub Economics

The programme allocates EUR 44M for regional hub operations (4 hubs at launch, 2 reserved for TEN-T extension). However, hub capacity demand is not modelled from carrier requirements: estimated 12-18 eligible carriers (proposed threshold) require hub integration by Month 30 (2029-04-08), but the actual volume of bookings per hub, the peak-hour throughput and the per-hub operating cost scaling are not quantified. Hub economics are fragile: estimated opex ~EUR 1.2M/year per hub vs fee revenue ~EUR 0.73M/year at capacity, leaving a gap of ~EUR 0.47M/year per hub (~EUR 1.9M/year for 4 hubs). If eligible carriers exceed 12-18 or if booking volumes are lower than forecast, hub utilization drops, and the economics gap widens, forcing either higher carrier fees (undermining adoption) or extended public subsidy beyond Month 48 (2030-10-08) (exhausting contingency).

Recommendation: Commission a detailed hub-capacity and economics analysis by Month 2 (2026-12-08) modelling: (1) carrier demand by hub region (number of eligible carriers, estimated annual cross-border bookings per carrier, peak-hour throughput per hub); (2) hub operating cost sensitivity (staffing, infrastructure, vendor fees) by volume; (3) fee-revenue sensitivity to throughput and carrier-willingness-to-pay; (4) breakeven volume per hub (at what booking volumes does fee revenue cover opex?). Define hub capacity gates per corridor: if bookings fall 20% below forecast at Month 24 (2028-10-08), trigger cost-reduction review (shared staffing, vendor consolidation) or carrier-fee increase (negotiate with carriers at Month 27 = 2029-01-08). Set hub cost-recovery transition date at Month 42 (2030-04-08) (6 months earlier than Month 48 = 2030-10-08 plan) to begin fee-revenue ramp and reduce public subsidy by Month 60 (2031-10-08). If hub economics do not improve by Month 42 (2030-04-08), escalate to Steering Committee for decision: (a) consolidate hubs (reduce from 6 to 4), (b) allow selective carrier subsidy to subsidise hub use, or (c) extend public funding.

4. Vendor Lock-In Risk in API Hosting, Data-Centre and Clearing Infrastructure

The programme procures cloud-based API hosting and data-centre infrastructure (Months 3-6 = 2027-01-08 to 2027-04-08) and commits 2-3 accredited payment institutions for settlement. These procurement decisions create long-term vendor dependencies: if a cloud provider raises prices, degrades performance or exits the market, or if an accredited payment institution fails or withdraws, the programme faces switching costs (estimated EUR 5-10M per incident), operational disruption (2-4 weeks), and potential re-architecture (6-12 months). No multi-vendor strategy or exit clause is defined for critical infrastructure.

Recommendation: Embed vendor-independence and exit-clause provisions in all major infrastructure procurements (Month 2-3 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-01-08): (1) API hosting: require contract portability (data export within 30 days, API specification migration toolkit) and price-cap guarantees (no annual increases >5%); procure from at least 2 competing cloud providers with load-balancing across both, ensuring neither is a single point of failure. (2) Accredited payment institutions: require contractual redundancy (if one provider fails, automatic failover to a backup partner; programme covers switching cost up to EUR 1-2M per incident); maintain at least 2 active providers at all times. (3) Data-centre and CDN infrastructure: use geographic diversity (at least 3 EU regions) with automatic regional failover. (4) OSDM and hub software: require open-source or escrow arrangements (source-code access if vendor fails). Reserve EUR 5-10M within free contingency for unplanned vendor switching and cost-mitigation. Include vendor-resilience audits (quarterly) starting Month 12 (2027-10-08).

5. Multimodal Integration Hooks (Buses, Ferries, Short-Haul Air) Deferred Without Clear Scope or Timeline

The programme plan mentions multimodal hooks for buses, ferries and short-haul air as scope, but no detailed workstream, timeline or resource allocation exists for their integration.
