Buses are the closest integrations (shared corridors with train networks); ferries (especially Baltic, Irish Sea, Mediterranean routes) require separate booking and ticketing systems; short-haul air integration (for competitive modal-shift analysis) requires access to airline inventory and pricing (politically sensitive). Absence of multimodal workstreams risks the following: (1) the through-ticket remains rail-only through Month 60 (2031-10-08), limiting door-to-door journey coverage; (2) modal-shift targets (air-to-rail) are harder to achieve without integrated bus-rail or rail-air options; (3) the 40% through-ticket target may be harder to reach in non-urban corridors where bus feeder services are required.

Recommendation: Defer detailed multimodal integration beyond the four priority corridors (Month 60 = 2031-10-08) but establish a Multimodal Integration Workstream by Month 3 (2027-01-08) to scope feasibility and governance: (1) Buses: design passenger-flow integration (e.g., real-time bus arrival affects train connection window) and revenue-sharing rules with local/regional bus operators; pilot on 1-2 corridors (e.g., Madrid-Barcelona with regional bus feeders) by Month 48 (2030-10-08). (2) Ferries: engage major ferry operators (Stena, P&O, others) to understand ticket and cargo-integration requirements; assess feasibility as a post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) add-on. (3) Short-haul air: engage IATA and major EU airlines on sharing non-discriminatory fare and availability data; establish data-governance safeguards (no collusion, price floors/ceilings prohibited); target exploratory MOU with 1-2 airlines by Month 30 (2029-04-08). Budget EUR 10-15M within EUR 225M contingency for multimodal pilots and integration planning (Months 30-60 = 2029-04-08 to 2031-10-08). Decision to extend multimodal scope beyond Month 60 (2031-10-08) by Month 48 (2030-10-08).

6. Absence of Through-Ticket Insurance and Passenger-Liability Coverage Requirements

The programme promises continuity-of-journey protection and single-contact liability for refunds and rerouting, but no requirement exists for through-ticket sellers (distributors, public reference distributor, or carriers acting as sellers) to carry errors-and-omissions (E&O) or passenger-liability insurance. If a through-ticket seller makes false promises (e.g., a distributor sells a risky itinerary as 'guaranteed continuity' when the connection time is tight) or fails to deliver promised assistance, passenger claims could exceed insurance capacity, leaving the passenger uncompensated. Additionally, no mechanism exists to pool liability across carriers and distributors if a cascading failure (hub outage + missed connections + delayed refunds) affects thousands of passengers.

Recommendation: Establish Through-Ticket Insurance and Passenger Liability Framework by Month 3 (2027-01-08): (1) Require all sellers (distributors, public reference distributor, carriers selling through-tickets) to carry E&O insurance with minimum coverage of EUR 5-10M per incident, EUR 20-30M aggregate annual; audit insurance annually starting Month 12 (2027-10-08). (2) Define a Passenger Liability Pool (EUR 10-20M reserve, funded from EUR 225M contingency) to cover uninsured or under-insured claims; administer claims within 5 working days with escalation to an independent arbitrator for disputed amounts. (3) Include insurance requirements in conformance checklist and quarterly compliance audits. (4) Publish a 'Passenger Compensation Information' notice on the public reference distributor and distributor-certification materials, specifying coverage limits and claims procedures. If an incident involves passenger injury or uncompensated losses exceeding EUR 1M, trigger Commission notification and a formal post-incident review (root-cause analysis, procedure update, insurance-coverage adjustment).

7. No Explicit Framework for Handling Non-Compliant Carriers at Month 30 (2029-04-08) API Mandate

The programme sets a hard deadline for mandatory API exposure (Month 30 = 2029-04-08) with a proposed threshold of at least 90% of corridor traffic bookable end-to-end. However, no escalation protocol exists if 1-2 major carriers (e.g., SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, ÖBB) signal continued non-compliance after the deadline or demand exemptions. The brief mentions 'enforcement action' by the Commission, but the mechanics (fines, license suspensions, mandatory hubs, restrictions on domestic sales) are not defined. Absence of clarity allows large incumbents to negotiate weaker compliance terms at the last minute (Month 24-30 = 2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08), fragmenting the network.

Recommendation: Establish a Non-Compliance Escalation and Enforcement Protocol by Month 6 (2027-04-08), defining mandatory actions if a carrier does not achieve API readiness by Month 30 (2029-04-08): (1) Month 24 (2028-10-08): DG MOVE formally notifies any carrier not projected to meet the deadline, specifying 'remedial actions' (e.g., accelerated integration, mandatory hub use, public distributor provisioning for that carrier's routes); (2) Month 27 (2029-01-08): escalation to Commission if carrier does not commit to a remedial path; (3) Month 30 (2029-04-08): if carrier is still non-compliant, invoke enforcement consequences: (a) co-funding hold (any outstanding tranches withheld), (b) mandatory hub routing (passengers cannot book that carrier directly; routing through hub with SLA guarantees), (c) regulatory escalation (Commission opens formal infringement procedure, fines up to 5-10% of annual turnover in the affected member state, or license review). (4) Publish compliance status quarterly (starting Month 18 = 2028-04-08) so the market knows which carriers are meeting obligations and which are not. Include this protocol in the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) and in the Commitment Letters signed by carriers (Month 3 = 2027-01-08).

8. Energy and Climate Volatility Not Explicitly Managed in Modal-Shift Planning

Modal shift from air to rail (5-15% planning range) depends on fuel prices (EUR 40-150/barrel historical range) and aviation-tax policy (proposed EU CO2-tax, member-state kerosene-tax harmonization). These external factors are largely outside the programme's control. If fuel prices drop 30-40% by Month 36 (2029-10-08) or aviation taxes are repealed, airline fares fall and the through-fare (EUR 70-90) is no longer competitive. Absence of energy-price scenarios and contingency planning leaves the programme's infrastructure case (environmental benefits, capacity relief) exposed to external shocks. By Month 48 (2030-10-08), if actual modal shift is 2-5% instead of 10-20%, the political case for the programme weakens.

Recommendation: Establish an Energy and Climate Sensitivity Monitoring Programme by Month 3 (2027-01-08): (1) Define modal-shift target ranges by fuel-price scenario in Month 4 (2027-02-08): if fuel <EUR 60/barrel, target 5-10% shift; EUR 60-100/barrel, 10-20% shift; >EUR 100/barrel, 15-30% shift. (2) Establish quarterly fuel-price and aviation-tax monitoring (starting Month 6 = 2027-04-08) using Bloomberg, IEA data and European Commission aviation-tax proposals; update modal-shift forecasts in quarterly dashboards. (3) If energy prices or policy shift materially (fuel drops >30% or aviation tax is repealed) by Month 24 (2028-10-08), trigger a mid-course programme review to reassess modal-shift viability and adjust communication strategy (emphasise 'cross-border rail journey convenience' rather than air competition). (4) If actual modal shift by Month 48 (2030-10-08) is <10% and fuel prices remain low, escalate to Steering Committee with contingency options: (a) extend distributor co-marketing funds (EUR 10-20M additional campaign budget), (b) pilot through-fare subsidies on 1-2 high-competition corridors (air vs. rail), or (c) reframe programme success narrative as 'through-ticket market share' (40% target) rather than modal shift, decoupling infrastructure investment from climate benefits (accepting reputational risk).

9. Accessibility Compliance Measurement and Escalation Framework Weak; Risk of Post-Launch Accessibility Failures

The programme commits to accessibility (24-hour assistance confirmation, 90%+ confirmation rate, 95%+ delivery rate, <2% complaint rate). However, the measurement framework is aspirational: no definition of 'confirmed assistance delivered' (e.g., does a lift failure en route count as non-delivery if alternative assistance is provided?), no independent auditing mechanism, and no escalation protocol if a corridor's delivery rate falls below 95%. BEUC and disability-rights organizations are invited to the working group but have no binding enforcement role. If accessibility failures are discovered post-launch (Month 18-24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), corrective actions are reactive (redesign, retraining, additional staffing), consuming unplanned budget (estimated EUR 5-10M per correction) and inviting regulatory intervention (member-state disability authorities, DG Justice).

Recommendation: Establish an Accessibility Compliance and Enforcement Framework by Month 4 (2027-02-08), including: (1) Detailed definition of 'confirmed assistance delivered': assistance is logged by both the passenger and the carrier/station staff; any deviation (no-show, equipment failure, alternative-assistance substitution) is documented; monthly reporting by all carriers and stations. (2) Independent quarterly audits (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 onward) by external accessibility-testing firm (1 FTE, EUR 500K-1M/year) conducting unannounced spot-checks on 5-10 randomly selected assisted journeys per quarter per corridor, with ratings (pass/fail) and corrective-action tracking. (3) Escalation protocol: if a corridor's assistance-delivery rate falls below 95% for 2+ consecutive months, suspend new bookings on that corridor pending root-cause analysis (estimated 2-4 week suspension); if <90%, trigger carrier remedial plan (additional staffing, equipment upgrades, training) with defined completion by Month +4. (4) Public accessibility dashboard (quarterly, anonymised by corridor) showing assistance-request volumes, confirmation rates, delivery rates and complaint rates; invite BEUC and disability-rights representatives to quarterly review forums (starting Month 9 = 2027-07-08). (5) Bind accessibility metrics into carrier licence agreements or conformance certifications (leverage regulatory enforcement if delivery fails).

10. Technology Obsolescence Risk for Legacy Carriers Not Addressed; Remediation Timeline Ambiguous

The programme assumes carriers with booking systems older than 10 years (hub-eligible criterion) can be served via regional hubs until they modernise. However, some carriers may face technical or financial barriers preventing modernisation even beyond Month 60 (2031-10-08) (e.g., national operators with limited budgets, or public-sector carriers unable to secure capital investment). No explicit sunset date exists for hub dependency: if hubs remain necessary indefinitely, they become permanent infrastructure, locking carriers into legacy-system costs (external hub fees vs. internal IT investment). Additionally, if hub operators use proprietary or unmaintainable mapping logic, hub obsolescence becomes a risk by Month 48-60 (2030-10-08) as technology standards evolve.

Recommendation: Establish a Technology Modernisation and Hub Dependency Management Programme by Month 6 (2027-04-08): (1) Require each hub-eligible carrier to submit a modernisation roadmap by Month 12 (2027-10-08) specifying: target date for OSDM-native API implementation (no later than Month 48 = 2030-10-08), budget required (co-funding ceiling EUR 2-5M per carrier), and phased milestones. (2) Set a hub-dependency sunset date of Month 48 (2030-10-08): all carriers must either be native-OSDM-compliant or have binding commitments to migrate by this date. (3) From Month 36-48 (2029-10-08 to 2030-10-08), transition hub fee-recovery: gradually shift from programme subsidy (EUR 0.47M/year per hub) to full carrier-fee recovery, signalling the cost of remaining on the hub to incentivise modernisation. (4) For carriers unable to modernise due to financial hardship, establish a Technology Modernisation Grant (EUR 50-100M reserved within EUR 225M contingency) to co-fund native API implementation at 50-70% cost, contingent on carrier commitment to complete by Month 48 (2030-10-08). (5) Require hub operators to maintain code modularity and export capability: if a hub is decommissioned at Month 48 (2030-10-08), carriers must be able to migrate with <4 week notice and no loss of booking data.

Potential Improvements

1. Strengthen Arbitration Panel Authority and Speed Through Formal Written Delegation and Penalty Escalation

The lightweight arbitration panel (8-12 FTE) is designed to resolve technical disputes in 60 days without building a new legal entity. However, without explicit written Council delegation (target Month 2 = 2026-12-08) and pre-agreed financial penalties (0.5-1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue in escrow), large carriers can contest rulings and delay implementation. Strengthening the panel's legal foundation and penalty framework would improve compliance credibility and reduce dispute-resolution cycles from 60+ days to 30-45 days, protecting the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate.

Recommendation: Secure explicit written Council and Commission Delegation of Authority by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), specifying binding technical-decision authority with 60-day cycles and 14-day compliance windows. Require all carriers >EUR 50M cross-border revenue to sign binding Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08) accepting arbitration outcomes and agreeing to financial penalties (0.5-1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue held in escrow) for non-compliance. Establish a Standing Regulators Committee (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23) with authority to enforce panel rulings consistently; escalate non-enforcement to the Commission within 5 business days. Draft a Memorandum of Understanding among DG MOVE, the EU Agency for Railways and the panel, locking in staffing, budget and escalation procedures. Include enforcement penalties in the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) so they are legally anchored.

2. Implement Real-Time Budget Burn Monitoring and Contingency-Tier Automation to Prevent Mid-Programme Overruns

The EUR 1.5 billion budget is fixed and fragile: carrier co-funding demand (EUR 290M), hub economics (EUR 1.9M/year gap), extended distributor operations and unplanned costs could trigger 20-30% overruns by Month 24 (2028-10-08). Monthly burn-rate dashboards are planned, but no automated escalation triggers or contingency-tier decision algorithms exist. Manual mid-course review processes (Months 12, 24 = 2027-10-08, 2028-10-08) risk 4-8 week delays between overspend detection and corrective decision, eroding the time available to protect conformance testing and capacity building.

Recommendation: Establish automated budget-burn monitoring by Month 3 (2027-01-08) with real-time dashboards and escalation triggers: if quarterly spend exceeds 115% of pro-rata budget, automatically escalate to the Programme Director and Steering Committee within 5 working days. Pre-define contingency-tier responses (Tier 1: 10-15% overrun → defer app polish, reduce distributor co-marketing by 20%; Tier 2: 15-25% → reduce carrier co-funding from 20% to 10%, limit hubs to priority corridors; Tier 3: >25% → suspend new hub openings, scale regulator capacity building to 3-4 priority member states) and require decision within 10 working days. Secure DG MOVE commitment to seek supplementary budget authority by Month 12 (2027-10-08) if Tier 2 is triggered, targeting EUR 100-200M supplementary allocation. Tie disbursements to verified milestone completion (API readiness gates, data-quality attestation) to avoid moral hazard in co-funding.

3. Establish Formal Data Quality and Inventory Accuracy Standards With Independent Auditing for Hubs and APIs

Regional hubs translate legacy carrier inventory into OSDM standards, and mapping errors (double-counted seats, incorrect fares, missed restrictions) can cause 2-5% booking-failure rates. The programme plans dual-run testing (2-4 weeks per carrier) but lacks pre-deployment validation and post-launch auditing. Independent auditing (quarterly from Month 18 = 2028-04-08 onward) would catch data-quality drift early and enforce remediation timelines, reducing refund disputes and passenger complaints.

Recommendation: Define data-quality SLAs by Month 4 (2027-02-08): booking-failure rate <0.5%, oversell rate <0.1%, inventory-freshness <5 minutes. Conduct external validation of hub mapping by Month 6 (2027-04-08) using an independent test lab with 30-50 real inventory samples per carrier. Require dual-run (hub and native) for 2-4 weeks per carrier (Month 15-18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08) before cutover. Establish quarterly independent audits (external testing firm, 1 FTE) from Month 18 (2028-04-08) onward, sampling 50-100 journeys per corridor per quarter and comparing search results (hub) against native implementations. Require hub operators to carry E&O liability insurance (EUR 2-5M minimum) covering overstated availability and inventory errors. If a hub's booking-failure rate exceeds 2% for >1 week, suspend new carrier onboarding to that hub until resolved.

4. Clarify Through-Ticket Definition and Measurement Operationally by Month 2 (2026-12-08) to Prevent Target Disputes

The programme targets '40% of cross-border rail journeys sold as through-tickets by Month 60 (2031-10-08)', but definition is aspirational: is it (a) single booking reference + single payment only, or (b) + continuity-of-journey rights, or (c) only via distributor platforms (excluding operator direct sales)? Ambiguity invites disputes by Month 24 (2028-10-08) over whether the target is being met, undermining stakeholder confidence and making mid-course corrections difficult.

Recommendation: Define 'through-ticket' operationally by Month 2 (2026-12-08): single booking reference + single payment + continuity-of-journey rights (rerouting/refund if connection missed) on a multi-carrier journey, sold via any distributor or carrier platform. Publish this definition in the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08) so it is legally anchored and not re-interpreted by carriers or member states. Establish mandatory carrier and distributor reporting of through-ticket volumes (monthly from Month 18 = 2028-04-08 onward), with data aggregated and published quarterly with a 1-month lag to protect commercial sensitivity. Commission an independent evaluator (contract Month 3 = 2027-01-08) to build a counterfactual model comparing through-ticket adoption on priority corridors to control routes (non-rollout corridors), separating programme effects from fuel prices and aviation-policy changes. Conduct a baseline survey (Months 0-2 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-12-08) validating baseline through-ticket share and complaint rates. Use quarterly dashboards to trigger mid-course corrections if through-ticket share is <15% at Month 24 (2028-10-08) (proposed threshold).

5. Establish Pre-Agreed Escalation and Communication Protocols for Major Carrier Non-Compliance Signalling

Large carriers (SNCF, Deutsche Bahn, ÖBB) have political leverage: if one signals non-compliance by Month 12-15 (2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08), others may follow, fragmenting the coalition. No pre-agreed escalation or political-engagement protocol exists for these scenarios. Clarity on consequences (co-funding holds, mandatory hubs, regulatory escalation) would deter signalling and strengthen carrier commitment.

Recommendation: Establish a Major-Carrier Engagement and Escalation Protocol by Month 2 (2026-12-08): (1) Conduct quarterly roundtables (Month 1 = 2026-11-08 onward) with carriers >EUR 50M cross-border revenue to air concerns early and negotiate timeline flexibility in exchange for binding commitments. (2) Require signed Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08) specifying API readiness date (no later than Month 30 = 2029-04-08) and acceptance of arbitration outcomes. (3) If a major carrier signals non-compliance in Month 9-12 (2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08), escalate immediately to DG MOVE and CER leadership; offer contingency options (extended integration timeline with co-funding, mandatory hub use, phased rollout). (4) If non-compliance is confirmed by Month 15 (2028-01-08), escalate to Commission and invoke penalties (co-funding hold, mandatory hub routing, regulatory escalation). (5) Build political cover early: secure visible member-state support (Belgium, Netherlands, Austria, Spain) and regular reporting to the European Parliament TRAN committee to signal political commitment and deter carrier resistance.

6. Enhance Distributor Incentive and Engagement Strategy to Secure Early API Integration Commitments

Commercial distributors (Trainline, Omio) are essential for achieving the 40% through-ticket target but their involvement is assumed rather than contractually secured. If distributor margins are compressed or if they prioritise other markets, their integration could slip from Month 18 (2028-04-08) to Month 24+ (2028-10-08), reducing market reach and forcing the public reference distributor to expand (consuming budget and crowding out commercial platforms).

Recommendation: Establish formal Distributor Advisory Working Groups by Month 1 (2026-11-08) with Trainline, Omio and smaller platforms. Conduct detailed margin and IT-capacity analysis (Months 2-4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) to understand their integration costs and requirements. Offer early API access (Month 9-12 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-10-08) and data-access priority to platforms committing to full integration and promotion by Month 18 (2028-04-08). Negotiate margin-support measures (Months 4-6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08): co-marketing funds (EUR 5-10M over 24 months), performance bonuses for through-ticket volumes and transaction-fee waivers (programme covers 50-70% of payment-institution fees for first 12-18 months). Require signed Distributor Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08) specifying integration timeline, promotion commitment and penalties for non-compliance (loss of early API access, withholding of co-marketing funds). Reserve dedicated conformance-testing slots for distributor systems (Month 12-18 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-04-08) with free technical support to accelerate integration. Monitor quarterly progress and escalate any slippage >2 weeks to Steering Committee within 5 working days.

7. Develop Clear Regulator Capacity-Building Twinning Programme With Enforcement SLAs and Accountability

National regulators across 27 member states vary widely in resources, expertise and enforcement traditions. Weaker-capacity regulators (Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary) cannot enforce access duties or resolve cross-border disputes quickly, creating two-tier compliance. A twinning programme (training, shared inspection checklists, experience exchange) is planned but lacks structure, accountability measures and enforcement SLAs. Regulators in weak-capacity states should commit to <30-day dispute resolution and <60-day cross-border case handling by Month 30 (2029-04-08); if they slip, escalate to Commission for targeted support or enforcement-authority adjustment.

Recommendation: Establish a Regulator Capacity-Building and Enforcement-Alignment Programme by Month 1 (2026-11-08): (1) Conduct regulator-capacity audit (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) identifying staff, budget and IT-system gaps in 27 member states; prioritise 8-12 weaker-capacity regulators for targeted support (EUR 10-15M over 5 years). (2) Fund twinning partnerships pairing strong regulators (France, Germany, Netherlands, Austria, Sweden, Belgium) with weaker ones (Poland, Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, Slovakia, Slovenia, Croatia, Malta); define SOW including 3-4 week joint training (access-enforcement, data-quality auditing, complaint handling), shared inspection checklists (Month 8 = 2027-06-08) and quarterly joint reviews (Month 12 = 2027-10-08 onward). (3) Establish Standing Regulators Committee (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23), chaired by EU Agency for Railways, meeting monthly; define enforcement SLAs: all access-related disputes resolved within 30 days (max 60 days), all refund claims processed within 10 days. (4) Define enforcement penalties: if a regulator fails to meet SLAs consistently (>60-day resolution in 2+ cases per quarter), escalate to Commission for targeted support or enforcement-authority adjustment. (5) Require lead-authority recognition: the affected carrier's home-state regulator leads cross-border disputes, with other affected states' support; lead-authority decisions are recognised across all member states without re-litigation. (6) Include enforcement capability and SLAs in the binding standards (Month 18 = 2028-04-08).

8. Design Clearer Contingency Pathways for Payment-Provider Accreditation Shortfalls to Avoid Settlement Delays

Payment-institution accreditation (call Month 2 = 2026-12-08, decision Month 8 = 2027-06-08) risks attracting <2 qualified providers, leaving no competitive choice. If the sole accredited provider fails post-launch, the fallback is undefined (bilateral settlement? emergency procurement?). EUR 1-2M switching-cost reserve exists, but mechanisms are vague. Clearer contingency pathways would reduce settlement delays and allow faster provider replacement if needed.

Recommendation: Define payment-provider accreditation contingencies by Month 1 (2026-11-08): (1) Market sounding (Months 0-1 = 2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) to gauge provider interest and capacity; communicate accreditation timeline and criteria publicly to encourage competition. (2) If fewer than 2 qualified providers apply by Month 6 (2027-04-08), trigger Contingency Path A: extend application deadline to Month 10 (2027-08-08) and launch targeted outreach to alternative payment institutions (e.g., incumbent banks with PSD2 licenses, fintech payment platforms). (3) If still <2 providers by Month 10 (2027-08-08), activate Contingency Path B: fallback to bilateral carrier settlement with a common message standard (SEPA, ISO 20022) and a neutral dispute-resolution body; implement by Month 15 (2028-01-08) (slower than accredited providers but known). (4) Require at least 2 accredited providers operational by Month 12 (2027-10-08) for production launch (Month 18 = 2028-04-08). (5) Contractual redundancy: if an accredited provider fails during Months 18-30 (2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08), automatic failover to backup partner; programme covers switching cost up to EUR 1-2M, with EUR 10M reserve for emergencies. (6) Quarterly provider performance reviews (uptime, settlement cycle, refund processing, dispute handling) starting Month 12 (2027-10-08); if a provider breaches SLAs, activate remediation plan (penalty deductions, accelerated provider replacement).

9. Strengthen Consumer-App User-Testing and Accessibility Compliance From MVP Phase

The public reference distributor app is central to adopting through-tickets; if it is poorly designed (confusing refund flows, missing accessibility features) or launches late, through-ticket volumes drop 10-20 percentage points. User-testing is planned for MVP (Month 9 = 2027-07-08), but accessibility testing and structured usability iteration are minimal. Early integration of WCAG 2.1 AA compliance, real-time assistance-request tracking and multilingual support would improve user satisfaction and accessibility-delivery metrics, reducing post-launch redesign costs.

Recommendation: Establish rigorous user-testing and accessibility-compliance processes for the MVP (Month 9 = 2027-07-08): (1) Conduct user research and personas (Months 2-4 = 2026-12-08 to 2027-02-08) with diverse user groups (frequent travellers, elderly users, persons with mobility limitations, non-native speakers). (2) Build wireframes and prototypes (Months 4-6 = 2027-02-08 to 2027-04-08) embedding accessibility as a core feature: keyboard navigation, screen-reader support, high-contrast modes, real-time assistance-request tracking. (3) MVP for one-corridor pilot (Month 9 = 2027-07-08) with at least 50-100 real users (diverse demographics); conduct unmoderated usability testing (UserTesting or equivalent) weekly for 4 weeks (Months 9-10 = 2027-07-08 to 2027-08-08). (4) Iterate on feedback (Months 10-12 = 2027-08-08 to 2027-10-08) with fortnightly releases; track Net Promoter Score (NPS) weekly and user-satisfaction ratings (target >4.0/5 stars) bi-weekly. (5) Accessibility testing: quarterly WCAG 2.1 AA audits (external firm) and monthly screen-reader testing with assistive-technology users (persons with visual impairments) from MVP phase. (6) Embed BEUC and disability-rights representatives in user-testing sessions (Months 9-15 = 2027-07-08 to 2028-01-08) to validate accessibility usability and complaint-handling flows. (7) If MVP satisfaction is <3.8/5 or accessibility audit identifies >5 critical issues at Month 12 (2027-10-08), extend MVP phase 4-6 weeks (delay public launch to Month 19 = 2028-05-08 vs. Month 15 = 2028-01-08) to prioritise quality over schedule.

10. Establish Quarterly Stakeholder Satisfaction Surveys and Adaptive Engagement Strategy

Stakeholder buy-in is assumed but not systematically measured. Smaller carriers, weaker regulators and disability-rights organizations may feel marginalised if engagement is top-down and decision-making appears concentrated at Brussels level. By Month 18 (2028-04-08), if stakeholder satisfaction falls below 70%, political pressure could force weaker standards or extend timelines. Quarterly satisfaction surveys and an adaptive engagement strategy would surface concerns early and allow corrective outreach.

Recommendation: Conduct quarterly stakeholder-satisfaction surveys (Month 3 = 2027-01-08 onward, administered anonymously via Qualtrics or equivalent) with segments: major carriers, smaller carriers, national regulators, BEUC, disability-rights organizations and distributors. Ask: (1) Are you satisfied with programme communication and decision transparency? (2) Do you feel your concerns are heard? (3) Are co-funding and support allocations fair? (4) Are the timelines realistic for your organisation? Target satisfaction >80% across segments; if any segment falls to 60-70%, trigger a focused outreach campaign (1:1 interviews, dedicated working group, adjustment of engagement mechanisms). Publish an annual Stakeholder Engagement Report (Month 12, 24, 36, 48 = 2027-10-08, 2028-10-08, 2029-10-08, 2030-10-08) with anonymised results, concerns raised and responses taken. Establish a Stakeholder Ombudsman role (1 FTE from Month 6 = 2027-04-08) for escalating unresolved concerns directly to the Programme Director (target resolution within 2 weeks). If stakeholder satisfaction remains <70% for 2+ consecutive quarters, conduct a full programme review (Month 24 = 2028-10-08) with Commission and Council to assess whether approach adjustments (governance model, co-funding rebalancing, timeline extension) are needed to maintain coalition.

1.3 Follow Up Consultation

By Month 3 (2027-01-08), review the status of the three critical preconditions: (1) Regulation adoption tracked to Month 8 (2027-06-08) gate with shadow standards pre-work progress; (2) Council delegation secured and Commitment Letters signed; (3) cost model and contingency tiers finalized. Address the killer-application commercial strategy: share customer-research findings and product-design decisions. Clarify the post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding model decision date (Month 48 = 2030-10-08 target) and any trigger for supplementary budget authority (Month 10 = 2027-08-08 target). Identify any political resistance from incumbents or member states and agree escalation protocols.

1.4.A Issue - Killer Application Missing—Competitive Positioning Against Airlines Undefined

The plan lacks a flagship product that makes through-tickets compelling on their own merits. Sum-of-segment fares with no regulated ceilings will rarely beat budget airlines on the competitive short-haul routes (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon, Copenhagen–Hamburg–Berlin). The modal-shift planning range (5–15%) is aspirational without proof that travellers prefer a guaranteed connection over separate tickets or flying. This is a core commercial risk: if through-fares do not compete, the 40% target and distributor adoption collapse.

1.4.B Tags

  • missing-commercial-strategy
  • weak-modal-shift-case
  • pricing-non-competitive
  • airline-undercut-risk

1.4.C Mitigation

By Month 3 (2027-01-08), commission customer-research and willingness-to-pay studies on the four priority corridors (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln as the lead pilot). Test two flagship products: (1) 'one ticket, guaranteed connection' with 4-hour reroute decision and 10-day refund, plus reduction-card recognition (~10–15% effective discount); (2) air-rail city-pair offer (e.g. Brussels–Barcelona with a connecting flight, priced to beat direct air). Pilot one product on one corridor from Month 9 (2027-07-08) with the consumer app; measure booking intent, completion rate and price sensitivity. If the pilot shows <5% modal shift or <8% through-ticket share by Month 24 (2028-10-08), commission a strategic review (Month 24–27 = 2028-10-08 to 2029-01-08) to consider regulated fare ceilings or subsidised through-fares on competitive routes, accepting antitrust risk or extra budget cost.

1.4.D Consequence

Without a compelling product, distributors (Trainline, Omio) lack margin incentive to push through-tickets, smaller carriers see no revenue uplift, and incumbents (DB, SNCF) offer minimal API access. The programme could hit the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate technically but miss the 40% target and halved-complaints goals by Month 60 (2031-10-08), leaving the programme seen as a technical exercise, not a passenger win.

1.4.E Root Cause

The plan prioritizes structural delivery (standards, APIs, clearing, governance) over customer value proposition. Commercial strategy, pricing rules and product design are delegated to later phases ('high levers refine...fares') rather than locked in early as the basis for carrier and distributor buy-in. Modal shift is stated as an outcome without evidence-based willingness to pay or customer research anchoring the feasibility.

1.5.A Issue - Arbitration Panel Lacks Real Enforcement Power; Incumbent Resistance Not Mitigated

The plan's arbitration panel is described as holding 'binding technical-decision authority' with '60-day cycles' and '14-day compliance deadlines,' yet the governance prerequisite is only 'written Council delegation by Month 2 (2026-12-08).' No mechanism exists to compel compliance from major carriers (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, ÖBB). The penalty structure (0.5–1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue in escrow) is toothless against a carrier that refuses the Commitment Letter or contests the panel's authority. If DB or SNCF signals non-compliance or seeks exemptions, the panel becomes advisory, the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate becomes unenforceable, and the entire network fragments.

1.5.B Tags

  • governance-enforcement-gap
  • incumbent-resistance-unmitigated
  • penalty-insufficient
  • authority-not-durable

1.5.C Mitigation

By Month 1.5 (2026-11-23), secure an explicit Council Regulation or Delegated Act (not just a letter) that designates the arbitration panel as a binding dispute-resolution body with force-of-law recognition across all member states. Include a compliance-escalation protocol: (1) first non-compliance = written notice + 5-day cure; (2) second = 1% of annual cross-border revenue withheld by paying carriers (held in escrow) until compliance; (3) third = Commission enforcement action (Article 258 TFEU or targeted sanctions). Require all carriers >EUR 50M annual revenue to sign the Commitment Letter by Month 3 (2027-01-08); if a major carrier refuses, escalate to DG MOVE for political intervention (Minister of Transport level) by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23). Conduct a dry-run arbitration case (e.g. access-term dispute) in Months 6–9 (2027-04-08 to 2027-07-08) to test the panel's speed and enforce compliance; publicize the outcome to signal credibility.

1.5.D Consequence

Without durable enforcement, large incumbents can contest arbitration rulings, delay or refuse API exposure, and negotiate their own 'special' access terms. Smaller carriers comply and lose competitive position. The network becomes two-tier: fast carriers with good APIs, slow carriers gatekept by non-compliance. 2.4.A Issue - Killer Application Missing—Fares Won't Beat Airlines Without Explicit Competitive Positioning

The plan targets 40% through-ticket share and 5-15% modal shift from air, yet the through-fare rule is 'sum of segment prices with no regulated ceilings.' This means passengers see uncompetitive prices versus budget airlines on short-haul routes—the very corridors where modal shift matters most. Without a flagship product (e.g. guaranteed-connection ticket, air-rail city-pair, or reduction-card bundling), the plan relies on convenience alone, which is insufficient. A 15% modal shift requires fares that beat airlines on 2-3 key corridors, not aspirational convenience.

2.4.C Mitigation

Define and pilot a flagship through-ticket product on one high-demand corridor (e.g. Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln) by Month 6 (2027-04-08). Propose: 'One ticket, guaranteed connection' with <4-hour reroute decision, 10-day refund, and reduction-card recognition honoured cross-border (10-15% effective discount). Run a willingness-to-pay study (Months 1-3 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-01-08) to confirm fares can undercut airlines. Pilot the product on one corridor (Month 9 = 2027-07-08) and launch with the public app (Month 15 = 2028-01-08). If modal shift is below 8% at Month 24 (2028-10-08), escalate and consider regulated fare ceilings (pending competition-law review) or subsidised through-fares as a contingency decision by Month 30 (2029-04-08).

2.4.D Consequence

Without a competitive through-fare or killer application, passengers default to separate tickets or flying. The 40% target and modal-shift planning range will be missed, eroding programme credibility and downstream funding justification. Distributor interest and consumer-app adoption will plateau below 15% by Month 24 (2028-10-08), requiring budget reallocation and scope cuts (Tier 2-3 contingency). Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) political support for sustained operation funding (EUR 45M/year unfunded) will evaporate.

2.4.E Root Cause

The plan treats through-ticketing as a technical and convenience problem, not a commercial one. The regulatory mandate (non-discriminatory access) and the cargo system (OSDM, clearing, hubs) are sound, but they do not inherently create a product passengers prefer over existing alternatives. Fares are left to carriers' segment pricing, which maximises revenue per leg, not per journey. No explicit analysis of price elasticity, airline response or willingness-to-pay grounds the 40% and 5-15% targets.

2.5.A Issue - Arbitration Panel Lacks Binding Enforcement Power Over Major Incumbents—Relies on Unconfirmed Council Delegation

The plan hinges on a time-boxed arbitration panel with binding decision authority by Month 2 (2026-12-08). 4.4.A Issue - Passenger-Rights Backstop Lacks Funded Guarantee Mechanism and Fault-Allocation Rules

The passenger-rights backstop (Decision 8) assigns the selling distributor as single contact for rerouting and refund, but the plan lacks: (1) a funded guarantee pool for carrier insolvency or cascade failures; (2) a fault-allocation schedule for missed connections specifying which carrier pays when multiple carriers cause a delay; (3) insurance requirements with verified coverage before operational go-live; (4) a dispute-resolution SLA (<5 business days for routine claims). The actuarial study (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) estimates 3-5% claim rate (EUR 10-40M), but without explicit funding within the EUR 1,500 million cap and enforceable fault rules, distributors will decline risky itineraries or claim disputes will consume 5-10% of through-ticket value, undercutting the 40% target.

Establish a Dispute Resolution Panel with rotating carrier and distributor representatives, empowered to rule on contested claims within 5 business days; set a dispute rate SLA (target <5% of claims escalated). Without funded guarantees and fault rules, distributors will demand escrow or insurance from carriers before selling through-tickets on weaker segments (e.g., small regional operators), which delays onboarding and fragments the network. This leaves the backstop as a design aspiration without an operational or financial anchor.

4.5.A Issue - GDPR and Competition-Law Firewall Risks Not Anchored to Binding Legal Consensus Before Standards Lock

The plan commits to binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-08), but GDPR (Decision on DPIA and DPA consensus by Month 4 = 2027-02-08) and competition-law clearance are downstream dependencies. If a national DPA or the EDPB challenges the cross-border data-flow architecture (e.g., requiring data residency in home state, blocking certain PII fields, or demanding consent mechanisms that slow booking), the remediation will require re-engineering the data layer and settlement message formats. This cannot be fixed within the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards window without compromising either GDPR compliance or standards completeness. Similarly, if the Commission's competition directorate requires data minimisation more strict than the current plan, real-time seat availability for distributors becomes impossible, weakening search quality and the 40% target.

6.5.D Consequence

If Council delegation is not legally adopted by Month 3 (2027-01-08), the Commitment Letters signed in Month 3 (2027-01-08) carry no legal weight. The plan underestimates the legal and political lead time for Council delegation to a novel governance body. 7.4.A Issue - Passenger-Rights Backstop Is Underfunded and Liability Framework Is Incomplete

The plan estimates claim rates at 3–5% (EUR 10–40M over 5 years), but EU Regulation 1371/2007 and disruption risk under multicarrier through-tickets typically trigger 8–12% claim rates on competitive, dense corridors. The backstop lacks: (1) fault-allocation protocol (who decides which carrier caused the missed connection?); (2) insolvency reserve for a major carrier collapse; (3) distributor indemnification rules if a carrier disputes liability; (4) cross-border enforcement of refund orders (does a French carrier refund a claim filed in Poland?). Without these, the clearing mechanism cannot settle disputes within 10 days, distributor confidence erodes, and through-ticket sales stall. The EUR 10M residual reserve is insufficient for tail-risk scenarios (cascading delays, force-majeure events). The plan assumes refund liability is 'recovered from the responsible carrier via accredited payment providers,' but no enforcement protocol specifies how a refund advance is recovered if the carrier contests fault.

Require all operational entities (distributors, hubs, clearing mechanism) to carry errors-and-omissions insurance with EUR 2–10M limits. 7.4.D Consequence

Without a clear fault-allocation and recovery protocol, disputed refund claims will accumulate; the 10-day refund SLA will be missed on 20–40% of claims; distributors will lose confidence and reduce through-ticket inventory; and carriers will contest refund advances, leading to 6–12 month collection disputes. The result is a loss of 10–20 percentage points on the 40% through-ticket target (i.e., 20–30% instead of 40%), higher consumer complaints (not 50% reduction but 10–20% reduction), and potential litigation that delays the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate by 3–6 months. If a major carrier becomes insolvent during a peak season, the EUR 10M reserve will be exhausted and the programme will be forced into emergency restructuring or a claim freeze that will severely damage credibility.

7.4.E Root Cause

The plan inherits EU Regulation 1371/2007 passenger-rights duties but does not translate them into operational procedures for multi-carrier through-tickets. Fault allocation under the regulation is carrier-specific (the carrier liable for a delay is responsible for rerouting, care, and compensation), yet the plan does not specify how fault is determined when three carriers are involved and the missed connection was caused by a delayed segment run by Carrier B but the distributor sold the ticket and the passenger claims against Distributor A. This design gap—whether fault flows back from distributor to carrier, or whether the distributor must advance cost and later recover—is not resolved. The result is a liability framework that is incomplete and exposes the programme to claims that exceed the reserve by 5–10x.

(3) Accessibility data (mobility restrictions, medical conditions) is special-category data under GDPR Article 9; the plan requires 'explicit consent' at booking time, but if a passenger refuses consent, can the platform complete the booking without accessibility data? 7.5.D Consequence

7.5.E Root Cause

The plan treats GDPR compliance as a box-ticking exercise (complete DPIA, reach DPA consensus by Month 4 = 2027-02-08) but does not recognise that GDPR governance for multicarrier through-tickets is genuinely novel and requires bespoke clarification from the EDPB or national DPAs. EU Regulation 1371/2007 requires passenger data to be retained for dispute resolution, but cross-border through-ticketing creates data flows that are not covered by existing DPA guidance. Accessibility data is particularly fraught: EU Accessibility Directive obligations (passengers with reduced mobility must be able to request assistance) collide with GDPR Article 9 (special-category data requires explicit consent and heightened protection). If consent is mandatory, a passenger who refuses accessibility data disclosure cannot book an accessible ticket; if it is optional, the platform cannot fulfil accessibility obligations. The plan does not resolve this tension. Additionally, DPA consensus at the EDPB level is not the same as national DPA approval; some member states may issue unilateral stop orders if they believe SCCs are insufficient.

7.6.A Issue - Arbitration Panel Lacks Enforcement Power; Panel Rulings Against Incumbents Are Not Binding Without Council Delegation

The plan specifies an arbitration panel with '8–12 FTE, binding technical rulings within 60 days, 14 days to comply or escalate to the Commission,' but it does not secure the foundational legal authority. The panel is described as 'layered on top of existing institutions' (DG MOVE, EU Agency for Railways) and lacks direct enforcement power. When Deutsche Bahn, SNCF or ÖBB contest a panel ruling—e.g., rejecting a requirement to expose real-time inventory at <2-second latency or refusing to recognise a third-party distributor's access rights—the plan's escalation route is 'to the Commission.' But the Commission has no standing executive power over a carrier's technical operations; it can only issue an enforcement directive or threaten an antitrust investigation, both of which take 6–12 months. The plan assumes 'written Council/Commission delegation' by Month 2 (2026-12-08), but such delegation is not yet secured and is not binding until formally adopted by Council decision. The Commitment Letters signed by carriers (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) include penalties of '0.5–1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue in escrow,' but those penalties are enforceable only if the panel's ruling is valid under EU law; if a carrier challenges the ruling before an EU court, the escrow can be tied up in litigation for 2–3 years. The result is that the panel has the appearance of authority but lacks the legal force to bind incumbents, and smaller carriers have no confidence that the panel will protect their access rights.

7.6.B Tags

  • governance-gap
  • panel-enforcement-undefined
  • delegation-not-secured
  • commission-escalation-slow
  • litigation-risk-high

7.6.C Mitigation

Immediately (Month 0 = 2026-10-08, within 2 weeks of project start), prepare a draft Council Decision delegating binding technical decision-making authority to the arbitration panel. The delegation must specify: (1) panel has authority to issue binding rulings on access-term templates, settlement message standards, data-quality SLAs, and conformance test criteria; (2) rulings are issued within 60 days and are final (not subject to administrative appeal, only judicial review if a carrier claims the ruling violated EU law); (3) compliance deadline is 14 days from notification; (4) non-compliance triggers a penalty (0.5–1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue in escrow, escalated to 1–2% if non-compliance persists beyond 30 days); (5) the Commission or EU Agency for Railways enforces penalties (not the Commission's discretionary choice, but a mandatory enforcement protocol). Submit the draft decision to the Council Legal Service for review by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23) and secure Council adoption by Month 2 (2026-12-08). Obtain a written Commission opinion affirming the panel's authority by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23). Prepare a secondary legal instrument (e.g., an Agency decision or a memorandum of understanding) that clarifies the panel's authority if the Council decision is delayed; this secondary instrument should be sufficient to begin standards work even if full Council delegation is not complete. Require all carriers above EUR 50M cross-border revenue to sign the Commitment Letters (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) with explicit acknowledgment that they accept the panel's authority and agree to penalties; use legal counsel to negotiate with SNCF, Deutsche Bahn and ÖBB leadership (Month 2.5 = 2026-12-23) to secure incumbent buy-in before Month 3 (2027-01-08). If a carrier refuses to sign by Month 4 (2027-02-08), escalate to DG MOVE and the Commission for enforcement action (threaten suspension of EU funding or antitrust investigation).

7.6.D Consequence

If the Council delegation is not secured by Month 2 (2026-12-08), the panel will be advisory only, and major incumbents can contest technical rulings without consequence. The standards-setting process (Months 4–18 = 2027-02-08 to 2028-04-08) will be paralysed by disputes over access-term templates and data-quality SLAs; carriers will submit competing proposals and block consensus, extending the standards phase by 6–12 months. The Month 18 (2028-04-08) binding standards milestone will be missed. If the delegation is delayed beyond Month 4 (2027-02-08), the standards work must pause pending legal clarity, and the critical path will slip by 3–6 months. Litigation risk is high: if a carrier challenges a panel ruling in the EU courts and wins on grounds that the panel lacked authority, all subsequent rulings are vulnerable to challenge, and the programme will face a cascading crisis of credibility. The result is likely a 6–18 month delay to the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate and a fragmented through-ticket network on only 1–2 corridors by Month 60 (2031-10-08), missing the 40% target by 30–40 percentage points.

7.6.E Root Cause

The plan opts for 'a small independent standards arbitration panel' to avoid the legal set-up time of a dedicated joint undertaking (which would take 12–18 months to establish), but in doing so it sacrifices binding authority. An arbitration panel has authority only if it is: (1) explicitly delegated that authority by a competent legal body (Council, Commission or a member state); (2) empowered to issue enforceable rulings (not advisory opinions); and (3) backed by a clear escalation and penalty mechanism that does not depend on the Commission's discretionary enforcement. The plan assumes these conditions are met by Month 2 (2026-12-08), but the Council decision delegating authority is not in progress and no legal draft has been prepared. The Commitment Letters (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) are a proxy for buy-in, but they are not a substitute for legal authority. If a carrier refuses to comply with a panel ruling and contests it in court (claiming the panel lacked authority), the ensuing litigation will paralyse the programme and delay the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards milestone.

Smaller carriers and state-weak operators need tailored incentives (milestone co-funding, hub access, accessible support). Advise on distributor co-marketing budget allocation and early API access gates to ensure Trainline and Omio prioritise the programme.

8.4.A Issue - Killer Application Undefined: Programme Relies on Generic Convenience, Not Compelling Traveller Value

The plan targets 40% through-ticket share and 5-15% modal shift from air, yet no flagship product is defined that makes a traveller choose rail over flying or separate tickets. Through-fares are merely sums of segment prices with no competitive ceiling; reduction-card discounts (~10-15%) do not offset low-cost-airline pricing on short-haul routes. The programme assumes adoption through broad convenience (single booking, single payment) without demonstrating what travellers actually value or will pay for. This is a critical gap: without a clear, testable killer application (e.g., guaranteed-connection product with 4-hour reroute, 10-day refund, and reduction-card recognition), distributor incentive and carrier willingness to invest remain weak.

8.4.C Mitigation

Commission customer research by Month 1 (2026-11-08) to validate traveller willingness to pay for three candidate killer applications: (1) guaranteed-connection through-ticket (4-hour reroute, 10-day refund, single contact), (2) air-rail city-pair offer (all-inclusive fare vs. flight competitor), (3) assisted-travel journey (confirmed assistance + priority seating + platform handover). Pilot the winning product on one high-demand corridor (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln or Wien–München–Zürich) by Month 9 (2027-07-08) with real traveller bookings and satisfaction tracking. If any product achieves >4.0/5 satisfaction and >15% uptake over separate tickets, scale it to all four corridors by Month 27 (2029-01-08). If none achieves this, escalate to the Steering Committee by Month 12 (2027-10-08) and propose a regulated through-fare ceiling or modal-shift subsidy (decision outside current scope).

8.4.D Consequence

Without a validated killer application, the programme risks missing the 40% through-ticket and halved-complaints targets. Distributors (Trainline, Omio) may delay integration if margins are weak. Carriers may comply with the API mandate passively, offering poor through-fare competitiveness or unreliable assistance. Modal shift remains in the 0-5% range instead of the planning range of 5-15%, undermining the environmental case and political credibility. Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding approval becomes harder if outcomes are ambiguous.

8.4.E Root Cause

The plan prioritises regulatory and technical architecture over traveller demand validation. It assumes that removing friction (single booking, single payment) is sufficient motivation, yet does not test whether the resulting through-fares or journey experience are actually more attractive than alternative options (flying, separate tickets, or car). The SWOT analysis flagged this as a strength opportunity ('killer application can be developed') but the plan does not resource its development or make it a gated milestone, allowing it to remain unresolved into execution.

8.5.A Issue - Arbitration Panel Lacks Binding Enforcement over Major Incumbents Without Explicit Delegation and Penalty Mechanism

The Pragmatic Foundation scenario relies on a lightweight arbitration panel with 60-day decision cycles and 14-day compliance deadlines. However, the plan does not secure the written Council/Commission Delegation of Authority until Month 2 (2026-12-08), and Commitment Letters from major carriers are not due until Month 3 (2027-01-08). Without formal legal authority and documented penalties, large incumbents (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, ÖBB) can contest technical rulings, demand arbitration review, or simply delay implementation. The proposed escrow penalties (0.5–1% of quarterly through-ticket revenue) are aspirational; no enforcement mechanism or jurisdictional route is specified. If a carrier refuses to comply by Month 3 (2027-01-08) or Month 12 (2027-10-08 or 2027-10-08), the plan has no credible escalation path, risking fragmentation of the network and failure to meet the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate.

  • enforcement_mechanism_missing
  • critical_path_vulnerability

8.5.C Mitigation

Secure written Council/Commission Delegation of Authority by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23, 10:00), not Month 2 (2026-12-08). The delegation must specify: (1) binding decision authority over technical standards, access terms and settlement rules; (2) 60-day decision cycles and 14-day compliance deadlines; (3) force-of-law language so rulings are recognised across all member states; (4) escalation path to the Commission if a carrier does not comply within 14 days, with automatic Commission enforcement action within 5 business days. Require all carriers with >EUR 50M cross-border revenue to sign a binding Commitment Letter by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23, 14:00), accepting arbitration outcomes and penalties (revised: 0.5% of quarterly through-ticket revenue on first violation, 1% on second, withheld until resolution). Establish a Standing Regulators Committee (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23, 09:00) with explicit power to enforce panel rulings in their jurisdictions and escalate non-enforcement to the Commission within 5 working days. Negotiate directly with SNCF, Deutsche Bahn and ÖBB leadership by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23, 11:00) to secure buy-in; offer them early API-design input in exchange for Commitment Letters.

8.5.D Consequence

If the delegation and Commitment Letters are not in place by Month 3 (2027-01-08), major incumbents can delay compliance indefinitely. The Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards deadline will slip if standards cannot be finalized without incumbent consensus. The Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate becomes unenforceable if the panel's rulings are not backed by Commission authority. The through-ticket network fragments: early-adopting carriers go live on time, while incumbents remain non-compliant, leaving travellers unable to book consistent end-to-end journeys. The 40% through-ticket target becomes unrealistic if key corridors (Wien–München–Zürich, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon) are held up by one non-compliant carrier.

8.5.E Root Cause

The plan assumes that arbitration panel authority will be formally delegated, but does not resource the political negotiation or legal drafting needed to secure it. It treats the Delegation and Commitment Letters as routine administrative steps, not as critical blockers that require high-level political engagement and legal certainty. The contingency and risk-mitigation sections note governance risk but do not specify the escalation path or who is responsible for securing delegation by the required date.

8.6.A Issue - Fixed Budget (EUR 1.5B) Is Fragile Against 20–30% Overrun; Free Contingency (EUR 215M) Is Insufficient; Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) Funding Cliff Is Unresolved

The plan allocates EUR 1.5 billion across standards (EUR 280M), clearing (EUR 120M), reference distributor (EUR 215M), capacity building (EUR 100M), consumer rollout (EUR 150M), carrier co-funding (EUR 290M), data layer (EUR 60M) and governance (EUR 60M), with EUR 225M contingency held at DG MOVE (EUR 215M free, EUR 10M earmarked for passenger-rights residual). A 20–30% overrun (EUR 300–450M) exceeds the free contingency by EUR 85–235M. Major cost risks are unmitigated: distributor operating costs (budgeted EUR 43M/year, estimate EUR 50–65M/year if extended), hub economics gap (EUR 0.47M/year per hub × 4 hubs = EUR 1.9M/year unfunded), payment-provider fee subsidies (EUR 15M budget, estimate EUR 20–25M if through-ticket adoption is slow), and carrier co-funding demand (budgeted EUR 290M, estimate 12–18 carriers × EUR 20–30M each = EUR 240–540M). Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08), recurring run costs of approximately EUR 45M/year (distributor + hub gap + data layer + regulator costs) are explicitly unfunded. The plan assumes supplementary budget authority of EUR 100–200M from the Commission by Month 12 (2027-10-08), but this is outside the cap and not confirmed. No decision on post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding model exists, risking programme collapse after 5 years.

8.6.C Mitigation

Commission an independent cost-modelling firm by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23, 11:00) to produce a detailed activity-based cost forecast by Month 2 (2026-12-08, 17:00), specifying: carrier co-funding per carrier (EUR 2–8M per SME, EUR 10–15M per mid-size, EUR 0.5–2M per major), hub operating cost per hub (EUR 1.2M/year vs. EUR 0.73M/year revenue = EUR 0.47M/year gap per hub), public distributor annual operating cost (EUR 50–65M/year for full retail, EUR 20–30M/year for reference implementation), and payment-institution fee exposure (EUR 80–160M over five years at 0.5–1.0% per transaction). Establish monthly budget-burn dashboards by Month 3 (2027-01-08, 10:00) showing cumulative spend vs. pro-rata forecast with automatic trigger if quarterly spend exceeds 115% of budget line; escalate any trigger to DG MOVE within 5 working days. Define three contingency tiers: Tier 1 (10–15% overrun): defer consumer-app polish, reduce distributor co-marketing by 20%; Tier 2 (15–25% overrun): reduce carrier co-funding rate from 20% to 10%, limit hub openings to priority corridors only; Tier 3 (>25% overrun): suspend new hub openings, scale back capacity building to 3–4 priority member states. Secure DG MOVE commitment by Month 3 (2027-01-08, 14:00) to seek supplementary budget authority from the Commission by Month 12 (2027-10-08) if Tier 2 is triggered, with target allocation EUR 100–200M. Establish a post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding decision task force by Month 36 (2029-10-08) to model sustainability of distributor, hubs and data layer on fee recovery, member-state co-funding or voluntary carrier contributions. Decide the post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding model by Month 48 (2030-10-08), with implementation from Month 55 (2031-05-08).

8.6.D Consequence

If cost overruns are not detected and mitigated early, contingency is exhausted by Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08). Conformance testing, capacity building and smaller-carrier support are cut, causing 20–30% of carriers to miss the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API deadline. Smaller carriers and weaker-capacity regulators are disproportionately affected, fragmenting the network and reducing through-ticket coverage to 60–70% of potential corridors. Distributor operations are scaled back; app quality and consumer support suffer. Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08), if no sustainable funding model is decided, the distributor shuts down, hubs cease operations, and the data layer is abandoned, reverting cross-border rail to the pre-programme fragmentation. The 40% through-ticket target becomes unrealistic; the investment is stranded.

8.6.E Root Cause

The plan aggregates estimated costs (EUR 0.5–2B private carrier IT, EUR 10–40M passenger-rights backstop, EUR 45M/year post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) run costs) as separate from the cap, treating the cap as if it covers only 'core' infrastructure. However, no independent cost audit has validated the EUR 1.5B allocation or the hidden costs in distributor operations, hub subsidies and payment-provider fees. The plan assumes supplementary budget authority without securing it or triggering it at a decision point. Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding is not addressed until Month 48 (2030-10-08), leaving only 12 months for a political and operational redesign if sustainability cannot be assured.
