Review 1: Critical Issues

  1. Regulation adoption delay compresses the standards-setting window, threatening Month 18 (2028-04-08) deadline. If the Commission Regulation is not adopted by Month 9 (2027-07-08), the standards window shrinks: adoption at Month 9 (2027-07-08) leaves 9 months to Month 18 (2028-04-08), and each month of slip removes one month (Month 12 = 2027-10-08 leaves 6; Months 14-15 = 2027-12-08 to 2028-01-08 leave 3–4), eliminating stakeholder consensus margin. Shadow pre-work mitigates this, but a slipped adoption forces either non-consensus standards (carriers contest rulings, fragmenting the network) or a 6–12 month standards delay, cascading to the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate and the 40% through-ticket target. Recommendation: establish weekly adoption tracking with Parliament TRAN rapporteurs and key member-state ministers by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); contract external standards consortium by Month 8.5 (2027-06-23) if adoption slips past Month 8 (2027-06-08).

  2. Arbitration panel lacks binding enforcement authority without formal Council delegation by Month 2 (2026-12-08), enabling incumbent resistance. Without explicit written delegation specifying force-of-law rulings and Commission enforcement for non-compliance, large carriers (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, ÖBB) can contest technical decisions and delay implementation by 6–12 months, preventing the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards completion and fragmenting the network across carriers and member states. Carrier Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08) are unenforceable without legal authority. Recommendation: draft Council decision specifying binding authority by Month 1 (2026-11-08); complete legal review and agree text by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) (target); secure signed Council delegation by Month 2 (2026-12-08); negotiate directly with SNCF and Deutsche Bahn leadership by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23).

  3. Free contingency (EUR 215 million) is exhausted by Month 24 (2028-10-08) under realistic cost scenarios, forcing cuts to core infrastructure. Carrier co-funding demand (12–18 carriers × EUR 2–15M bands, vs. EUR 290M budget), hub economics gap (EUR 1.9M/year unfunded), distributor cost creep (estimate EUR 50–65M/year vs. EUR 43M budget), and payment-fee subsidy (EUR 20–25M actual vs. EUR 15M cap) total EUR 50–200M unaccounted. A 20–30% overrun (EUR 300–450M) exceeds contingency by EUR 85–235M; the proposed supplementary authority (EUR 100–200M) is not yet secured. Recommendation: establish monthly burn-rate dashboards by Month 3 (2027-01-08) with 115% pro-rata trigger; secure DG MOVE commitment to seek EUR 100–200M supplementary authority by Month 12 (2027-10-08) if Tier 2 overrun signals emerge.

Review 2: Implementation Consequences

  1. Successful Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate (90%+ corridor coverage) requires private carrier IT spend (planning value EUR 1.25 billion, estimate) treated as mandated compliance cost. If carriers invest the planning-value EUR 1.25 billion in private IT to meet the mandate, the 40% through-ticket target (40% of ~3–5 million annual cross-border passengers = 1.2–2.0 million through-tickets/year at EUR 50–100 average fare = EUR 60–200 million annual revenue pool, estimate); the business case must be rebuilt on a stated passenger base, showing revenue, avoided costs and mandated compliance separately. Compliance depends on achieving regulatory compliance (arbitration panel enforcement), distributor uptake (Trainline/Omio API integration), and travel-market rebound post-2027. If the API mandate slips to Month 36+ (2029-10-08+) due to governance delays or regulation adoption failure, carrier ROI erodes by 20–30% (reduced months of operation before cost-recovery thresholds), triggering a cascading reduction in private IT investment and fragmenting the network to 20–30% through-ticket coverage (vs. 40% target). Recommendation: lock arbitration panel delegation (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) and Commitment Letters (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) to signal binding authority and reduce carrier investment uncertainty.

  2. Achievable 40% through-ticket target by Month 60 (2031-10-08) depends on killer-application product validation, which lacks a willingness-to-pay baseline and risks 15–25 percentage-point underperformance. The plan assumes through-fares (sum of segments, no ceilings) and convenience (single booking) drive the 40% target, yet no customer research validates whether travellers prefer a through-ticket over separate tickets or budget airlines on competitive routes (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln, Madrid–Barcelona–Lyon). A willingness-to-pay study (planned Months 1–6 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-04-08) may reveal actual modal-shift potential is 5–10% (vs. planning range 5–15%), or through-fares are uncompetitive, forcing either a contingency decision (regulated fare ceilings, subsidies) or a downward target revision to 15–25% by Month 24 (2028-10-08). This slippage cascades: lower through-ticket volume reduces payment-provider transaction-fee revenue (EUR 15M subsidy consumed faster), forces cuts to distributor co-marketing (EUR 5–10M reduction), and delays consumer-app momentum. Recommendation: commission and complete killer-application research by Month 4 (2027-02-08); if survey preference is below 8% (proposed threshold) at Month 4 (2027-02-08) or pilot conversion is below 3% (proposed threshold) at Month 12 (2027-10-08), escalate and propose contingency (subsidised through-fares or regulated ceilings).

  3. Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding cliff (EUR 45 million/year unfunded recurring costs) risks programme collapse unless cost-recovery or sustained political commitment is locked by Month 48 (2030-10-08). The EUR 1,500 million cap ends at Month 60 (2031-10-08), but the distributor (~EUR 43M/year), hub economics gap (~EUR 1.9M/year), data-layer operations, and regulator capacity have no post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding source. If a post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) model is not decided by Month 48 (2030-10-08), the programme risks operating under a 12-month funding cliff with no transition path: the public distributor may shut down (eliminating a key consumer channel and forcing commercial platforms to carry full load), hubs may cease operations (leaving smaller carriers unsupported and fragmenting the network), and the shared data layer may be abandoned (reverting to pre-programme fragmentation). This interacts with contingency exhaustion: if free contingency is consumed by Month 24–30 (2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08) due to cost overruns, no buffer exists to fund an emergency transition by Month 60 (2031-10-08). Recommendation: establish a post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability task force by Month 36 (2029-10-08); model three funding scenarios (fee-recovery, member-state co-funding, carrier contributions); secure written political commitment from the Commission and member states by Month 48 (2030-10-08).

Review 3: Recommended Actions

  1. Establish monthly budget-burn dashboards with 115% pro-rata trigger by Month 3 (2027-01-08); expected impact: detect EUR 85–235M overrun gap 6–12 months earlier, enabling contingency-tier cost cuts (Tier 1–3) before conformance testing or capacity building are damaged; priority: Critical. Delayed detection compresses the Month 24 (2028-10-08) mid-course review, leaving only 6 months to cut EUR 150–225M before the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate. Implementation: commission cost model by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); deploy dashboards tracking pro-rata spend (EUR 25M/month baseline) by Month 3 (2027-01-08); escalate any quarterly overspend above 115% to DG MOVE within 5 working days for pre-approved Tier response.

  2. Commission killer-application customer research and willingness-to-pay study by Month 1 (2026-11-08); complete by Month 4 (2027-02-08); expected impact: validate whether through-fares can undercut budget airlines (EUR 40–70 flight vs. EUR 70–90 through-fare estimate), reducing modal-shift achievement risk from 50–75% miss (to 5–10% actual) to validated 10–20% baseline; priority: Critical. If pilot conversion is below 3% (proposed threshold) at Month 12 (2027-10-08), escalate contingency decision (regulated fare ceilings or subsidies). Implementation: pilot one flagship product (guaranteed-connection ticket with 4-hour reroute + 10-day refund) on Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln corridor by Month 9 (2027-07-08); measure booking uptake and satisfaction (target ≥4.0/5) by Month 24 (2028-10-08).

  3. Secure written Council/Commission Delegation of Authority for the arbitration panel's binding technical-decision power by Month 2 (2026-12-08) (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23 target for text agreed); expected impact: enable Commitment Letters from carriers above EUR 50M by Month 3 (2027-01-08) with enforceable penalties (0.5–1% quarterly revenue in escrow), reducing incumbent resistance risk and month-long disputes from 6–12 months to 4–6 weeks; priority: Critical. Without legal authority, standards-setting cannot proceed, threatening Month 18 (2028-04-08) and Month 30 (2029-04-08) milestones. Implementation: draft delegation document by Month 1 (2026-11-08); circulate to DG MOVE and Council Legal Service by Month 1 (2026-11-08); secure signed Council delegation by Month 2 (2026-12-08) (legal review complete by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23, target); negotiate SNCF and Deutsche Bahn buy-in by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23).

Review 4: Showstopper Risks

  1. Payment-provider accreditation attracts fewer than 2 qualified bidders by Month 6 (2027-04-08), forcing fallback to bilateral settlement and delaying operationalization by 6–12 months. Impact: Month 12 (2027-10-08) go-live slips to Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08); settlement cycle extends from <48 hours to 5–7 days; refund processing delays from <10 days to 20–30 days, eroding distributor confidence and reducing through-ticket volumes by 15–25 percentage points (40% target becomes 15–25%). Likelihood: Medium. Interaction: Payment delays compound with hub onboarding delays (both Month 9 = 2027-07-08 gate); together they cascade Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate to Month 33–36 (2029-07-08 to 2029-10-08). Recommendation: launch market sounding by Month 0 (2026-10-08); if <2 applicants by Month 6 (2027-04-08), immediately activate fallback: bilateral carrier settlement with common message standard by Month 10 (2027-08-08). Contingency: if bilateral settlement remains unstable (>5% disputes unresolved within 5 days), commission emergency procurement of a custom clearing service from free contingency by Month 15 (2028-01-08) (cost EUR 5–10M estimate).

  2. GDPR consensus from national DPAs fails to materialize by Month 4 (2027-02-08); a single DPA veto on cross-border data flows blocks payment-institution accreditation and forces 6–12 month architectural redesign. Impact: data-layer shifts from central cache to federated queries only; API latency increases 3–5 seconds per search; search timeout rate rises from <1% to 5–10%; through-ticket volumes drop 15–25 percentage points. Month 12 (2027-10-08) payment-provider operationalization slips to Month 18–24 (2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08); standards timeline unaffected but clearing compliance is blocked. Likelihood: Medium. Interaction: GDPR delay compounds with payment-provider accreditation delay; both hit the same Month 12 (2027-10-08) gate, creating dual critical-path risk. Recommendation: conduct early 1-on-1 DPA consultations with Bulgaria, Romania, Austria by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23); publish DPIA and seek EDPB guidance by Month 3 (2027-01-08); secure written sign-off from at least 8 of 27 member-state DPAs by Month 4 (2027-02-08). Contingency: if consensus is not reached, escalate to EDPB for expedited guidance (4-week target) and commission supplementary legal instrument (Commission adequacy decision) by Month 6 (2027-04-08) (cost EUR 3–5M estimate from governance budget).

  3. Hub mapping errors cause 2–5% booking-failure rates post-launch (Months 18–24 = 2028-04-08 to 2028-10-08), forcing 4–8 week remediation per hub and cascading 20–30% of smaller carriers (4–6 carriers) past the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API deadline. Impact: through-ticket coverage drops from 90% to 70–75% of potential traffic; TEN-T extension (Month 36 = 2029-10-08) slips to Month 42–48 (2030-04-08 to 2030-10-08); refund disputes spike 8–12% as passengers experience ticket-validation failures. Likelihood: Medium. Interaction: Hub failures compound with budget contingency exhaustion (if costs consume EUR 50M remediation, free contingency shrinks to EUR 165M, exhausted by Month 30 = 2029-04-08 if concurrent overruns occur); together they fragment the network and trigger Tier 3 contingency cuts. Recommendation: mandate dual-run testing (2–4 weeks per hub, Months 15–18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08) with independent external lab validation by Month 6 (2027-04-08); establish booking-failure stop threshold (2% for >1 week); hire regional support coordinators (5 FTE) by Month 4 (2027-02-08). Contingency: if a hub's booking-failure rate exceeds 2%, suspend new carrier onboarding immediately and activate cost-recovery renegotiation (reduce hub opex from EUR 1.2M to EUR 0.8M/year) or consolidate to 2–3 highest-utilization hubs by Month 36 (2029-10-08) (estimated recovery EUR 5–10M over five years).

Review 5: Critical Assumptions

  1. Assumption: Private carrier IT investment (EUR 1.25 billion planning value) materializes on schedule without regulatory/market shock delays. If actual private spend falls 30–50% below estimate (EUR 0.6–0.9 billion instead of EUR 1.25 billion), fewer carriers achieve native API compliance by Month 30 (2029-04-08); through-ticket coverage drops to 70–80% (vs. 90% target threshold), pushing smaller-carrier integration 6–12 months past deadline. This compounds hub dependency (more carriers forced into hubs, straining EUR 44M hub budget) and interacts with arbitration-panel enforcement risk: if incumbents delay private IT investment pending governance certainty, the Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate becomes non-binding. Recommendation: validate carrier IT budgets and procurement timelines in Commitment Letters (Month 3 = 2027-01-08); establish a carrier investment tracking dashboard by Month 12 (2027-10-08) reporting cumulative private spend vs. forecast; trigger co-funding accelerator (increase from EUR 234M to EUR 280M) if cumulative actual spend is <70% of plan by Month 18 (2028-04-08).

  2. Assumption: Distributor engagement (Trainline, Omio, public reference distributor) drives through-ticket volume to 40% without margin compression or competitive platform withdrawal. If distributor margins are squeezed by low through-fares or high payment-fee costs (actual fees EUR 1.0% vs. capped EUR 0.5%), or if Trainline/Omio delay full integration past Month 18 (2028-04-08), commercial uptake stalls at 10–15% and the public distributor must expand to fill the gap (cost escalates from EUR 43M/year to EUR 60–100M/year, consuming EUR 150–250M from free contingency by Month 48 = 2030-10-08). This interacts with killer-application validation risk: if willingness-to-pay research reveals uncompetitive through-fares, distributors lose confidence and cut co-marketing. Recommendation: finalize distributor partnership agreements and margin-support terms by Month 6 (2027-04-08); lock co-marketing budget (EUR 10M) and early API access (Month 9 = 2027-07-08) in signed MOUs; monitor Trainline/Omio integration progress quarterly (starting Month 12 = 2027-10-08); if either platform signals <50% integration readiness by Month 18 (2028-04-08), activate public distributor expansion contingency and escalate co-funding demand.

  3. Assumption: Regulation adoption by Month 9 (2027-07-08) and standards completion by Month 18 (2028-04-08) occur without material rework triggered by Parliament amendments or legal challenge. If final Regulation text diverges materially from the May 2026 proposal on liability allocation, data-sharing scope, or mandatory API exemptions, the Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards must be re-scoped (4–8 week delay); if adoption is blocked or delayed past Month 10 (2027-08-08), the standards window shrinks by one month per month of slip (Month 12 = 2027-10-08 leaves 6 months; Months 14-15 = 2027-12-08 to 2028-01-08 leave 3–4), forcing either non-consensus standards (carriers contest, fragmenting the network) or a 6–12 month slip (Month 24–30 = 2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08). This compounds with governance delegation risk: if the Council delegation is delayed past Month 2 (2026-12-08), arbitration-panel authority is questioned, and carriers withhold Commitment Letters, making standards non-binding. Recommendation: establish weekly Regulation adoption tracking with Parliament TRAN rapporteurs and member-state ministers by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); publish shadow standards pre-work gap analysis by Month 6 (2027-04-08); if adoption probability drops below 70% by Month 6 (2027-04-08) or material text divergence is flagged, contract external standards consortium (EUR 1–2M) by Month 8.5 (2027-06-23) for accelerated drafting.

Review 6: Key Performance Indicators

  1. Through-Ticket Share: 40% of cross-border rail journeys by Month 60 (2031-10-08); interim gate 15% at Month 24 (2028-10-08). Success requires: validated baseline by Month 9 (2027-07-08), monthly carrier/distributor reporting from Month 18 (2028-04-08), and independent counterfactual evaluation to isolate programme effects from fuel prices and aviation policy. If actual share falls below 15% at Month 24 (2028-10-08), escalate and assess killer-application willingness-to-pay; if below 8% (stop level) at Month 24 (2028-10-08), trigger contingency decision (regulated fare ceilings or subsidies). Monitor quarterly; compounded risk if distributor engagement slips or through-fare competitiveness is poor. Recommendation: establish monthly dashboards by Month 18 (2028-04-08); commission independent evaluator by Month 3 (2027-01-08) to build counterfactual separating programme effects from external factors.

  2. API Readiness: At least 90% of corridor traffic bookable end-to-end by Month 30 (2029-04-08); smaller-carrier conformance (hubs or native) by Month 30 (2029-04-08). Success requires: binding standards by Month 18 (2028-04-08), hub operationalization by Month 9 (2027-07-08), accredited payment providers live by Month 12 (2027-10-08), and staggered carrier conformance testing Months 18–30 (2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08). If actual readiness is below 90% at Month 30 (2029-04-08), Commission review is triggered; below 80% is a severe case in which the network fragments. Monitor via monthly carrier readiness surveys and gate compliance tracking (Month 24 = 2028-10-08, projection gate 80% projected ready as stop rule, target higher). If compliance slips, activate hub-failure contingency (gateway or bilateral settlement) or extend timeline. Compounded with budget and hub risks. Recommendation: establish conformance testing steering committee by Month 12 (2027-10-08) with weekly carrier readiness updates.

  3. Distributor Complaints: At or below 50% of the Month 9 (2027-07-08) baseline by Month 60 (2031-10-08); interim gate 75% of baseline at Month 24 (2028-10-08). Success requires: standardized complaint taxonomy by Month 3 (2027-01-08), 24/7 multilingual support operational by Month 15 (2028-01-08), refund processing under 10 days, and dispute resolution under 5 business days. If complaints remain above 75% of baseline at Month 24 (2028-10-08) or refund cycle exceeds 15 days, escalate and activate support surge or process redesign. Interacts with passenger-rights backstop and accessibility SLAs; compounded if settlement delays or hub mapping errors cause booking failures. Recommendation: deploy real-time complaint tracking dashboard by Month 15 (2028-01-08); conduct monthly trend reviews with distributor partners and carriers; reserve EUR 5–10M from free contingency for unplanned support surge if complaint rates spike.

Review 7: Report Objectives

  1. Primary Objective: Inform DG MOVE and the Steering Committee on the viability and critical dependencies of the Pragmatic Foundation scenario (certified access, accredited payment institutions, milestone co-funding, regional hubs, arbitration panel) for delivering EUR 1,500 million cross-border rail through-ticketing infrastructure by Month 60 (2031-10-08). The report establishes baseline assumptions, quantifies budget allocations (EUR 280M standards, EUR 120M clearing, EUR 215M distributor, EUR 290M carrier co-funding), identifies three critical prerequisites (regulation adoption by Month 9 = 2027-07-08, arbitration panel delegation by Month 2 = 2026-12-08, Commitment Letters by Month 3 = 2027-01-08), and flags 20 material risks with mitigation strategies. Intended for: DG MOVE leadership, Programme Director, Steering Committee, carrier executives, and member-state transport ministers deciding governance and budget authority.

  2. Key Decisions to Inform: (1) Whether to proceed with the Pragmatic Foundation (vs. more aggressive or conservative alternatives); (2) who holds binding technical authority and how it is enforced (arbitration panel vs. joint undertaking); (3) how to allocate the fixed EUR 1,500 million across eight budget lines and protect EUR 215M free contingency from 20–30% overrun exposure; (4) which three flagship actions to prioritize immediately (regulation tracking, killer-application research, budget dashboards) to reduce critical-path risk. The report quantifies trade-offs: tight governance avoids legal delays but risks incumbent resistance; milestone co-funding accelerates smaller-carrier adoption but consumes EUR 290M (19% of cap); through-fare rules avoid antitrust risk but may not compete with airlines (5–15% modal shift planning range vs. implied higher expectations).

  3. Version 2 should deepen: (1) Contingency trigger specifics—operationalize the three budget tiers with pre-approved cost-cutting options, named decision-owners, and 10-day escalation timelines; (2) Killer-application validation—complete willingness-to-pay research (Month 4 = 2027-02-08 target) with binding commitment to contingency decisions if survey preference is below 8% (proposed threshold); (3) Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability model—lock funding decision and secure member-state written commitment by Month 48 (2030-10-08), not left as a future task. Version 1 establishes the architecture; Version 2 must operationalize the gates, contingencies, and long-term viability.

Review 8: Data Quality Concerns

  1. Carrier IT investment estimate (EUR 1.25 billion planning value) lacks vendor cost validation and market-shock scenario testing. This figure underpins private-spend ROI projections and the decision to co-fund only EUR 290 million (19% of carrier costs). If actual costs are 30–50% lower (EUR 0.6–0.9 billion), co-funding becomes oversized and budget is misallocated; if higher (EUR 1.8–2.0 billion), carriers defer integration awaiting co-funding expansion. Consequence: Month 30 (2029-04-08) readiness drops 15–25 percentage points (to 65–75% vs. 90% target), fragmenting the network. Recommendation: obtain binding IT cost quotes from 8–12 representative carriers (major, mid-size, SME) by Month 6 (2027-04-08); cross-check against historical rail modernisation benchmarks; if estimates diverge >20% from planning value, trigger cost-model re-baseline and adjust co-funding allocation by Month 12 (2027-10-08).

  2. Modal-shift planning range (5–15% reduction in short-haul air trips) is not grounded in real demand elasticity or airline competitive response modelling. This range implies 50–100% variance in environmental and capacity-benefit justification for the EUR 1,500 million investment. If actual modal shift is below 8% by Month 48 (2030-10-08), the ROI case and political support erode. Consequence: post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) sustainability funding approval becomes difficult if infrastructure benefits are overstated. Recommendation: complete killer-application willingness-to-pay research by Month 4 (2027-02-08) with elasticity estimates (price sensitivity, convenience premium vs. competitors); model airline capacity and pricing response on each priority corridor; if modal shift is projected below 8%, flag contingency decision (regulated fare ceilings or subsidies) by Month 12 (2027-10-08) before deployment costs crystallize.

  3. Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) unfunded recurring cost (EUR 45 million/year estimate) lacks detailed cost breakdown and member-state co-funding commitment. The EUR 45 million estimate includes distributor (~EUR 43M) and hub economics gap (~EUR 1.9M) but excludes data-layer operations and regulator capacity costs not quantified. Consequence: if actual run costs are EUR 60–75 million/year, and no sustainable funding model is locked by Month 48 (2030-10-08), the programme risks collapse within 12 months of Month 60 (2031-10-08). Recommendation: decompose the EUR 45 million estimate into distributor (break-even fee revenue vs. retail scope), hub (by region and carrier concentration), data-layer (hosting, neutral operator), and regulator (staffing by member state) by Month 36 (2029-10-08); obtain written co-funding commitments from at least 15 member states by Month 48 (2030-10-08); if gap exceeds EUR 50 million/year, trigger decision to sunset public distributor or consolidate hubs.

Review 9: Stakeholder Feedback

  1. Arbitration panel delegation legal authority and enforcement mechanism clarity from the Council and Commission. The report assumes written Council/Commission delegation by Month 2 (2026-12-08) specifying binding technical decision-making power, 14-day compliance deadlines, and Commission enforcement for non-compliance, yet no formal legal instrument exists. Without explicit stakeholder sign-off, carriers may refuse Commitment Letters (Month 3 = 2027-01-08), rendering standards non-binding and delaying Month 18 (2028-04-08) and Month 30 (2029-04-08) milestones by 6–12 months (estimated EUR 100–200M value at risk if ROI is deferred). Recommendation: obtain written legal opinion from DG MOVE and Council Legal Service by Month 1 (2026-11-08) confirming feasibility of delegation; secure formal stakeholder endorsement (Commission, Council, CER, major carriers) in a joint statement by Month 1.5 (2026-11-23) before draft text is finalised.

  2. Carrier private IT investment commitment and readiness timeline validation from major incumbents (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, ÖBB, Renfe, Trenitalia). The report allocates EUR 290 million co-funding (19% of the EUR 1.5 billion cap) and assumes EUR 1.25 billion private spend materialises on schedule; if actual private investment falls 30–50% below plan, through-ticket coverage drops to 70–80% and Month 30 (2029-04-08) mandate is unachievable. Carriers have not yet committed binding IT budgets or integration timelines. Recommendation: obtain signed IT cost quotes and integration timelines from all 8 major carriers by Month 4 (2027-02-08); validate against historical rail-modernisation benchmarks; if estimates diverge >20% from EUR 1.25 billion planning value, trigger mid-course co-funding adjustment by Month 12 (2027-10-08).

  3. Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding model and member-state political commitment for recurring EUR 45 million/year unfunded costs. The report identifies that the public distributor (~EUR 43M/year), hub economics gap (~EUR 1.9M/year), data-layer operations, and regulator capacity lack post-programme funding. If no sustainable model is locked by Month 48 (2030-10-08), the programme risks operational collapse within 12 months of Month 60 (2031-10-08), stranding all prior investment. Member states have not signalled co-funding willingness. Recommendation: commission a sustainability task force by Month 36 (2029-10-08) modelling three fee-recovery, co-funding, and sunset scenarios; obtain written political commitment from at least 15 member states by Month 48 (2030-10-08) specifying post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding source or shutdown procedures.

Review 10: Changed Assumptions

  1. Regulation adoption timeline assumption (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 gate) may slip due to Parliament amendments or member-state delays. If adoption is delayed past Month 10 (2027-08-08), the 9-month standards-drafting window shrinks by one month per month of slip (Month 12 = 2027-10-08 leaves 6; Months 14-15 = 2027-12-08 to 2028-01-08 leave 3–4), risking lost margin and rework, forcing either non-consensus standards (carriers contest, blocking Month 30 = 2029-04-08 API mandate) or a 6–12 month slip (estimated EUR 100–200M ROI deferral and 15–25 percentage-point reduction in through-ticket volumes). This amplifies arbitration-panel enforcement risk: without timely Regulation clarity, carriers withhold Commitment Letters (Month 3 = 2027-01-08), undermining standards credibility. Recommendation: track weekly adoption probability with Parliament TRAN rapporteurs by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); trigger external standards consortium procurement by Month 8.5 (2027-06-23) if adoption probability falls below 70%.

  2. Private carrier IT investment (EUR 1.25 billion planning value) assumes market stability and no technology disruption; actual spend volatility (±30–50%) is unvalidated. If private investment falls to EUR 0.6–0.9 billion (30–50% undershoot), fewer carriers achieve native API compliance by Month 30 (2029-04-08); through-ticket coverage drops to 70–80% (vs. 90% threshold), requiring hub expansion (EUR 44M budget strained) and pushing 20–30% of smaller carriers past the deadline. This interacts with budget contingency exhaustion: if hub spending exceeds EUR 50M to absorb excess carrier demand, free contingency drops below EUR 165M. Recommendation: obtain binding IT cost quotes from 12 representative carriers (major, mid-size, SME) by Month 6 (2027-04-08); if estimates diverge >20% from EUR 1.25 billion planning value, adjust co-funding allocation and trigger cost-model re-baseline by Month 12 (2027-10-08).

  3. Killer-application willingness-to-pay assumption (through-fares competitive enough to drive 40% adoption) lacks baseline customer research and airline response modelling. If willingness-to-pay research (Months 1–4 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-02-08) reveals actual modal-shift potential is below 8% (vs. 5–15% planning range), or through-fares cannot undercut budget airlines (EUR 40–70 flight vs. EUR 70–90 estimate), the 40% target becomes unachievable without contingency measures (regulated fare ceilings, subsidies) not yet funded. This compounds distributor and payload-volume risk: lower through-ticket conversion reduces payment-provider fee revenue (EUR 15M subsidy consumed faster) and forces public distributor expansion (EUR 43M/year to EUR 65M/year). Recommendation: complete willingness-to-pay study by Month 4 (2027-02-08); if through-fare elasticity is below 8% modal shift, escalate to Steering Committee and propose contingency decision (subsidised fares or price regulation) by Month 12 (2027-10-08).

Review 11: Budget Clarifications

  1. Distributor operating-cost allocation within EUR 215 million budget lacks clarity on retail vs. reference-implementation scope. The allocation assumes ~EUR 43M/year (EUR 215M over 5 years), yet scope is undefined: full retail consumer service (EUR 60–100M/year estimate) or reference-implementation only (EUR 20–30M/year estimate). If retail is chosen and actual costs reach EUR 65M/year, the programme consumes EUR 50–110M more than budgeted by Month 48 (2030-10-08), exhausting free contingency and forcing Tier 2–3 cuts (reduced co-funding, delayed smaller-carrier support). Recommendation: finalize distributor scope decision by Month 2 (2026-12-08); obtain binding annual operating-cost quotes from candidate operators by Month 4 (2027-02-08); if costs exceed EUR 50M/year, trigger mid-course budget review and adjust allocations.

  2. Carrier co-funding allocation (EUR 290 million = EUR 234M grants + EUR 44M hubs + EUR 12M accessibility) is demand-driven and unvalidated against actual per-carrier integration costs. The allocation assumes 12–18 eligible carriers demand EUR 2–8M per SME and EUR 10–15M per mid-size operator; if actual per-carrier costs are 30–50% higher (EUR 3–12M per SME, EUR 15–22M per mid-size), cumulative demand reaches EUR 350–400M, exceeding budget by EUR 60–110M and consuming free contingency by Month 18 (2028-04-08). Recommendation: obtain binding IT cost quotes from all 12–18 hub-eligible carriers by Month 6 (2027-04-08); establish quarterly co-funding demand tracking by Month 12 (2027-10-08); if total demand exceeds EUR 290M early-warning level (20% over, about EUR 348M, is the failure level), trigger Tier 2 response (reduce co-funding rate from 20% to 10%, saving EUR 50M).

  3. Payment-institution accreditation and fee-subsidy sustainability lacks confirmed provider cost structure and volume-dependency assumptions. The clearing allocation (EUR 120M) includes EUR 15M fee subsidy (60% of fees in Months 0–24 = 2026-10-08 to 2028-10-08), yet actual fee exposure ranges EUR 80–160M over 5 years depending on transaction volume and provider pricing (estimated 0.5–1.0% per transaction). If through-ticket volumes are 30–50% below plan or payment providers demand higher fees (0.7–1.0% vs. 0.3–0.5% cap), fee subsidy extends beyond Month 24 (2028-10-08) and consumes an additional EUR 10–25M from free contingency. Recommendation: lock payment-provider fee quotes during accreditation (Month 8 = 2027-06-08); model three volume scenarios (conservative, baseline, upside) by Month 12 (2027-10-08); if subsidy demand exceeds EUR 20M, reduce duration (subsidy ends Month 18 = 2028-04-08) or negotiate volume discounts with providers.

Review 12: Role Definitions

  1. Programme Director accountability for critical-path milestones and budget discipline. This role must hold binding authority over Month 18 (2028-04-08) standards completion, Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate readiness, and EUR 215 million free-contingency protection. If unclear, mid-course cost overruns consume contingency without escalation; milestone slippage accumulates without corrective decision (estimated 6–12 month downstream delay to Month 30 = 2029-04-08 and Month 60 = 2031-10-08 deadlines). Recommendation: define in writing by Month 1 (2026-11-08): decision authority over Tier 1–3 contingency responses, budget line reallocation, and escalation to DG MOVE within 5 working days of any 115% pro-rata spend trigger.

  2. Arbitration panel chair and binding-decision authority over technical standards disputes. This role resolves contested access-term templates, settlement message formats, and conformance criteria within 60-day cycles, with force-of-law status enforced by the Commission. If unclear, incumbent carriers contest rulings and delay standards by 6–12 months, fragmenting the network and jeopardizing Month 18 (2028-04-08) and Month 30 (2029-04-08) deadlines. Recommendation: specify in the Council Delegation document (Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23): chair selection process, decision quorum (majority of 8–12 members sufficient), voting rules, and escalation to Commission enforcement within 14 days of non-compliance.

  3. Hub operation and smaller-carrier integration lead, responsible for 4–6 hub operators and 12–18 eligible carriers. This role ensures hubs are operational by Month 9 (2027-07-08), achieve <0.5% booking-failure rate, and onboard carriers by Month 30 (2029-04-08). If unclear, hub delays cascade to 20–30% of smaller carriers missing the API mandate, fragmenting through-ticket coverage to 70–80% (vs. 90% threshold). Recommendation: assign by Month 1 (2026-11-08) with P&L accountability for EUR 44 million hub budget, authority to suspend carrier onboarding if failure rate exceeds 2%, and weekly readiness reporting to the Programme Director.

Review 13: Timeline Dependencies

  1. Regulation adoption (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 gate) shortens the standards-drafting window (9 months to Month 18 = 2028-04-08 if adopted at Month 9 = 2027-07-08; one month lost per month of slip) if delayed past Month 9 (2027-07-08), cascading to Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate and through-ticket targets. If standards-drafting Months 4–18 (2027-02-08 to 2028-04-08) slips due to late regulation clarity, carrier integration window (Months 18–30 = 2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08) is compressed, delaying smaller-carrier hub onboarding and pushing 20–30% of carriers past Month 30 (2029-04-08) deadline (estimated 15–25 percentage-point reduction in corridor coverage). This interacts with arbitration-panel authority risk: late regulation delays Council delegation (target Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23), weakening Commitment Letter credibility by Month 3 (2027-01-08). Recommendation: establish weekly regulation tracking by Month 0.5 (2026-10-23); contract external standards consortium by Month 8.5 (2027-06-23) if adoption probability drops below 70%.

  2. Hub operationalization (Month 9 = 2027-07-08 gate) must precede staggered carrier conformance testing (Months 18–30 = 2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08); if hubs delay beyond Month 9 (2027-07-08), dual-run pilots (Months 15–18 = 2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08) are compressed from 2–4 weeks to <2 weeks per carrier, risking data-quality validation gaps. Hub delays cascade to 4–6 carriers slipping past Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate (estimated 10–15 percentage-point coverage reduction). This compounds with payment-provider operationalization (target Month 12 = 2027-10-08): if both hubs and payment providers are not operational by Month 12 (2027-10-08), the conformance-testing and settlement-integration gates (Months 18–30 = 2028-04-08 to 2029-04-08) cannot proceed in parallel, serializing the critical path. Recommendation: award hub contracts by Month 3 (2027-01-08); require contractual hub go-live by Month 9 (2027-07-08) with liquidated damages; conduct integration pilots no later than Month 15 (2028-01-08).

  3. Consumer app public launch (Month 15 = 2028-01-08 gate) depends on through-ticket definition lock (Month 2 = 2026-12-08), killer-application validation (Months 1–4 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-02-08), and booking-interface API integration (Months 12–15 = 2027-10-08 to 2028-01-08); if definition or killer-app research slips beyond Month 4 (2027-02-08), app development is delayed 6–8 weeks and launch slips from Month 15 (2028-01-08) to Month 21–24 (2028-07-08 to 2028-10-08). Late app launch reduces early-corridor momentum and through-ticket consumer awareness, lowering adoption by 10–20 percentage points (estimated 2–4 percentage-point hit to the 40% target). This cascades with measurement baseline timing: if app launch is delayed past Month 15 (2028-01-08), baseline reporting (starting Month 18 = 2028-04-08) lacks early consumer-volume data to validate the 15% interim gate at Month 24 (2028-10-08). Recommendation: lock through-ticket definition by Month 2 (2026-12-08); complete killer-application research by Month 4 (2027-02-08); begin app MVP development by Month 4 (2027-02-08), not Month 6 (2027-04-08).

Review 14: Financial Strategy

  1. Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding model (EUR 45 million/year unfunded recurring costs) remains undecided; leaving it unanswered risks operational collapse within 12 months of programme end. Distributor (~EUR 43M/year), hub economics gap (~EUR 1.9M/year), data-layer operations and regulator capacity have no post-programme funding source. If no sustainable model is locked by Month 48 (2030-10-08), carriers cannot rely on through-ticket infrastructure continuity, reducing private IT ROI by 20–30% (estimated EUR 150–400M value loss). This compounds with budget contingency exhaustion risk: if free contingency (EUR 215M) is consumed by Month 30 (2029-04-08) due to cost overruns, no buffer exists to fund emergency transition or bridge to Month 60 (2031-10-08). Recommendation: establish sustainability task force by Month 36 (2029-10-08); model fee-recovery, member-state co-funding and shutdown scenarios; secure written political commitment from at least 15 member states by Month 48 (2030-10-08).

  2. Through-fare competitiveness and modal-shift viability (5–15% planning range) lack willingness-to-pay validation; if uncompetitive, the 40% through-ticket target drops 15–25 percentage points. The programme assumes sum-of-segment pricing with no regulated ceilings achieves competitive fares against budget airlines (EUR 40–70 flight vs. EUR 70–90 through-fare estimate) yet no customer research grounds this assumption. If through-ticket share is below 8% at Month 24 (2028-10-08), contingency decisions (subsidised fares or regulated ceilings) are unfunded and outside the EUR 1,500 million cap, requiring supplementary authority (estimated EUR 50–100M additional). This interacts with distributor incentive and payment-fee risk: lower through-ticket volume erodes distributor margins and payment-provider transaction-fee revenue. Recommendation: complete killer-application research by Month 4 (2027-02-08); if survey preference is below 8% at Month 4 (2027-02-08) or pilot conversion below 3% at Month 12 (2027-10-08), propose contingency decision (subsidies or price regulation).

  3. Carrier co-funding allocation (EUR 290 million = EUR 234M grants + EUR 44M hubs + EUR 12M accessibility) is demand-driven and unvalidated; a 30–50% cost underestimate at per-carrier level (actual EUR 3–12M per SME vs. budgeted EUR 2–8M) consumes EUR 60–110M additional, exhausting free contingency by Month 18 (2028-04-08). If total co-funding demand exceeds EUR 290M, Tier 2 response cuts the rate from 20% to 10% (saving EUR 50M), forcing 20–30% of smaller carriers to defer integration and miss the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate (estimated 10–15 percentage-point corridor-coverage loss). This compounds hub-economics tension: if hub costs rise 20–30% (EUR 6–8M per hub vs. EUR 5–6M budget), both co-funding and hub resilience reserves are strained simultaneously. Recommendation: obtain binding IT cost quotes from all 12–18 hub-eligible carriers by Month 6 (2027-04-08); establish quarterly co-funding demand tracking by Month 12 (2027-10-08); trigger contingency re-baseline if total requests exceed EUR 290M.

Review 15: Motivation Factors

  1. Clear early wins and tangible progress visibility maintain stakeholder confidence and justify continued private IT investment through Month 30 (2029-04-08). If the first corridor (Paris–Brussels–Amsterdam–Köln) does not go live by Month 30 (2029-04-08) with measurable through-ticket volumes (≥5% of corridor traffic, estimate), carriers lose confidence and defer private integration spending (EUR 1.25 billion planning value), reducing Month 60 (2031-10-08) readiness from 90%+ to 70–80% (estimated 15–25 percentage-point shortfall on the 40% through-ticket target). This cascades with payment-provider and hub risk: if accredited providers and hubs are not operationally stable by Month 12 (2027-10-08), the Month 30 (2029-04-08) go-live credibility erodes immediately. Recommendation: establish public quarterly progress dashboards by Month 12 (2027-10-08) showing binding-standards completion (Month 18 = 2028-04-08), hub readiness (Month 9 = 2027-07-08), and payment-provider operationalization (Month 12 = 2027-10-08); celebrate each milestone publicly to reinforce momentum.

  2. Transparent budget tracking and timely escalation of cost overruns prevent silent contingency exhaustion and maintain stakeholder trust in financial discipline. If budget overruns are not detected and reported until Month 24 (2028-10-08) or later, free contingency (EUR 215 million) is already consumed by 20–30% shortfalls, leaving no buffer for corrective mid-course action. This compounds governance risk: if Steering Committee learns of a 20–30% overrun (EUR 300–450M, exceeding contingency by EUR 85–235M) after Month 18 (2028-04-08), trust in programme management collapses and stakeholder consensus for contingency tiers fractures, delaying remedial decisions by 6–12 weeks and deepening the overrun. Recommendation: establish monthly burn-rate dashboards by Month 3 (2027-01-08); escalate any quarterly spend above 115% of pro-rata budget to DG MOVE within 5 working days with pre-approved Tier response options; hold budget review steering sessions at Months 12 and 24 (2027-10-08, 2028-10-08).

  3. Political commitment from member states and major carriers signalled through binding Commitment Letters (Month 3 = 2027-01-08) and Council delegation (Month 2 = 2026-12-08) sustains engagement and prevents strategic delay by incumbents. If arbitration-panel authority is not formally delegated or carriers refuse Commitment Letters by Month 3 (2027-01-08), standards-setting lacks enforceability and incumbents can contest technical decisions, deferring Month 18 (2028-04-08) completion by 6–12 months and pushing the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate to Month 33–36 (2029-07-08 to 2029-10-08) (estimated EUR 100–200M ROI loss and 15–25 percentage-point reduction in through-ticket volumes). Recommendation: secure signed written Council/Commission delegation by Month 2 (2026-12-08) (text agreed by Month 1.5 = 2026-11-23, target); conduct direct bilateral negotiations with SNCF, Deutsche Bahn and ÖBB leadership by Month 2.5 (2026-12-23); publish signed Commitment Letters publicly by Month 3 (2027-01-08) to signal binding intent to all stakeholders.

Review 16: Automation Opportunities

  1. Automate monthly budget-burn tracking and Tier contingency triggering by Month 3 (2027-01-08); potential savings: EUR 2–3 million avoidance of manual reporting overhead and 4–6 weeks faster escalation detection. Deploying a real-time dashboard integrating carrier invoices, payment-provider settlements, and distributor spending eliminates manual variance analysis (estimated 500–800 FTE-hours/year). Early Tier detection (within 5 working days of 115% pro-rata trigger) enables faster Tier 1–3 response, reducing decision lag from 6–12 weeks to 2–4 weeks and preventing contingency exhaustion by Month 24 (2028-10-08). Recommendation: procure budget-tracking software (e.g. Anaplan, OneStream) by Month 2 (2026-12-08); integrate carrier/distributor/payment-provider data feeds by Month 3 (2027-01-08); activate automated escalation alerts within 5 working days of overspend.

  2. Standardize and automate conformance-testing data collection and carrier readiness reporting from Month 12 (2027-10-08) onward; potential savings: EUR 1–2 million in testing-lab overhead and 3–4 weeks faster gate compliance validation. Implement a centralized testing-lab management system (e.g. JIRA, custom portal) capturing API latency, availability, booking-failure rates and settlement integration status in real time per carrier. This replaces 200–400 FTE-hours/year of manual test scheduling and result compilation, accelerates carrier readiness signaling to Month 24 (2028-10-08) and Month 30 (2029-04-08) gates, and provides early warning of carriers slipping past deadlines (enabling pre-emptive hub or gateway escalation). Recommendation: procure test-lab portal and integration APIs by Month 6 (2027-04-08); pilot with 3–4 volunteer carriers by Month 12 (2027-10-08); full rollout across all 25+ carriers by Month 18 (2028-04-08).

  3. Automate distributor complaint intake, triage and escalation to the dispute-resolution panel by Month 15 (2028-01-08); potential savings: EUR 1–1.5 million/year in support labor and 5–7 day faster resolution time. Deploy a multilingual chatbot (NLP-based) and intake workflow routing 70–80% of routine complaints (booking failures, status updates) to automated self-service or tier-2 support, reserving 20–30% complex disputes for the human dispute panel. This reduces support labor from estimated EUR 3–5 million/year to EUR 1.5–3.5 million/year and improves median resolution time from 15–20 days (current plan) to 8–10 days (target 10 days per SLA). Recommendation: procure complaint-management platform (e.g. Zendesk, Intercom with multilingual NLP) by Month 9 (2027-07-08); deploy by Month 15 (2028-01-08); monitor resolution-time KPI starting Month 18 (2028-04-08) and adjust escalation thresholds quarterly.

Q1: What does the Pragmatic Foundation scenario mean by 'certification-based tiered access' for distributor participation, and how does it differ from the alternative approaches?

A1: Certification-based tiered access (Decision 1) awards distributors tiered inventory access rights based on passing conformance and consumer-protection tests, with carriers able to audit distributors in return. This avoids fixing a regulated reference price before the Regulation's final text and cost data exist. Alternative approaches are: (1) a single regulated price enforced by national regulators (more restrictive, higher compliance cost for incumbents); or (2) self-published FRAND terms with complaints-driven enforcement only (weaker, incumbent-influenced). The certification model balances carrier buy-in against non-discrimination goals.

Q2: What does the plan mean by 'regional shared booking hubs' for smaller carriers, and what are the key risks if hubs fail to deliver?

A2: Regional hubs (Decision 4) translate legacy carrier inventory and business rules into OSDM standards, allowing 12–18 smaller carriers (those with cross-border revenue under EUR 50M, systems older than 10 years, or IT staff under 10 FTE) to meet the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate without expensive native integration. Hubs are operational by Month 9 (2027-07-08), with 2–4 week dual-run pilots in Months 15–18 (2028-01-08 to 2028-04-08). Key risks: (1) hub mapping errors cause 2–5% booking failures (triggering refunds and disputes); (2) hub outages strand 4–6 dependent carriers; (3) cost-recovery gap (opex EUR 1.2M/year vs. fee revenue EUR 0.73M/year per hub) creates EUR 1.9M/year unfunded liability. If hubs fail, smaller carriers slip past the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API deadline, fragmenting the through-ticket network to 70–80% coverage instead of the 90% target.

Q3: The plan mentions a 'free contingency' of EUR 215 million within the EUR 1,500 million cap. What triggers contingency cuts, and how aggressive can those cuts be before core infrastructure is damaged?

A3: The EUR 215 million free contingency (of EUR 225 million total, minus EUR 10 million earmarked for passenger-rights residual) is triggered if quarterly spend exceeds 115% of pro-rata budget (i.e., EUR 86.25M in a 3-month quarter vs. EUR 75M baseline). Three contingency tiers are pre-defined: Tier 1 (10–15% overrun): defer consumer-app polish, cut co-marketing by 20%; Tier 2 (15–25% overrun): reduce carrier co-funding from 20% to 10%, limit hubs to priority corridors only; Tier 3 (>25% overrun): suspend new hub openings, scale capacity building to 3–4 member states. A 20–30% overrun (EUR 300–450 million) exceeds free contingency by EUR 85–235 million, forcing severe cuts to conformance testing or smaller-carrier support, which damages Month 30 (2029-04-08) readiness.

Q4: What is the 'killer application' the plan mentions as missing from the through-ticketing value proposition, and why is validating it critical for achieving the 40% target?

A4: The killer application is a flagship through-ticket product (e.g., 'one ticket, guaranteed connection' with 4-hour reroute decision, 10-day refund, and reduction-card recognition) that makes through-tickets compelling to travellers compared to budget airlines or separate tickets. The plan targets 40% through-ticket share and 5–15% modal shift from air, yet assumes sum-of-segment pricing (no regulated ceilings) and convenience alone drive adoption. No customer research yet validates whether through-fares (EUR 70–90 estimated) can compete with budget airlines (EUR 40–70). If willingness-to-pay research (Months 1–4 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-02-08) reveals demand is below 8%, contingency decisions (subsidised fares or regulated ceilings) are unfunded and require new authority. The killer application pilot (Month 9 = 2027-07-08, one corridor) is essential to confirm demand before full-scale rollout.

Q5: The plan identifies 'post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) funding cliff' as a major unresolved risk. What are the unfunded recurring costs after the public budget ends, and what happens if no sustainable model is decided by Month 48 (2030-10-08)?

A5: Post-Month 60 (2031-10-08), recurring costs of approximately EUR 45 million/year are unfunded: the public reference distributor (~EUR 43M/year), hub economics gap (~EUR 1.9M/year per hub for regional hubs), data-layer operations, and member-state regulator capacity maintenance. If no sustainable funding model (fee-recovery, member-state co-funding, or carrier contributions) is locked by Month 48 (2030-10-08), the programme risks operational collapse within 12 months of Month 60 (2031-10-08): the public distributor may shut down (eliminating a consumer channel), hubs may cease operations (leaving smaller carriers stranded), and the shared data layer may be abandoned (reverting to pre-programme fragmentation). This compounds budget contingency exhaustion risk: if free contingency (EUR 215M) is consumed by Month 30 (2029-04-08) due to cost overruns, no buffer exists to fund an emergency transition by Month 60 (2031-10-08).

Q6: The plan allocates EUR 1,500 million to public coordination but estimates private carrier IT investment at EUR 0.5–2.0 billion (planning value EUR 1.25 billion), outside the cap. What ethical or fairness issues arise from this cost split, and who bears the risk if private investment falls short?

A6: The cost split creates an asymmetric burden: smaller carriers and weaker-capacity operators may lack the private capital to fund EUR 10–15 million native API integration, forcing hub dependency and potential lock-in to a publicly funded intermediary. If private carrier IT spend falls 30–50% below the EUR 1.25 billion planning value, smaller carriers slip past the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API deadline, fragmenting the network and excluding their passengers from through-tickets. The ethical tension: public funds (EUR 1,500 million) subsidise infrastructure benefiting large carriers' customers, while smaller operators' customers face exclusion or delayed access. Risk allocation: carriers bear private IT cost (known in advance); the programme bears co-funding risk (if demand exceeds EUR 290 million, contingency is exhausted). No mechanism exists to recover private spend if the network fails post-Month 60 (2031-10-08).

Q7: The plan proposes a 'killer application' (guaranteed-connection through-ticket with reroute and refund commitments) that has not yet been validated for traveller demand or airline competitiveness. What happens to the 40% through-ticket target and the programme's credibility if customer research reveals the killer application is uncompetitive or unwanted?

A7: If willingness-to-pay research (Months 1–4 = 2026-11-08 to 2027-02-08) reveals through-fares cannot compete with budget airlines (EUR 40–70 flight vs. EUR 70–90 through-fare estimate) or demand for guaranteed connections is below 8%, the 40% through-ticket target becomes unachievable without contingency measures (subsidised fares or regulated price ceilings). These measures are unfunded and outside the EUR 1,500 million cap, requiring new budget authority and political debate about market intervention. The programme's credibility hinges on the killer application: if unvalidated and subsequently fails, stakeholder trust in the entire infrastructure collapses, deterring private carrier IT investment and distributor engagement, cascading to 15–25% through-ticket share (vs. 40% target) by Month 60 (2031-10-08). Escalation required by Month 12 (2027-10-08) if pilot results are disappointing.

Q8: The programme commits to halving distributor complaints by Month 60 (2031-10-08), yet the plan identifies a 10–day refund turnaround and 5-business-day dispute-resolution SLA without specifying how these will be enforced across 27 member states with uneven regulator capacity. How realistic is the complaints-reduction target, and what happens if regulators cannot enforce refund timelines?

A8: The complaints-reduction target (from baseline at Month 9 = 2027-07-08 to 50% of baseline by Month 60 = 2031-10-08) depends on three unproven elements: (1) accredited payment institutions meeting <48-hour settlement SLAs without breaching GDPR; (2) national regulators enforcing 10-day refund timelines consistently across 27 member states (twinning partnerships are planned but untested); (3) a dispute-resolution panel ruling in 5 business days, which assumes clear fault allocation (not yet defined in the liability framework). If any element fails, refund delays extend to 20–30 days, eroding passenger confidence and distributor willingness to sell risky itineraries. Regional regulators with weak capacity (central and southeast Europe) may lack staffing to audit settlement disputes, creating a two-tier enforcement landscape. The interim gate (75% of baseline complaints at Month 24 = 2028-10-08) will signal whether the SLA framework is working; if not, a major contingency redesign is needed.

Q9: The plan requires a written Council/Commission delegation of binding authority to the arbitration panel by Month 2 (2026-12-08), yet acknowledges this prerequisite has not been secured. What is the political and legal risk if major member states or large carriers refuse the delegation or contest the panel's authority?

A9: The delegation is critical: without it, the arbitration panel cannot enforce technical standards, and incumbent carriers (Deutsche Bahn, SNCF, ÖBB) can contest rulings, deferring standards completion from Month 18 (2028-04-08) to Month 24–30 (2028-10-08 to 2029-04-08) and pushing the Month 30 (2029-04-08) API mandate to Month 33–36 (2029-07-08 to 2029-10-08) (estimated EUR 100–200 million ROI loss). Political risk: member states may resist delegating binding authority to an arbitration panel over technical standards, fearing loss of sovereignty in national regulatory matters. If the Council refuses or attaches conditions (e.g., every decision subject to a national veto), the panel becomes advisory, not binding, fracturing the standards consensus. Legal risk: if a major carrier challenges the panel's authority in the EU courts, claiming the delegation exceeds the Commission's mandate, years of litigation could ensue. Carrier Commitment Letters signed by Month 3 (2027-01-08) depend entirely on the delegation being real and enforceable; if the delegation is questioned, carriers will refuse to commit.

Q10: The plan identifies EUR 45 million/year in unfunded recurring costs post-Month 60 (2031-10-08) (distributor operations and hub economics gap), yet defers the decision on a sustainable funding model until Month 48 (2030-10-08). If no member state or carrier commitment materialises by then, what is the contingency plan to avoid programme collapse?

A10: The plan does not specify a contingency if political or financial commitment fails by Month 48 (2030-10-08). Current options are: (1) cost-recovery model (charge carriers and distributors higher fees for hub and data-layer access, risking through-ticket competitiveness), (2) member-state co-funding (secure written commitment from at least 15 member states for EUR 45+ million/year, not pre-negotiated), or (3) sunset (shut down the public distributor, consolidate hubs, and devolve data-layer operations to the EU Agency for Railways with reduced feature set). If none materialises, the programme risks operational collapse at Month 60 (2031-10-08): the public distributor closes (eliminating a consumer channel), hubs cease operations (stranding smaller carriers and fragmenting the network), and the shared data layer is abandoned, reverting to pre-programme fragmentation. This interacts with budget contingency exhaustion: if the EUR 215 million free contingency is consumed by Month 30 (2029-04-08) due to cost overruns, no bridge funding exists to manage the transition. Escalation and decision required by Month 42 (2030-04-08) if funding prospects are poor.

A premortem assumes the project has failed and works backward to identify the most likely causes.

Assumptions to Kill

These foundational assumptions represent the project's key uncertainties. If proven false, they could lead to failure. Validate them immediately using the specified methods.

Any carrier above EUR 100M cross-border revenue states in writing it will not accept binding rulings or escrow penalties, or Council Legal Service estimates delegation takes more than 4 months.

Run one-to-one pre-engagement sessions with Austria, Germany, France, Poland, Bulgaria and Romania DPAs in Months 1-2 (2026-11-08 to 2026-12-08) using a draft DPIA data-flow map. Fewer than 8 DPAs give written non-objection by Month 4 (2027-02-08), or any DPA signals a residency or explicit-consent requirement for accessibility data.
A6 Trainline, Omio and other commercial distributors will integrate OSDM APIs and actively promote through-tickets by Month 18 (2028-04-08) in exchange for early API access and co-marketing support (EUR 5-10M), without demanding preferential inventory terms. Hold structured sessions with Trainline, Omio and two smaller platforms in Month 1 (2026-11-08) to obtain written integration timelines, margin requirements and preconditions. A major distributor states in writing that integration will not complete before Month 24 (2028-10-08), or conditions participation on preferential or advance inventory access.
A7 The 4 regional hubs can be contracted by Month 3 (2027-01-08) and operational by Month 9 (2027-07-08), and their legacy-to-OSDM mapping will keep booking failures below the 2% threshold (proposed threshold). Run market sounding and issue the hub RFP in Month 0-1 (2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08); count qualified bidders and have an independent consultant test bid SLAs against 99.9% uptime and 2 h recovery. Fewer than 3 qualified bidders respond, or no bidder credibly commits to operational start by Month 9 (2027-07-08), or sample mapping tests show failure above 2%.
A8 At least 2 regulated payment institutions will apply, be accredited by Month 8 (2027-06-08) and be operational by Month 12 (2027-10-08), at fees capped at 0.3-0.5% per transaction, with settlement under 48 h. Publish draft accreditation criteria and fee cap in the Month 0-1 (2026-10-08 to 2026-11-08) market sounding; request written indications of interest and indicative fee quotes from licensed PSD2 institutions. Fewer than 2 written indications of interest, or indicative fees above 0.7% per transaction, or providers refuse the settlement and dispute SLAs.
A9 Confirmed accessibility assistance (24 h confirmation, delivery above 95%) can be delivered on platforms across borders by carriers and station staff the programme funds only indirectly, with a EUR 12M accessibility programme. Survey the 8 largest carriers and 4 corridor station operators by Month 3 (2027-01-08) on current assistance confirmation windows, staffing and handover records; pilot one cross-border handover with disability-rights bodies. Baseline delivery on pilot journeys is below 90%, or carriers state in writing they cannot confirm within 24 h without funding beyond the EUR 12M line.

Failure Scenarios and Mitigation Plans

Each scenario below links to a root-cause assumption and includes a detailed failure story, early warning signs, measurable tripwires, a response playbook, and a stop rule to guide decision-making.

Summary of Failure Modes

ID Title Archetype Root Cause Owner Risk Level

FM2 The Toothless Panel and the Brittle Hubs Technical/Logistical A1 Chief Technical Standards Officer CRITICAL (20/25)

FM4 The Clock That Stopped in Parliament Process/Financial A4 Programme Director CRITICAL (15/25)
FM5 The Data Layer That Had to Stay Home Technical/Logistical A5 Data Layer and Real-Time Systems Architect HIGH (12/25)
FM6 The Platforms That Waited Market/Human A6 Consumer Product and App Development Lead HIGH (12/25)
